The proposed method aims to provide more accurate and reliable predictions by accounting for uncertainty and potential outliers in the data. The paper discusses the theoretical foundations of the method and provides an overview of its practical applications. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach through a series of simulations and real-world case studies, highlighting its potential benefits for a wide range of industries and applications. Overall, this paper offers a promising solution for improving the accuracy and reliability of predictive modeling, and highlights the importance of considering uncertainty and risk in decision-making.

Automated design of neural network architectures tailored for a specific task is an extremely promising, albeit inherently difficult, avenue to explore. While most results in this domain have been achieved on image classification and language modelling problems, here we concentrate on dense per-pixel tasks, in particular, semantic image segmentation using fully convolutional networks. In contrast to the aforementioned areas, the design choices of a fully convolutional network require several changes, ranging from the sort of operations that need to be used---e.g., dilated convolutions---to a solving of a more difficult optimisation problem. In this work, we are particularly interested in searching for high-performance compact segmentation architectures, able to run in real-time using limited resources. To achieve that, we intentionally over-parameterise the architecture during the training time via a set of auxiliary cells that provide an intermediate supervisory signal and can be omitted during the evaluation phase. The design of the auxiliary cell is emitted by a controller, a neural network with the fixed structure trained using reinforcement learning. More crucially, we demonstrate how to efficiently search for these architectures within limited time and computational budgets. In particular, we rely on a progressive strategy that terminates non-promising architectures from being further trained, and on Polyak averaging coupled with knowledge distillation to speed-up the convergence. Quantitatively, in 8 GPU-days our approach discovers a set of architectures performing on-par with state-of-the-art among compact models on the semantic segmentation, pose estimation and depth prediction tasks. This study aims to investigate social dynamics within collaborative environments. Specifically, we examine opinions, conflicts, and consensus-building processes among individuals working together on complex projects where collaboration is essential. Utilizing data from real-world case studies, our research develops computational models that capture key aspects of these phenomena, including opinion formation, conflict resolution strategies, and factors influencing group decision making. Our results provide valuable insights into how sociometric analysis can inform design principles for more effective online platforms enabling productive collaborations across diverse groups of stakeholders. Overall, this work contributes to understanding the interplay between individual behavior and collective outcomes in dynamic socio-technical systems.

Medical image segmentation is a fundamental task in medical imaging analysis, which involves dividing an image into its constituent parts or structures. However, achieving robust general medical Image segmentation remains a challenging problem due to variations In image quality, modality, and anatomy. In this paper, we propose A novel approach towards robust general Medical image segmentation, which combines the strengths of deep learning and traditional computer vision techniques. Our approach leverages a hybrid segmentation framework that integrates a deep neural network with a robust feature extraction method, resulting in improved segmentation accuracy and robustness across different medical imaging modalities. We evaluate our approach on several publicly available medical image datasets, including CT, MRI, and US images, and demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that our approach is able to effectively Handle variations in image Quality, modality, and anatomy, and is able to segment medical images with high accuracy and robustness. This work has the potential to significantly Impact Various medical image analysis applications, such as disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring.

This study presents a novel high-resolution segmentation approach for tooth root fuzzy edges based on polynomial curve fitting and landmark detection. The proposed method utilizes an automated algorithm to detect key landmarks along the toothroot boundary, which are then used to fit a polynomial curve that accurately captures the complex shape of the tooth root. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed technique provides superior results compared to existing methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, making it well suited for practical applications in dental image analysis. Overall, this research represents a significant advance in the field of oral imaging and has important implications for clinical practice.

In this study, we propose a novel approach to improve microscopy image segmentation using lifted multicuts. Our method leverages domain knowledge by incorporating prior information about the structure and organization of objects in the images into the segmentation process. We demonstrate that our technique outperforms existing methods on several benchmark datasets, achieving more accurate segmentations and faster computation times. Overall, our findings suggest that integrating domain expertise into machine learning algorithms can significantly enhance their performance in complex imaging tasks.

In this work, we address the challenging task of few-shot segmentation. Previous few-shot segmentation methods mainly employ the information of support images as guidance for query image segmentation. Although some works propose to build cross-reference between support and query images, their extraction of query information still depends on the support images. We here propose to extract the information from the query itself independently to benefit the few-shot segmentation task. To this end, we first propose a prior extractor to learn the query information from the unlabeled images with our proposed global-local contrastive learning. Then, we extract a set of predetermined priors via this prior extractor. With the obtained priors, we generate the prior region maps for query images, which locate the objects, as guidance to perform cross interaction with support features. In such a way, the extraction of query information is detached from the support branch, overcoming the limitation by support, and could obtain more informative query clues to achieve better interaction. Without bells and whistles, the proposed approach achieves new state-of-the-art performance for the few-shot segmentation task on PASCAL-5$^{i}$ and COCO datasets.

S-folds are a class of compactifications of M-theory that preserve supersymmetry and lead to 4d N=3 theories. The paper reviews the basics of S-folds and 4d N=3 theories, and then explores the relationship between the two. It shows that S-folds can be used to construct new 4d N=3 theories, and that these theories can be used to study the properties of S-folds. The paper also discusses some recent developments in the field, including the use of S-folds to study the properties of M5-branes and the relationship between S-folds and other types of compactifications. Overall, the paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of research on S-folds and 4d N=3 superconformal field theories, and highlights some of the exciting directions for future research in this area.

In this paper, we investigate the equivalence of multi-letter quantum finite automata (QLA) and their ability to recognize certain languages. We present several results that establish connections between various types of QLA and their classical counterparts, including the well-known notion of non-deterministic finite automata (NFA). Firstly, we show that every deterministic QLA can be simulated by a NFA, providing a characterization of the class of languages recognizable by these devices. Subsequently, we extend this result to the probabilistic setting, demonstrating that any probabilistic QLA can be approximated by a probabilistic NFA with comparable performance guarantees. Notably, our methods in this section rely on an intricate combination of techniques from linear programming relaxations and Markov chain analysis. Furthermore, we explore the connection between QLA and memoryless symmetries in language recognition. By introducing a suitable adaptation of the Myhill-Nerode theorem, we prove that a language is recognizable by a QLA if and only if it possesses specific properties related to spectral symmetry. This fundamental insight enables us to generalize celebrated results from algebraic combinatorics to the realm of quantum computing, ultimately leading to new insights into the computational capabilities and limitations of QLAs. Our findings contribute significantly towards a deeper understanding of quantum formal language theory and its relationships to other areas within theoretical computer science. Particularly, they shed light on the role of quantum effects when dealing with complex patterns in data streams, with potential implications for applications such as natural language processing or information security.

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the first cause of death in many countries. CRC originates from a small clump of cells on the lining of the colon called polyps, which over time might grow and become malignant. Early detection and removal of polyps are therefore necessary for the prevention of colon cancer. In this paper, we introduce an ensemble of medical polyp segmentation algorithms. Based on an observation that different segmentation algorithms will perform well on different subsets of examples because of the nature and size of training sets they have been exposed to and because of method-intrinsic factors, we propose to measure the confidence in the prediction of each algorithm and then use an associate threshold to determine whether the confidence is acceptable or not. An algorithm is selected for the ensemble if the confidence is below its associate threshold. The optimal threshold for each segmentation algorithm is found by using Comprehensive Learning Particle Swarm Optimization (CLPSO), a swarm intelligence algorithm. The Dice coefficient, a popular performance metric for image segmentation, is used as the fitness criteria. Experimental results on two polyp segmentation datasets MICCAI2015 and Kvasir-SEG confirm that our ensemble achieves better results compared to some well-known segmentation algorithms.

> We present novel approach to image editing that is based on language descriptions. Our method is able to edit images by generating new image that is consistent with a given text description. We use a recurrent neural network to generate sequence of image patches that are then combined to form a new image. The recurrent network is trained to predict next patch given previous patches and the text description. We show that our method is able to generate images that are consistent with the text description and that are visually plausible. In this paper, we investigate the problem of overfitting in neural networks under class imbalance, with a focus on its impact on image segmentation tasks. We analyze the effects of class imbalance on the training dynamics of neural networks and demonstrate that overfitting is exacerbated in such scenarios. We propose several techniques to address this issue, including oversampling the minority class, undersampling the majority class, and using class-balanced batch normalization. Our experiments on several benchmark datasets show that these techniques can significantly improve segmentation performance in the presence of class imbalance. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the effects of oversampling and undersampling on the generalization error of the network, and show that oversampling the minority class can lead to a bias-variance trade-off that can be detrimental to performance. Our findings have important implications for the design and training of neural networks for image segmentation and other imbalanced classification tasks.

In this work, we present an extension to Semantics and Information Retrieval (SIER) that combines automatic feature selection and semantic segmentation in an innovative fashion using image-based style generation for segmentation training. Specifically, we use images derived using hierarchical clustering based on a modified version of the style grid from Apte and colleagues. Our system learns how humans categorize pictures in terms of their visual content and then constructs these hierarchies from these descriptions by combining these definitions from both human reviewers as well as machine learning algorithms based on image descriptors such as color, shape, lighting etc.. To test our model, which uses very few labels or features, we performed classification of human annotated images for which we have no way of finding similar examples without manually adding them manually before presenting these results at the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 2016 where they were first presented. We find that our scheme, which has shown promising performances previously on several classes of problem, may be beneficial when used together with advanced multi-labeling techniques for supervised classification. Moreover, we predict significant improvement over state-of-the-art models using the existing style-grapher utility package developed earlier.

A keyboard is just a list of switches. There is several ways to connect those switches but basically when a switch is pressed, it allows current to flow thru and a microcontroller (a smart chip if you wish) will detect this current and basically record which one was pressed or released. In turn the microcontroller will send this information to the computer via a serial connection (PS2 or USB), the computer receive this information and the operating system acknowledges it and send it thru the program that "own" the keyboard at that time. We propose a new method based on hierarchical linear algebra (HLA) that can be efficiently used to segment an entyre tooth root. Instead of attempting to use a very high amount of parametres or gradient computation in order obtain optimal results, we directly incorporate the best features of individual teeth into our model in a parametre-dependent manner and leverage their overlap to achieve a good result. Our procedure was confirmed after performing hundreds of thousands of steps per hour using real human and simulated teeth. While results were inconsistent (due to the variance inherent in sampling), they were statistically significant at p<0.001 when considering 10 000 steps/hour. Abstract We evaluate methods for learning to generate visual stimuli using an ensemble of random noise shapes extracted dynamically from a grid. Using hypercube contours and deep convolutional neural networks we learn to find new categories by adjusting values of all weights in nonlinear kernel gradient descent over time, yielding stable, robust visual classifiers on images generated using unmodified hypercubes. Our analysis reveals that our model performs equally well even when restricted to visual stimuli with only one or two classes, which were not considered prior to training. The key contribution lies in our approach to use hypercube distributions as inputs to gradient descent, making it possible to learn visually similar objects across different environments. Our analysis shows clear benefit of working on hypercube surfaces instead of randomly selecting them directly from the spatial coordinates at each stage of gradient ascent; in fact we can learn better results on both cases because gradients on hyper cube manifolds propagate further on the surface than on normal cubes. Abstract — Object detection in images with different orientations, such as landscape images, vertical images etc, has always been considered to be challenging due to the large gap between the two domains: horizontal image and portrait image. To adress this issue, we present Crosslink Net (CoLink), which consists of four key features: horizontal-vertical cascaded fusion strategy, double branch segmentation network architecture, dynamic convolutional filter design and gradient back-propagation across modalities through an adaptive cross-modality attention module. By introducing these mechanisms into one model, CoLink not only takes advantage of horizontal and vertical information learned at same stage but also learns higher level features jointly during training by minimizing mutual information loss between those two branches. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for object detection both offline and online modes on all metrics compared over 37 scenes using multiple detectors on a single stream mobile device without any other preprocessing or calibration stages. Furthermore, based on our proposed method, we have built one application for indoor localization through scene classification (as shown below) and will continue extending it further into semantic mapping and multi target tracking based applications soon.

The abstract of an academic paper is a concise summary of the paper's main contributions and findings. Here's a possible abstract for the paper "A Multidimensional Szemerédi Theorem in the Primes": In this paper, we establish a multidimensional version of the Szemerédi theorem in the primes, generalizing the classical result of Szemerédi (1975) and its subsequent extensions to higher dimensions. Our main theorem states that for any k ≥ 2, there exists a positive integer N such that any subset of the prime numbers of size at least N contains a k-term arithmetic progression. We prove this result using a combination of techniques from additive combinatorics, erdős-turán theory, and the study of prime numbers. Our proof involves constructing a suitable weight function and applying the Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem, combined with a careful analysis of the distribution of prime numbers in short intervals. We also establish a stronger version of the theorem for "typical" subsets of the primes, which implies a multidimensional version of the Green-Tao-Ziegler theorem. Our results have implications for other problems in additive combinatorics and number theory, such as the study of sum-free sets, and provide a new perspective on the distribution of prime numbers. They also demonstrate the power of the multidimensional approach to additive combinatorics, which has been successful in tackling a range of problems in recent years. Overall, our paper provides a significant contribution to the study of additive combinatorics and number theory, and opens up new avenues for research in these areas.

The reliability of Deep Learning systems depends on their accuracy but also on their robustness against adversarial perturbations to the input data. Several attacks and defenses have been proposed to improve the performance of Deep Neural Networks under the presence of adversarial noise in the natural image domain. However, robustness in computer-aided diagnosis for volumetric data has only been explored for specific tasks and with limited attacks. We propose a new framework to assess the robustness of general medical image segmentation systems. Our contributions are two-fold: (i) we propose a new benchmark to evaluate robustness in the context of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) by extending the recent AutoAttack natural image classification framework to the domain of volumetric data segmentation, and (ii) we present a novel lattice architecture for RObust Generic medical image segmentation (ROG). Our results show that ROG is capable of generalizing across different tasks of the MSD and largely surpasses the state-of-the-art under sophisticated adversarial attacks.

In this paper we consider image segmentation as an edge refinement problem, where we allow the iterative application of edges during the inference loop to guide the intermediate output of each iteration towards the desired class labels by means of conditional normal flow (CNF). Our model has two main advantages over previous CINs that also use iterative processes in the training loop; it requires no special memory architecture and does not use any features or labels that are associated with only a very short time interval because of its fully autoregressive structure, and because all iterations are conditioned by simple gradients on the cross-layers instead of global attention mechanisms such as seen in other works, it performs very efficiently, which allows us to train many forward passes without the need for additional data, while still achieving competitive results with the best CINs on public test sets like CamVid 2017. This makes our method more widely applicable than previous methods, enabling improvements in performance to be made by tinkering with hyper-parameters rather than by changing any of the network’s components. Thanks to the aforesaid advantages of the model, which will certainly encourage its wide-ranging deployment given how easy to deploy neural networks have become today, compared to just five years ago when most networks were implemented in different frameworks designed specifically for neural networks.

In this paper, we describe a new method of training deep neural networks to segment neural structures in microscopic images. The method, called Icon, is based on the principle of combining the advantages of deep learning and interactive segmentation, and is designed to facilitate the manual annotation of neural structures in large-scale microscopy images, where the annotation of images by hand is time-consuming and expensive. Our method relies on iteratively correcting the deep neural network output by hand, which can lead to a more accurate segmentation of complex neural structures. We have evaluated Icon on several standard datasets and compared its performance with other state-of-the-art methods. The results show that Icon achieves high accuracy and outperforms other methods in terms of efficiency and scalability. We also demonstrate the versatility of Icon by applying it to different neural structures and different modalities of images. The high scalability and accuracy of Icon can be used in a variety of applications, including neurology, drug discovery and regenerative medicine, and the interactive nature of the method can be used by experts to ensure that the accuracy of the data is not lost in the next steps of analysis. Our paper represents a significant advance in the development of deep learning methods for neural structure segmentation, and we believe that Icon will be a useful tool for the scientific community.

The deep learning framework has brought substantial advances to some segmentation tasks such as semantic and instance-level segmentation. However, many important practical applications are still unsolved, particularly in the case of real-time, poorly supervised, unannotated scenes (see Fig. 1). While existing interactive segmentation methods have achieved promising results on simple objects such as cars and chairs, they have failed on high-resolution images with complex geometry and large amounts of occlusion. Moreover, even when the input is annotated, these methods tend to degrade rapidly, limiting their utility even with highly structured object labels. In this paper, we address these issues by guiding the segmentation process by boundaries between objects. We propose “EdgeFlow,” an edge-aware flow-based optimization framework that takes advantage of the deep learning framework to extract boundary guidance features on synthetic data and combine them with the input from deep learning models trained on RGB images or depth images captured by a Kinect-like device (see Fig. 2). Unlike existing methods, our method does not require densely annotated input, as the training data only need to be annotated with partial, sparse edge information. On four popular datasets, EdgeFlow achieves better performance than the best-in-class methods on weakly annotated data, matching the performance of fully supervised methods at a fraction of the cost. Moreover, on four popular datasets, EdgeFlow runs at an interactive speed using commercial off-the-shelf hardware components, and achieves superior performance on both quantitative and qualitative measures.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to referring image segmentation that leverages comprehensive multi-modal interactions between humans and machines. Our proposed method enables users to interact with an image using natural language commands, gestures, and visual attention, allowing them to accurately refer to specific regions of interest within the image. We propose a unified framework that combines these multiple modalities into a single coherent representation, enabling effective communication and collaboration between humans and machines. This is achieved through a combination of deep learning techniques, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and multi-modal fusion algorithms. The key contribution of our work lies in its ability to effectively integrate and reconcile the strengths of different modalities to improve image segmentation accuracy. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on several challenging benchmark datasets, where it outperforms existing methods that rely solely on language or vision inputs. Through extensive user studies, we also investigate the impact of modality switching strategies and identify optimal combinations of modalities that maximize performance. Our findings have important implications for applications such as object recognition, medical imaging analysis, and human-robot interaction, where effective multi-modal communication can significantly enhance task efficiency and accuracy.

The recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) combined with the extensive amount of data generated by today's clinical systems, has led to the development of imageing AI solutions across the whole value chain of medical imageing, including image reconstruction, medical image segmentation, image-based diagnosis and treatment planning. Notwithstanding the successes and future potential of AI in medical imageing, many stakeholders are concerned of the potential risks and ethical implications of imageing AI solutions, which are perceived as complex, opaque, and difficult to comprehend, utilise, and trust in critical clinical applications. Despite these concerns and risks, there are currently no concrete guidelines and best practises for guiding future AI developments in medical imageing towards increased trust, safety and adoption. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a careful selection of guiding principles drawn from the accumulated experiences, consensus, and best practises from five large European projects on AI in Health Imageing. These guiding principles are named FUTURE-AI and its building blocks consist of (i) Fairness, (ii) Universality, (iii) Traceability, (iv) Usability, (v) Robustness and (vi) Explainability. In a step-by-step approach, these guidelines are further translated into a framework of concrete recommendations for specifying, developing, evaluating, and deploying technically, clinically and ethically trustworthy AI solutions into clinical practise.

We introduce a method that allows to automatically segment images into semantically meaningful regions without human supervision. Derived regions are consistent across different images and coincide with human-defined semantic classes on some datasets. In cases where semantic regions might be hard for human to define and consistently label, our method is still able to find meaningful and consistent semantic classes. In our work, we use pretrained StyleGAN2~\cite{karras2020analyzing} generative model: clustering in the feature space of the generative model allows to discover semantic classes. Once classes are discovered, a synthetic dataset with generated images and corresponding segmentation masks can be created. After that a segmentation model is trained on the synthetic dataset and is able to generalize to real images. Additionally, by using CLIP~\cite{radford2021learning} we are able to use prompts defined in a natural language to discover some desired semantic classes. We test our method on publically available datasets and show state-of-the-art results.

In this research, we propose an effective few-shot segmentation approach that combines global and local contrastive learning to achieve outstanding performance. Our method utilizes self-supervision techniques by leveraging two types of contrasts: global contrast which aligns features from different parts in a single image patch, and local contrast which aligns feature maps across patches from nearby regions of different images. By integrating these contrasts simultaneously, our approach can learn robust semantic segmented representations with high discrimination against diverse backgrounds while remaining computationally efficient. We validate our model's efficacy on multiple datasets with limited training data, demonstrating state-of-the-art results and outpacing prior methods in terms of accuracy, tradeoff between speed and quality, and generalization ability across unseen or challenging classes and scenes.

Variational Auto-Encoders have often been used for unsupervised pretraining, feature extraction and out-of-distribution and anomaly detection in the medical field. However, VAEs often lack the ability to produce sharp images and learn high-level features. We propose to alleviate these issues by adding a new branch to conditional hierarchical VAEs. This enforces a division between higher-level and lower-level features. Despite the additional computational overhead compared to a normal VAE it results in sharper and better reconstructions and can capture the data distribution similarly well (indicated by a similar or slightly better OoD detection performance).

Weakly Threshold Graphs: A Study on Algorithmic Applications =========================================================== A threshold graph is a widely used data structure to store and process real-world, binary edge relation databases. Its efficient connectivity modeling has led to its successful use in numerous applications, such as computer networking and bioinformatics. However, we discover that some of these scenarios may tolerate certain levels of disconnectedness within graph while still processing efficiently due to their inherent locality or distributed nature. This paper presents our initial study into weakly connected threshold graphs - those with a user specified tolerance level (or 'threshold') for edge connectivity. The central aim is to design and evaluate new algorithms tailored specifically for these cases by taking advantage of inherently existing structural properties. Our analysis uncovers interesting connections between weakly threshold graphs and other data structures like matrix representations and vertex colorings, allowing us to apply known methods from their fields, and provide novel hybrid algorithmic approaches. We demonstrate how the concept can improve both computational efficiency and robustness of multiple common threshold graph traversal problems including Dijkstra's single source shortest path algorithm, breadth-first search and depth first search when dealing with large, highly sparse datasets. Further, our results indicate promising potential in developing family of scalable, distributed algorithms applicable across multiple domains.

In this paper, we explore some complexity results in the theory of normal numbers. Normal numbers are real numbers that have a certain uniform distribution property with respect to their digits in base $b$. We investigate the computational complexity of various problems related to normality, including the decision problem of wether a given number is normal and the problem of computing the density of a normal number. Our main results show that these problems are computationally hard, even for very simple instances. Specifically, we prove that it is NP-hard to decide wether a given rational number is normal, and that computing the density of a normal number is #P-complete. These results demonstrate that normal numbers exhibit intrinsic mathematical properties that make them resistant to efficient algorithmic processing. Furthermore, our work implies that many natural questions related to normal numbers are unlikely to be resolved by algorithms that run in polynomial time or polynomial space. This has significant implications for fields such as number theory, cryptography, and randomness. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental limits of computability and have far-reaching consequences for studying complex phenomena using computational methods.

We investigate Referring Image Segmentation (RIS), which outputs a segmentation map corresponding to the given natural language description. To solve RIS efficiently, we need to understand each word's relationship with other words, each region in the image to other regions, and cross-modal alignment between linguistic and visual domains. We argue that one of the limiting factors in the recent methods is that they do not handle these interactions simultaneously. To this end, we propose a novel architecture called JRNet, which uses a Joint Reasoning Module(JRM) to concurrently capture the inter-modal and intra-modal interactions. The output of JRM is passed through a novel Cross-Modal Multi-Level Fusion (CMMLF) module which further refines the segmentation masks by exchanging contextual information across visual hierarchy through linguistic features acting as a bridge. We present thorough ablation studies and validate our approach's performance on four benchmark datasets, showing considerable performance gains over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper presents the findings of a data mining study of teachers' grades to identify key courses in an educational curriculum. Certain materials will stretchcompressbend more easily than others, and this is known as the material's stiffness. Up to a certain amount of stress, if you let go, the material will snap back to its original size and shape. It will be as if the deformation never happened. This is known as [elastic deformation] (URL0). With many materials, if you put too much load on them, if you deform them too far, they will suddenly snap. These are brittle materials, like glass or porcelain. But other materials don't snap immediately. These are ductile materials. In ductile materials, an interesting thing happens: yield. At the yield point, the elastic deformation gives way to [plastic deformation] (URL2). In plastic deformation, the material becomes much less stiff, and begins to deform permanently. Even when you let go and stop stressing it, it will never return back to its original shape. The usual examples for discussing elastic vs. plastic deformation are slinkies or paperclips: stretchbend them a little bit and they're fine, but stretchbend them too far and you can't get them back into their proper shape. Amazon has revealed two new robots at the re:MARS conference that are designed to move products around its warehouses. The Xanthus is an upgrade for Amazon's shelf-bots that will let them operate in more environments, and the Pegasus is a completely new system that replaces the conveyors normally employed. 3D Convolution Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely applied to 3D scene understanding, such as video analysis and volumetric image recognition. However, 3D networks can easily lead to over-parameterization which incurs expensive computation cost. In this paper, we propose Channel-wise Automatic KErnel Shrinking (CAKES), to enable efficient 3D learning by shrinking standard 3D convolutions into a set of economic operations e.g., 1D, 2D convolutions. Unlike previous methods, CAKES performs channel-wise kernel shrinkage, which enjoys the following benefits: 1) enabling operations deployed in every layer to be heterogeneous, so that they can extract diverse and complementary information to benefit the learning process; and 2) allowing for an efficient and flexible replacement design, which can be generalized to both spatial-temporal and volumetric data. Further, we propose a new search space based on CAKES, so that the replacement configuration can be determined automatically for simplifying 3D networks. CAKES shows superior performance to other methods with similar model size, and it also achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art with much fewer parameters and computational costs on tasks including 3D medical imaging segmentation and video action recognition. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/yucornetto/CAKES

We present a novel method to automatically segment scenes composed of millions of pixels from large data sets by extracting coarse and fine gradients from their noise images. The method achieves good results on both visual objects, where features are robust against noisy data, and semantic or object representation problems involving small groups (e.g., a facial expression). We applied it successfully to a data set of 4 million high resolution face images, producing a global and local score representation that was indistinguishable from that produced by conventional segmentation approaches. The proposed system exhibits high temporal fidelity and thus can replace human segmentation techniques in many types of situations. (via @joshuarei)

This paper presents novel approach to ranking response surfaces using deep learning techniques. The proposed method is applied to optimal stopping problems, where the goal is to determine the optimal time to stop a process in order to maximize reward. The response surface is a function that describes expected reward as a function of stopping time. The proposed method uses a deep neural network to learn response surface and rank it based on its expected reward. The results show that the proposed method outperforms traditional methods for ranking response surfaces and can be applied to wide range of optimal stopping problems.

In this work, we study semantic segmentation in few-shot scenario (i.e., training on only a small set of labeled images per class). Given that standard CNNs achieve better performance for classification over segmentation tasks; one natural attempt to adapt them would be through the combination of a 2D convolutional neck with an additional head producing pixel predictions -- a direct yet naive approach called `Vanilla'. To tackle such issues, we propose two novel approaches that boost the base-line models performance by learning complementary representations suitable for dense prediction under low shot scenarios . A feature matching attention module is introduced in order to explicitly enforce consistency between high level visual features extracted by backbone modules for segmentation and downstream task heads. In addition, we also show how adopting global contrastive loss not only improves generalization power but can lead towards discovering more discriminative latent projections. Experimental results verify the effectiveness of our proposed method, yielding superior performances compared against other recent works while being much lighter which leads to faster convergence as well during optimizations.

The Mathematical Foundations of the GraphBLAS The graph-structured linear algebra subsystems (GraphBLAS) are widely used to solve problems in science and engineering. In this paper, we provide a review of mathematical foundations related to these algorithms. We begin by defining vectorized matrix operations on arrays and develop formalism necessary to understand the parallelization techniques applied by GraphBLAS. Next, we explain matrix-vector product operations with block vectors and define the concept of the local matrix blocks. These lead us to define various data structures commonly used in the graph-structured linear algebra. Finally, we introduce the graph-based indexing schemes, which allow efficient access to vertex and edge indices from their global positions. Overall, our work provides an accessible introduction to the mathematical foundations required for understanding the implementation details of popular GraphBLAS libraries such as BoomerAMG and Trilinos.

The screening of baggage using X-ray scanners is now routine in aviation security with automatic threat detection approaches, based on 3D X-ray computed tomography (CT) images, known as Automatic Threat Recognition (ATR) within the aviation security industry. These current strategies use pre-defined threat material signatures in contrast to adaptability towards new and emerging threat signatures. To address this issue, concept of adaptive automatic threat recognition (AATR) was proposed in previous work. In this paper, we present a solution to AATR based on such X-ray CT baggage scan imagery. This aims to address the issues of rapidly evolving threat signatures within the screening requirements. Ideally, the detection algorithms deployed within the security scanners should be readily adaptable to different situations with varying requirements of threat characteristics (e.g., threat material, physical properties of objects). We tackle this issue using novel adaptive machine learning methodology with our solution consisting of a multi-scale 3D CT image segmentation algorithm, multi-class support vector machine (SVM) classifier for object material recognition and a strategy to enable adaptability of our approach. Experiments are conducted on both open and sequestered 3D CT baggage image datasets specifically collected for AATR study. Our proposed approach performs well on both recognition and adaptation. Overall our approach can achieve the probability of detection around 90% with a probability of false alarm below 20%. Our AATR shows capabilities of adapting to varying types of materials, even unknown materials which are not available in the training data, adapting to varying required probability of detection and adapting to varying scales of threat object.

An innovative 3-D radar imaging technique is developed for fast and efficient identification and characterization of radar backscattering components of complex objects, when the collected scattered field is made of polarization-diverse measurements. In this context, all the polarimetric information seems irretrievably mixed. A direct model, derived from a simple but original extension of the widespread "multiple scattering model" leads to a high dimensional linear inverse problem. It is solved by a fast dedicated imaging algorithm that performs to determine at a time three huge 3-D scatterer maps which correspond to HH, VV and HV polarizations at emission and reception. It is applied successfully to various mock-ups and data sets collected from an accurate and dedicated 3D spherical experimental layout that provides concentric polarization-diverse RCS measurements.

In this paper, we present novel approach to modeling social dynamics in collaborative environments. Our work focuses on understanding how opinions, conflicts, and consensus emerge and evolve over time in groups of individuals working together on a shared task. We propose a computational framework that captures the complex interplay between individual perspectives, social influence, and collective decision-making processes. Our model incorporates several key features, including the ability to represent diverse opinion distributions, handle conflicting views, and simulate emergence of consensus through repeated interactions. We evaluate our approach using a series of simulations and case studies, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing realistic patterns of behavior and predicting outcomes of group deliberations. The insights gained from our models have important implications for understanding and improving collaboration in various contexts, such as multidisciplinary teams, organizational decision-making, and online community discussions. By providing better understanding of social forces that shape collective decision-making, our work can inform strategies for promoting effective communication, resolving conflicts, and fostering consensus in diverse group settings.

> The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment that will use a 40-kilotonne liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) as its far detector. The LArTPC will be located in the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in Lead, South Dakota, 1,300 km from the neutrino source at Fermilab. The LArTPC will be instrumented with 10,000 photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) to detect the Cherenkov light produced by the charged particles created in neutrino interactions. The PMTs will be arranged in a 10-layer, 10-column array. The DUNE Collabouration has developed a simulation framework to study the performance of the LArTPC. The simulation framework is based on the Geant4 toolkit and includes a detailed description of the LArTPC and its instrumentation. The simulation framework is used to study the performance of the LArTPC in a variety of configurations. This paper describes the simulation configurations used in the DUNE Collabouration's Conceptual Design Report (CDR). The full paper can be found here.

This paper proposes a new statistical test, the Smoothed P-Value Test, for situations where there is a nuisance parameter under the alternative hypothesis. The test is designed to account for the effects of the nuisance parameter on the test statistic, resulting in improved power and accuracy. The test is based on a smoothed p-value function that incorporates information from the nuisance parameter distribution. The paper provides a detailed derivation of the test and demonstrates its effectiveness through simulations and an application to a real data set. Overall, the Smoothed P-Value Test offers a valuable tool for researchers working with nuisance parameters in their statistical models.

The abstract of the paper entitled “Iterative, Deep and Unsupervised Synthetic Aperture Sonar Image Segmentation” is as follows: “A new iterative, deep and unsupervised approach to the synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) image segmentation is proposed. The proposed method employs a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and graph-based methods to process the SAS images into target and clutter regions. The CNNs are used to extract features from the sonar images, and the graph-based methods to refine the segmentation. This method is unsupervised, meaning that it does not require labelled training data and can be applied to a wide range of sonar images. The results of the proposed method are compared with a supervised learning method and show significantly improved accuracy.”

In this article, we investigate the transient behavior of a sequence of packetsbits traversing a multi-hop wireless network. Our work is motivated by novel applications from the domain of process automation, Machine-Type Communication (MTC) and cyber-physical systems, where short messages are communicated and statistical guarantees need to be provided on a per-message level. In order to optimize such a network, apart from understanding the stationary system dynamics, an understanding of the short-term dynamics (i.e., transient behavior) is also required. To this end, we derive novel Wireless Transient Bounds (WTB) for end-to-end delay and backlog in a multi-hop wireless network using stochastic network calculus approach. WTB depends on the initial backlog at each node as well as the instantaneous channel states. We numerically compare WTB with State-Of-The-Art Transient bounds (SOTAT), that can be obtained by adapting existing stationary bounds, as well as simulation of the network. While SOTAT and stationary bounds are not able to capture the short-term system dynamics well, WTB provides relatively tight upper bound and has a decay rate that closely matches the simulation. This is achieved by WTB only with a slight increase in the computational complexity, by a factor of O (T N), where T is the duration of the arriving sequence and N is the number of hops in the network. We believe that the presented analysis and the bounds can be used as base for future work on transient network optimization, e.g., in massive MTC, critical MTC, edge computing and autonomous vehicle.

Abstract: In quantum gravity, theories involving closed timelike curves (CTCs) have led to concerns about potential singularities and their possible impact on global topology. In this paper, we revisit these issues by discussing recent results regarding asymptotic safety in quantum gravity. Specifically, we focus on avoiding the presence of singularities through deformation of matter fields that couple with curvature. Furthermore, using a combination of perturbative methods and numerical simulations, we show how to modify initial conditions for scalar field configurations to eliminate the formation of CTCs during evolution. These results demonstrate the possibility of constructing consistent theories without violating causality or global conformal symmetries, providing important insights into the nature of quantum gravity and its implication for fundamental physics.

This paper provides a robust approach to large-scale image segmentation through the utilization of distributed clustering algorithms. With the increasing availability of high-dimensional databases, conventional centralized processing techniques have become extremely obsolete and limited by computational limitations. To address this challenge, we propose a novel methodology that allows the optimization of image segmentation over many nodes in a distributed computing ecosystem. Our proposed approach uses the power of distributed clustering algorithms, which are proven to be very efficient in handling large databases, to perform pixel-level classification and segmentation of pictures. By partitioning the input image into larger fragments and spreading them over different processors, our technique delivers extraordinary levels of efficiency and performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to many large-scale image datasets, yielding excellent reliability and reliability compared to state-of-the-art centralized techniques. The important contributions of this paper can be described as follows: 1. A distributed clustering-based methodology for large-scale image segmentation is adopted, which enabled the efficient processing of large pictures through parallel algorithms. 2. An optimization approach was adopted to efficiently distribute the workload and reduce communication overheads between processor clusters. 3. Thorough tests were conducted on several large-scale image datasets to improve the efficiency of the proposed approach against existing centralized methods. The findings show substantial changes in both performance and reliability. 4. The proposed approach paves the way for tackling far smaller imaging datasets, formerly considered too large for practical research, opening up new possibilities in technologies such as computer vision, machine learning, and multimedia processing. In conclusion, this paper provides a groundbreaking solution to the issue of large-scale image segmentation, employing an attractive blend of distributed computing and clustering algorithms that enables robust and reliable extraction of large quantities of image data. Our approach has far-reaching consequences for pursuing research and creating innovative technologies outside the realm of big data analytics.

In this paper, we propose a novel self-supervised learning framework called Prior-Guided Local Self-supervised Learning (PGL) for 3D medical image segmentation. Existing self-supervised learning methods for medical image segmentation rely solely on the internal information of the images and neglect the valuable prior knowledge available in the field. Our proposed method incorporates prior knowledge into the self-supervised learning process to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation task. We designed PGL with two main components: 1) a prior guide module that utilizes external knowledge from large-scale datasets of labeled images to learn a spatial heirarchy of anatomical priors; 2) a local self-supervised module that learns contextual features by enforcing similarity between neighboring pixels or voxels in the input volume. Unlike traditional self-supervised learning approaches, our local module does not require explicit annotations or artificial augmentations, making it more interpretable and robust to variations in data quality. Our experiments show that PGL outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised and fully supervised methods on several challenging tasks including brain tumor segmentation, liver segmentation, and lung nodule detection. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating our method with transfer learning and explore its potential in domain adaptation scenarios. The results suggest that prioritizing prior knowledge can significantly enhance the performance of self-supervised learning models in medical imaging applications. This work has important implications for future research in medical image analysis. By leveraging the rich expertise and knowledge accumulated over decades of manual annotation efforts, self-supervised learning frameworks like PGL are poised to revolutionize the field. With improved accuracy, efficiency, and generalizability, these advances may enable new possibilities such as active contouring, semi-supervised learning, and multi-modal fusion - ultimately leading to better patient outcomes.

We also show that our approach can be used for semi-supervised learning, where a small amount of labeled data is used to train a generative model, which can then generate annotations for unseen images. EdgeFlow is a novel interactive segmentation method that utilizes Edge-guided flow to achieve practical and efficient segmentation of images. The method is designed to handle complex and dynamic scenes, where traditional segmentation techniques may struggle. Edge-guided flow is used to guide the segmentation process by identifying and tracking edges in the image. This allows for more accurate and precise segmentation, even in the presence of noise and occlusions. The Method is also designed to be interactive, allowing users to adjust the segmentation Parameters and view the results in real-time. The paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of EdgeFlow, demonstrating Its effectiveness on a variety of Image datasets and use cases. Overall, EdgeFlow represents a significant advancement in the field of interactive segmentation, providing a practical and efficient solution for A wide range of applications.

New Yorkers were shocked to hear of an unusual case recently argued in court, where a woman successfully managed to avoid drink-driving charges after claiming to suffer from a rare condition often referred to as "auto-brewery syndrome." The woman was pulled over by police in the state of New York for allegedly driving under the influence of alcohol. Upon breathalyser tests, her blood-alcohol content (BAC) was found to be three times the legal limit. However, she argued that she had not consumed any alcohol - rather, her BAC levels were due to her auto-brewery syndrome. Auto-brewery syndrome is a rare condition where sugar in the body is converted into alcohol by yeast present in the intestines. This can occur spontaneously or after consuming carbohydrates and sugary foods, leading to an elevated BAC level without having ingested any ethanol. This is the first case in the US of someone successfully arguing in court that they suffer from auto-brewery syndrome, which has been recorded only in very few cases around the world. In 2016, a man from Italy won a similar case and avoided being charged with drunk-driving. Despite prosecutors being unconvinced, the judge ruled in favour of the woman and dismissed the charges. The defence team presented evidence from doctors, who confirmed the presence of yeast in the woman's system, proving that auto-brewery syndrome was the cause of her high BAC levels. The woman's lawyer said: "We are glad that justice was served and that the court accepted our argument that this woman was not guilty of drink-driving because of her medical condition." The case has sparked discussions about how auto-brewery syndrome should be handled in the courts, with some experts suggesting that more research needs to be done in order to properly understand and diagnose the condition.

Despite deep convolutional neural networks achieved impressive progress in medical image computing and analysis, its paradigm of supervised learning demands large number of annotations for training to avoid overfitting and achieving promising results. In clinical practices, massive semantic annotations are difficult to acquire in some conditions where specialized biomedical expert knowledge is required, and it is also a common condition where only few annotated classes are available. In this work, we proposed a novel method for few-shot medical image segmentation, which enables a segmentation model to fast generalize to unseen class with few training images. We construct our few-shot image segmentor using a deep convolutional network trained episodically. Motivated by the spatial consistency and regularity in medical images, we developed an efficient global correlation module to capture the correlation between a support and query image and incorporate it into deep network called global correlation network. Moreover, we enhance discriminability of deep embedding to encourage clustering of feature domains of same class while keep feature domains of different organs far apart. Ablation Study proved effectiveness of the proposed global correlation module and discriminative embedding loss. Extensive experiments on anatomical abdomen images on both CT and MRI modalities are performed to demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our proposed model.

> We study the problem of finding a longest path in a task-precedence poset. A task-precedence poset is a poset in which each element is either a task or a milestone, and the order relation is a partial order on the tasks and a total order on the milestones. The problem is to find a longest path in the poset that contains no two consecutive milestones. We show that the problem is NP-complete, and we give a polynomial-time algorithm for the special case in which the poset is a chain. We also give a polynomial-time algorithm for the special case in which the poset is a tree. The paper is available here.

This paper presents a scalable approach to large-scale image segmentation through the utilization of distributed clustering algorithms. With the growing availability of high-dimensional data, traditional centralized processing methods have become increasingly inefficient and limited by computational constraints. To adress this challenge, we propose a novel framework that enables the parallelization of image segmentation across multiple nodes in a distributed computing environment. Our proposed method leverages the power of distributed clustering algorithms, which are proven to be highly effective in handling massive datasets, to perform pixel-level classification and segmentation of images. By partitioning the input image into smaller chunks and distributing them across multiple processors, our approach achieves unprecedented levels of scalability and efficiency. We demonstrate the efficacy of our technique by applying it to several large-scale image datasets, yielding superior performance and accuracy compared to state-of-the-art centralized methods. The key contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: 1. A distributed clustering-based framework for large-scale image segmentation is introduced, which enabled the efficient processing of massive images via parallel computation. 2. An optimization strategy was developed to effectively distribute the workload and minimize communication overheads between processor nodes. 3. Thorough experiments were conducted on various large-scale image datasets to evaluate the performance of the proposed method against existing centralized approaches. The results show significant improvements in both efficiency and accuracy. 4. The proposed method paves the way for tackling even larger imaging datasets, previously considered too vast for practical analysis, opening up new opportunities in applications such as computer vision, machine learning, and multimedia processing. In conclusion, this paper offers a groundbreaking solution to the problem of large-scale image segmentation, providing an elegant combination of distributed computing and clustering algorithms that facilitates efficient and accurate processing of huge amounts of image data. Our approach has far-reaching implications for advancing research and developing innovative applications within the realm of big data analytics.

In this paper, we present a general framework for studying the polynomiality property of the structure coefficients of double-class algebras. By introducing a certain grading on the algebra and its module category, we are able to establish a connection between the polynomiality of the structure coefficients and the existence of certain types of finite-dimensional representations of the algebra. We show that if the structure coefficients of an arbitrary double-class algebra satisfy a set of polynomiality conditions, then the algebra has a Finite number of Isomorphism classes of simple modules, and every module has a Composition Series Whose factors are direct sums of simple modules. We also prove that if the algebra has a Finite number of isomorphism classes of simple modules and Every module has a composition series whose factors are direct sums of simple modules, then the structure coefficients of the algebra satisfy the polynomiality conditions. Our results provide a new perspective on the relationship between the polynomiality property and the representation theory of double-class algebras, and they have important implications for the study of these algebras And their applications In geometry and physics.

Several, recently proposed methods of surface manufacturing based on ion beam sputtering, which involve dual beam setups, sequential application of ion beams from different directions, or sample rotation, are studied with the method of kinetic Monte Carlo simulation of ion beam erosion and surface diffusion. In this work, we only consider erosion dominated situations. The results are discussed by comparing them to a number of theoretical propositions and to experimental findings. Two ion-beams aligned opposite to each other produce stationary, symmetric ripples. Two ion beams crossing at right angle will produce square patterns only, if they are exactly balanced. In all other cases of crossed beams, ripple patterns are created, and their orientations are shown to be predictable from linear continuum theory. In sequential ion beam sputtering we find a very rapid destruction of structures created from the previous beam direction after a rotation step, which leads to a transient decrease of overall roughness. Superpositions of patterns from several rotation steps are difficult to obtain, as they exist only in very short time windows. In setups with a single beam directed towards a rotating sample, we find a non-monotonic dependence of roughness on rotation frequency, with a very pronounced minimum appearing at the frequency scale set by the relaxation of prestructures observed in sequential ion beam setups. Furthermore we find that the logarithm of the height of structures decreases proportional to the inverse frequency.

In this paper, we present a novel unsupervised semantic segmentation method based on the two state-of-the-art models, namely, the GAN and the CLIP models. GAN is used to generate different styles for an image, and CLIP is used to learn the representation of an image with a text caption. By combining these two models, a rich set of features can be learned that can be used for semantic segmentation. We propose a novel combining loss function based on the image-text pair and the cross-style pair to optimize the semantic segmentation. The proposed method is tested on a number of datasets including Pascal VOC and COCO, and its performance is evaluated on several evaluation metrics. The experiments show that our method can produce accurate and semantically accurate segmentation masks for images. We also analyze the effectiveness of different components of our model using the procedure of ablation. The results show that the combination of GAN and CLIP plays an important role in the performance of the model, and the proposed loss function also plays an important role in the quality of the segmentation. The application of our method to object recognition, scene understanding, image and video analysis is very significant. Since our method can obtain semantic segmentation without any supervision, it can be widely used in many applications where annotation is not available or is difficult to obtain. In summary, the proposed method of semantic segmentation in style is a significant development in the field of unsupervised semantic image segmentation.

This academic paper presents a new framework for predictive modeling that is distribution-free and risk-controlling. The authors propose a novel prediction set methodology that utilizes statistical measures Of risk and uncertainty to construct sets of predictions with guaranteed performance characteristics. Unlike traditional methods that assume knowledge about the underlying data distribution, the proposed approach allows for flexibility in terms of selecting appropriate distributions. Additionally, the authors demonstrate How their technique Can be applied to nonlinear regression models and provide several examples to illustrate its effectiveness. Overall, this work Represents an important Advancement into the realm of robust and reliable predictive analytics, which has critical applications across many diverse disciplines.

Abstract: Deep learning has made major progress on several segmentation tasks such as semantic and instance segmentation. However, many important practical applications are not covered by existing methods, especially when it comes to interactive segmentation settings including weakly or poorly supervised, unsegmented scenes (Figure 1). While state-of-the-art interative segmentation techniques often do well in these scenarios for simple objects like cars and chairs, they struggle with high resolution datasets that involve complex geometry and large occlusion. Moreover, we find significant performance degradation even under fully supervi- sion which limits their use even with highly structured object labels. In this work, we address these challenges through an intuitive approach guided by boundaries between objects. We propose 'EdgeFlow,' a boundary-aware flow optimization algorithm that uses edge guidance features learned on synthetic data paired with deep network inputs (e.g., RGB) captured from either raw video capture or depth sensors such as Kinect (see Figure 3). Our approach requires neither strong nor dense object labeling for training; instead we only require low supervision of edges through depth input that encodes partial ordering information. On four popular benchmarks, EdgeFlow generalizes better than existing weak-supervision based approaches while achieving comparable accuracy with fully supervised baselines at one tenth of the computational cost. At interactive speed using off-the-shelf hardware components our method outperforms previous works across all datasets for both quantitative metrics and qualitative visualizations.

Samuel was a middle-aged man who lived alone in a small, one bedroom apartment. He had never been married and had no children, so he spent most of his days working at his job as a janitor. Every Thursday, it was his job to take the trash from the building out to the dumpster. He had been doing this for years, but today something felt different. When he pulled up to the dumpster, he noticed a young woman standing near it. She seemed to be waiting for someone, but he couldn't tell who. He got out of his truck and walked over to her. "Can I help you?" he asked, trying to sound friendly. The woman smiled at him and said she was waiting for her boyfriend, who was supposed to be helping her take out the trash. Samuel offered to help instead and the woman gratefully accepted. Together they loaded all the bags into the back of his truck and then drove them to the dumpster. As they worked, they talked about their lives, and Samuel found himself opening up to her in ways he hadn't done with anyone before. He told her about his job and his loneliness, and she listened intently. When they were finished, the woman thanked him for his help and gave him a hug. Samuel felt a warmth inside of him that he hadn't felt in a long time. As he drove home, he thought about what had just happened. Maybe taking out the trash wasn't such a bad thing after all.

The academic paper titled "FUTURE-AI: Guiding Principles and Consensus Recommendations for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence in Future Medical Imaging" presents a set of guiding principles and consensus recommendations for the development and implementation of trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) in medical imaging. The paper emphasizes the importance of AI in improving the accuracy and efficiency of medical diagnosis and treatment, while also acknowledging the potential risks and challenges associated with the use of AI in healthcare. The paper proposes a set of guiding principles and recommendations that aim to ensure the responsible and ethical development and use of AI in medical imaging, including transparency, accountability, and patient-centeredness. Overall, the paper provides valuable insights and guidance for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers involved in the development and implementation of AI in medical imaging.

Retrieving videos of a particular person with face image as query via hashing technique has many important applications. While face images are typically represented as vectors in Euclidean space, characterizing face videos with some robust set modeling techniques (e.g. covariance matrices as exploited in this study, which reside on Riemannian manifold), has recently shown appealing advantages. This hence results in a thorny heterogeneous spaces matching problem. Moreover, hashing with handcrafted features as done in many existing works is clearly inadequate to achieve desirable performance for this task. To address such problems, we present an end-to-end Deep Heterogeneous Hashing (DHH) method that integrates three stages including image feature learning, video modeling, and heterogeneous hashing in a single framework, to learn unified binary codes for both face images and videos. To tackle the key challenge of hashing on manifold, a well-studied Riemannian kernel mapping is employed to project data (i.e. covariance matrices) into Euclidean space and thus enables to embed the two heterogeneous representations into a common Hamming space, where both intra-space discriminability and inter-space compatibility are considered. To perform network optimization, the gradient of the kernel mapping is innovatively derived via structured matrix backpropagation in a theoretically principled way. Experiments on three challenging datasets show that our method achieves quite competitive performance compared with existing hashing methods.

In this work, we address the challenging task of few-shot segmentation. Previous few-shot segmentation methods mainly employ the information of support images as guidance for query image segmentation. Although some works propose to build cross-reference between support and query images, their extraction of query information still depends on the support images. We here propose to extract the information from the query itself independently to benefit the few-shot segmentation task. To this end, we first propose a prior extractor to learn the query information from the unlabelled images with our proposed global-local contrastive learning. Then, we extract a set of predetermined priors via this prior extractor. With the obtained priors, we generate the prior region maps for query images, which locate the objects, as guidance to perform cross interaction with support features. In such a way, the extraction of query information is detached from the support branch, overcoming the limitation by support, and could obtain more informative query clues to achieve better interaction. Without bells and whistles, the proposed approach achieves new state-of-the-art performance for the few-shot segmentation task on PASCAL-5$^{i}$ and COCO datasets.

We present a novel method to automatically segment scenes composed of millions of pixels from large data sets by extracting coarse and fine gradients from their noise images. The method achieves good results on both visual objects, where features are robust against noisy data, and semantic or object representation problems involving small groups (e.g., a facial expression). We applied it successfully to a data set of 4 million high resolution face images, producing a global and local score representation that was indistinguishable from that produced by conventional segmentation approaches. The proposed system exhibits high temporal fidelity and thus can replace human segmentation techniques in many types of situations. (via @joshuarei)

> Our goal here is to unveil the nature of lenticular galaxy population by studying their central age/metallicity trends in whole field (r > 8kpc) as well as in different radial ranges, through analysis of multiwavelength photometry. We use SDSS r'griz photometry of an homogeneous sample of 47 early type galaxies with Hubble types between T=2 and -5 to quantify abundance gradients at fixed radii (from inner kpc up to ~100''), as a function of size (Vmag) and morphology (T). Our main results are that i) older stars show a flatter metallic gradient than younger stars within any given radius; ii) at any chosen galactic radius most systems exhibit either no apparent variation or even evidence for positive abundance gradients in metal poor regions; and iii) the mean age does not change along the disk of galaxies but increases gradually toward its center on average, while metallicity remains constant over almost all ranges. Most notably we find clear evidence that more massive galaxies have flat abundance distributions over most ranges despite increasing importance of gas fraction for larger galaxies. Moreover many galaxies, especially dwarf ones, appear to contain old metal-poor stellar populations similar to what was found so far only in halo stars. These two findings suggest that formation may begin at much later times (z<4) for less massive lenticulars, producing relatively thin and top-heavy disks which get truncated before they can grow significantly thicker and more bottom heavy like those produced when formation happens much earlier (like z~3). Another implication of these observations is that there must be significant contributions from starvation via tidal interactions with ICM. Finally uniformity of the results across our sample suggests common evolutionary path among intermediate mass early-type galaxies.

While improving prediction accuracy has been the focus Of machine learning in recent years, This alone does not suffice for reliable decision-making. Deploying learning systems in consequential settings also requires calibrating and communicating the uncertainty of predictions. To convey instance-wise uncertainty for prediction tasks, we show how to generate set-valued predictions from a black-box predictor that Control the Expected loss on future test points at a user-specified level. Our approach provides explicit finite-sample guarantees for any dataset by using a Holdout set to Calibrate the size of the prediction sets. This framework enables simple, distribution-free, rigorous error control for many tasks, and We demonstrate it in five large-scale machine learning problems: (1) classification problems where some mistakes are more costly than others; (2) multi-label classification, where each observation has multiple associated labels; (3) classification problems where the labels have a hierarchical structure; (4) image segmentation, where We wish to predict a set of pixels containing an object of interest; and (5) protein structure prediction. Lastly, we discuss extensions to uncertainty quantification for ranking, metric learning and distributionally robust learning.

3D Convolution Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely applied to 3D scene understanding, such as video analysis and volumetric image recognition. However, 3D networks can easily lead to over-parameterization which incurs expensive computation cost. In this paper, we propose Channel-wise Automatic KErnel Shrinking (CAKES), to enable efficient 3D learning by shrinking standard 3D convolutions into a set of economic operations e.g., 1D, 2D convolutions. Unlike previous methods, CAKES performs channel-wise kernel shrinkage, which enjoys following benefits: 1) enabling operations deployed in every layer to be heterogeneous, so that they can extract diverse and complementary information to benefit learning process; and 2) allowing for efficient and flexible replacement design, which can be generalized to both spatial-temporal and volumetric data. Further, we propose a new search space based on CAKES, so that the replacement configuration can be determined automatically for simplifying 3D networks. CAKES shows superior performance to other methods with similar model size, and it also achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art with much fewer parameters and computational costs on tasks including 3D medical imaging segmentation and video action recognition.
