This paper provides an unsupervised domain adaptation network for computational image segmentation, which uses a category-centric prototype aligner to address the challenge of domain transition between source and target domains. The proposed network consists of a feature extractor and a model aligner, which is trained in an end-to-end way without needing any labeled data from the target domain. The model aligner is created to learn a category-centric representation of the target domain, which is aligned with the source domain prototypes. Experimental findings on three biomedical image segmentation datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in reducing the segmentation efficiency in the target domain, especially when there is a large domain change between the source and target domains.

Referring expression comprehension (REC) aims to interpret referring expressions about objects and actions in images. However, there has been little exploration on REC under diverse interaction modalities; how people interact with machines varies greatly based on their goals, contexts, environments/conditions they are faced with and available resources at hand. In this work, we introduce Comprehensive REC (CoRE), image segmentation benchmark comprising 20 subsets that capture multi-modal user interactions via webcam or microphone, text input only, or various combinations among these. To ensure a comprehensive measure across human-machine referral interaction paradigm, our CoRE incorporates all existing large-scale datasets into a unified framework including TACoS-Interactive, RefCOCO+WebCam & Flickr30k Entities. It is expected to facilitate better understanding by bridging gaps within current research, as well as motivate more fine-grained studies when analyzing REC performance based on different conditions, tasks, and dataset sizes. Moreover, leveraging the wide variety of interactive styles offered in CoRE , we provide baselines built upon Transformer models and show potential generalization ability towards diverse settings. We hope this will encourage further studies on modeling real world scenarios or developing systems capable of such flexibility in human computer interactions (HCIs).

The recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) combined with the extensive amount of data generated by today's clinical systems, has led to the development of imaging AI solutions across the whole value chain of medical imaging, including image reconstruction, medical image segmentation, image-based diagnosis and treatment planning. Notwithstanding the successes and future potential of AI in medical imaging, many stakeholders are concerned of the potential risks and ethical implications of imaging AI solutions, which are perceived as complex, opaque, and difficult to comprehend, utilise, and trust in critical clinical applications. Despite these concerns and risks, there are currently no concrete guidelines and best practices for guiding future AI developments in medical imaging towards increased trust, safety and adoption. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a careful selection of guiding principles drawn from the accumulated experiences, consensus, and best practices from five large European projects on AI in Health Imaging. These guiding principles are named FUTURE-AI and its building blocks consist of (i) Fairness, (ii) Universality, (iii) Traceability, (iv) Usability, (v) Robustness and (vi) Explainability. In a step-by-step approach, these guidelines are further translated into a framework of concrete recommendations for specifying, developing, evaluating, and deploying technically, clinically and ethically trustworthy AI solutions into clinical practice.

Using neural architecture search (NAS) has become a popular method to automate the design of deep learning networks. However, many of the NAS methods available today still use inefficient methods, such as random samples or nave evolution, which often results in slow convergence and low performance. In this paper, we propose a new method, called 'poisoning', which biases the neural architecture search process towards sub-optimal solutions, with the aim of increasing the exploration speed while maintaining a good generalization ability. By injecting targeted errors into the initialization of the weight and the landscape during the training, our approach is not only able to obtain competitive architectures, but also reduces the complexity of the usual NAS optimization methods used by the machine learning community. Our experimental results show significant improvements in accuracy (a 27% increase) and the reduction in the wall clock time needed to achieve the above excellent results, which are achieved through carefully designed modifications tailored to the problems in the field of neural network architecture search. Our overall conclusion highlights the significance of these advances in future, by paving the way for future developments in the automation of the generating pipeline., which may lead to better performing AI systems and, resulting in an improvement in humanity's ability to learn.

In this study, we proposed a high-resolution segmentation method to extract tooth root edge in radiographic images. Our approach combined polynomial curve fitting and landmark detection techniques. Firstly, we located 10 significant landmarks of each root using image processing techniques including template matching, edge detection and contour analysis. Then the remaining root edges were extracted by applying polynomial curve fitting algorithm, obtaining smooth and continuous functions that represented root edges' distribution patterns. Finally, the fuzzy connectivity among these curves was adjusted through membership function calculation and distance between roots' surfaces computation methods. The performance evaluation showed our proposed method outperformed other state of the art algorithms based on quantitative assessment metrics indicating accuracy and computational complexity. This work could provide valuable information in developing efficient automation tools for dental professionals to improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce patient exposure time from complex radiographs.

VoteNet is a deep learning label fusion method aimed at enhancing segmentation accuracy in multi-atlas networks. The system employs a variety of convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures to generate individual predictions on each input image, then applies a fusion algorithm that combines these results into a final output. Using this approach, VoteNet can effectively harness the strengths of different CNNs and overcome their limitations. The authors propose three label fusion methods: 1D-Majority, which aggregates the outputs of all individual models; Kullback–Leibler (KL)-divergence, which measures the similarity between model outputs and estimates model uncertainty; and Attention-based, which assigns weights to inputs based on their contribution to the overall result. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets, they demonstrate the effectiveness of VoteNet and compare it with other state-of-the-art approaches. Overall, VoteNet represents an important advance in the field of medical imaging analysis, offering an effective solution to improve multi-atlas segmentation performance by leveraging multiple labels.

The Solar North Polar Coronal Hole (SNPCH) is a region of the Sun's corona that is characterized by a lack of magnetic activity and a high-speed plasma flow. In this paper, we present a new model for the heating of the SNPCH. Our model is based on the idea that the lack of magnetic activity in the SNPCH leads to a higher degree of plasma turbulence, which in turn generates heat through the dissipation of kinetic energy. We use numerical simulations to test our model and find that it is able to accurately reproduce the observed temperature and plasma density profiles in the SNPCH. Our results provide new insights into the heating mechanisms of the SNPCH and have important implications for our understanding of the Sun's corona as a whole.

The task of semantic image segmentation aims to determine object labels with sharp boundaries, but suffers from the usual problems of overfitting. Recent data augmentation strategies such as local dropout and local mix have been proposed to alleviate this problem. These strategies have proved to be effective in guiding the model to less discriminative features. But because these strategies operate at the image level, affecting both the objects and the background, these strategies are ineffective in enhancing object boundaries in the fixed semantic context. We propose ObjectAug, a novel strategy to augment the object-level features for semantic image segmentation. The method first decomposes the image into its constituent objects and background, using the image’s own semantic labels. Each object is then independently augmented with standard augmentation methods such as scaling, translation and rotation, and then the area in black, where the augmentation has taken place, is filled in with an inpainting method. Objects and backgrounds are then merged to create an augmented image, in which the objects’ boundaries are enhanced in all semantic contexts. In addition, ObjectAug supports augmentation with object category information, which provides each object with a range of possibilities. It is easy to combine with other existing augmentation methods to further improve performance. A comprehensive evaluation on natural image and medical image data shows that ObjectAug clearly improves the performance of semantic segmentation.

High-resolution segmenting of tooth crown fissures using nonparametric multivariate regularization for feature-free, polygonal, parametrical reconstruction. We propose new method based on hierarchical linear algebra (HLA) that can be efficiently used to segment entire tooth root. Instead of attempting to use a very high amount of parameters or gradient computation in order obtain optimal results, we directly incorporate best features of individual teeth into our model in parameter-dependent manner and leverage their overlap to achieve a good result. The resulting curve fit to each landmark provides a continuous indication on where to focus further investigation in terms of determining the most likely path to take (i.e. tooth edge). For this paper, we present experiments using state-of-the-art DRSM hardware with a sampling rate of 100 times per second, as well as several thousand data points collected over period of weeks by multiple users over 8 consecutive days to evaluate effectiveness of our method. Our procedure was confirmed after performing hundreds of thousands of steps per hour using real human and simulated teeth. While results were inconsistent (due to the variance inherent in sampling), they were statistically significant at p<0.001 when considering 10 000 steps/hour. With additional refinement using several more datasets, we found similar positive correlations: correlation coefficient = 0.891, Pearson r2 = 0.844, η p 2 = 0.88

This study aims to develop a robust and general medical image segmentation method, a thorough review of existing methods has been done, and a novel hybrid approach combining deep learning and machine learning has been proposed, and the effectiveness of this method has been verified by extensive experiments on multiple images with different anatomical structures and different modalities. The results show that the proposed method is superior to the existing methods in terms of accuracy, and is a promising tool for the research of medical image data.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for referring image segmentation that incorporates comprehensive multi-modal interactions between the user and the system. Our approach allows users to interact with the system through various modalities, including speech, gesture, and touch, to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation process. We propose a deep learning-based framework that integrates multiple modalities and leverages their complementary information to improve the segmentation performance. The framework consists of several components, including a speech recognition module, a gesture recognition module, a touch-based interaction module, and a segmentation module. These components work together to enable the user to provide rich and diverse inputs that can effectively convey their desired segmentation goals. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional single-modal interaction methods. Our experiments show that the proposed approach can significantly improve the segmentation accuracy and reduce the interaction time, making it more efficient and user-friendly. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: * We propose a comprehensive multi-modal interaction framework for referring image segmentation that integrates speech, gesture, and touch modalities. * We develop a deep learning-based model that fuses the complementary information from multiple modalities to improve the segmentation performance. * We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional single-modal methods. Our work has important implications for various applications, such as medical imaging, robotics, and human-computer interaction. The proposed approach can help improve the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation tasks, making it more accessible and user-friendly for a wide range of users.

This study proposes an ensemble learning approach that combines classifier prediction confidence with comprehensive learning particle swarm optimization (CLPSO) to improve the accuracy of polyp localization in colonoscopy images. The method utilizes a variety of traditional machine learning algorithms, such as decision trees, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors, and naive Bayes, which are trained using different feature sets extracted from the input data. The output predictions of these classifiers are then combined by weighting them according to their individual predictive performance scores derived from cross validation experiments. Additionally, CLPSO is employed to optimize the weight allocation process further enhancing the overall system's robustness against overfitting issues while improving its generalization capacity. Experimental results show significant improvements compared to standalone approaches demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed technique. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into designing efficient computer aided diagnostic systems capable of detecting polyps during endoscopies enabling improved patient outcomes through timely diagnosis and therapy interventions.

Our aim is to automatically segment images into semantically meaningful regions without the help of human supervision. Our method automatically creates semantic classes that are consistent across different images, and overlaps with human-defined semantic classes on some of the datasets. However, even in the situations where it is difficult for human beings to clearly define and consistently classify semantic regions, our method is able to create meaningful and consistent semantic classes. In this paper, we used the generative network, styleGAN2, which is pre-trained on the NIST image dataset. By clustering in the feature space of the generative network, we automatically found semantic classes. Once we have identified semantic classes, we can generate synthetic images with corresponding segmentation masks, and then train a semantic segmentation model on the synthetic images. Also, we can learn to discover some of the semantic classes with CLIP-based learning. We then tested our method on several publicly available datasets, and achieved state-of-the-art results.

High-resolution segmentation of crown fissures by multivariate regularization for featureless, polygonal, reconstructed image. We propose a new method based on hierarchical linear algebra (HLA) which is able to efficiently segment a tooth. Instead of calculating the optimum for all cases or using an extremely large number of parameters, we directly integrate the best features of the teeth into our model, depending on the values of the parameters, and exploit their superimposition to achieve a good result. The curve fitted to each landmark gives us an indication of where to investigate in order to find the most probable line (i.e. the edge of the tooth). We report on our experiments on the state-of-the-art hardware of the DRSM system, which is able to sample at a rate of 100 times/s, using several thousand points collected by different operators during a week. We subsequently performed up to one hundred thousand measurements/h using real human and simulated teeth, and although our results were somewhat inconsistent because of the variations in the data set, they were nevertheless significant at p 0.0001 for the data sampled at 10,000 points/h. With the additional data of several other specimens, we obtained a similar correlation: r2 = 0.891, p2 = 0.88, p 0.01, for an average distance of 0.35 between the landmarks.

Fully convolutional deep neural networks have been asserted to be fast and precise frameworks with grate potential in image segmentation. One of the major challenges in training such networks raises when data is unbalanced, which is common in many medical imaging applications such as lesion segmentation where lesion class voxels are often much lower in numbers than non-lesion voxels. A trained network with unbalanced data may make predictions with high precision and low recall, being severely biased towards the non-lesion class which is particularly undesired in most medical applications where FNs are more important than FPs. Various methods have been proposed to adress this problem, more recently similarity loss functions and focal loss. In this work we trained fully convolutional deep neural networks using an asymmetric similarity loss function to mitigate the issue of data imbalance and acheive much better tradeoff between precision and recall. To this end, we developed a 3D FC-DenseNet with large overlapping image patches as input and an asymmetric similarity loss layer based on Tversky index (using Fbeta scores). We used large overlapping image patches as inputs for intrinsic and extrinsic data augmentation, a patch selection algorithm, and a patch prediction fusion strategy using B-spline weighted soft voting to account for the uncertainty of prediction in patch borders. We applied this method to MS lesion segmentation based on two different datasets of MSSEG and ISBI longitudinal MS lesion segmentation challenge, where we achieved top performance in both challenges. Our network trained with focal loss ranked first according to the ISBI challenge overall score and resulted in the lowest reported lesion false positive rate among all submitted methods. Our network trained with the asymmetric similarity loss led to the lowest surface distance and the best lesion true positive rate.

While improving prediction accuracy has been the focus of machine learning in recent years, this alone does not suffice for reliable decision-making. Deploying learning systems in consequential settings also requires calibrating and communicating the uncertainty of predictions. To convey instance-wise uncertainty for prediction tasks, we show how to generate set-valued predictions from a black-box predictor that control the expected loss on future test points at a user-specified level. Our approach provides explicit finite-sample guarantees for any dataset by using a holdout set to calibrate the size of the prediction sets. This framework enables simple, distribution-free, rigorous error control for many tasks, and we demonstrate it in five large-scale machine learning problems: (1) classification problems where some mistakes are more costly than others; (2) multi-label classification, where each observation has multiple associated labels; (3) classification problems where the labels have a hierarchical structure; (4) image segmentation, where we wish to predict a set of pixels containing an object of interest; and (5) protein structure prediction. Lastly, we discuss extensions to uncertainty quantification for ranking, metric learning and distributionally robust learning.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to few-shot segmentation, which leverages both global and local contrastive learning To achieve state-of-the-art Performance. Our proposed method, called FSGL (Few-Shot segmentation with Global and Local Contrastive Learning), combines the strengths of global contrastive learning and local contrastive learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of few-shot segmentation. Global contrastive learning is used to learn high-level features that are robust across Different datasets and tasks, while local contrastive learning is employed to learn task-specific features that are important for segmenting specific objects or regions in an image. By combining these two types of contrastive learning, our model can Learn both generalizable and Task-specific knowledge, leading to improved performance on few-shot segmentation tasks. FSGL consists of two Main components: a global feature Extractor and a local feature refiner. The global feature extractor uses a self-supervised loss function to learn high-level features from a large dataset, while the local feature refiner uses a supervised loss function to fine-tune the learned features for a specific segmentation task. We also propose a novel technique called multi-scale dense connections To integrate the global and local features effectively. Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets show that FSGL outperforms existing state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods by a significant margin. Notably, FSGL achieves an average IoU score of 86.5% on PASCAL vOC, which Is 10.2% higher than the previous state-of-the-art method. Moreover, FSGL requires only 320k parameters, making it much more efficient compared to other state-of-the-art models. Our Work demonstrates the effectiveness Of incorporating both global and local contrastive learning into few-shot segmentation models. The proposed FSGL model has important implications for real-world applications where accurate segmentation is required, such as autonomous driving, robotics, And medical imaging.

Many recent medical segmentation systems rely on powerful deep learning models to solve highly specific tasks. To maximize performance, it is standard practice to evaluate numerous pipelines with varying model topologies, optimization parameters, pre- & postprocessing steps, and even model cascades. It is often not clear how the resulting pipeline transfers to different tasks. We propose a simple and thoroughly evaluated deep learning framework for segmentation of arbitrary medical image volumes. The system requires no task-specific information, no human interaction and is based on a fixed model topology and a fixed hyperparameter set, eliminating the process of model selection and its inherent tendency to cause method-level over-fitting. The system is available in open source and does not require deep learning expertise to use. Without task-specific modifications, the system performed better than or similar to highly specialized deep learning methods across 6 separate segmentation tasks. In addition, it ranked 6-th and 6-th in the first and second round of the 2018 Medical Segmentation Decathlon comprising another 10 tasks. The system relies on multi-planar data augmentation which facilitates the application of a single 2D architecture based on the familiar U-Net. Multi-planar training combines the parameter efficiency of a 2D fully convolutional neural network with a systematic train- and test-time augmentation scheme, which allows the 2D model to learn a representation of the 9D image volume that fosters generalization.

In this study, we propose a novel few-shot segmentation approach that leverages both global and local contrastive learning. Our method is based on the idea of encoding image features in an efficient manner to enable rapid adaptation to new tasks without requiring extensive training data. We demonstrate through experiments conducted on various datasets that our model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods while achieving faster convergence rates thanks to its ability to capture high-level semantic information as well as detailed contextual cues using contrasting examples at multiple scales. Overall, these results suggest that combining different types of contrasts can lead to significant improvements in few-shot performance for segmentation problems.

The field of biomedical image segmentation has seen significant advancements in recent years, with deep learning techniques such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) being widely adopted. However, these methods often struggle with handling complex and diverse image structures, leading to inaccurate segmentation results. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to biomedical image segmentation using a multi-compound transformer architecture. Our model is designed to handle complex image structures by leveraging the power of transformer-based attention mechanisms, which allow for more efficient and accurate information processing. We evaluate our model on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CNN-based methods. Our results highlight the potential of transformer-based architectures for biomedical image segmentation and pave the way for further research in this area.

> Differential privacy is a notion of privacy that has been widely studied in the past decade. It is a notion that is based on the idea that the output of a query on a database should not change much if a single record is added or removed from the database. This notion has been studied in the context of both statistical databases and machine learning. > > In this paper, we propose a Bayesian formulation of differential privacy. We show that differential privacy can be viewed as a form of Bayesian inference, where the prior is the distribution of the database and the likelihood is the distribution of the query output. We show that this formulation provides a natural way to think about differential privacy, and that it can be used to derive new results about differential privacy. > > We also show that our formulation can be used to derive a new definition of differential privacy, which we call Bayesian differential privacy. This definition is based on the idea that the output of a query should be independent of the database, given the query output. We show that this definition is equivalent to the standard definition of differential privacy, and that it can be used to derive new results about differential privacy. > > Finally, we show that our formulation can be used to derive a new definition of differential privacy, which we call Bayesian differential privacy. This definition is based on the idea that the output of a query should be independent of the database, given the query output. We show that this definition is equivalent to the standard definition of differential privacy, and that it can be used to derive new results about differential privacy. The paper is available here.

Despite deep convolutional neural networks achieved impressive progress in medical image computing and analysis, its paradigm of supervised learning demands a large number of annotations for training to avoid overfitting and achieving promising results. In clinical practices, massive semantic annotations are difficult to acquire in some conditions where specialized biomedical expert knowledge is required, and it is also a common condition where only few annotated classes are available. In this work, we proposed a novel method for few-shot medical image segmentation, which enables a segmentation model to fast generalize to an unseen class with few training images. We construct our few-shot image segmentor using a deep convolutional network trained episodically. Motivated by the spatial consistency and regularity in medical images, we developed an efficient global correlation module to capture the correlation between a support and query image and incorporate it into the deep network called global correlation network. Moreover, we enhance discriminability of deep embedding to encourage clustering of the feature domains of the same class while keep the feature domains of different organs far apart. Ablation Study proved the effectiveness of the proposed global correlation module and discriminative embedding loss. Extensive experiments on anatomical abdomen images on both CT and MRI modalities are performed to demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our proposed model.

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the first cause of death in many countries. CRC originates from a small clump of cells on the lining of the colon called polyps, which over time might grow and become malignant. Early detection and removal of polyps are therefore necessary for the prevention of colon cancer. In this paper, we introduce an ensemble of medical polyp segmentation algorithms. Based on an observation that different segmentation algorithms will perform well on different subsets of examples because of the nature and size of training sets they have been exposed to and because of method-intrinsic factors, we propose to measure the confidence in the prediction of each algorithm and then use an associate threshold to determine whether the confidence is acceptable or not. An algorithm is selected for the ensemble if the confidence is below its associate threshold. The optimal threshold for each segmentation algorithm is found by using Comprehensive Learning Particle Swarm Optimization (CLPSO), a swarm intelligence algorithm. The Dice coefficient, a popular performance metric for image segmentation, is used as the fitness criteria. Experimental results on two polyp segmentation datasets MICCAI2015 and Kvasir-SEG confirm that our ensemble achieves better results compared to some well-known segmentation algorithms.

This paper provides a fully convolutional multi-scale residual DenseNet design for cardiac segmentation and automated cardiac diagnosis utilizing an ensemble of classifiers. The proposed approach uses a multi-scale approach to extract features at various levels of abstraction, and residual connections to solve the vanishing gradient problem. DenseNet blocks are used to reduce feature reuse and reduce the model's capability to tell from limited data. The ensemble of classifiers is designed to combine the predictions of different models for improved reliability and reliability. Experimental findings on a publicly accessible cardiac MRI database show the efficacy of the proposed technique, improving state-of-the-art performance in cardiac segmentation and automated treatment.

The system we have designed is an integration of recent progress in neural networks and probabilistic graphical models, and is intended for general use on medical images of different modalities. It is based on a hybrid framework which combines the advantages of a fully convolutional network (FCN) with the power of a probabilistic graphical model. We use the FCN to extract features of a particular modality from a given input image, and feed these features into a PGM, which models the spatial relationships between the resulting labelled regions and enforces consistency in the labelling of neighboring regions. This PGM is trained using different datasets, including different modalities and pathologies, to learn a robust model of the underlying anatomy. To improve the model’s ability to deal with variations in image quality and artefacts, we introduce uncertainty estimates into the segmentation process. With this method, we use dropout regularization to introduce random errors during training, and combine them with the uncertainty from the PGM, allowing us to obtain high-quality segmentations from noisy or low-resolution input images. We evaluated our method using a number of well-known datasets of medical images, including CT, MRI and ultrasound. Our results show that our method is able to outperform existing methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness. We also conducted a series of ablation experiments to understand the individual components of the method, and provide insight into how it works. The main contribution of our method is its ability to effectively combine anatomical knowledge with uncertainty estimates, to obtain robust segmentations from medical images. Our method has important implications for clinical applications where reliable and accurate segmentations are required, such as tumour detection, organ isolation, and treatment planning.

Deep learning has not been routinely employed for semantic segmentation of seabed environment for synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) imagery due to the implicit need of abundant training data such methods necessitate. Abundant training data, specifically pixel-level labels for all images, is usually not available for SAS imagery due to the complex logistics (e.g., diver survey, chase boat, precision position information) needed for obtaining accurate ground-truth. Many hand-crafted feature based algorithms have been proposed to segment SAS in an unsupervised fashion. However, there is still room for improvement as the feature extraction step of these methods is fixed. In this work, we present a new iterative unsupervised algorithm for learning deep features for SAS image segmentation. Our proposed algorithm alternates between clustering superpixels and updating the parameters of a convolutional neural network (CNN) so that the feature extraction for image segmentation can be optimized. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on a realistic benchmark dataset. Our results show that the performance of our proposed method is considerably better than current state-of-the-art methods in SAS image segmentation.

We adapt our light Dialectica interpretation to usual and light modal formulas (with universal quantification on boolean and natural variables) and prove it sound for a non-standard modal arithmetic based on Goedel's T and classical S4. The range of this light modal Dialectica is the usual (non-modal) classical Arithmetic in all finite types (with booleans); the propositional kernel of its domain is Boolean and not S4. In this paper, we investigate the phenomenon of spin-flip reflection of electrons from a potential barrier in heterostructures. Heterostructures are materials composed of alternating layers of different materials, and they have attracted significant interest in recent years due to their potential for applications in a wide range of fields, including electronics, optoelectronics, and spintronics. One of the key properties of heterostructures is the ability to manipulate the spin of electrons, which is a fundamental property of particles that determines their intrinsic angular momentum. Spin-flip reflection, where an electron's spin is flipped upon reflection from a potential barrier, is a phenomenon that has been observed in heterostructures and has important implications for the design and operation of spintronic devices. In this paper, we present a theoretical study of spin-flip reflection in heterostructures using a combination of analytical and numerical methods. We develop a model that takes into account the spin-dependent transport properties of the heterostructure and the potential barrier, and we investigate the effects of various parameters, such as the barrier height, width, and spin-orbit coupling, on the spin-flip reflection probability. Our results show that spin-flip reflection is a strong function of the barrier height and width, and that it can be significantly enhanced by increasing the spin-orbit coupling in the heterostructure. We also find that the spin-flip reflection probability can be controlled by applying an external magnetic field, which offers a way to manipulate the spin properties of electrons in heterostructures. Our findings have important implications for the design and operation of spintronic devices, such as spin-based transistors and logic gates, which rely on the manipulation of electron spin to perform logical operations. By understanding and controlling spin-flip reflection in heterostructures, we can improve the performance and efficiency of these devices, and pave the way for the development of new spintronic technologies.

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the first cause of death in many countries. CRC originates from a small clump of cells on the lining of the colon called polyps, which over time might grow and become malignant. Early detection and removal of polyps are therefore necessary for the prevention of colon cancer. In this paper, we introduce an ensemble of medical polyp segmentation algorithms. Based on an observation that different segmentation algorithms will perform well on different subsets of examples because of the nature and size of training sets they have been exposed to and because of method-intrinsic factors, we propose to measure the confidence in the prediction of each algorithm and then use an associate threshold to determine whether the confidence is acceptable or not. An algorithm is selected for the ensemble if the confidence is below its associate threshold. The optimal threshold for each segmentation algorithm is found by using Comprehensive Learning Particle Swarm Optimization (CLPSO), a swarm intelligence algorithm. The Dice coefficient, a popular performance metric for image segmentation, is used as the fitness criteria. Experimental results on two polyp segmentation datasets MICCAI2015 and Kvasir-SEG confirm that our ensemble achieves better results compared to some well-known segmentation algorithms.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to referring image segmentation that leverages comprehensive multi-modal interactions between humans and machines. Our proposed method enables users to interact with image using natural language commands, gestures, and visual attention, allowing them to accurately refer to specific regions of interest within the image. We propose a unified framework that combines these multiple modalities into single coherent representation, enabling effective communication and collaboration between humans and machines. This is achieved through a combination of deep learning techniques, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and multi-modal fusion algorithms. The key contribution of our work lies in its ability to effectively integrate and reconcile strengths of different modalities to improve image segmentation accuracy. We demonstrate efficacy of our approach on several challenging benchmark datasets, where it outperforms existing methods that rely solely on language or vision inputs. Through extensive user studies, we also investigate the impact of modality switching strategies and identify optimal combinations of modalities that maximize performance. Our findings have important implications for applications such as object recognition, medical imaging analysis, and human-robot interaction, where effective multi-modal communication can significantly enhance task efficiency and accuracy.

S-folds are generalizations of orientifolds in type IIB string theory, such that the geometric identifications are accompanied by non-trivial S-duality transformations. They were recently used by Garcia-Etxebarria and Regalado to provide the first construction of four dimensional N=3 superconformal theories. In this note, we classify the different variants of these N=3 preserving S-folds, distinguished by an analog of discrete torsion, using both a direct analysis of the different torsion classes and the compactification of the S-folds to three dimensional M-theory backgrounds. Upon adding D9-branes, these variants lead to different classes of N=3 superconformal field theories. We also analyze the holographic duals of these theories, and in particular clarify the role of discrete gauge and global symmetries in holography. In the main part of the paper, certain properties of cohomology groups associated to the S-folds were conjectured and used. This arXiv version includes an appendix written by Kiyonori Gomi in 4238 providing the proofs of the required properties using the technique of Borel equivariant cohomology, whose brief review is also provided.

A Comprehensive Benchmark of Object Segmentation in Large Scale Videos presents a large scale dataset of over two thousand youtube videos for object segmentation. The dataset includes a variety of scenes and objects, which makes it an ideal platform for testing the robustness of VOS approaches. We provide annotations and five well-known metrics to allow the objective assessment of the performance of their own methods. Our analysis shows the effectiveness of several state-of-the-art models on this challenging task and the directions for future research. Youtube-VoS is a useful resource for advancing computer vision techniques for visual understanding and recognition.

We describe a Fourier transform spectroscopy technique for directly measuring band structures, and apply it to a spin-1 spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensate. In our technique, we suddenly change the Hamiltonian of the system by adding a spin-orbit coupling interaction and measure populations in different spin states during the subsequent unitary evolution. We then reconstruct the spin and momentum resolved spectrum from the peak frequencies of the Fourier transformed populations. In addition, by periodically modulating the Hamiltonian, we tune the spin-orbit coupling strength and use our spectroscopy technique to probe the resulting dispersion relation. The frequency resolution of our method is limited only by the coherent evolution timescale of the Hamiltonian and can otherwise be applied to any system, for example, to measure the band structure of atoms in optical lattice potentials.

Semantically Meaningful Class Prototypes for One-Shot Image Semantic Segmentation In this paper we propose a novel method for one-shot image semantic segmentation that uses semantically meaningful class prototypes to improve the performance of the model. Our method is based on the idea that the prototypes should capture the semantic meaning of the classes rather than just their visual appearance. This is achieved by combining supervised and unsupervised learning techniques and integrating semantic information into the learning process. Our method is evaluated on several image datasets and it is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods both in terms of accuracy and speed.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for referring image segmentation that incorporates comprehensive multi-modal interactions between the user and the system. Our approach allows users to interact with the system through various modalities, including speech, gesture, and touch, to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation process. We propose a deep learning-based framework that integrates multiple modalities and leverages their complementary information to improve the segmentation performance. The framework consists of several components, including a speech recognition module, a gesture recognition module, a touch-based interaction module, and a segmentation module. These components work together to enable the user to provide rich and diverse inputs that can effectively convey their desired segmentation goals. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional single-modal interaction methods. Our experiments show that the proposed approach can significantly improve the segmentation accuracy and reduce the interaction time, making it more efficient and user-friendly. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: * We propose a comprehensive multi-modal interaction framework for referring image segmentation that integrates speech, gesture, and touch modalities. * We develop a deep learning-based model that fuses the complementary information from multiple modalities to improve the segmentation performance. * We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional single-modal methods. Our work has important implications for various applications, such as medical imaging, robotics, and human-computer interaction. The proposed approach can help improve the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation tasks, making it more accessible and user-friendly for a wide range of users.

EdgeFlow is a novel approach to achieving practical interactive segmentation with edge-guided flow. By utilizing edge-guided flow, EdgeFlow is able to achieve interactive segmentation with high accuracy and efficiency. This approach is particularly useful in applications where real-time performance is critical, such as in video analysis and image processing. EdgeFlow's use of edge-guided flow also allows for more robust segmentation results, as it is able to better handle complex scenes and objects with varying textures. Overall, EdgeFlow represents a significant advancement in the field of image processing and has the potential to revolutionize the way we approach interactive segmentation.

We consider the problem of constructing a prediction set for a random variable X from n previous observations of X. The set must be small, and have a high probability of containing the future value. We propose a new method of constructing such a prediction set, which is based on the notion of using a distribution-free confidence interval for the mean of X. We prove that the resulting prediction set has a small expected size, and high probability of containing the future value. The paper is available here.

This academic paper presents a novel approach to learning food portion sizes from monocular images using cross-domain feature adaptation. The proposed method aims to address the challenge of domain shift between training and testing data by adapting the features of the source domain to the target domain. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in accurately estimating food portion sizes from monocular images, even when the data distribution shifts between training and testing. This work contributes to the development of automated systems for food portion estimation and has potential applications in nutrition research and diet management.

High-quality training data are a prerequisite for any image segmentation task. Conventional pixel-level annotations are expensive, time-consuming, and tedious for large-scale data. To reduce the cost of labeling and improve segmentation accuracy, many interactive methods have been proposed that can be performed with a few mouse clicks. But their performance is not satisfactory for practical segmentation tasks in terms of speed and accuracy. In this work, we propose a novel architecture called EdgeFlow that combines edge-directed flow with the interactivity of mouse clicks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance without any post-processing or iterative learning. Extensive experiments on both public and private datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method. Based on the proposed method, we also developed an efficient interactive tool called PaddleSeg for practical data annotation. The source code and the tool are available at https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleSeg.

This paper proposes a new method to learn food portion estimation from monocular images by transforming the features from the source domain to the target domain by using the deep convolutional network. In the cross-domain feature transformation, the proposed method uses deep convolutional neural networks to extract features from the source and target domains, followed by a mutual information method to align the features of the two domains. In extensive experiments on various data sets, the proposed method shows a high estimation accuracy of the food portions from the monocular images. It is hoped that this paper can be a reference for the development of the automatic food portion analysis system, and help people to control their diets more accurately.

The phrase "Hiding behind (or'watching from behind the sofa" entered British pop culture, signifying in humour the stereotypical early-series behaviour of children who wanted to avoid seeing frightening parts of a television programme while remaining in the room to watch the remainder of it. The phrase retains this association with Doctor Who, to the point that in 1991 the Museum of the Moving Image in London named their exhibition celebrating the programme "Behind the Sofa." The electronic theme music too was perceived as eerie, novel, and frightening, at the time. A 2012 article placed this childhood juxtaposition of fear and thrill "at the center of many people's relationship with the show," and a 2011 online vote at Digital Spy deemed the series the "scariest TV show of all time."

This scientific journal provides an ensemble learning method based on classifier prediction confidence and comprehensive learning particle swarm optimization for polyp localization. The proposed approach uses different classifiers to reduce the reliability of polyp detection and localization. The prediction confidence of each algorithm is designed to weight the contributions of individual classifiers to the next decision. Comprehensive learning particle swarm optimization is employed to improve the parameters of the ensemble simulation. Experimental findings on a publicly accessible database demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed approach compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

[Abstract] At present, future medical imaging is increasingly being used to diagnose patients with cancer or other life-threatening problems without a physician's input (1⇓⇓–4). In fact, this level of patient monitoring has emerged as an urgent need and a cost effective alternative to a conventional surgical strategy of operationally treating disease when clinical findings warrant it (5, 6). However, current techniques are relatively costly compared to human surgeons who still perform a significant portion of total imaging-related revenue (7). Consequently, healthcare systems must now prioritize not just what images should be captured but how they ought to be collected and organized (8). To date, many experts have agreed that large volumes do require to be recorded (9) for certain types of health issues such as cardiac infarction detection in which information is revelant beyond simply allowing doctors to detect atrial fibrillation [6]. These guidelines also dictate use of standardized storage methods for storing medically useful clinical information on large-scale data centers (10), although others would like to see greater transparency about which institutions hold the most medical data, thereby enabling citizens to decide wether privacy is important when making healthcare decisions using mass data (11). Despite these differences, no concensus approach exists regarding the best way forward with respect to both capturing mass imaging images and maintaining appropriate access, quality and security while recording them on centralized data sources. This raises the question: Should we seek solutions which maximize efficiency while minimizing the amount stored or rely only on technologies for storing information? We propose the following guiding principles for designing trustworthy artificial inteligence in the field of medical imaging and apply them to several challenges currently facing contemporary diagnostic machine learning that include: identifying common diseases in high volume samples; detecting noncontroversial features in large quantities at low accuracy through pattern recognition or image classification based on prior knowledge, like heart rate, pupil size; locating and cataloguing images to obtain revelant contextual context that may contribute to treatment recommendations and identify potential anomalies; performing post-processing routines such as pre and/or post activation (activation steps) and noise correction, as well as creating customized visualization programs by automatically modifying predefined templates in order to better understand what is represented in these files; and providing continuous feedback as to how the algorithms are interpreting the medical data and helping healthcare physicians make decisions regarding management

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to few-shot segmentation, which is a challenging task in computer vision that involves segmenting objects from a small number of labeled examples. Our approach, called Few-Shot Segmentation with Global and Local Contrastive Learning (FSS-GCL), combines the strengths of global and local contrastive learning to improve segmentation accuracy. Global contrastive learning has been shown to be effective in learning high-level representations that are useful for few-shot learning. However, it may not capture local information that is crucial for segmentation tasks. Local contrastive learning, on the other hand, can capture local information but may not generalize well to new examples. In FSS-GCL, we propose a two-stage training strategy that first uses global contrastive learning to learn high-level representations and then uses local contrastive learning to refine the segmentation masks. We also introduce a novel mask-based contrastive loss function that encourages the model to produce accurate segmentation masks. Experiments on several benchmark datasets show that FSS-GCL outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods, including those that use global or local contrastive learning alone. We also perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the different components of our approach. Our main contributions are: * A novel few-shot segmentation approach called FSS-GCL that combines global and local contrastive learning * A two-stage training strategy that leverages the strengths of global and local contrastive learning * A mask-based contrastive loss function that encourages accurate segmentation masks * State-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets Overall, FSS-GCL demonstrates the effectiveness of combining global and local contrastive learning for few-shot segmentation, and provides a promising direction for future research in this area.

This study proposes a novel image quality assessment method named Gradient Magnitude Similarity Deviation (GMSD). GMSD is based on the gradient magnitude of an image and measures the deviation between two images by calculating the difference in their gradients. The proposed index was designed to be highly efficient, computationally simple yet perceptually robust. Extensive experiments were conducted using standard databases including LIVE, CSIQ, TID2008, and ICCV'11 with different distortion types such as blur, noise, JPEG compression etc., which demonstrate that our approach outperforms several other state-of-the art perceptual metrics both quantitatively and qualitatively while maintaining high efficiency making it suitable for practical applications. Overall this work provides insight into designing new IQA methods focusing more towards robustness rather than just computational complexity.

This article explores the concept of witness structures in knowledge representation and their relationship with immediate snapshot complexity. Witness structures allow for efficient querying of information by providing a compressed representation that can be quickly accessed without decoding unnecessary data. However, this compression also leads to increased susceptibility to errors due to the loss of redundancy and contextual connection within the compressed structure. Immediate snapshot complexity is introduced as a measure of how much compression can occur before the ability to reconstruct original information drops off significantly, highlighting the limitations of witness structures in representing more complex or interconnected entities. The article presents empirical evidence of these limits through an evaluation of varying levels of immediate snapshot complexity on different types of datasets, demonstrating that the performance of witness structures decreases rapidly beyond certain threshold levels. Overall, the findings suggest that while witness structures have practical applications in areas such as approximate nearest neighbor search, they may not be suitable for all types of database representations, particularly those requiring high fidelity and detailed connectivity between information points.

We introduce edge flow, a new class of directed graph structures capable of operating as interactive segmentation procedures on large distributed networks. We evaluate its performance by training two approaches to classify images in real time using two different ways of computing the error functions over image pixels (correlation and covariance). These methods jointly characterize an image's boundaries automatically, yielding reliable boundary detection in practical data sets, such as Facebook photos, videos, and Web pages. In addition, we demonstrate that these methods can produce accurate model invariants across images at low cost and are very sensitive to small inputs; thus they provide a fast path towards scalable algorithms for performing real-time segmentation operations over larger datasets. It's known as a technique called "cupping" where heated cups are placed on the skin. Cupping is done by lighting flammable liquid in a small glass cup. Once the flame goes out, the drop in temperature creates suction, making the cups stick to the body. Then, we have considered interacting model between $F(R,T)$ gravity and modified Chaplygin gas. In order to calculate cosmological solutions, we obtained Friedmann equations and also equation of state (EoS) parameter of dark energy. By employing interacting model we considered the total energy density and the total pressure of Universe as the combination of components of dark energy and Chaplygin gas. Subsequently, we reconstructed the model by an origin of a scalar field entitled quintessence model with a field potential. The field potential has been calculated in terms of free parameters of $F(R,T)$ gravity and modified Chaplygin gas. In what follows, we used a parametrization, and the cosmological parameters have been written in terms of redshift $z$. Next, we plotted cosmological parameters with respect to three variable of cosmic time, redshift $z$ and $e$-folding number $N=ln(a)$, and the figures showed us an accelerated expansion of Universe. Also, we have described the scenario in three status early time, late time and future time by $e$-folding number. Finally, the stability of scenario has been investigated by a useful function named sound speed, and the graph of sound speed versus $e$-folding number has been showed us that there is the stability in late time.

What is aging? Mechanistic answers to this question remain elusive despite decades of research. Here, we propose a mathematical model of cellular aging based on a model gene interaction network. Our network model is made of only non-aging components - the biological functions of gene interactions decrease with a constant mortality rate. Death of a cell occurs in the model when an essential gene loses all of its interactions to other genes, equivalent to the deletion of an essential gene. Gene interactions are stochastic based on a binomial distribution. We show that the defining characteristic of biological aging, the exponential increase of mortality rate over time, can arise from this gene network model during the early stage of aging. Hence, we demonstrate that cellular aging is an emergent property of this model network. Our model predicts that the rate of aging, defined by the Gompertz coefficient, is approximately proportional to the average number of active interactions per gene and that the stochastic heterogeneity of gene interactions is an important factor in the dynamics of the aging process. This theoretic framework offers a mechanistic foundation for the pleiotropic nature of aging and can provide insights on cellular aging.

This study aims to improve the quality of medical image segmentation by developing an efficient supervisory approach that can effectively handle label noise. We propose a two-stage distillation method, which employs both pixel-wise and feature-level knowledge dissemination from a well-trained teacher model to several student models trained on incomplete or corrupted annotations. Extensive experiments conducted using two popular datasets demonstrate significant performance gains achieved through our proposed technique compared to other state-of-the-art methods in dealing with challenging scenarios involving high levels of training data corruption due to inaccurate labeling. Overall, this work highlights the importance of carefully designed supervisions strategies when working with limited labeled samples prone to errors.

Direct white matter bundle segmentation is a crucial task in neuroimaging that involves identifying and separating white matter bundles from the surrounding tissue. This task is challenging due to the complex and overlapping structures of the brain. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to direct white matter bundle segmentation using stacked U-Nets. Our approach involves training a series of U-Nets with increasing depth and number of channels to improve the accuracy of the segmentation. We evaluate our approach on a publicly available dataset of human brain MRI scans and demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our approach has the potential to improve the accuracy of white matter bundle segmentation, which can have important applications in neuroscience and clinical medicine.

We study gradient descent, which takes as input some sequence of points and produces as output value corresponding to cumulative probability sum of the elements in that interval. This method performs well on large data sets but also has significant computational efficiencies given its sequential nature. We show how these efficient execution methods can be obtained with little extra memory by parallelizing the algorithm under a common scheduler and leveraging a cache-based approach. At low level, we show the advantages of this approach compared to running more than one stochastic process simultaneously. Compared to earlier model optimized only by locality, our simple version is faster even on highly concurrent machines by nearly a factor of two. Our optimization reduces overall time for gradient descent operations by substantial 10-40% depending on number of training iterations for small perturbations of a target variable at each step point. Overall, parallelism scales down to as much as 50X the total amount of instruction memory per machine via fast parallel programming techniques using OpenMP. This paper presents a computer vision pipeline for automated determination of cardiac structure and function and detection of disease by two-dimensional echocardiography. The pipeline consists of several stages, including image preprocessing, segmentation, feature extraction, and classification. The image preprocessing stage involves noise reduction, contrast enhancement, and registration. The segmentation stage uses a deep learning-based approach to segment the cardiac region from the background. The feature extraction stage extracts relevant features from the segmented images, including left ventricular volume, ejection fraction, and strain. Finally, the classification stage uses a support vector machine to classify the images as normal or abnormal based on the extracted features. The pipeline was trained on a large dataset of echocardiographic images and achieved high accuracy in determining cardiac structure and function and detecting disease. The pipeline has the potential to improve the efficiency and accuracy of echocardiographic diagnosis and monitoring.

This problem can be avoided by considering Imbalancing the distribution of positive signals in the activation functions of every layer during computation time to address over-exposure to negative signals. Experiments demonstrate the advantages of This technique resulting in stable Learning rates even if dealing with extremely unbalanced ratios of ground-true target Labels. In this research, we propose an effective few-shot segmentation approach that combines global and local contrastive learning to achieve outstanding performance. Our method utilizes self-supervision techniques by leveraging two types of contrasts: global contrast which aligns features from different parts in a single image patch, and local contrast which aligns feature maps across patches from nearby regions of different images. By integrating these contrasts simultaneously, our approach can learn robust semantic segmented representations with high discrimination against diverse backgrounds while remaining computationally efficient. We validate our model's efficacy on multiple datasets with limited training data, demonstrating state-of-the-art results and outpacing prior methods in terms of accuracy, tradeoff between speed and quality, and generalization ability across unseen or challenging classes and scenes.

We propose a new method based on hierarchical linear algebra (HLA) that can be efficiently used to segment an entire tooth root. Instead of attempting to use a very high amount of parameters or gradient computation in order obtain optimal results, we directly incorporate the best features of individual teeth into our model in a parameter-dependent manner and leverage their overlap to achieve a good result. The resulting curve fit to each landmark provides a continuous indication on where to focus further investigation in terms of determining the most likely path to take (i.e. tooth edge). In this paper we propose a new approach to high-resolution, boundary-based tooth-root edging using landmark-based polynomial curve fitting with polynomial smoothing. Our method utilizes the theory of algebraic curves to model and accurately seg-ment the complex boundaries of the tooth-root boundaries in medical images. The existing methods have shortcomings, such as low accuracy, sensitivity to noise, and difficulties in handling ambiguous or unclear boundaries. Our proposed method uses the strength of polynomial curve fitting to model the tooth-root boundary, and can thus detect its exact shape and structure even in the presence of noise or distortion. The proposed method is in three stages: first, the input image is enhanced and filtered to improve the contrast; then the landmark is used to set up control points on the tooth-root boundary, and third, the polynomial curve is used to edge the tooth-root boundary from the background. The evaluation is based on 40 digitized -rays of dental -rays, annotated by expert radiographers. We use three measurements: the mean absolute error, the intersection over union, and the Dice coefficient. Our result is that the Dice coefficient is 93.1%, and the IoU is 96.6%, eclipsing the majority of the existing methods. The proposed method has great potential to increase the accuracy of dental and dental health applications, such as computer-aided diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring of periodontal and orthodontic treatment.

This academic paper presents a robust video-based eye tracking method using recursive estimation of pupil characteristics. The proposed approach utilizes a camera to capture the eye image and extracts the pupil region using an adaptive thresholding technique. The pupil characteristics, such as size and position, are then recursively estimated to improve the accuracy of eye tracking. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated using various datasets and demonstrates superior accuracy and robustness compared to existing video-based eye tracking methods. Overall, this paper provides a promising solution for video-based eye tracking with practical applications in human-computer interaction, psychology, and healthcare.

In this study, we proposed a high-resolution segmentation method to extract tooth root edge in radiographic images. Our approach combined polynomial curve fitting and landmark detection techniques. Firstly, we located 10 significant landmarks of each root using image processing techniques including template matching, edge detection and contour analysis. Then the remaining root edges were extracted by applying polynomial curve fitting algorithm, obtaining smooth and continuous functions that represented root edges' distribution patterns. Finally, fuzzy connectivity among these curves was adjusted through membership function calculation and distance between roots' surfaces computation methods. The performance evaluation showed our proposed method outperformed other state of art algorithms based on quantitative assessment metrics indicating accuracy and computational complexity. This work could provide valuable information in developing efficient automation tools for dental professionals to improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce patient exposure time from complex radiographs.

> Quantum cryptography is field of research that aims to provide security guarantees for cryptographic protocols by exploiting the laws of quantum mechanics. The most prominent application of quantum cryptography is quantum key distribution (QKD), which allows two parties to establish a shared secret key over insecure quantum channel. In this paper, we present new approach to quantum cryptography that goes beyond QKD. We introduce a new primitive called quantum-proof cryptography (QPC), which is cryptographic primitive that is secure against quantum adversaries. We show that QPC can be used to construct a variety of cryptographic protocols that are secure against quantum adversaries, including digital signatures, public-key encryption, and zero-knowledge proofs. We also show that QPC can be used to construct new type of quantum cryptography protocol called quantum-proof key distribution (QPKD), which is a protocol that allows two parties to establish shared secret key over insecure quantum channel, even if one of parties is a quantum adversary. We show that QPKD is secure against quantum adversaries, and we present a protocol for QPKD that is based on the quantum-proof cryptography primitive. The paper is available here.

As a lifelong classical musician, I am absolutely in love with the repertoire of symphony orchestras, opera, and chamber music. I am always trying to think of ways to introduce the music to a wider audience and get more people to love listening to classical music. So here it is: I believe that the main reason people don't like listening to classical music as much as other genres is because classical music rarely includes a drum set. Definitions I use in this CMV: Classical music: not only music from the classical period. I'm using the blanket term to describe any music typically performed by orchestras, or chamber ensembles. What a non-musician would think of as "classical." Everything from Bach to Mahler to Bartok to Ives. Popular music: not just the narrow genre of "pop," but the broad term to include anything listened to by a more mainstream audience. Could include anything from oldies, to country, to EDM, to metal, and beyond. Now to explain my view: I really don't think there's that much difference between classical music and other genres. -Both genres use the same 12 notes. (The exception obviously being microtonal classical music, which even as a career classical musician, sometimes I have a really hard time appreciating. But 99.9 of classical music uses the same 12 notes as popular music.) -Both use the same basic palette of harmonies and tonalities (majorminor chords, added 7ths, 9ths, etc.). -Both have the same basic choices of meters. (44 time, mixed meter, etc.) -Both use many of the same instruments. 3D convolution Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely applied to 3D scene understanding, Such as video analysis and volumetric image recognition. However, 3D networks can easily lead to over-parameterization which incurs expensive computation cost. In this paper, we propose Channel-wise Automatic KErnel Shrinking (CAKES), to enable efficient 3D learning by shrinking standard 3D Convolutions into a set of economic operations e.g., 1D, 2D convolutions. Unlike previous methods, CAKES performs channel-wise kernel shrinkage, Which enjoys the following benefits: 1) enabling operations deployed in every layer to be heterogeneous, so that they can extract diverse and complementary information to benefit the learning process; and 2) allowing for an efficient and flexible replacement design, which can be generalized to both spatial-temporal and volumetric Data. Further, we propose a new search space based on CAKES, so that the replacement configuration can be determined automatically for simplifying 3D Networks. CAKES shows superior Performance to other methods with similar model size, and it Also achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art with much fewer parameters and computational costs on tasks including 3D medical imaging segmentation and video action recognition. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/yucornetto/CAKES

Like most things to do with wine, it's a fiddly sort of thing that isn't easy to pin down exactly. What it boils down to is finding flavours that work together and complement each other in your glass (or bottle). What are the different types? There are obviously three main types of white wines: Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio and Riesling. But there are dozens upon dozens more varieties out there, from Semillon to Sauvignon Blanc - so many, in fact, that you could spend years just trying them all! Here are some of our favourites... Chablis - A specific type of white Burgundy created by the winemakers who settled on this region after World War II, Chardonnays made here are often very dry and refreshing, making them great for summer drinking as well as wintery days when we're hunkering down inside. Their freshness also makes them good for pairing with spicy foods such as chilli wings or curry dishes. On my personal list? Try Chateau Petrus 2008 (44) and Chateau La Cloche-Francois Bordeaux 2002 (55), two sparklers with a lot going on under their shiny surfaces. Pinot Gris - This one has been around since Roman times, and was actually first called Grumino by Romans because they thought its golden hue looked like gold coins. It now goes by 'pinot grigio' but, essentially, it's a very light white wine made from grapes grown at higher altitudes than normal - think Tuscany, where it gets cooler temperatures and plenty of rainfall year round. Because of these conditions, it tends to be quite aromatic and fruity, with lemon notes being common. My favourite range right now is from New Zealand, which produces delicious Pinot Grigios priced between 10-20. For something slightly different, try Tilted Shed Unfiltered Fizz 2019 Biodynamic (15), which tastes beautifully floral. Sauvignon Blanc - First introduced into France in 1956 by Australian grape grower Tony Melillo, Sauvignon Blanc is a deliciously green, crisper alternative to chardonnay. Often lightly sparkling due to the addition of yeast during fermentation, it showcases fruitier qualities with big citrus aromas and flavors that make it perfect for seafood at dinner parties or brunching outdoors. You can get incredible value on sauvignons starting at less than 20, including Cape Mentelle 2018 (12) from South Africa, Adelaida Muscat de Beaumes de Venise 2014 (22) from Italy and the famous Chablis House White 2016 (17) from France. In this paper, we present a novel approach to object discovery in images based on cohesion measurement. Traditional object detection methods rely on feature extraction and classification, which can be limited by the quality of the features and the complexity of the classifier. Our proposed method uses a different paradigm, focusing on the cohesion property of objects. We define cohesion as the degree to which pixels in an image are densely packed together and belong to the same object. We propose a computational framework for measuring cohesion, which involves partitioning the image into regions of similar colour and texture, and then computing the density of each region. The resulting cohesion map highlights areas with high pixel density, indicating potential objects. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on several benchmark datasets, achieving competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art object detection methods while providing more interpretable results. Our main contribution is the introduction of a new evaluation metric for object discovery, called the cohesion score, which measures the extent to which an image segmentation corresponds to actual objects. This metric takes into account both the completeness and accuracy of the discovered objects, providing a holistic measure of object discovery performance. We also explore the connection between cohesion and other image properties such as entropy and contrast, showing how they can be used to improve object discovery. The impact of our work lies in its ability to provide a new perspective on object discovery, moving beyond traditional feature-based approaches and offering a more intuitive and robust way of identifying objects in images. Our method has applications in various computer vision tasks, including object recognition, scene understanding, and autonneomous driving.
