The goal of this paper is to develop medical matting as a novel method to clinical image segmentation that creates uncertainty. Clinical imaging plays a key role in diagnosis and treatment planning, but accurate segmentation of organs is important due to dramatic differences in appearance between images. Traditional techniques use deterministic techniques, which lack flexibility and do not capture uncertainties. We propose medical matting as an extension of generative adversarial systems (GANs) that captures visual interactions among pixels. Our approach employs stochastic mapping from unsegmented to segmented images while propagating probability maps representing uncertainty. These maps offer useful insights into uncertain areas, enabling scientific interpretation. Our findings show improved segmentation reliability and efficiency compared to state-of-the-art models. This work paves the way toward more sophisticated and consistent medical segmentation tasks using uncertainty.

In this work, we present an extension to Semantics and Information Retrieval (SIER) that combines automatic feature selection and semantic segmentation in an innovative fashion using image-based style generation for segmentation training. Specifically, we use images derived using hierarchical clustering based on a modified version of the style grid from Apte and colleagues. Our system learns how humans categorize pictures in terms of their visual content and then constructs these hierarchies from these descriptions by combining these definitions from both human reviewers as well as machine learning algorithms based on image descriptors such as color, shape, lighting etc.. To test our model, which uses very few labels or features, we performed classification of human annotated images for which we have no way of finding similar examples without manually adding them manually before presenting these results at the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 2016 where they were first presented. We find that our scheme, which has shown promising performances previously on several classes of problem, may be beneficial when used together with advanced multi-labeling techniques for supervised classification. Moreover, we predict significant improvement over state-of-the-art models using the existing style-grapher utility package developed earlier.

"Those two blanks are "z." "So..... Zyzzyva?" "Sure. It's a word." I smirk triumphantly as I put down the tiles for my triple-word-score word, putting me 64 points ahead of the other players dumbfounded at my success. David, my father and our scrabble group's dictionary holder, gives a sigh. "It's a word," he reluctantly admits, "a small weevil apparently." I pick out the last seven tiles of the game - K, W, Y, J, B, I, O - and give an inward groan. Messing with time like this gives me such a headache. At first I'd only add small words. Qi, zi, zu - idiotic point earners because I used to be terrible at scrabble. My dad's a two time champion of the North American Scrabble Championship, and damned if he'd let his kid grow up as a disappointment. But I was a disappointment, I won only once every dozen games but that got me hooked. I dropped out of university to play more often, and since I was failing my physics degree I didn't care anyway. But I was terrible, and my vocabulary was too. That gave me an idea. So, with a microwave with no door, a cell phone and a TV, I created a time machine - quite by accident, but that's irrelevant. Future gadget no. 8 I called it, now 1-7 being stupid things I'd made with a university friend and computer hacker. And, with a bunch of made up words, I began winning matches. People would accuse me of cheating, but of course they were all there in the dictionary. My dad stopped thinking of me as a disappointment after that and if I had to cheat to make my dad look favourably on me, it was worth it. Besides, what's the harm? "Excuse me," I tell the group around the table as I head into the kitchen. Setting the microwave to 120 seconds, I enter the letters onto my phone. "Kwyjibo." "Kwyjibo?!" I smile smugly as I lay down the last tiles of the game. David, my father and our group's dictionary holder, sighs as he relates that a Kwyjibo is a big, dumb, balding North American ape with no chin. The rest throw down their tiles. I've won the game.

To solve RIS efficiently, we need to Understand each word's relationship with other words, each region in the image to other regions, and Cross-modal alignment between linguistic and visual domains. We argue that one of the limiting factors in the recent Methods is that they do not handle these interactions simultaneously. To this End, we propose a novel architecture called JRNet, which uses a Joint Reasoning Module(JRM) to concurrently capture the inter-modal and intra-modal Interactions. The output of jRM is passed through a novel Cross-Modal Multi-Level Fusion (CMMLF) module which further refines the segmentation masks by exchanging Contextual information across visual hierarchy through linguistic features acting as a bridge. We present thorough ablation studies and validate our approach's performance on four benchmark datasets, showing considerable performance gains over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper presents a novel approach for high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy edges based on polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection. The proposed method aims to accurately separate the tooth roots from the surrounding dental tissues in digital dental images. Existing methods for tooth root segmentation are often limited by their reliance on hand-crafted features, low accuracy, and high computational complexity. In contrast, our approach leverages the power of polynomial curve fitting to accurately model the fuzzy edges of tooth roots and detect landmarks that define the boundary between the tooth roots and the surrounding tissues. The proposed method consists of three stages: 1) preprocessing, 2) polynomial curve fitting, and 3) landmark detection. In the preprocessing stage, the input image is philtreed to enhance the contrast and remove noise. In the polynomial curve fitting stage, a cubic polynomial curve is fitted to the fuzzy edge of the tooth root using a non-linear least squares optimisation algorithm. The curve is then used to separate the tooth root from the surrounding tissues. Finally, landmarks are detected by identifying the points on the curve that correspond to the maxeimum gradient values. The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of 20 digital dental images using a leave-one-out cross-validation scheme. The results show that our method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. The mean absolute error was found to be 0.15 mm, and the processing time was less than 30 seconds per image. The proposed method has important implications for dental image analysis and related applications such as orthodontic treatment planning, dental implant planning, and oral disease diagnosis. With its high accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, the method has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of dental procedures and contribute to better patient outcomes.

In this research, we proposed a high-resolution segmentation technique to extract tooth root edge in radiographic images. Our method combined polynomial curve fitting and landmark detection methods. Firstly, we located 10 significant landmarks of each root using image extraction methods including template matching, edge detection and contour prediction. Then the remaining root vertices were obtained by using polynomial curve fitting algorithms, finding smooth and steady functions that represented root edges' distribution patterns. Then, the fuzzy convergence among these curves was measured through membership function analysis and distance between roots' surfaces computation techniques. The performance analysis showed our proposed method outperformed other state of the art algorithms based on quantitative assessment metrics indicating reliability and computational simplicity. This work will give useful data in creating efficient automation techniques for medical professionals to reduce clinical reliability and improve patient exposure time from complex radiographs.

Large-scale image segmentation is a critical task in many applications. In this paper, we present a novel approach to perform image partitioning by utilizing distributed clustering methods such as k-means and hierarchical clustering. The aim of our method is to overcome the challenges of large-scale data processing by partitioning the image into smaller parts that can be treated independently, and then combining their results to obtain the final result. We also propose a new method to rearrange small clusters without using extra communication, thus increasing scalability. The proposed method converges faster than previous methods using the message-passing mechanism of MPI for the communication between nodes. The experiments show that our method outperforms other clustering methods in both speed and accuracy.

Despite deep convolutional neural networks achieved impressive progress in medical image computing and analysis, its paradigm of Supervised learning demands a large number of annotations for training to avoid overfitting and achieving promising results. In clinical practices, massive semantic annotations are difficult to acquire in some conditions where specialized biomedical Expert knowledge is required, and it is also a common condition where only few annotated classes are available. In this work, we proposed a novel method for few-shot medical image segmentation, which enables a segmentation model to fast generalize to an unseen class With few training images. We construct our few-shot image segmentor using a deep convolutional network trained episodically. motivated by the spatial consistency and regularity in medical images, we developed an efficient global correlation module to capture the correlation between a support and query image and incorporate it into the deep network called global correlation network. Moreover, we enhance discriminability of deep embedding to encourage clustering of the feature domains of the same class while keep the feature Domains Of different organs far Apart. Ablation Study proved the effectiveness of the proposed Global correlation module and Discriminative Embedding loss. Extensive experiments on anatomical abdomen images on both CT and MRI modalities are performed to demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our proposed model.

The state-of-the-art method for automatically segmenting white matter bundles in diffusion-weighted MRI is tractography in conjunction with streamline cluster selection. This process involves long chains of processing steps which are not only computationally expensive but also complex to setup and tedious with respect to quality control. Direct bundle segmentation methods treat the task as a traditional image segmentation problem. While they so far did not deliver competitive results, they can potentially mitigate many of the mentioned issues. We present a novel supervised approach for direct tract segmentation that shows major performance gains. It builds upon a stacked U-Net architecture which is trained on manual bundle segmentations from Human Connectome Project subjects. We evaluate our approach \textit{in vivo} as well as \textit{in silico} using the ISMRM 2015 Tractography Challenge phantom dataset. We achieve human segmentation performance and a major performance gain over previous pipelines. We show how the learned spatial priors efficiently guide the segmentation even at lower image qualities with little quality loss.

In this paper, we introduce a large-scale, realistic object segmentation challenge, based on the popular and rich YouTube data. In the current age, the huge amount of video data and the high demand for automatic video analysis have created an urgent need for robust and efficient methods that can handle complex scenes with many objects, occlusions, and clutter. Existing challenges are limited in scale, simplicity, or focus on particular application areas. Instead, the YouTube-VoS dataset comprises a huge collection of videos from YouTube, which covers different categories such as sports, music, animation, and education. The dataset contains 133,000 clips of approximately 10-second duration, which yields about 47 hours of video. The data are annotated with high-quality object masks that contain a broad range of object categories such as humans, animals, vehicles, indoors, outdoors, and special objects. This enables us to create a rich collection of subsets within the full dataset, which allows for the evaluation of algorithms for specific tasks (e.g., human and vehicle segmentation) while at the same time contributing to the goal of improving generalized object segmentation methods. We provide a comprehensive set of evaluation metrics to facilitate comparisons. In addition, we report extensive experiments with popular state-of-the-art methods, which demonstrate the strength of the dataset in revealing the limitations of current methods. Our hope is that the challenge will lead to improved object segmentation methods, and ultimately to more accurate and robust multimedia analysis and applications.

In this work, we study semantic segmentation in few-shot scenario (i.e., training on only a small set of labeled images per class). Given that standard CNNs achieve better performance for classification over segmentation tasks; one natural attempt to adapt them would be through the combination of a 2D convolutional neck with an additional head producing pixel predictions -- a direct yet naive approach called `Vanilla'. To tackle such issues, we propose two novel approaches that boost the base-line models performance by learning complementary representations suitable for dense prediction under low shot scenarios . A feature matching attention module is introduced in order to explicitly enforce consistency between high level visual features extracted by backbone modules for segmentation and downstream task heads. In addition, we also show how adopting global contrastive loss not only improves generalization power but can lead towards discovering more discriminative latent projections. Experimental results verify the effectiveness of our proposed method, yielding superior performances compared against other recent works while being much lighter which leads to faster convergence as well during optimizations.

We present XMM-Newton and Chandra observations of two low-metallicity cometary blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxies, Mrk 59 and Mrk 71. The first BCD, Mrk 59, contains two ultraluminous X-ray (ULX) sources, IXO 72 and IXO 73, both associated with bright massive stars and H II complexes, as well as one fainter extended source associated with a massive H II complex at head of the cometary structure. The low-metallicity of Mrk 59 appears to be responsible for the presence of two ULXs. IXO 72 has varied little over last 10 yr, while IXO 73 has demonstrated variability factor of ~4 over the same period. The second BCD, Mrk 71, contains two faint X-ray point sources and two faint extended sources. One point source is likely a background AGN, while the other appears to be coincident with a very luminous star and a compact H II region at the "head" of cometary structure. The two faint extended sources are also associated with massive H II complexes. Although both BCDs have the same metallicity, three sources in Mrk 71 have X-ray luminosities ~1-2 orders of magnitude fainter than those in Mrk 59. The age of starburst may play a role.

In this research, we introduce distribution-free prediction sets that control risk. These methods seek to provide uncertainty quantification without relying on specific assumptions about the underlying data generating process, making them suitable for a wide range of applications. Through simulations and real-data examples, we demonstrate excellent performance in terms of predicting outcomes while controlling risks. Our approach offers an effective alternative or complement to traditional predictive models based on point estimates alone. Overall, these results suggest that our proposed method can be valuable tool predict uncertain events with confidence intervals which are not limited by any assumption about population’s properties thus has broad applicability across domains including finance, epidemiology and engineering among others.

This research presents a large-scale image segmentation approach that leverages distributed clustering algorithms. The proposed method utilizes parallel computing capabilities to efficiently process vast amounts of data, making it suitable for processing high resolution and large images. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant improvements in terms of computational efficiency compared to centralized approaches while maintaining comparable accuracy levels. Overall, this study showcases how distributed clustering can be effectively applied to address challenging problems such as large scale image segmentation whilst providing improved scalability and performance benefits.

In this paper, we propose a novel multi-modal interaction module to model the interaction between the referring expression and the image. The proposed module consists of two parts: a multi-modal attention module and a multi-modal fusion module. The multi-modal attention module is used to capture the semantic information of the referring expression and the visual information of the image. The multi-modal fusion module is used to fuse the semantic information and the visual information. The proposed module is simple and effective, and it can be easily integrated into existing models. Large-scale image segmentation is a critical task in computer vision applications. In this work, we present a novel technique to perform image partitioning utilizing distributed clustering algorithms such as K-means and hierarchical clustering. Our approach aims at addressing the challenges of large data processing by dividing the image into smaller subimages that can be processed independently and then combining their results to derive a final output. We also propose an adaptive method to rearrange the partitions of small clusters with minimum communication overhead, which improves scalability. The algorithm converges faster than conventional techniques by leveraging MPI (Message Passing Interface) for parallel communication between nodes. Results show that our proposed method outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior accuracy with reduced computational time and communicative cost.

[Abstract] At present, future medical imaging is increasingly being used to diagnose patients with cancer or other life-threatening problems without a physician's input (1⇓⇓–0). In fact, this level of patient monitoring has emerged as an urgent need and a cost effective alternative to a conventional surgical strategy of operationally treating disease when clinical findings warrant it (5, 6). However, current techniques are relatively costly compared to human surgeons who still perform a significant portion of total imaging-related revenue (7). Consequently, healthcare systems must now prioritize not just what images should be captured but how they ought to be collected and organized (8). To date, many experts have agreed that large volumes do require to be recorded (6) for certain types of health issues such as cardiac infarction detection in which information is relevant beyond simply allowing doctors to detect atrial fibrillation [6]. These guidelines also dictate use of standardized storage methods for storing medically useful clinical information on large-scale data centers (09), although others would like to see greater transparency about which institutions hold the most medical data, thereby enabling citizens to decide whether privacy is important when making healthcare decisions using mass data (74). Despite these differences, no consensus approach exists regarding the best way forward with respect to both capturing mass imaging images and maintaining appropriate access, quality and security while recording them on centralized data sources. This raises the question: Should we seek solutions which maximize efficiency while minimizing the amount stored or rely only on technologies for storing information? We propose the following guiding principles for designing trustworthy artificial intelligence in the field of medical imaging and apply them to several challenges currently facing contemporary diagnostic machine learning that include: identifying common diseases in high volume samples; detecting noncontroversial features in large quantities at low accuracy through pattern recognition or image classification based on prior knowledge, like heart rate, pupil size; locating and cataloguing images to obtain relevant contextual context that may contribute to treatment recommendations and identify potential anomalies; performing post-processing routines such as pre and/or post activation (activation steps) and noise correction, as well as creating customized visualization programs by automatically modifying predefined templates in order to better understand what is represented in these files; and providing continuous feedback as to how the algorithms are interpreting the medical data and helping healthcare physicians make decisions regarding management

The purpose of this article is to develop a novel unsupervised approach for semantic image segmentation that leverages both Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) andCLIP, two state-of-the-art methods for style synthesis and vision. Specifically, we propose to use Segmentation-GANs (Seg-GANs), which are GAN models specifically designed for generating realistic images within a specified domain, alongside CLIP, an image embedding model trained on a massive dataset. Our method uses these pre-trained models to create a novel conditional GAN architecture that can be fine-tuned for the task of image segmentation based solely on labeled regions instead of requiring pixel-level labels. Results show that our proposed method achieves comparable performance to supervised learning algorithms while significantly reducing computational demands and training time required, making it a more feasible solution for real-world applications in areas such as medical imaging or autonomous vehicles.

Infrared (IR) image segmentation is essential in many urban defence applications, such as pedestrian surveillance, vehicle counting, security monitoring, etc. Active contour model (ACM) is one of the most widely used image segmentation tools at present, but existing methods only utilize the local or global single feature information of image to minimize the energy function, which is easy to cause false segmentations in IR images. In this paper, we propose a multi-feature driven active contour segmentation model to handle IR images with intensity inhomogeneity. Firstly, especially-designed signed pressure force (SPF) function is constructed by combining the global information calculated by global average gray information and the local multi-feature information calculated by local entropy, local standard deviation and gradient information. Then, we draw upon adaptive weight coefficient calculated by local range to adjust the afore-mentioned global term and local term. Next, SPF function is substituted into level set formulation (LSF) for further evolution. Finally, LSF converges after finite number of iterations, and IR image segmentation result is obtained from the corresponding convergence result. Experimental results demonstrate that the presented method outperforms the state-of-the-art models in terms of precision rate and overlapping rate in IR test images.

We aim to estimate food portion size, a property that is strongly related to the presence of food object in 3D space, from single monocular images under real life setting. Specifically, we are interested in end-to-end estimation of food portion size, which has great potential in the field of personal health management. Unlike image segmentation or object recognition where annotation can be obtained through large scale crowd sourcing, it is much more challenging to collect datasets for portion size estimation since human cannot accurately estimate the size of an object in an arbitrary 2D image without expert knowledge. To address such challenge, we introduce a real life food image dataset collected from a nutrition study where the groundtruth food energy (calorie) is provided by registered dietitians, and will be made available to the research community. We propose a deep regression process for portion size estimation by combining features estimated from both RGB and learned energy distribution domains. Our estimates of food energy achieved state-of-the-art with a MAPE of 51.46%, significantly outperforms non-expert human estimates by 27.04%.

3D Convolution Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely applied to 7D scene understanding, such as video analysis and volumetric image recognition. However, 8D networks can easily lead to over-parameterization which incurs expensive computation cost. In this paper, we propose Channel-wise Automatic KErnel Shrinking (CAKES), to enable efficient 3D learning by shrinking standard 3D convolutions into a set of economic operations e.g., 1D, 2D convolutions. Unlike previous methods, CAKES performs channel-wise kernel shrinkage, which enjoys the following benefits: 2) enabling operations deployed in every layer to be heterogeneous, so that they can extract diverse and complementary information to benefit the learning process; and 4) allowing for an efficient and flexible replacement design, which can be generalized to both spatial-temporal and volumetric data. Further, we propose a new search space based on CAKES, so that the replacement configuration can be determined automatically for simplifying 3D networks. CAKES shows superior performance to other methods with similar model size, and it also achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art with much fewer parameters and computational costs on tasks including 8D medical imaging segmentation and video action recognition. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/yucornetto/CAKES

A good segmentation result relies on a set of "correct" choice for the seeds. When the input images are noisy, the seeds can fall on atypical pixels that are not representative of the region statistics. This can lead to incorrect segmentation results. In this paper, an automatic seeded area growing algorithm is proposed for cellular image segmentation. First, the areas of interest (ROIs) generated from the preprocessed imagery. Second, the initial plants are automatically chosen based on ROIs retrieved from the picture. Fourth, the most reprehensive plants are chosen using a machine learning algorithm. Then, the cellular image is segmented into areas where each area corresponds to a seed. The goal of the proposed is to automatically extract the Region of Interests (ROI) from in the cellular images in terms of avoiding the explosion, under segmentation and over segmentation problems. Experimental findings show that the proposed optimization can reduce the segmented image and the segmented results are less noisy as compared to some existing algorithm.

We introduce a method that allows to automatically segment images into semantically meaningful regions without human supervision. Derived regions are consistent across different images and coincide with human-defined semantic classes on some datasets. In cases where semantic regions might be hard for human to define and consistently label, our method is still able to find meaningful and consistent semantic classes. In our work, we use pretrained StyleGAN2~\cite{karras2020analysing} generative model: clustreing in the feature space of the generative model allows to discover semantic classes. Once classes are discovered, a synthetic dataset with generated images and corresponding segmentation masks can be created. After that a segmentation model is trained on the synthetic dataset and is able to generalise to real images. Additionally, by using CLIP~\cite{radford2021learning} we are able to use prompts defined in a natural language to discover some desired semantic classes. We test our method on publicly available datasets and show state-of-the-art results.

We present a novel method to automatically segment scenes composed of millions of pixels from large data sets by extracting coarse and fine gradients from their noise images. The method achieves good results on both visual objects, where features are robust against noisy data, and semantic or object representation problems involving small groups (e.g., a facial expression). We applied it successfully to a data set of 4 million high resolution face images, producing a global and local score representation that was indistinguishable from that produced by conventional segmentation approaches. The proposed system exhibits high temporal fidelity and thus can replace human segmentation techniques in many types of situations. (via @joshuarei)

This article introduces a learning approach based on classifier confidence and comprehensive learning based on particle swarm optimization for polyp localization. The proposed method employs a set of multiple classifiers to improve the accuracy of polyp detection and localization. The confidence of each classifier is used to weight the contribution of each classifier to the final decision. Particle swarm optimization is used for comprehensive learning to optimize the parameters of the ensemble model. The experiments on publicly available images demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed method compared to the best-known state-of-the-art methods.

While findings were incomplete (due to the variance inherent in sampling), they were statistically meaningful at p<0.001 when comparing 10 000 steps/hour. Here is a possible abstract: Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest cancers worldwide, with early detection being crucial for its successful treatment. Accurate CT scan-based segmentation of pancreatic tumours can aid in the development of effective treatment plans and improve patient outcomes. In this study we propose a deep learning-based graph-guided 3D segmentation model to accurately segment pancreatic tumours on contrast-enhanced CT scans. Our methodology utilises multi-scale voxel-wise convolutional layers as well as graph attention mechanisms explicitly modelling inter-voxel connectivities within the spatial neighbourhoods of the target tissue to jointly learn low-level shape features and high-level contextual patterns of pancreatic tumour morphology. We evaluate our approach on MIAOCR-10T dataset where the accuracy outperforms state-of-the-art methods by considerable margin, achieving mean average precision (mAP) values at the slice-level as high as 95%.

The paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation that utilizes comprehensive multi-modal interactions to improve the accuracy and robustness of the segmentation results. The proposed method integrates multiple modalities, including visual, auditory, and haptic information, to enhance the segmentation process. The visual modality is used to provide contextual information, while the auditory and haptic modalities are used to provide additional cues for segmentation. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through experiments on various datasets and shows that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. The results highlight the potential of multi-modal interactions for improving image segmentation and pave the way for future research in this area.

Millwall Football Club have sealed a dramatic aggregate win over Bradford City to reach the League One play-off final at Wembley. The sides drew 1-1 in the second leg of their semi-final tie at The Den on Sunday, but Millwall's 3-1 victory in the first leg proved enough for them to make it through. The result means that the Lions will face Barnsley in the final on 27 May, with the winner earning a place in the Championship next season. Millwall had taken a commanding lead in the first leg of the semi-final last Thursday, thanks to goals from Lee Gregory, Steve Morison and Shaun Williams. Bradford were able to reduce the deficit in the return leg on Sunday, when Mark Marshall scored an early penalty to give the visitors a lifeline. However, Millwall held firm and managed to keep Bradford at bay until the final whistle, meaning they progress to the final with a 4-2 aggregate victory. Manager Neil Harris praised his side's performance after the game, saying: "I'm delighted with the overall result, we've worked so hard over the two games and it's great to see the players rewarded with a trip to Wembley for the final. "We weren't at our best today, but we showed real character to hold onto our lead and get the job done." Millwall now have just over a week to prepare for the final, which is sure to be a tense affair given the high stakes involved. Whichever team wins the match will be playing in the Championship next season - making it a date not to be missed.

Deep learning has not been consistently used for semantic segmentation of seabed environment for artificial aperture radar (SAS) imagery due to the implicit need of abundant training data such methods necessitate. abundant training data, specifically pixel-level labels for all images, is often not available for SAS imagery due to the complex operations (e.g., diver survey, chase boat, precision position information) needed for achieving precise ground-truth. Several hand-crafted feature based algorithms have been proposed to segment SAS in an unsupervised fashion. Unfortunately, there is not space for improvement as the feature extraction step of these techniques is fixed. In this work, we present a new iterative unsupervised algorithms for learning deep features for SAS image segmentation. Our proposed algorithms alternates between clustering superpixels and updating the parameters of a convolutional neural network (CNN) so that the feature extraction for image segmentation can be optimized. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a realistic benchmark dataset. Our findings show that the efficiency of our proposed technique is significantly greater than previous state-of-the-art techniques in SAS image segmentation.

In this paper, we present YouTube-VOS, a novel sequence-to-sequence method for video object segmentation. Our approach uses the large quantity of video data available on video to train a deep neural network that can efficiently segment objects in video. Existing videos object segmentation tools rely on manually compiled data, which are limited in length and diversity. In comparison, YouTube-VOS provides a large-scale database of videos with manually created object proposals, allowing the training of a more efficient and generalizable model. YouTube-VOS is based on a sequence-to-sequence design, where the input sequence consists of frames from a video, and the output sequence consists of bounding boxes around the objects in each frame. We use a mix of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to model the interactions between frames and objects. We evaluate YouTube-VOS on various benchmark datasets, including YouTube-VOS-Test, YouTube-VOS-Val, and Cityscapes. Our tests demonstrate that YouTube-VOS outperforms state-of-the-art technologies in terms of segmentation accuracy and performance. We also demonstrate the flexibility of our technique by applying it to other video analysis activities, such as object tracking and human-object relationship detection. Our major contributions are: * A large-scale video object segmentation dataset (YouTube-VOS) with automatically created object proposals. * A sequence-to-sequence method for video object segmentation that uses the large quantity of video data available on YouTube. * A novel design that uses CNNs and RNNs to model the interactions between frames and objects. * State-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets, outperforming existing techniques in terms of segmentation accuracy and performance. YouTube-VOS has the potential to provide a broad variety of video analysis technologies, such as autonomous driving, monitoring, and video editing. Our data and code are publicly accessible, creating a useful resource for scholars and professionals in the field.

> We study an interior object detection problem in RVGs (Room-centered viewing graphs). In this setting, we are given a set of images of 3D objects taken around the entire object with respect to a fixed camera in center and are required to recover the poses of these objects. Although there are many indoor scene understanding results, most of them focus on static scenes with limited number of clutter background such as table-top datasets like Pascal Sintel; more realistic cases containing movable dynamic furniture have not received much attention. We propose a method that simultaneously solves pose refinement by geometric constraints from different views and segmentation via global color consistency and shape regularity priors among different regions. To deal with challenges coming from both high computational complexity and large inter-class variations within each region under different viewings, our proposed algorithm consists of multiple pipelines running together on GPU, where each step has its own local optimization goals. Each pipeline works independently but collaborates well through joint outputs. By introducing novel objective function and carefully designed loss terms in learning process, all those independent components can be trained end-to-end without explicit handcrafted features or predetermined rules for geometry estimation. We conduct extensive experiments on real world synthetic and human generated datasets, showing promising performance of the unified network for generalized interior semantic segmentation task based on which reliable viewpoint estimation could also be achieved.

The field of image segmentation in neuroscience has been developing rapidly in recent years, and there are many challenges that can be addressed. We consider here a problem where these challenges collide and where they create the greatest value; namely, the use in medical imageing to infer what part of the brain has been damaged or destroyed by disease. In this work, we present an approach based on direct cortical and subcortical surface morphometry. During this work, we focus entyrely in two directions: (1) We use cortical and subcortical surface morphology as indicators of structural change associated with disease and (2) the development of a robust method which allows reconstruction of complex images directly from cortical data, allowing us to recover a highly structured representation of large numbers of voxels without requiring a knowledge of any other structures or their properties. Our central hypothesis is that once defined well enough, this representation will be capable to reconstruct almost perfectly realistic faces from simple images.

The abstract of the academic paper on “Multicell Coordinated Beamforming with Rate Outage Constraint--Part II: Efficient Approximation Algorithms” is: In this study, we present efficient approximation algorithms to solve the multicell coordinated beamforming problem under rate outage constraints. We first propose a new constraint set called the rate-outage feasibility set (ROFS) and show that it guarantees that every transmission achieves minimum expected rate within its outage probability interval while maximising the expected rate over all transmissions. Then we develop an iterative algorithm based on alternating minimization principles to efficiently approximate ROFS. Finally, we prove global convergence properties of our proposed algorithm and also investigate properties of the approximated feasible regions. Overall, the results in this work make significant contributions to the optimisation of the joint transmission design in multiple cell networks with rate outage constraints, filling an important gap in litreature.

– This work is a penetrating study of the future of jet modification during the next ten years. Combined with rapid technological developments and the increasing need for more efficient and sustainable modes of transport, the jet industry is facing great change. It is the purpose of this study to investigate the trends and developments in jet modification, such as the use of electric and hybrid-electic propulsion systems, aerodynamic improvements and the introduction of artificial intelligence. Moreover, it is necessary to consider the difficulties and limitations associated with introducing these modifications, such as safety issues, regulatory restrictions and cost-effectiveness. This work concludes with a summary of the benefits that jet modification can bring to the industry, such as reduced emissions, increased efficiency and improved passenger comfort. The authors claim that the next ten years will be decisive for the jet industry, determining the direction of jet modification for the next decade.

For mobile robots navigating on sidewalks, it is essential to be able to safely cross street intersections. Most existing approaches rely on the recognition of the traffic light signal to make an informed crossing decision. Although these approaches have been crucial enablers for urban navigation, the capabilities of robots employing such approaches are still limited to navigating only on streets that contain signalized intersections. In this paper, we address this challenge and propose a multimodal convolutional neural network framework to predict the safety of a street intersection for crossing. Our architecture consists of two subnetworks; an interaction-aware trajectory estimation stream IA-TCNN, that predicts the future states of all observed traffic participants in the scene, and a traffic light recognition stream AtteNet. Our IA-TCNN utilizes dilated causal convolutions to model the behavior of all the observable dynamic agents in the scene without explicitly assigning priorities to the interactions among them. While AtteNet utilizes Squeeze-Excitation blocks to learn a content-aware mechanism for selecting the relevant features from the data, thereby improving the noise robustness. Learned representations from the traffic light recognition stream are fused with the estimated trajectories from the motion prediction stream to learn the crossing decision. Incorporating the uncertainty information from both modules enables our architecture to learn a likelihood function that is robust to noise and mispredictions from either subnetworks. Simultaneously, by learning to estimate motion trajectories of the surrounding traffic participants and incorporating knowledge of the traffic light signal, our network learns a robust crossing procedure that is invariant to the type of street intersection. Furthermore, we extend our previously introduced Freiburg Street Crossing dataset with sequences captured at multiple intersections of varying types, demonstrating complex interactions among the traffic participants as well as various lighting and weather conditions. We perform comprehensive experimental evaluations on public datasets as well as our Freiburg Street Crossing dataset, which demonstrate that our network achieves state-of-the-art performance for each of the subtasks, as well as for the crossing safety prediction. Moreover, we deploy the proposed architectural framework on a robotic platform and conduct real-world experiments which demonstrate the suitability of the approach for real-time deployment and robustness to various environments.

The Knowledge-Based Fully Convolutional Networks (KB-FCN) is a novel method to segment lung structures on computed tomography images using deep learning. This network delivers experience from radiologists with an end-to-end trainable architecture, resulting in improved reliability compared to existing protocols. The KB-FCN was trained and validated on a database of 126 high-resolution CT scans and achieved Dice Similarity Coefficients higher than 90% for both lungs and respiratory tumors. Additionally, we showed that our technique can be employed as a tool by radiation oncologists during treatment planning for patients undergoing stereotactic body therapy (SBRT). Overall, this research provides a promising solution towards accurate segmentation of chest CTs which will have considerable effect on computer aided diagnosis systems.

Convolutional neural networks have shown to achieve superior performance on image segmentation tasks. However, convolutional neural networks, operating as black-box systems, generally do not provide a reliable measure about the confidence of their decisions. This leads to various problems in industrial settings, amongst others, inadequate levels of trust from users in the model's outputs as well as non-compliance with current policy guidelines (e.g., EU AI Strategy). To address these issues, we use uncertainty measures based on Monte-Carlo dropout in context of a human-in-the-loop system to increase the system's transparency and performance. In particular, we demonstrate the benefits described above on real-world multi-class image segmentation task of wear analysis in machining industry. Following previous work, we show that the quality of a prediction correlates with model's uncertainty. Additionally, we demonstrate that multiple linear regression using the model's uncertainties as independent variables significantly explains the quality of prediction (\(R^2=0.718\)). Within the uncertainty-based human-in-the-loop system, the multiple regression aims at identifying failed predictions on image-level. The system utilizes a human expert to label these failed predictions manually. A simulation study demonstrates that the uncertainty-based human-in-the-loop system increases performance for different levels of human involvement in comparison to random-based human-in-the-loop system. To ensure generalizability, we show that the presented approach achieves similar results on the publicly available Cityscapes dataset.

3D Convolution Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely applied to 3D scene understanding, such as video analysis and volumetric image recognition. However, 3D networks can easily lead to over-parameterization which incurs expensive computation cost. In this paper, we propose Channel-wise Automatic KErnel Shrinking (CAKES), to enable efficient 3D learning by shrinking standard 3D convolutions into a set of economic operations e.g., 1D, 2D convolutions. Unlike previous methods, CAKES performs channel-wise kernel shrinkage, which enjoys the following benefits: 1) enabling operations deployed in every layer to be heterogeneous, so that they can extract diverse and complementary information to benefit the learning process; and 2) allowing for an efficient and flexible replacement design, which can be generalized to both spatial-temporal and volumetric data. Further, we propose a new search space based on CAKES, so that the replacement configuration can be determined automatically for simplifying 3D networks. CAKES shows superior performance to other methods with similar model size, and it also achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art with much fewer parameters and computational costs on tasks including 3D medical imaging segmentation and video action recognition. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/yucornetto/CAKES

The reliability of Deep Learning systems depends on their accuracy but also on their robustness against adversarial perturbations to the input data. Several attacks and defenses have been proposed to improve the performance of Deep Neural Networks under the presence of adversarial noise in the natural image domain. However, robustness in computer-aided diagnosis for volumetric data has only been explored for specific tasks and with limited attacks. We propose a new framework to assess the robustness of general medical image segmentation systems. Our contributions are two-fold: (i) we propose a new benchmark to evaluate robustness in the context of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) by extending the recent AutoAttack natural image classification framework to the domain of volumetric data segmentation, and (ii) we present a novel lattice architecture for RObust Generic medical image segmentation (ROG). Our results show that ROG is capable of generalizing across different tasks of the MSD and largely surpasses the state-of-the-art under sophisticated adversarial attacks.

The abstract of the article is as follows: Semantic segmentation is a critical task in remote sensing image processing, which divides the image into a number of regions, and gives a name to each region. But the performance of semantic segmentation is often limited by the boundary between the regions, which leads to labeling errors. This paper presents a new way to solve this problem by adding a boundary loss to the objective function of the semantic segmentation. This loss can guide the model to learn more accurate boundaries between regions, and thus improve the performance of the semantic segmentation. We test this method on several public data sets and show that the accuracy of the labeling is greatly improved compared with state-of-the-art methods.

The development and deployment of parallel systems to perform large scale visual computing tasks have become widely available in recent years, making it possible to use them to process images with unprecedented resolution. However, these processing platforms still lack necessary tools that enable users to conveniently access their resources to solve data driven problems. In this work we describe techniques for performing parallel and scalable image analysis using distributed iterative region growing methods running over range of different computational models including shared memory threads, message passing interface (MPI), Mapred and Spark based clusters on both small laptops as well as huge supercomputers. We show two key points; firstly how to adapt clustering methods so they can be implemented efficiently across a wide variety of hardware ranging from single processor machines up to petascale clusters. Secondly, rather than just providing benchmarks about these systems we focus our efforts towards developing end user toolkit around large image segmentations so people interested in performing such analyses are no longer required to know how or what type of system would best fit their requirements. Our current software allows us to test various segmentation tools such as Otsu, Mean Cut, Hue Saturation Value, Chocolate Box algorithm or watershed transformer to name some few which all run very easily through our library. We tested extensively different configuration strategies like SIMD, MPI+OpenMp, hybrid MPI/shared memory programs among others against a number of real life applications which include 100’s Millions of pixels per second. As future goals our toolbox will provide not only implementations but also the corresponding performance results on top cluster architectures along with the availability of several segmented databases generated over time which might serve other researchers to further examine new analysis approaches on high dimensional datasets coming from either astronomy or biomedicine fields of study.

The proposed method utilizes a convolutional neural network that is trained in an unsupervised manner using generative adversarial networks. Through multiple iterations of refinement, the algorithm segments SAS images into distinct classes without requiring any labeled data or prior knowledge of target characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology by achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets while also reducing computational complexity compared to traditional supervised approaches. The recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) combined with the extensive amount of data generated by today's clinical systems, has led to the development of imaging AI solutions across the whole value chain of medical imaging, including image reconstruction, medical image segmentation, image-based diagnosis and treatment planning. Notwithstanding the successes and future potential of AI in medical imaging, many stakeholders are concerned of the potential risks and ethical implications of imaging AI solutions, which are perceived as complex, opaque, and difficult to comprehend, utilise, and trust in critical clinical applications. Despite these concerns and risks, there are currently no concrete guidelines and best practices for guiding future AI developments in medical imaging towards increased trust, safety and adoption. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a careful selection of guiding principles drawn from the accumulated experiences, consensus, and best practices from five large European projects on AI in Health Imaging. These guiding principles are named FUTURE-AI and its building blocks consist of (i) Fairness, (ii) Universality, (iii) Traceability, (iv) Usability, (v) Robustness and (vi) Explainability. In a step-by-step approach, these guidelines are further translated into a framework of concrete recommendations for specifying, developing, evaluating, and deploying technically, clinically and ethically trustworthy AI solutions into clinical practice.

The field of quantum computing has seen rapid growth in recent years, with many researchers focusing their attention on understanding and simplifying complex quantum systems. One important concept that arises frequently is that of quantum finite automaton (QFA) equivalence – the idea that two different QFAs can perform the same computational tasks, despite their aparrent differences in structure or behavior. In this paper, we provide several key results on the equivalence of multi-letter quantum finite automata. We show that any QFA can be transformed into a equivalent but smaller one through operations such as deletions, insertions, and permutations. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain families of QFAs are universally equivalent, even when restricted to specific input sizes. Our findings contribute significantly to our understanding of quantum computation, and have applications in fields such as cryptography and optimization.

This paper presents a novel approach to estimating body schema through Bayesian inference, utilizing tactile information obtained from coordinated random movements. The proposed method combines insights from cognitive science and robotics to enable a human-like body awareness in robots. By leveraging the concept of body schemas, which are internal models that humans use to represent their own bodies, we can improve the ability of robots to interact with their environment and perform tasks that require an understanding of self-body relationships. Our approach uses coordinated random movements to generate tactile data, which is then processed using Bayesian inference to update the body schema estimate. We evaluate our method on various simulation environments and show that it outperforms traditional methods relying solely on visual or auditory sensing. Additionally, we discuss how this work paves the way towards more advanced AI systems capable of emulating human-like sensorimotor capabilities.

Despite deep convolutional neural networks achieved impressive progress in medical image computing and analysis, its paradigm of supervised learning demands a large number of annotations for training to avoid overfitting and achieving promising results. In clinical practises, massive semantic annotations are difficult to acquire in some conditions where specialised biomedical expert knowledge is required, and it is also a common condition where only few annotated classes are available. In this work, we proposed a novel method for few-shot medical image segmentation, which enables a segmentation model to fast generalise to an unseen class with few training images. We construct our few-shot image segmentor using a deep convolutional network trained episodically. Motivated by the spatial consistency and regularity in medical images, we developed an efficient global correlation module to capture the correlation between a support and query image and incorporate it into the deep network called global correlation network. Moreover, we enhance discriminability of deep embedding to encourage clustreing of the feature domains of the same class while keep the feature domains of different organs far apart. Ablation Study proved the effectiveness of the proposed global correlation module and discriminative embedding loss. Extensive experiments on anatomical abdomen images on both CT and MRI modalities are performed to demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our proposed model.

In this paper, we investigate properties of a superconductor with pair hopping and magnetic interactions at half-filling using a tight-binding model. We focus on the effects of pair hopping and magnetic interactions on the superconducting state, and compare our results to experimental observations. We find that presence of pair hopping and magnetic interactions leads to a rich phase diagram, with multiple superconducting phases emerging as function of temperature, doping, and external magnetic field. We observe that superconducting state is strongly influenced by the competition between pair hopping and magnetic interactions, leading to novel phenomena such as suppression of superconductivity at high temperatures and re-emergence of superconductivity at lower temperatures. Our results also reveal interesting correlations between the superconducting gap and density of states at Fermi level, which provide insight into the underlying pairing mechanism. Furthermore, we find that effectiveness of pair hopping in promoting superconductivity is strongly dependent on the strength and range of magnetic interactions. Overall, our study provides new insights into complex interplay between pair hopping, magnetic interactions, and superconductivity in systems at half-filling. The observed phenomena have important implications for the design and optimization of superconductors, and may lead to new strategies for enhancing their performance.

As a young soldier, I was eager to serve my country during the First World War. Little did I know, the next few years of my life would be spent in the trenches, fighting for survival alongside my fellow soldiers. The trenches were an entirely different world. The mud, the rats, the lice - it was all so overwhelming. The stench of death was constant, with the sound of exploding shells and gunfire becoming a lullaby to us all. During the day, we spent our time repairing the trenches, digging new ones, and gathering supplies for the next battle. We were always on high alert, ready to fight at a moment's notice. Our fear was palpable, but we had to remain stoic in the face of danger. The nights were a different story. Illuminated by the moon and the enemy's flares, we played a deadly game of cat and mouse. The darkness provided much-needed cover, enabling us to launch surprise attacks on our enemies. But the price for this was high. Every night, we would lose men, friends, and brothers, and the thought of not making it back home haunted us. The tiniest mistake could end in an instant, striking terror in our hearts. I remember the endless months of the war, where we sat in the same position, barely able to stretch our legs, eat, or sleep. The rain was our greatest enemy, and trench foot was a constant threat. As the months trudged on, the war lost its nobility for us. The camaraderie of joining the army and fighting for a noble cause slowly transformed into a grim determination to stay alive. Finally, after years of living in utter despair, peace was announced. The war ended, and we were free to go home. But for me, the horrors of the trench never left me. It remains etched in my mind till this day, a solemn reminder of the sacrifices made in the name of freedom.

We consider the problem of fitting variational posterior approximations using stochastic optimization methods. The performance of these approximations depends on (1) how well the variational family matches the true posterior distribution, (2) the choice of divergence, and (3) the optimization of the variational objective. We show that even in the best-case scenario when the exact posterior belongs to the assumed variational family, common stochastic optimization methods lead to poor variational approximations if the problem dimension is moderately large. We also demonstrate that these methods are not robust across diverse model types. Motivated by these findings, we develop a more robust and accurate stochastic optimization framework by viewing the underlying optimization algorithm as producing a Markov chain. Our approach is theoretically motivated and includes a diagnostic for convergence and a novel stopping rule, both of which are robust to noisy evaluations of the objective function. We show empirically that the proposed framework works well on a diverse set of models: it can automatically detect stochastic optimization failure or inaccurate variational approximation.

X-ray images of the oral cavity have been used as a diagnostic aid in root canal treatment. But it has always been difficult to segment the teeth roots, because of their blurred boundary, using the traditional image-processing methods. In this paper, we propose a high-resolution model based on polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection (HS-PCL). The model, based on the detection of multiple landmarks evenly distributed along the teeth roots, is used to determine the boundary of the teeth roots by a smooth polynomial curve, thus resolving the problem of the blurred boundary. In addition, a new maximum shortest distance-based distance estimation method (MNSD) was developed to automatically remove the bad influence of those landmarks which have been detected by mistake, which are out of the root-edge region. In our experiments, the proposed method reduced the root-edge distance (as measured by the Haussdorff distance) by 33.9 per centimeter and the average-surface-distance by 42.2%, compared with the existing method. It also produced good results for the data set, making it feasible to evaluate root canal treatment automatically using a medical image-processing system.

Our approach offers effective alternative or complement to traditional predictive models based on point estimates alone. Overall, these results suggest that our proposed method can be valuable tool predict uncertain events with confidence intervals which are not limited by any assumption about population’s properties thus has broad applicability across domains including finance, epidemiology and engineering among others.

In this study, we propose a novel few-shot segmentation approach that leverages both global and local contrastive learning. Our method is based on the idea of encoding image features in an efficient manner to enable rapid adaptation to new tasks without requiring extensive training data. We demonstrate through experiments conducted on various datasets that our model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods while achieving faster convergence rates thanks to its ability to capture high-level semantic information as well as detailed contextual cues using contrasting examples at multiple scales. Overall, these results suggest that combining different types of contrasts can lead to significant improvements in few-shot performance for segmentation problems.

The aim of this paper is to present a method of unsupervised semantic image segmentation, which uses a combined strategy of Stylegan and CLIP to generate high-quality segmentation masks. Using Stylegan, we first extract the masks that are specific to the particular visual style, and these masks are used as input to the CLIP model to obtain the segmentation masks that are specific to the semantics. Using this method, high-quality and accurate segmentation masks can be obtained without the need for any training data, which is useful for the application where data are rare or expensive to obtain. We show that the proposed method can obtain segmentation masks that are as good as those obtained by supervised methods in experiments on several standard datasets.

A display created by Misapplied Sciences and partially funded by Delta is able to produce multiple displays at different angles, meaning that multiple people viewing the same screen are able to see different information. Researchers at MIT's Tangible Media Group are developing a new type of display that can produce multiple views on the same screen, depending on the angle from which it's being seen. Misapplied Sciences, a startup spun out from MIT's Media Lab, recently unveiled a demonstration of the technology in collaboration with Delta. The result is a display that's able to produce multiple views, meaning that multiple people viewing the same screen are able to see different information. "You want to create displays that are interactive for a group of people so that you can create something that everyone can be engaged with," said Sebastian Wernicke, co-founder of Misapplied Sciences. The technology, called Digitouch, consists of two parts. There's a set of sensors on the front of the screen that can determine where the viewer's hand is and also how far away it is from the screen. It can then produce a 3D image that the person can interact with. There's also a program that can create multiple views on the same screen. A simple example is to have two viewers side by side, with one person able to see a different set of information than the person next to them. That's a big step beyond what current technologies are able to do. In a demonstration, a group of people looked at the same screen that was displaying a simple image. One person was able to make changes to a certain element of the image, while the other people were unable to see the changes. The key to the technology is the software that's able to generate the various views. The Digitouch technology could be used in a variety of settings, including retail. A retailer, for instance, could have shoppers try on different clothing items on a screen, and then pass the item over to a tablet to pay for it. "The key idea is that you can create a shared experience, but for different people," Wernicke said.

The task of segmenting objects within an image requires a Comprehensive understanding of spatial relationships between different segments. Traditional interactive semantic segmentation methods usually rely on global changes to images or regions, which may be detrimental to maintaining local context and relationship between adjacent pixel groups. In this work, we introduce a novel approach called EdgeFlow that uses edge information as Input to achieve practical interactive segmentation while considering the local dependencies in real-time. Our proposed framework learns robust edge maps from both low and high resolution levels, Utilizing temporal correlations through dynamic motion estimates based on optical flow. We then combine Edge cues from high and low resolution level with a set of locally-adapted Filter weights to create a fine-tuned intermediate map, Capturing the delicate details across space and time. Finally, our model performs interactive manipulation using gradient descent until Convergence, resulting in accurate segmentation output without the need for human Intervention. Furthermore, we evaluate our method on three benchmark datasets, demonstrating outperformances over classical approaches by preserving more detailed spatial patterns while achieving significantly faster processing times.

We investigate Referring Image Segmentation (RIS), which outputs a segmentation map corresponding to the given natural language description. To solve RIS efficiently, we need to understand each word's relationship with other words, each region in the image to other regions, and cross-modal alignment between linguistic and visual domains. We argue that one of the limiting factors in the recent methods is that they do not handle these interactions simultaneously. To this end, we propose a novel architecture called JRNet, which uses a Joint Reasoning Module(JRM) to concurrently capture the inter-modal and intra-modal interactions. The output of JRM is passed through a novel Cross-Modal Multi-Level Fusion (CMMLF) module which further refines the segmentation masks by exchanging contextual information across visual hierarchy through linguistic features acting as a bridge. We present thorough ablation studies and validate our approach's performance on four benchmark datasets, showing considerable performance gains over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

'A novel method for detecting saliency is presented here, based on the idea of aggregating complementary contrasts. We start from the observation that the saliency of a region of an image is determined by the contrast between that region and its surroundings. To measure this contrast, we use two complementary contrasts, the contrast in color and the contrast in edges. The color contrast is the difference between the color of the region and the average color of its surroundings. The contrast in edges is the difference between the intensity of the edges in the region and the average intensity of the edges in the region's surroundings. The contrast in color and the contrast in edges are combined by a weighted sum whose weights are determined by a coherence measure based on the strength of the edges. The proposed method is evaluated on the Pascal S and the MIT-Saliency data sets. The results show that the proposed method outperforms the best of the existing methods on both data sets. In spite of the spectacular success of deep convolutional neural networks in medical image processing and analysis, their supervised learning architectures require a large amount of annotated training data in order to avoid overfitting and achieve good performance. However, in clinical practices, it is difficult to obtain large amounts of annotated data because of the involvement of biomedical experts, and in many cases only a few classes are available. In this work, we propose a few-shots method for medical image segmentation, which can generalize quickly to unseen classes from a few images of a given class. We construct our few-shots method using a deep convolutional network trained episodically, which exploits the spatially consistent and repetitive nature of medical images to extract global correlations between the support and the query images and introduce it into the deep network as a “global correlation network”. Moreover, to enhance the discriminability of the embedding, we use a dilation and permutation (D & P) operation to force the region of interest to cluster features of the same class, while separating the regions of interest of different classes. Testing on an anatomical abdomen, we show the effectiveness of our method on a number of different image modalities, including CT and MRI.

The proposed CPA is composed of a self-complementary metasurface and a metallic ground plane. The self-complementary metasurface is composed of a periodic array of split-ring resonators (SRRs) and a periodic array of metallic wires. The proposed CPA can be used in various applications, such as terahertz imaging, terahertz sensing, and terahertz communication. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is set to launch on Halloween this year, after decades of careful planning and development. It will travel from Earth to a gravitational eddy located nearly one million miles from Earth. From there, it will potentially be able to spot the first generation of stars to ever shine in the early universe, as well as exoplanets in our galaxy. The JWST will focus on the infrared part of the spectrum. It has 100 times the observational power of the Hubble Space Telescope, and scientists are hoping it will reveal galaxies that Hubble can't see.

Toronto's City Council will soon hold a vote on whether to allow Sidewalk Labs to privatize much of the city's lakeshore to create a'smart city' owned by Alphabet. Sidewalk Labs has a plan to create a corporate-owned city similar to Lake Buena Vista with privately owned and regulated roads, chartered schools, the power to levy and spend property taxes, a corporate criminal justice system, and continuous surveillance. Residents can choose to decline to share information with Sidewalk Labs, but doing so will mean that they will not receive the same level of services as those who choose to share information. For example, they will not be able to access automated taxi services and some merchants might be unable to accept cash. Sidewalk Labs plans to use reputation tools, effectively establishing a social credit system.

As COVID-19 grabs the attention of the world, the war against antibiotic-resistant bacteria wages on. The number of people dying from bacterial infections could grow from 700,000 annually last year to 10 million annually by 2050. Bacteria evolves resistance against antibiotics over time, and this process is accelerated by overuse. Felix, a biotech startup, believes that it can program viruses to target specific sites in bacteria, killing bad bacteria and halting its ability to evolve and become more resistant. The treatment is now in trials. This approach can potentially re-sensitize bacteria to traditional antibiotics.

This paper presents a Quality-Aware Memory Network (QAMN) for interactive volumetric image segmentation. The QAMN integrates a quality prediction module that estimates the segmentation quality of each voxel in real-time, allowing the user to interactively refine the segmentation results by focusing on regions with low quality. The QAMN is trained end-to-end using a novel loss function that combines segmentation and quality prediction losses. Experimental results on three volumetric medical image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the QAMN in achieving high-quality segmentation results while reducing user interaction time. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, the QAMN achieves comparable or better performance with significantly reduced user interaction time.

The construction and application of a variable temperature environmental capsule for scanning electron microscopy in fluids and fluids at atmospheric conditions is presented in this journal. The capsule provides for the observation of samples under different ambient conditions, varying from -180°C to 600°C, and in various situations, including low vacuum, low pressure fluids, and fluids. The capsule's design, operation, and performance are shown in detail, along with its potential applications in other fields, such as materials engineering, biology, and geology. The paper shows the versatility and utility of the variable temperature environmental capsule in developing the abilities of scanning particle microscopy for analyzing complex phenomena at the micro- and nanoscale.
