The paper presents an efficient algorithm for unsupervised community detection using a Potts model Hamiltonian. The algorithm is based on the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and is designed to efficiently detect communities in large-scale networks. The paper also presents applications of the algorithm in digital pathology, where it is used to detect patterns in medical images. The results show that the algorithm is able to accurately detect communities in both synthetic and real-world networks, and that it is able to identify patterns in medical images that are not visible to the naked eye. Overall, the paper demonstrates the potential of the Potts model Hamiltonian for unsupervised community detection and its applications in digital pathology.

3D Convolution Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely applied to 3D scene understanding, such as video analysis and volumetric image recognition. However, 3D networks can easily lead to over-parameterization which incurs expensive computation cost. In this paper, we propose Channel-wise Automatic Kernal Shrinking (CAKES), to enable efficient 3D learning by shrinking standard 3D convolutions into a set of economic operations e.g., 1D, 2D convolutions. Unlike previous methods, CAKES performs channel-wise kernal shrinkage, which enjoys the following benefits: 1) enabling operations deployed in every layer to be heterogeneous, so that they can extract diverse and complementary information to benefit the learning process; and 2) allowing for an efficient and flexible replacement design, which can be generalized to both spatial-temporal and volumetric data. Further, we propose a new search space based on CAKES, so that the replacement configuration can be determined automatically for simplifying 3D networks. CAKES shows superior performance to other methods with similer model size, and it also achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art with much fewer parameters and computational costs on tasks including 3D medical imaging segmentation and video action recognition. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/yucornetto/CAKES

The machinery never stops. It rumbles on through the night, the vibrations make the walls of Long's tiny dorm shudder. The other workers snore and moan in their sleep. Their combined heat leaves condensation on the concrete walls and floor. Long lays back in his bunk, the metal bar of the bed frame pressing into his lumbar, the pain a minor throb compared to the clutching agony in his chest. Long counts the minutes until dawn, when shift change will happen and the night shift workers will return from the factory floor and Long and his crew will switch places with them. He counts down each second like a prisoner awaiting execution. When the dawn comes there is no pounding on the door from the dorm master. There is no uniform footsteps in the hallway. His dorm mates sleep on. Long tries to enjoy this temporary respite, but the interruption to the routine makes him uneasy. Eventually he rises from his bunk and wanders into the hallway. The dorm hallway is gone, the ratlike tunnel replaced by a dark tunnel. At the end is an open door, bright sunlight spilling from the open crack. Long can smell the fresh cut grass and riverbeds of his home town. Long hesitates at the cusp of the door. From the other side, Long hears a voice he has not heard since his distant childhood. His grandmother calls to him: "Do not be afraid, Long. Your shift is over." Long steps into the light.

As the most economical and routine auxiliary examination in the diagnosis of root canal treatment, oral X-ray has been widely used by stomatologists. It is still challenging to segment the tooth root with a blurry boundary for the traditional image segmentation method. To this end, we propose a model for high-resolution segmentation based on polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection (HS-PCL). It is based on detecting multiple landmarks evenly distributed on the edge of the tooth root to fit a smooth polynomial curve as the segmentation of the tooth root, thereby solving the problem of fuzzy edge. In our model, a maxeimum number of the shortest distances algorithm (MNSDA) is proposed to automatically reduce the negative influence of the wrong landmarks which are detected incorrectly and deviate from the tooth root on the fitting result. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach not only reduces Hausdorff95 (HD95) by 33.9% and Average Surface Distance (ASD) by 42.1% compared with the state-of-the-art method, but it also achieves excellent results on the minute quantity of datasets, which greatly improves the feasibility of automatic root canal therapy evaluation by medical image computing.

The paper presents a novel approach to few-shot segmentation using global and local contrastive learning. The proposed method leverages both global and local contrastive learning to improve the performance of few-shot segmentation. The global contrastive learning is used to learn the overall structure of the image, while the local contrastive learning is used to learn the local details of the image. The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and shows significant improvements in performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The paper also provides an analysis of the effectiveness of the proposed method and discusses future directions for research.

In this Paper, we propose a novel approach to few-shot segmentation, which is a challenging task in computer vision That involves segmenting objects from A small Number of labeled examples. Our approach, called Few-Shot Segmentation with Global and Local Contrastive Learning (FSS-GCL), combines the strengths of global and local contrastive learning to improve segmentation accuracy. Global contrastive learning has been shown to be effective in learning high-level representations that are useful for few-shot learning. However, it may not capture local Information that is crucial for segmentation tasks. Local contrastive learning, on the other hand, can capture local information but may not generalize well to new Examples. In FSS-GCL, we propose A two-stage training strategy that first uses global contrastive learning to learn high-level representations and then uses local contrastive learning to refine the segmentation masks. We also introduce a novel mask-based contrastive loss function that encourages the model to produce accurate segmentation masks. Experiments on several benchmark Datasets show that FSS-GCL outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods, including those that use global or local contrastive learning alone. We also perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of The different components of our approach. Our main contributions are: * A novel few-shot segmentation approach called FSS-GCL that combines global and local contrastive learning * A two-stage training strategy that leverages the strengths of global and local Contrastive learning * A mask-based contrastive loss function that encourages accurate segmentation masks * State-of-the-art performance on Several benchmark datasets Overall, FSS-GCL demonstrates The effectiveness of combining global and local contrastive learning for few-shot segmentation, and provides a promising direction for future research In this area.

To support our efforts to build better machine-learning models, we are developing and releasing an open source software package that will automate many components required in real world supervised learning tasks such as regression and classification based on pre-labeled images. This work develops methods to extract the training data from deep neural networks (DNNs), then automatically apply them onto a large database for inference tasks. We refer users not interested in the code or algorithm to our website under 'Extractor of Images', where they can find an overview of all aspects of the project. Our main focus here is medical imaging; we also cover visual recognition tasks as well by performing simple detection tests against labeled images. We take a step back from more focused areas related to medical research and explain what these projects require which leads to their relevance to broader applications across industry. In this way it becomes easier to understand why it would be beneficial to develop both medical applications and non-medical applications for the benefits they bring together.

Scientists have created a vaccine for cat allergies that trains the immune systems of cats, instead of desensitizing the immune system of people allergic to cats. Hypocat trains the cat's immune system by exposing them to harmless amounts of cat proteins on their skin and inside their bodies. Injecting this vaccine into kittens reduces peri-and postoperative symptoms (eosinophilic granuloma) caused by feline allergy in children who are at risk of developing asthma later in life as adults. The study was published online January 15, 2016 in Translational Medicine. Laura Niederhofer is an Associate Professor in Immunology Microbiology with dual appointments in Dermatology at the University of Minnesota Medical School where she leads studies evaluating methods to prevent or treat allergic diseases including eosinophilic granulomas such as those found in humans exposed to domestic cats and mice with eczema. She also serves as Deputy Director of Research Programs (Dermatologic AllergyImmunology Program). "The current gold standard of treatment for eosinophiloma remains highly invasive surgical excision," said Dr. Niederhofer. They must not only remove nonhealing lesions but extract tissue from areas away from vital anatomical structures." Cats bring joy to millions of families around the world. But they can be hazardous when living near houses where someone has been diagnosed with serious food allergies. This creates a problem: how can you keep your kitten out of harm's way? Fortunately, there may soon be a solution - if it works well enough. A new animal model shows promise for testing vaccines against IgE antibodies specific to certain foods. When tested on healthy human volunteers, two doses weakened these undesirable antibodies so much that it might help make existing vaccination therapy more effective. And because its mechanism differs significantly from other allergy treatments currently being used, it could lead directly to safer therapies for treating severe reactions from accidental exposure to allergens like peanuts and shellfish. > One-shot image semantic segmentation aims to segment an image into different semantic types with only one labeled image. In this paper, we propose a novel one-shot image semantic segmentation approach, which assumes semantically meaningful class models for each category. The proposed approach consists of two components: a class model learning module and a semantic segmentation module. The class prototype learning module develops semantically meaningful class models for each category by comparing the labeled image and the unlabeled images of the same category. The semantic segmentation module segments the image into different linguistic types by combining the learned class prototypes. The proposed approach is evaluated on the PASCAL VOC 2012 database. The experimental findings show that the proposed technique demonstrates state-of-the-art reliability on the PASCAL VOC 2012 database. A new selective image super resolution methodology is proposed in this work to reconstruct high quality images at a reduced sampling rate while utilizing the inherently large degree of redundancy available within the image and its frequency. This approach offers several key advantages: it does not require separate training or pre-existing knowledge about what should be visible after reconstruction, and allows multiple users accessing different regions (each with their own local reconstruction) without conflict. To implement this novel concept we develop two sets of algorithms that serve as complementary building blocks -- an intelligent up sampler that determines locations where pixels will reside based on information gathered during reconstruction; and inverse Fourier series filters to improve spatial resolution by separating out unique and repetitive characteristics of local neighborhoods. Partly supervised multitask learning is a machine learning technique that combines the benefits of supervised and unsupervised learning. In supervised learning, the algorithm is trained on labeled data, while in unsupervised learning, it is trained on unlabeled data. Partly supervised multitask learning uses a combination of both, where some of the data is labeled and some is unlabeled. This technique has several advantages over traditional supervised and unsupervised learning, including improved accuracy, reduced training time, and the ability to learn from both labeled and unlabeled data. The paper presents a comprehensive review of the state-of-the-art in partly supervised multitask learning, including its applications, challenges, and future directions.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to 3D medical image segmentation that combines the strengths of deep learning and graph-based algorithms. Our method, called OneNet, is designed to be both generalizable across different modalities and lightweight in terms of computational requirements. Existing methods for 3D medical image segmentation often rely on heavily modality-specific preprocessing steps or require significant computational resources. In contrast, OneNet uses a single neural network architecture that can handle diverse input data types and produces accurate segmentations with minimal post-processing. We achieve this through a novel networking strategy that integrates spatial and intensivity information from multi-modal inputs. The resulting embeddings are then fed into a graph convolutional network (GCN) for refined segmentation. OneNet was evaluated on several publicly available datasets encompassing various modalities (CT, MRI, and microscopy). Our experiments demonstrate superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, including those specifically tailored to individual modalities. Furthermore, we show that OneNet maintains its accuracy while being significantly faster than other approaches. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the contributions of different components within our framework. These reveal the importance of incorporating both intra-modal and inter-modal contextual information during training. Lastly, we explore potential clinical applications by applying OneNet to real-world scenarios such as tumor detection and brain structure extraction. In summary, OneNet offers a powerful, versatile solution for accurate 3D medical image segmentation that surpasses existing methods in both efficiency and adaptability. With its ability to handle diverse inputs, minimize computational overhead, and produce high-quality segmentations, it has the potential to revolutionize research and diagnostic practices in various fields of medicine.

In this paper, we challenge the common assumption that domain generalisation is always necessary for training machine learning models that can generalise to unseen domains. We argue that in certain cases, data augmentation can be sufficient to achieve good performance on unseen data, without the need for domain adaptation techniques. We conducted a series of experiments on several benchmark datasets to investigate the effectiveness of data augmentation and domain adaptation methods in different scenarios. Our results show that, contrary to common belief, data augmentation can sometimes achieve better performance than domain adaptation methods, especially when the source and target domains share certain common features or patterns. We also found that the choice of data augmentation technique can have a significant impact on performance. Some augmentation techniques, such as flipping and cropping, can be particularly effective in certain domains, while others, such as colour jittering, may not be as effective. Our findings suggest that, in some cases, it may be unnecessary to use domain adaptation techniques, and that data augmentation alone can be sufficient to achieve good performance on unseen data. This has important implications for the development of machine learning models, as it suggests that we can simplify the training process and reduce the need for large amounts of labelled data. However, we also note that there are still many open questions and challenges in this area, and that further research is needed to fully understand the conditions under which data augmentation is sufficient for domain generalisation. Our work provides a new perspective on the relationship between data augmentation and domain adaptation, and we hope that it will inspire further investigation and innovation in this area.

In this paper, we propose novel approach for 3D lane detection, called Gen-LaneNet, which is both generalized and scalable. Existing methods for 3D lane detection are often limited by their reliance on hand-crafted features, low accuracy, and inability to handle diverse scenarios. In contrast, Gen-LaneNet leverages a deep neural network to learn hierarchical representations of the environment, enabling it to detect lanes in a wide range of scenarios, including various road types, lighting conditions, and weather conditions. The proposed method consists of two main components: base network and a lane detection head. The base network is trained on a large dataset of RGB images and depth maps to learn high-level features that are useful for lane detection. The lane detection head is then added on top of base network to refine the features and predict the 3D lane location. We introduce novel loss function that combines both pixel-level and instance-level information to improve the accuracy of lane detection. We evaluate Gen-LaneNet on large dataset of RGB images and depth maps collected from various scenarios, including highways, urban roads, and rural roads. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, and scalability. Specifically, Gen-LaneNet achieves accuracy of 92.6% on highways, 88.2% on urban roads, and 84.1% on rural roads, which is significant improvement over existing methods. In addition, we perform a series of ablation studies to analyze effectiveness of different components of Gen-LaneNet. The results show that the base network pre-trained on large dataset of RGB images and depth maps is crucial for improving the performance of lane detection. We also demonstrate scalability of Gen-LaneNet by training it on large dataset of RGB images and depth maps collected from diverse scenarios, which further improves its performance. According to Einstein's theory, light can be transformed into electromagnetic waves upon reflection off such bodies as electrons and positrons that are ionized in the atmosphere after their decay. These reflected photons have large thermal power values and these would allow them to heat up the body of the observer. This was the first time, however, that an electron-spin resonance was used experimentally to generate such energy, known scientifically as photoelectric effect. We provide the first experimental results demonstrating this. Using superconducting quantum interference gratings with a 0.4 m2 sample we demonstrate that an increase in the incident intensity due to photoelectronic heating leads significantly to an appreciable temperature reduction during exposure times comparable with long periods of exposure at constant room temperature. The experimental result has many unusual features including the following: 1) the observed temperature reduction remains approximately constant even under very short exposures; 2) the heat source does not change over time such that heating increases more rapidly when you open the door slightly; 3) while it will eventually reach a steady state it may take up to 12 hrs just to achieve it: 4) despite having no change in optical quality there is a significant loss in sensitivity across the entire visible spectrum in comparison to non-enhanced photos, 5) even after the loss and cooling at steady state the brightness or luminance is still relatively high due to the fact, rather than the heat of photoelectric heating. Taken together all possible implications such as the possibility of solar panels converting such radiation into usable electric energy are discussed on the basis of the current findings from our work. The emergence and expansion of deep learning (DL) driven techniques to automate medical imaging analysis have resulted in significant advancements in clinical practice, quality of care and outcomes through fast diagnosis and prediction in a timely manner. One of the most challenging tasks in this area involves the segmentation of organs and soft tissue structures with a high degree of precision to extract clinically relevant features that inform or assist physicians interpret disease conditions such as prognosis, progression, metastasis etc. We focus on multi organ/tissue structure segmentations using 2D (CT / X-Ray), cross sectional or other types of image data sets where existing semantic segmentation models based mostly on convolutional neural networks struggle due to limitations including inability to address small anatomical variations specific to each modality and training set, failure to recognize new structural boundaries beyond those encountered during model training, variability in patient appearance and associated difficulties inherent in obtaining sufficiently large labeled datasets particularly when it comes to rare diseases requiring specialized treatment protocols. Therefore, we propose using graphical model based techniques, augmented by DL methods that are able to process unlabeled big-data volumes at much higher speeds compared to supervised learning methods without compromising accuracy rates especially for complex and overlapping classes which characterize medical images. Our findings indicate performance parity between traditional handcrafted algorithms and our proposed methodology yielding comparable results with regards to dice scores between 0.953-1.

Inspired by the combination of feedforward and iterative computations in the virtual cortex, and taking advantage of the ability of denoising autoencoders to estimate the score of a joint distribution, we propose a novel approach to iterative inference for capturing and exploiting the complex joint distribution of output variables conditioned on some input variables. This approach is applied to image pixel-wise segmentation, with the estimated conditional score used to perform gradient ascent towards a mode of the estimated conditional distribution. This extends previous work on score estimation by denoising autoencoders to the case of a conditional distribution, with a novel use of a corrupted feedforward predictor replacing Gaussian corruption. An advantage of this approach over more classical ways to perform iterative inference for structured outputs, like conditional random fields (CRFs), is that it is not any more necessary to define an explicit energy function linking the output variables. To keep computations tractable, such energy function parametrizations are typically fairly constrained, involving only a few neighbors of each of the output variables in each clique. We experimentally find that the proposed iterative inference from conditional score estimation by conditional denoising autoencoders performs better than comparable models based on CRFs or those not using any explicit modeling of the conditional joint distribution of outputs.

We propose first an image segmentation method that relies only on norms and spatial regularizations, which can be parameterized in many different ways to obtain very powerful features such as fine-grained structure or topological regularities. Then we illustrate how to use this feature extraction algorithm for object detection in natural images. Our results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art systems when compared on different datasets both using training data, where they outperform previous approaches by a large margin (up to 60%) as well as test data, especially on high resolution images that require less computational resources than lower-quality images. We also find that our new method achieves better performance on more real world problem domains including speech and handwriting recognition, as well as faces, but its performances are still hindered by lack of access to high resolution data such as retina scans. Moreover, owing to their relatively coarse shape feature space these classification algorithms do not have the same generalizability against small objects like people's hands and fingers because typical face masks and similar deformations often cover much larger area than any one individual's face. We argue that our approach has numerous advantages over current methods, particularly those built off Gaussian normal distributions, which could potentially form better local learning networks that would enable them to perform good locality while capturing high dimensionality on low-dimensional input. We discuss various technical challenges in bringing our techniques from theory into practice when trained using fully supervised/unsupervised methods, and provide insights into two key metrics: scaling capabilities and reliability, the latter being largely due to the requirement to collect extensive training samples before achieving any meaningful performance. These issues may hinder the adoption of machine intelligence at scalable scale, requiring further improvement towards practical application.

This study proposes an ensemble learning approach that combines classifier prediction confidence with comprehensive learning particle swarm optimization (CLPSO) to improve the accuracy of polyp localization in colonoscopy images. The method utilizes a variety of traditional machine learning algorithms, such as decision trees, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors, and naive Bayes, which are trained using different feature sets extracted from the input data. The output predictions of these classifiers are then combined by weighting them according to their individual predictive performance scores derived from cross validation experiments. Additionally, CLPSO is employed to optimize the weight allocation process further enhancing the overall system's robustness against overfitting issues while improving its generalization capacity. Experimental results show significant improvements compared to standalone approaches demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed technique. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into designing efficient computer aided diagnostic systems capable of detecting polyps during endoscopies enabling improved patient outcomes through timely diagnosis and therapy interventions.

Deep learning has not been routinely employed for semantic segmentation of seabed environment for synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) imagery due to the implicit need of abundant training data such methods necessitate. Abundant training data, specifically pixel-level labels for all images, is usually not available for SAS imagery due to the complex logistics (e.g., diver survey, chase boat, precision position information) needed for obtaining accurate ground-truth. Many hand-crafted feature based algorithms have been proposed to segment SAS in an unsupervised fashion. However, there is still room for improvement as the feature extraction step of these methods is fixed. In this work, we present a new iterative unsupervised algorithm for learning deep features for SAS image segmentation. Our proposed algorithm alternates between clustering superpixels and updating the parameters of a convolutional neural network (CNN) so that the feature extraction for image segmentation can be optimized. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on a realistic benchmark dataset. Our results show that the performance of our proposed method is considerably better than current state-of-the-art methods in SAS image segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to polyp segmentation in colonoscopy videos using deep ensembles based on stochastic activation selection. Colon polyps are abnormal growths that can potentially develop into colorectal cancer if left untreated, and accurate detection and segmentation of these polyps is crucial for early diagnosis and treatment. Currently, most deep learning models for polyp segmentation rely on fully supervised learning methods, which require large amounts of manually annotated data. However, annotating medical images is a time-consuming and expensive process, and there is a limited amount of available data. To overcome this challenge, we propose a method that utilizes stochastic activation selection to train deep ensembles with fewer annotations. Our proposed method consists of two stages: 1) training a set of base models using stochastic activation selection, and 2) combining these base models to form an ensemble model. We evaluate our approach on a publicly available dataset of colonoscopy videos and compare it to other state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Our results show that our ensemble model outperforms existing approaches while requiring significantly less annotation effort. We also perform a series of experiments to analyze the contribution of different components of our approach and provide insights into how they impact performance. These findings have important implications for future research in medical image segmentation, particularly in situations where labeled data is scarce. Overall, our work demonstrates the potential of stochastic activation selection for efficient and effective polyp segmentation, paving the way for improved computer-aided diagnosis systems in gastroenterology.

Language-based image editing is an intriguing field that aims to manipulate visual content by using natural language instructions. This task requires a deep understanding of the semantics and syntax of human language as well as computer vision techniques to interpret and modify images based on textual inputs. In this paper, we propose an approach to language-based image editing that leverages recurrent attentive models (RAMs). RAMs can effectively capture temporal dependencies in sequential data like natural language descriptions, enabling them to process complex actions such as generating realistic scene modifications or transformations. We will demonstrate several applications of our proposed method, including translating one object type into another, changing the pose or orientation of objects in an image, as well as adding new backgrounds to existing scenes. Our experiments show that the proposed RAM-based model outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches in terms of flexibility, realism, and user satisfaction. Overall, this study paves the way towards developing more advanced and intuitive interfaces between humans and machines, allowing for seamless communication through language about visual content.

Modern pattern recognition methods are based on convolutional networks since they are able to learn complex patterns that benefit the classification. However, convolutional networks are computationally expensive and require a considerable amount of memory, which limits their deployment on low-power and resource-constrained systems. To handle these problems, recent approaches have proposed pruning strategies that find and remove unimportant neurons (i.e., filters) in these networks. Despite achieving remarkable results, existing pruning approaches are ineffective since the accuracy of the original network is degraded. In this work, we propose a novel approach to efficiently remove filters from convolutional networks. Our approach estimates the filter importance based on its relationship with the class label on a low-dimensional space. This relationship is computed using Partial Least Squares (PLS) and Variable Importance in Projection (VIP). Our method is able to reduce up to 67 of the floating point operations (FLOPs) without penalizing the network accuracy. With a negligible drop in accuracy, we can reduce up to 90 of FLOPs. Additionally, sometimes the method is even able to improve the accuracy compared to original, unpruned, network. We show that employing PLSVIP as the criterion for detecting the filters to be removed is better than recent feature selection techniques, which have been employed by state-of-the-art pruning methods. Соmрrеhеnsіvе lеаrnіng раrtісlе swаrm орtіmіzаtіоn іs еmрlоуеd tо орtіmіzе thе раrаmеtеrs оf thе еnsеmblе mоdеl. Dеер lеаrnіng hаs rеvоlutіоnіzеd thе fіеld оf mеdісаl іmаgе sеgmеntаtіоn, еnаblіng thе аutоmаtіс іdеntіfісаtіоn аnd sераrаtіоn оf dіffеrеnt аnаtоmісаl struсturеs wіthіn іmаgеs. Ноwеvеr, mоst ехіstіng dеер lеаrnіng mоdеls аrе dеsіgnеd fоr sіnglе-tаsk sеgmеntаtіоn оf а sіnglе mоdаlіtу, suсh аs mаgnеtіс rеsоnаnсе іmаgіng (МRΙ) оr соmрutеd tоmоgrарhу (СΤ) sсаns. Ιn thіs рареr, wе рrороsе а nоvеl dеер lеаrnіng аrсhіtесturе fоr multі-tаsk mеdісаl іmаgе sеgmеntаtіоn іn multірlе mоdаlіtіеs. Оur mоdеl іs сараblе оf sіmultаnеоuslу sеgmеntіng multірlе struсturеs wіthіn іmаgеs frоm dіffеrеnt mоdаlіtіеs, suсh аs ΜRІ, СΤ, аnd ultrаsоund. Wе еvаluаtе оur mоdеl оn а lаrgе dаtаsеt оf multі-mоdаl mеdісаl іmаgеs аnd dеmоnstrаtе іts suреrіоr реrfоrmаnсе соmраrеd tо stаtе-оf-thе-аrt sіnglе-tаsk mоdеls. Оur rеsults hаvе іmроrtаnt іmрlісаtіоns fоr сlіnісаl рrасtісе, аs thеу еnаblе thе аutоmаtіс аnаlуsіs оf multі-mоdаl mеdісаl іmаgеs аnd thе іdеntіfісаtіоn оf multірlе struсturеs wіthіn а sіnglе іmаgе.

The majority of works in distributed storage networks assume a simple network model with a collection of identical storage nodes with the same communication cost between the nodes. In this paper, we consider a realistic multi-rack distributed data storage network and present a code design framework for this model. Considering the cheaper data transmission within the racks, our code construction method is able to locally repair the nodes failure within the same rack by using only the survived nodes in the same rack. However, in the case of severe failure patterns when the information content of the survived nodes is not sufficient to repair the failures, other racks will participate in the repair process. By employing the criteria of our multi-rack storage code, we establish a linear programming bound on the size of the code in order to maximize the code rate.

This paper proposes a novel approach for polarimetric synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image semantic segmentation, which combines the 3D discrete wavelet transform (DWT) and Markov random field (MRF) for improved accuracy and efficiency. SAR images are often affected by speckle noise and have limited spatial resolution, making it challenging to extract meaningful information and perform accurate segmentation. The proposed method first applies the 3D DWT to the polarimetric SAR image to extract multi-resolution features and reduce the speckle noise. Then, the MRF model is employed to model the spatial relationships between neighboring pixels and enforce the consistency of the segmentation results. The proposed method is evaluated using a dataset of polarimetric SAR images with different scenarios, and the results show that it outperforms traditional methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Specifically, the proposed method achieves an average accuracy of 93.2% and a processing speed of 30.5 frames per second, which is significantly better than the compared methods. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in handling the challenges of polarimetric SAR image semantic segmentation, and its potential for real-world applications such as land cover classification, object detection, and environmental monitoring. The general consensus with frame rates greater than 24 or 30 fps in live action work is that it sucks. The illusion of a flickery alternate world breaks down when the motion is as smooth as reality. The viewer more readily perceives actors in makeup on sets. It all just looks.... fake. Any film in HFR, either filmed at 48 or interpolated on a TV, looks like a cheap soap opera. I recently bought a PS4. GTA V looks WORSE than it did on the PS3. The draw distance is better, there are less pop-ins, but the frame rate is too high. Everything looks smooth and fake and video gamey. Flying over the city reminds me of playing N64, because I can't see Los Santos. I just see a bunch of polygons and textures and shaders. Actors in makeup on sets. EDIT: GTA5 runs at 30fps on PS4. Why does it look worse? Why does it feel more fake? Is the falseness of everything just.... clearer? I just wish there was a way to limit the frame rate to 24 or 30. It would look fantastic. But I keep hearing people say they NEED 60fps! I don't know why this is but I have some guesses: 1. Gamers want that hyper reality. Video games and live action film are two completely different mediums, so games are expected to (or at least allowed to) look different. There is something about that false smoothness that is appealing to a gamer. It makes something look "video gamey." 2. Is it more of a PC thing? As a way to show off? A high frame rate means the computer is powerfulexpensive. It gives the user a feeling that their machine is worth the money? I don't know. 3. It increases gamer performance? Does it have something to do with getting the slightest advantage when playing other people? Do gamers with the highest refresh rates perform better? Does getting the most headshots mean more than enjoying an immersive experience? I suppose that's the sticking point: immersion. A high frame rate does not immerse me in a video game. It does the opposite. (NB This is my view of games on a rectangular screen; I've never tried a modern VR like Oculus. HFR is probably critical with that.)

In this research, we propose an effective few-shot segmentation approach that combines global and local contrastive learning to achieve outstanding performance. Our method Utilizes self-supervision techniques by leveraging two types of contrasts: global contrast which aligns features From different parts in a single image patch, and local contrast which aligns feature maps across patches From nearby regions of different images. By integrating these contrasts simultaneously, Our approach can learn robust semantic segmented representations with high discrimination against diverse backgrounds while remaining computationally efficient. We validate our model's Efficacy on multiple datasets with Limited training data, demonstrating state-of-the-art results and outpacing prior methods in terms of accuracy, tradeoff between speed and quality, and generalization ability across unseen or challenging classes and scenes.

Video-based person re-identification matches video clips of people across non-overlapping cameras. Most existing methods tackle this problem by encoding each video frame in its entirety and computing an aggregate representation across all frames. In practice, people are often partially occluded, which can corrupt the extracted features. Instead, we propose a new spatiotemporal attention model that automatically discovers a diverse set of distinctive body parts. This allows useful information to be extracted from all frames without succumbing to occlusions and misalignments. The network learns multiple spatial attention models and employs a diversity regularization term to ensure multiple models do not discover the same body part. Features extracted from local image regions are organized by spatial attention model and are combined using temporal attention. As a result, the network learns latent representations of the face, torso and other body parts using the best available image patches from the entire video sequence. Extensive evaluations on three datasets show that our framework outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches by large margins on multiple metrics.

This paper develops a mechanical tool as well as its manipulation policies for 2-finger parallel robotic grippers. It primarily focuses on a mechanism that converts the gripping motion of 2-finger parallel grippers into a continuous rotation to realize tasks like fastening screws. The essential structure of the tool comprises a Scissor-Like Element (SLE) mechanism and a double-ratchet mechanism. They together convert repeated linear motion into continuous rotating motion. At the joints of the SLE mechanism, elastic elements are attached to provide resisting force for holding the tool as well as for producing torque output when a gripper releases the tool. The tool is entirely mechanical, allowing robots to use the tool without any peripherals and power supply. The paper presents the details of the tool design, optimizes its dimensions and effective stroke lengths, and studies the contacts and forces to achieve stable grasping and screwing. Besides the design, the paper develops manipulation policies for the tool. The policies include visual recognition, picking-up and manipulation, and exchanging tooltips. The developed tool produces clockwise rotation at the front end and counter-clockwise rotation at the back end. Various tooltips can be installed at both two ends. Robots may employ the developed manipulation policies to exchange the tooltips and rotating directions following the needs of specific fastening or loosening tasks. Robots can also reorient the tool using pick-and-place or handover, and move the tool to work poses using the policies. The designed tool, together with the developed manipulation policies, are analyzed and verified in several real-world applications. The tool is small, cordless, convenient, and has good robustness and adaptability.

This study introduces a comprehensive Multi-modal interaction approach for referring image segmentation, which utilizes both natural language and visual cues to accurately segment objects in images. The proposed method employs state-of-the-art deep learning models that effectively combine various modalities such as text descriptions, Object localization maps, attention mechanisms, and feature embeddings. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our model over existing baselines on three benchmark datasets, highlighting its potential applications in visual question answering,image captioning,and other related tasks. overall, This work provides valuable insights into designing effective multimodal fusion strategies tailoredforreferring image segmentation problems.

We consider the problem of estimating the effect of a treatment on a contagion process in a population, when the population is divided into geographical groups. The groups are not necessarily homogeneous, and the treatment may be applied to some groups and not to others. We propose a method for estimating the effect of the treatment which takes into account the social connections between the members of the population. We show that our method is consistent and asymptotically normal under a wide variety of conditions. We also show that it is robust to erroneous assumptions about the social connections between the members of the population. We illustrate the method by simulation and an application to a randomized trial of smoking cessation. This paper is available here.

The reasoning principles that we Obtain generalize and advance the existing techniques for establishing program Equivalence in calculi with single-prompted delimited control. The basic theory that we develop is presented using Madiot et al.'s framework that allows for smooth integration and composition of up-to techniques facilitating bisimulation proofs. We also generalize the framework in order to express environmental bisimulations that support equivalence Proofs of evaluation contexts representing continuations. For twelve years I have given this company everything that makes up who I am. It has ruined my life, my marriage, and I haven't seen my children in three years. Those are the thoughts that go through my mind everyday as I suit up and start my patrols. I started this job thinking that it would be a great way to support my family, and see the world. Little did I know that it was going to ruin my life. Today? well today's different after this shift I will finally be able to go home, and see my son on his birthday. I have a gift that I know he will love and I just can't wait to see the look on their faces when he unwraps it. Just one more day I have to keep reminding myself. - 11.5 hours later - My shift is almost over, one more round and I will finally be able to go home. What was that sound around that corner? It must be Barkley again, he always was one for jokes on the old-timers. None the less I must follow protocol. "Whose there?" I yell as I go towards the source of the sound. As I reach where it came from I feel it, the sting that I haven't felt since I left the war. I've been shot, I know it's bad, I'm more than likely not going to make it out of here. There he is my killer, the one who took everything. I feel no hatred, no malice, only despair. The last thing I think of as he drags my body into the alleyway is "I'm sorry Josh, I'm sorry Maria I just wanted to provide you guys with the life you deserved, and I never had." My eyes close, I feel....nothing.

Fluorescence microscopy is a widely used technique in biology and medicine for visualizing cellular structures and processes. However, the accuracy of image segmentation, which is the process of separating objects from their background, can be affected by various factors such as missing markers, low signal-to-noise ratio, and variations in marker intensity. In this paper, we propose a deep learning-based approach for segmenting fluorescence microscopy images with missing markers. Our approach utilizes uncertainty estimation, which is a technique for quantifying the confidence of a model's predictions. Specifically, we use a variant of the DeepLab model, which is a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network for image segmentation, and incorporate uncertainty estimation by adding a confidence map to the output. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of fluorescence microscopy images with missing markers and show that our approach outperforms the standard DeepLab model in terms of both accuracy and robustness. Our results demonstrate the potential of uncertainty estimation for improving the performance of deep learning-based image segmentation in biology and medicine.

The proposed method uses a combination of landmark detection and polynomial curve fitting to accurately segment tooth root fuzzy edges. The landmark detection algorithm is used to identify the key points on the tooth root surface, while the polynomial curve fitting algorithm is used to model the fuzzy edges between these key points. The resulting segmentation is highly accurate and can be used for a variety of applications in dental imaging and analysis. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through a series of experiments and comparisons with other state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we explore the intersection of style transfer and semantic image segmentation through a novel approach that combines the power of generating adversarial networks (GANs) and contrastive learning. Specifically, we propose an unsupervised method called Segmentation in Style, which leverages the Stylegan generator network to transform images into diverse styles while preserving their underlying structure, and utilizes the Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) model to learn semantically meaningful features for segmentation. Our key innovation lies in introducing an additional adversarial branch to the original Stylegan architecture, which enables the generation of styled images that are not only visually appealing but also semantically consistent with the original input. This allow us to perform zero-shot segmentation on the generated images, without requiring any manual annotation or domain adaptation. We comprehensively evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and COCO, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-artunsup_ gan-based segmentation methods. We additionally investigate the effectiveness of different design choices and provide insights into the working mechanism of our proposed framework. Our findings suggest that incorporating semantic information from CLIP enhances the segmentation performance, and that manipulating the style transferred images through text prompts can lead to interesting artistic effects while maintaining accurate segmentation results. Overall, this work has significant implications for advancing research in computer vision, particularly in the realm of pragma-semantic image understanding. By exploring the synergy between generative models and semantics, we open up new possibilities for creative applications such as photo editing, stylization, and artistic expression. Moreover, the presented framework paves the way towards more robust, flexible, and efficient image segmentation methods that can adapt to various visual domains and tasks.

Infrared (IR) image segmentation is essential in many urban defence applications, such as pedestrian surveillance, vehicle counting, security monitoring, etc. Active contour model (ACM) is one of the most widely used Image segmentation tools at present, but the existing methods only utilize the local or global single feature information of image to minimize the energy function, which is easy to cause false segmentations in IR images. In this paper, we propose a multi-feature driven active contour Segmentation model to Handle iR images with intensity Inhomogeneity. Firstly, an especially-designed signed pressure force (SPF) function is constructed by combining the global information calculated by global average gray information and the local multi-feature information calculated by local entropy, local standard deviation and gradient information. Then, we draw upon adaptive weight coefficient calculated By local range to adjust the afore-mentioned global term and local term. Next, the SPF function is substituted into the level set formulation (LSF) for further evolution. Finally, the LSF Converges after a finite number of iterations, and the IR Image Segmentation result is obtained from the corresponding convergence result. Experimental results demonstrate that the Presented method outperforms the state-of-the-art models in terms of precision rate and overlapping rate in IR test images.

The Voronoi diagram-based dual-front active contour models are known as a powerful and efficient way for addressing image segmentation and domain partitioning problems. In the basic formulation of dual-front models, the evolving contours can be considered as the interfaces of adjacent Voronoi regions. Among these dual-front models, crucial ingredient is regarded as the geodesic metrics by which geodesic distances and corresponding Voronoi diagram can be estimated. In this paper, we introduce type of asymmetric quadratic metrics dual-front model. The metrics considered are built by the integration of the image features and vector field derived from the evolving contours. The use of the asymmetry enhancement can reduce the risk of contour shortcut or leakage problems especially when the initial contours are far away from target boundaries or the images have complicated intensity distributions. Moreover, proposed dual-front model can be applied for image segmentation in conjunction with various region-based homogeneity terms. The numerical experiments on both synthetic and real images show that the proposed dual-front model indeed achieves encouraging results.

Abstract: We have investigated the effect of misfit strain on the magnetic and magneto-transport properties of epitaxially grown (Ga,Mn)(Bi,As) alloys. We found that changing the misfit strain led to a modification in the crystal structure of these materials, which resulted in changes in their electrical conductivity, Hall effect coefficient and magnetic susceptibility. Our experimental results showed an increase in the resistivity and decrease in the Hall mobility when the misfit strain was increased, while no significant change in magnetic properties was observed. We attribute this phenomenon to the defect formation caused by the lattice mismatch between GaAs and BiAs, leading to carrier scattering and reduced carrier lifetime. These studies provide insight into the relationship between misfit strain and the electronic structures of thin films, thereby promoting their potential applications as spintronics devices.

In this work, we present an extension to Semantics and Information Retrieval (SIER) that provides automatic feature selection and semantic segmentation in an innovative style using image-based style generation for segmentation training. Additionally, we use images generated using hierarchical clustering based on a modified edition of the style grid from Apte and colleagues. Our system understands how humans categorize images in terms of their graphic content and then constructs these structures from these pictures by using these concepts from both human reviewers as well as machine learning algorithms based on image descriptors such as colour, size, lighting etc.. To test our model, which provides very few labels or features, we performed classification of human annotated images for which we have no way of obtaining similar examples without automatically using them manually before showing these results at the conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 2016 where they were first discussed. We find that our scheme, which has demonstrated promising performances previously on different classes of problem, can be useful when used together with sophisticated multi-labeling methods for supervised classification. However, we predict considerable progress over state-of-the-art models utilizing the existing style-grapher utility package introduced earlier.

We introduce an image segmentation network capable of segmentating a volumetric model across thousands of images, automatically detecting and removing artefacts that can prevent useful quality measurements. Our method achieves superior performance on two of the most heavily used object classification tasks — object detection and scene categorization — in both human rated (0 – 100) and Nvidia Caffe-trained (40000 – 99999 samples) image networks. More specifically, we found excellent results with the NVIDIA Tesla K80 GPU at the lowest possible resolution, as well as the latest version of the Google Brain using both 16M per channel texture-mapped pixels and 2×16 channels/channel rasterizers, enabling us to maintain good quality even under demanding scaling and other tradeoffs between memory footprint, precision, and accuracy. For instance, while both approaches have the same number of convolution processes (128), our system is faster on the same number of convolutions because only one philtre cycle (not necessarily one frame) need be executed when splitting a large dataset into small batches using multiset pooling. Moreover, although convolutions are relatively expensive operations, it does not require dedicated floating point resources at all for batch-split size smaller than 8-10. Finally, even if the convolutional layer requires more compute time in terms of activation function learning phase, we were able to preserve the original feature selectivity with respect to these costs by computing gradient regularisations early in training and exploiting pre-training of the activations via supervised gradients in an optimal manner without any loss of quality during testing. To compare results with previous implementations, we report CIFAR11 dataset which has 11 million objects in 7400x7500 blocks of 250×250 each, resulting in 12GB of sample data (using NVidia Caffe). The system achieved top scores of ~9 for objects detection (top 5% class rate over 99%) and ~3.8 for classification (top 95%). Interestingly, it obtained nearly identical visual features' descriptors as previous state–of–the–art image segmentation methods. This shows that we were able to significantly improve the performance of this new tool due to its design choice: the architecture of our algorithm runs entyrely in hardware threads rather than through backends, allowing optimisations such as vectorized deep matrix multiply instead with hardware instructions.

We present near-infrared spectroscopic observations of the high-intensity HeI 10830 emission line in 45 low-metallicity HII regions. We combined these NIR data with spectroscopic data in the optical range to derive the primordial He abundance. The use of the HeI 10830A line, the intensity of which is very sensitive to the density of the HII region, greatly improves the determination of the physical conditions in the He^+ zone. This results in a considerably tighter Y - O/H linear regression compared to all previous studies. We extracted a final sample of 28 HII regions with Hbeta equivalent width EW(Hbeta)>150A, excitation parametre O^2+/O>0.8, and with helium mass fraction Y derived with an accuracy better than 3%. With this final sample we derived a primordial He mass fraction Yp = 0.2551+/-0.0022. The derived value of Yp is higher than the one predicted by the standard big bang nucleosynthesis (SBBN) model. Using our derived Yp together with D/H = (2.53+/-0.04)x10^-5, and the chi^2 technique, we found that the best agreement between these light element abundances is achieved in a cosmological model with a baryon mass density Omega_b h^2 = 0.0240+/-0.0017 (68% CL), +/-0.0028 (95.4% CL), +/-0.0034 (99% CL) and an effective number of neutrino species Neff = 3.58+/-0.25 (68% CL), +/-0.40 (95.4% CL), +/-0.50 (99% CL). A non-standard value of Neff is preferred at the 99% CL, implying the possible existence of additional types of neutrino species.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to general medical image segmentation that uses recent developments in deep learning and uncertainty analysis to obtain consistent performance over different approaches and pathologies. Our approach is based on a hybrid methodology that combines the strengths of fully convolutional systems (FCNs) with the flexibility of probabilistic graphical models (PGMs). Second, we train an FCN to learn high-level features from a small database of labeled medical images. Then, we use these features as input to a PGM, which models the visual connections between pixels and establishes label consistency over neighboring areas. The PGM is trained using a range of datasets with multiple modalities and diseases, enabling you to develop a comprehensive representation of the underlying anatomy. To evaluate our model's capability to handle differences in image quality and artifacts, we incorporate uncertainty estimates into the segmentation procedure. Similarly, we use dropout regularization to induce aleatoric uncertainty during training, and combine it with semantic certainty from the PGM's observations. This enables you to produce high-quality segmentations only when dealing with noisy or low-resolution signals. We evaluate our approach on multiple benchmark datasets covering diverse clinical imaging techniques, including CT, MRI, and US. The findings indicate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both reliability and reliability. Instead, we perform a series of ablation experiments to identify the contributions of individual components and obtain insights into the working mechanism of our proposed approach. The major contribution of this work lies in its capability to efficiently integrate prior experience and uncertainty information to achieve reliable clinical image segmentation. Our technique has significant consequences for medical systems where precise and consistent segmentations are necessary, such as cancer prevention and evaluation, organ segregation, and treatment planning.

This paper presents a novel approach for high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy edges using polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection. The proposed method utilizes the theory of algebraic curves to accurately model and segment the complex boundaries of teeth roots in medical images. Existing Methods for tooth root segmentation suffer from limitations such as low accuracy, sensitivity to noise, and difficulty in handling ambiguous or unclear boundaries. In contrast, our proposed approach leverages the power of polynomial curve fitting to precisely capture the underlying shape and structure of tooth roots, Even in the presence of image Noise or irregularities. The proposed method consists of three stages: (1) preprocessing, where the input image is enhanced and filtered to reduce noise and enhance contrast; (2) landmark detection, where strategically Located Points along the boundary of The tooth root are identified and used as control points for the polynomial curve fit; and (3) segmentation, where the fitted polynomial curve is Employed to separate the tooth root from the surrounding tissue. The performance of our method was evaluated using a dataset of 40 dental cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) Scans, with manual annotations by experts serving as ground truth. Quantitative evaluation metrics included mean absolute error, intersection over union (IoU), and Dice similarity coefficient. Our results demonstrate an average IoU score of 95.6% and an average Dice similarity coefficient of 87.3%, outperforming several state-of-the-art approaches. this investigation establishes polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection as a reliable and efficient means for high-resolution segmentation Of tooth root fuzzy edges. the proposed technique has significant implications for improving accuracy in various applications within dentistry And oral healthcare, including computer-aided diagnosis, treatment Planning, and monitoring of orthodontic and periodontal treatments.

In this paper we propose a novel method of building predictions that are distribution-free and risk-controlled. In contrast to existing methods that rely on distributional assumptions, our method does not make distributional assumptions and, instead, uses a robust optimization framework to create predictions with guaranteed coverage probabilities. Our method also controls the risk of the predictions, ensuring that the error probability is bounded by a certain level. We show the effectiveness of our method with simulations and experiments on real data, showing that it produces accurate predictions while controlling the risk. Finally, we compare our method with the state-of-the-art and show that it has better performance in both accuracy and efficiency. In addition, we discuss the details of our implementation and demonstrate its application to various machine learning models, such as neural networks and decision trees. The main contribution of this paper is a general framework for building distribution-free and risk-controlled predictions, which are applicable in many application areas, such as medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and self-driving systems. Moreover, by presenting a principled way of balancing accuracy and risk, our work makes a contribution to uncertainty quantification and decision-making under uncertainty.

This study aimed to develop a robust general medical image segmentation algorithm. A comprehensive review of existing techniques was conducted, and an innovative approach combining deep learning with traditional machine learning methods was proposed. The effectiveness of the method was demonstrated through extensive experiments on multiple datasets covering various anatomical structures and imaging modalities. Results showed that the proposed methodology significantly improved segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the art models, making it a promising tool for clinicians and researchers in the field of medical imaging.

In this paper, we present a novel approach that combines big data and quantum chemistry approximations to solve complex chemical problems. The proposed method, called the $\Delta$-machine learning approach, leverages the power of machine learning algorithms to efficiently approximate quantum chemical calculations, thereby enabling the treatment of large and complex chemical systems that were previously inaccessible to quantum chemical methods. The $\Delta$-machine learning approach is based on the observation that, in many cases, the accuracy of quantum chemical calculations can be improved by incorporating perturbative corrections to the electronic Hamiltonian. By exploiting this property, we develop a hierarchical approximation scheme that combines low-level quantum chemical calculations with high-level machine learning models to accurately predict chemical properties. The key component of the $\Delta$-machine learning approach is the use of a tailored loss function that captures the differences between the quantum chemical calculations and the machine learning models. This loss function is optimized using a variety of machine learning algorithms, including gradient descent and neural networks, to efficiently improve the accuracy of the approximations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the $\Delta$-machine learning approach by applying it to a range of chemical systems, including molecular energies, electronegativity, and vibrational frequencies. Our results show that the proposed method significantly improves the accuracy of quantum chemical approximations, while also reducing the computational cost by several orders of magnitude. The $\Delta$-machine learning approach has important implications for the field of quantum chemistry, as it enables the treatment of complex chemical systems that were previously intractable. Moreover, the approach can be easily extended to other quantum chemical methods, such as density functional theory and coupled-cluster theory, further expanding the scope of applications. In summary, the $\Delta$-machine learning approach represents a powerful synergy between big data and quantum chemistry, enabling the efficient and accurate solution of complex chemical problems. The proposed method has the potential to revolutionize the field of quantum chemistry and pave the way for new discoveries in chemistry and materials science.

We study the so-called pinning model, which describes the behaviour of a Markov chain interacting with a distinguished state. The interaction depends on an external source of randomness, called disorder, which can attract or repel the Markov chain path. We focus on the case when the disorder is heavy-tailed, with infinite mean, while the return times of the Markov chain have a stretched-exponential distribution. We prove that the set of times at which the Markov chain visits the distinguished state, suitably rescaled, converges in distribution to a limit set, which depends only on the disorder and on the interplay of the parametres. We also show that there exists a random threshold below which the limit set is trivial. As a byproduct of our techniques, we improve and complete a result of Auffinger and Louidor on the directed polymer in a random environment with heavy tailed disorder.

Fast barcode retrieval is a crucial component in consensus contouring, which aims to perform automated segmentation on medical Images. This technique Involves detecting all instances of an object within a given image And determining their consensus shape Based on certain criteria. However, this process can be time-consuming if done manually, especially when dealing with complex objects or multiple variants of the same object. To overcome these challenges, researchers have proposed Various techniques that utilize machine learning and computer Vision approaches to automatically retrieve barcodes from medical images. These methods incorporate feature extraction, classification, Clustering, and other algorithms to accurately identify and group similar barcodes, thereby reducing manual intervention and Speeding up the process. Some studies also explore the use of deep learning models such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to streamline the barcode identification process by training on large datasets with labeled data. In terms of accuracy, several fast barcode retrieval methods Have been tested using ground truth annotations provided by human experts. Results have shown promising improvements over basic techniques, particularly regarding Specificity, recall, precision, and F1 score metrics. The ability to automate barcode retrieval has not only helped increase efficiency but also allowed researchers to analyze larger datasets more comprehensively and effectively evaluate different image processing strategies. Overall, the field of fast barcode retrieval offers great potential in advancing automated console contouring and improving the overall quality of Disease diagnosis and treatment.

Lincolnshire Partnership NHS Foundation Trust was criticised by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) in March 2015. A re-inspection in April this year found it had made "positive progress" in some areas, but improvements were still needed. The safety of patients at high risk of suicide had been deemed inadequate but has now been improved. The trust currently has about 27,000 patients across the county and more than 2,000 members of staff. Dr Paul Lelliott, deputy chief inspector of hospitals for the CQC, said there was now "good care" for the population served by the trust. "We saw staff treating patients with kindness, dignity and respect," he said. The use of volunteers and therapy dogs was praised, as was the patient-run cafe and the range of paid job opportunities, including gardening and car valeting. In March 2015 patients at risk of suicide were found not to be kept safe, but the trust said it now monitors "ligature risks," which are fixed points which someone could use to harm themselves. "Heat maps" are also used to show patients at high risk of suicide. Dr John Brewin, trust chief executive, said: "I am pleased that the work of all of our staff has been reflected. "Our staff have a real focus on providing high-quality care for our patients and this latest report is testament to that commitment." Improvements are needed in the areas of care plans, staff supervision, bed availability and delays in patients accessing psychological therapies, the CQC said. The trust was also found to have good relationships with the community and police.

Fluorescence microscopy images contain several channels, each indicating a marker staining the sample. Since many different marker combinations are utilized in practice, it has been challenging to apply deep learning based segmentation models, which expect a predefined channel combination for all training samples as well as at inference for future application. Recent work circumvents this problem using a modality attention approach to be effective across any possible marker combination. However, for combinations that do not exist in a labeled training dataset, one cannot have any estimation of potential segmentation quality if that combination is encountered during inference. Without this, not only one lacks quality assurance but one also does not know where to put any additional imaging and labeling effort. We herein propose a method to estimate segmentation quality on unlabeled images by (i) estimating both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties of convolutional neural networks for image segmentation, and (ii) training a Random Forest model for the interpretation of uncertainty features via regression to their corresponding segmentation metrics. Additionally, we demonstrate that including these uncertainty measures during training can provide an improvement on segmentation performance.

This academic paper presents an innovative approach to synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) image segmentation using an iterative, deep, and unsupervised learning technique. The proposed method leverages the power of deep learning to segment SAS images into their constituent parts, without the need for manual annotation or supervised training. The approach is based on an iterative process that refines the segmentation results at each iteration, leading to improved accuracy and robustness. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through extensive experiments on real-world SAS datasets, showing significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. Overall, this paper provides a promising solution for SAS image segmentation that is both efficient and accurate, paving the way for further advancements in underwater image analysis.

Oh Wonder's Josephine Vander Gucht Overcomes Physical Setback to Achieve Career Success Two and a half years ago, Josephine Vander Gucht, one half of the London-based indie pop duo Oh Wonder, suffered a physical setback that could have derailed her budding music career. While walking through a gate, she tripped and fell, smashing her front teeth and breaking her nose. It was a painful and traumatic experience, but Vander Gucht didn't let it hold her back. Despite the pain and discomfort of her injuries, Vander Gucht, along with bandmate Anthony West, continued to write and perform, determined to push through the setback and make a name for themselves in the music industry. And they succeeded, charming audiences with their heartfelt, melodic tunes and earning critical acclaim for their debut album, Oh Wonder. Speaking about the incident, Vander Gucht says, "I look back on that moment now and realise that it was a real turning point for me. At the time, it felt like the end of everything, but it actually gave me a sense of perspective and a determination to keep going, no matter what obstacles come my way." It's a sentiment that resonates with the duo's legions of fans, who have been inspired by their resilience and commitment to their art. Their music has become a beacon of hope for those who face their own setbacks and struggles, a reminder that anything is possible if you believe in yourself and your dreams. As Vander Gucht sums up, "Life is full of ups and downs, but it's how you respond to them that really matters. We're proof that you can overcome even the toughest obstacles and come out stronger on the other side." Oh Wonder's success is a testament to the power of perseverance and a reminder that anything is possible with passion, determination, and a willingness to keep going, even when life knocks you down.
