Feature extraction from financial data is one of the most important problems in market prediction domain for which many approaches have been suggested. Among other modern tools, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have recently been applied for automatic feature selection and market prediction. However, in experiments reported so far, less attention has been paid to the correlation among different markets as a possible source of information for extracting features. In this paper, we suggest a CNN-based framework with specially designed CNNs, that can be applied on a collection of data from a variety of sources, including different markets, in order to extract features for predicting the future of those markets. The suggested framework has been applied for predicting the next day's direction of movement for the indices of SP 500, NASDAQ, DJI, NYSE, and RUSSELL markets based on various sets of initial features. The evaluations show a significant improvement in prediction's performance compared to the state of the art baseline algorithms.

The emergence and expansion of deep learning (DL) driven techniques to automate medical imaging analysis have resulted in significant advancements in clinical practice, quality of care and outcomes through fast diagnosis and prediction in a timely manner. One of the most challenging tasks in this area involves the segmentation of organs and soft tissue structures with a high degree of precision to extract clinically relevant features that inform or assist physicians interpret disease conditions such as prognosis, progression, metastasis etc. We focus on multi organ/tissue structure segmentations using 2D (CT / X-Ray), cross sectional or other types of image data sets where existing semantic segmentation models based mostly on convolutional neural networks struggle due to limitations including inability to address small anatomical variations specific to each modality and training set, failure to recognize new structural boundaries beyond those encountered during model training, variability in patient appearance and associated difficulties inherent in obtaining sufficiently large labeled datasets particularly when it comes to rare diseases requiring specialized treatment protocols. Therefore, we propose using graphical model based techniques, augmented by DL methods that are able to process unlabeled big-data volumes at much higher speeds compared to supervised learning methods without compromising accuracy rates especially for complex and overlapping classes which characterize medical images. Our findings indicate performance parity between traditional handcrafted algorithms and our proposed methodology yielding comparable results with regards to dice scores between 0.953-5.

Automotive companies increasingly adopt scaled agile methods to allow them to deal with their organisational and product complexity. Suitable methods are needed to ensure safety when developing automotive systems. On a small scale, R-Scrum and SafeScrum are two concrete suggestions for how to develop safety-critical systems using agile methods. However, for large-scale environments, existing frameworks like SAFe or LeSS do not support the development of safety-critical systems out of the box. We, therefore, aim to understand which challenges exist when developing safety-critical systems within large-scale agile industrial settings, in particular in the automotive domain. Based on an analysis of R-Scrum and SafeScrum , we conducted a focus group with three experts from industry to collect challenges in their daily work. We found challenges in the areas of living traceability, continuous compliance, and organisational flexibility. Among others, organisations struggle with defining a suitable traceability strategy, performing incremental safety analysis, and with integrating safety practices into their scaled way of working. Our results indicate a need to provide practical approaches to integrate safety work into large-scale agile development and point towards possible solutions, e.g., modular safety cases.

Scenario discovery is the process of finding areas of interest, commonly referred to as scenarios, in data spaces resulting from simulations. For instance, one might search for conditions - which are inputs of the simulation model - where the system under investigation is unstable. A commonly used algorithm for scenario discovery is PRIM. It yields scenarios in the form of hyper-rectangles which are human-comprehensible. When the simulation model has many inputs, and the simulations are computationally expensive, PRIM may not produce good results, given the affordable volume of data. So we propose a new procedure for scenario discovery - we train an intermediate statistical model which generalizes fast, and use it to label (a lot of) data for PRIM. We provide the statistical intuition behind our idea. Our experimental study shows that this method is much better than PRIM itself. Specifically, our method reduces the number of simulations runs necessary by 75 on average.

High-quality training data play a key role in image segmentation tasks. Usually, pixel-level annotations are expensive, laborious and time-consuming for the large volume of training data. To reduce labelling cost and improve segmentation quality, interactive segmentation methods have been proposed, which provide the result with just a few clicks. However, their performance does not meet the requirements of practical segmentation tasks in terms of speed and accuracy. In this work, we propose EdgeFlow, a novel architecture that fully utilizes interactive information of user clicks with edge-guided flow. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance without any post-processing or iterative optimization scheme. Comprehensive experiments on benchmarks also demonstrate the superiority of our method. In addition, with the proposed method, we develop an efficient interactive segmentation tool for practical data annotation tasks. The source code and tool is avaliable at https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleSeg.

The Earth is constantly changing and moving in predictable patterns and cycles. The water cycle and nutrient cycles (carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, etc.) are Earth's metabolism. The Homo sapiens component of Earth's ecosystems responds in predictable ways to the changes in the environmental cycles. The first part of the series introduces the geosphere, biosphere, and atmosphere as the three spheres of the Earth system. The second part then explores the three components of Earth's metabolism: the water cycle, the carbon cycle, and the nitrogen cycle. The third part focuses on the human response to the environmental cycles, primarily as observed in North America. The fourth part focuses on the impact of humanity on the environment, starting with agricultural practices, and continuing with increasing human population, human impact on the atmosphere, and human impact on water resources. The fifth part focuses on the impacts of environmental changes on humanity, from climate change to ocean acidification to overpopulation. On May 25, 2016 at 0312 UTC (5:00PM EST), we conducted multiple measurements of local intensity of light within left anteroinferior portion of the coronary artery to investigate whether structure of the arterial wall could be correlated with local intensity and shape priors (SMP). Following standard autoregressive time-domain modelling procedure [42], we found that there were very strong SMP relations between local gradient amplitude and local infraflood concentration of light (hereafter 'light' or 'LIS') and between global gradient strength and LIS (hereafter 'theta'). Thus, both gradient amplitude and shape of the coracoid segment are strongly related to light, which appears only weakly but positively coupled for theta. Further investigation showed more pronounced relationship between gradient size and theta values within the left atrium than between these parameters inside right ventricle. Moreover, after taking into account different spatial scales tested in our study, we find stronger significant correlation between gradient sizes and theta within anterior part of heart compared to posterior region. It is important to highlight that this work does not take place in the context of existing hypotheses on heart disease risk factors [23] since no direct causal relation has been made [43]. Rather, it uses a novel form of multimodal statistical analysis where gradient magnitude and direction at site can be decomposed as separate random effects. The fact that effect was so evident even when other known potential confounders such as sex, age groups and ethnic group were removed suggests use of the same dataset provides important clues regarding possible pathogenic mechanisms. Therefore, by studying gradient pattern within the right ventricles along with gradient patterns in all three regions, it may help us to better understand patient's propensity towards cardiovascular diseases rather than focusing primarily only around acute coronary syndromes like hypertension [40–44]. In future studies, using larger sample size we would love to investigate other interhemispheric connections and evaluate the clinical relevance and utility of these features in assessing the risk factor profiles of patients prior to initiating preventive measures such as early angioplasty.

Quantum memories are a fundamental of any global-scale quantum Internet, high-performance quantum networking and near-term quantum computers. A main problem of quantum memories is the low retrieval efficiency of the quantum systems from the quantum registers of the quantum memory. Here, we define a novel quantum memory called high-retrieval-efficiency (HRE) quantum memory for near-term quantum devices. An HRE quantum memory unit integrates local unitary operations on its hardware level for the optimization of the readout procedure and utilizes the advanced techniques of quantum machine learning. We define the integrated unitary operations of an HRE quantum memory, prove the learning procedure, and evaluate the achievable output signal-to-noise ratio values. We prove that the local unitaries of an HRE quantum memory achieve the optimization of the readout procedure in an unsupervised manner without the use of any labeled data or training sequences. We show that the readout procedure of an HRE quantum memory is realized in a completely blind manner without any information about the input quantum system or about the unknown quantum operation of the quantum register. We evaluate the retrieval efficiency of an HRE quantum memory and the output SNR (signal-to-noise ratio). The results are particularly convenient for gate-model quantum computers and the near-term quantum devices of the quantum Internet.

A NEW APPROACH TO THE STUDY OF PHYSICAL SYSTEMS IS HEREBY PRESENTED TO ASSESS THE METHODS OF DYNAMICS WHICH HAVE A HEAVY-TAIL DISORDER AND ITS EFFECTS ON A CLASS OF DYNAMIC STRUCTURES. We introduce a new PIN DYNAMICS MODEL WHICH COPIOUSLY REPRESENTS THE ESSENCE OF THE HEAVY-TAILED DISORDER, AND WITH WHICH WE STUDY ITS EFFECTS AND ITS MANIFESTATIONS. We then study the corresponding PIN problem using a combination of mathematical and numerical methods. We find that the pinner model shows a complex phase-diagram writable with respect to the intensity and range of the disorder. The system exhibits a transition from a pinned phase to a depinned phase which is characterized by a power-law distribution of pinning forces. We also observe a novel ‘sticky’ phase where the system shows a non-trivial scaling behaviour, and which is not to be confused with the pinned and depinned phases. Finally, we find that the system shows a non-trivial response to an external drive force which is characterized by a power-law relationship between the applied force and the velocity. This result is a consequence of the heavy-tailed disorder, which leads to a long-range correlation in the pinning forces. Our results offer a new insight into the behaviour of physical systems with long-range disorder and demonstrate the importance of considering the long-range character of the disorder in order to understand their properties. The pinning model which we propose provides a simple and resolvable model for the study of long-range disorder in physical systems, and it can be applied to a broad class of physical systems including granular materials, glasses and other complex materials.

In this research, we propose an effective few-shot segmentation approach that combines global and local contrastive learning to acheive outstanding performance. Our method utilizes self-supervision techniques by leveraging two types of contrasts: global contrast which aligns features from different parts in a single image patch, and local contrast which aligns feature maps across patches from nearby regions of different images. By integrating these contrasts simultaneously, our approach can learn robust semantic segmented representations with high discrimination against diverse backgrounds while remaining computationally efficient. We validate our model's efficacy on multiple datasets with limited training data, demonstrating state-of-the-art results and outpacing prior methods in terms of accuracy, tradeoff between speed and quality, and generalization ability across unseen or challenging classes and scenes.

The development of artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized various industries, including healthcare. With its potential to improve medical imaging accuracy and speed, AI is increasingly being integrated into clinical workflows for image analysis and interpretation. However, concerns arise about the reliability and trustworthiness of AI systems in this setting. In this paper, we outline guiding principles for building trustworthy AI in future medical imaging using consensus recommendations from a group of experts in the field. Our framework considers multiple dimensions such as data quality, model transparency, human oversight, ethical implications, and patient privacy. We also propose guidelines on how to measure and evaluate AI performance, validate models on new datasets, and incorporate knowledge exchange between humans and machines. These recommendations provide practical insights that can help ensure the responsible use of AI technologies with high stakes, ultimately leading to better outcomes for patients and improving healthcare delivery.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to language-based image editing using recurrent attentive models. Our proposed method enables users to edit images by simply providing natural language descriptions of the desired changes, without requiring any manual manipulation of visual elements or deep knowledge of image processing techniques. We introduce a new architecture that combines the strengths of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention mechanisms to effectively understand and execute natural language instructions. The RNNs are used to model the sequence of edits specified in the input text, while the attention mechanism allows the model to selectively focus on specific parts of the image and apply the required transformations. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in executing various editing tasks such as object removal, facial expression manipulation, and color adjustment. We also show that our model can generalize well to unseen data and outperform existing state-of-the-art methods. Our work has significant implications for empowering non-technical users to create sophisticated images with minimal effort. Moreover, it opens up new opportunities for multimodal interaction between humans and computers, where natural language can serve as a powerful instrument for communicating visual preferences and intentions. In summary, Language-Based Image Editing with Recurrent Attentive Models represents a substantial advancement in the field of computer vision and human-computer interaction. It introduces a simple yet efficient way for people to express their creative ideas visually, without requiring proficiency in complex graphical user interfaces or programming languages.

High-quality training data play a key role in image segmentation tasks. Usually, pixel-level annotations are expensive, laborious and time-consuming for the large volume of training data. To reduce labelling cost and improve segmentation quality, interactive segmentation methods have been proposed, which provide the result with just a few clicks. However, their performance does not meet the requirements of practical segmentation tasks in terms of speed and accuracy. In this work, we propose EdgeFlow, a novel architecture that fully utilizes interactive information of user clicks with edge-guided flow. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance without any post-processing or iterative optimization scheme. Comprehensive experiments on benchmarks also demonstrate the superiority of our method. In addition, with the proposed method, we develop an efficient interactive segmentation tool for practical data annotation tasks. The source code and tool is avaliable at https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleSeg.

We develop a concept of aggregation utilizing statistical mechanical techniques. An instance of a complicated aggregation system with multiple levels of structures is peptide/protein self-assembly. The problem of protein aggregation is crucial for the understanding and diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders and therefore for the development of bio-macromolecules as new materials. We write the effective Hamiltonian in terms of interaction energies between protein molecules, protein and solvent, as well as between protein filaments. The grand partition function can be expressed in terms of a Zimm-Bragg-like transfer matrix, which is calculated exactly and all thermodynamic properties can be derived. We start with two-state and three-state descriptions of protein monomers using Potts models that can be generalized to include q-states, for which the exactly solvable feature of the model remains. We focus on n x N lattice configurations, corresponding to the ordered systems seen in some real fibrils. We have obtained results on nucleation systems and phase diagrams, in which a protein property such as the sheet content of aggregates is expressed as a function of the number of molecules on the lattice and inter-protein or interfacial interaction energies. We have applied our techniques to A{\beta}(1-40) and Curli fibrils and obtained results in excellent agreement with experiments.

While improving prediction accuracy has been the focus of machine learning in recent years, this alone does not suffice for reliable decision-making. Deploying learning systems in consequential settings also requires calibrating and communicating the uncertainty of predictions. To convey instance-wise uncertainty for prediction tasks, we show how to generate set-valued predictions from a black-box predictor that control the expected loss on future test points at a user-specified level. Our approach provides explicit finite-sample guarantees for any dataset by using a holdout set to calibrate the size of the prediction sets. This framework enables simple, distribution-free, rigorous error control for many tasks, and we demonstrate it in five large-scale machine learning problems: (1) classification problems where some mistakes are more costly than others; (2) multi-label classification, where each observation has multiple associated labels; (3) classification problems where the labels have a hierarchical structure; (4) image segmentation, where we wish to predict a set of pixels containing an object of interest; and (5) protein structure prediction. Lastly, we discuss extensions to uncertainty quantification for ranking, metric learning and distributionally robust learning.

In this paper, we explore the connection between nonlocality and the central geometry of dimer algebras. Dimer algebras are a class of mathematical structures that have been used to model various physical systems, including quantum spin chains and lattice guage theories. One of their key features is the presance of nonlocal interactions between adjacent units, which give rise to a rich and interesting geometric structure. We demonstrate that the central geometry of dimer algebras is intimately tied to the notion of nonlocality in these systems. Specifically, we show that the central elements of the algebra can be understood as creating nonlocal excitations in the system, which correspond to defects in the geometric structure. We develop a framework for studying these excitations, which allows us to understand the relationships between different types of nonlocalities present in the system. Our work provides new insights into the interplay between nonlocality and geometry in the context of dimer algebras, and sheds light on the deep connections between these concepts. It also highlights the potential applications of dimer algebras in understanding complex systems with nonlocal interactions, both in physics and beyond. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the power of algebraic methods for understanding intricate geometric structures arising from nonlocal interactions.

In this paper, we present an interactive medical image segmentation framework using iterative refinement. Our approach leverages the strengths of both machine learning algorithms and human expertise to improve the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation. We propose a novel iteration-based method that integrates user feedback into the segmentation process, enabling the algorithm to learn from the user's inputs and adapt to their preferences. Our proposed framework consists of two main components: (1) a deep neural network that initially segments the medical images, and (2) an interactive module that allows users to correct the segmentation results and provide feedback. The neural network is trained on a large dataset of annotated medical images and utilises a combination of convolutional and recurrent layers to generate accurate segmentations. The interactive module is designed to facilitate efficient user interaction and incorporate user feedback into the segmentation process. Users can adjust the segmentation boundaries through intuitive visualisations and real-time updates, allowing them to quickly identify and correct any errors or inaccuracies. The module also includes a reinforcement learning mechanism that learns from user behaviour and adapts the segmentation model accordingly. We evaluate our framework on several public datasets of diverse medical imageing modalities, including MRI brain scans, CT lung scans, and ultrasound liver images. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly improves upon traditional segmentation approaches by incorporating valuable user knowledge and achieving higher Dice coefficients and lower mean absolute errors. Additionally, user studies show that our framework reduces the time and effort required for manual segmentation while maintaining high accuracy levels. Our work has important implications for various clinical applications where precise medical image segmentation is critical, such as tumour diagnosis, organ transplant planning, and surgical intervention guidance. By empowering experts with real-time, interactive tools, we can increase accuracy and confidence in decision-making processes while reducing the tedium associated with manual segmentation methods. This research sets a new direction towards intelligent, dynamic, and collabourative image segmentation systems, ultimately contributing to better patient outcomes.

The paper presents a novel approach to few-shot segmentation using global and local contrastive learning. The proposed method leverages both global and local contrastive learning to improve the performance of few-shot segmentation. The global contrastive learning is used to learn the overall structure of the image, while the local contrastive learning is used to learn the local details of the image. The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and shows significant improvements in performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The paper also provides an analysis of the effectiveness of the proposed method and discusses future directions for research.

This paper presents a comprehensive multi-modal interaction approach for referring image segmentation, which involves the use of natural language and visual cues to accurately segment objects in images. The proposed method utilizes a deep neural network to process the visual information and a language model to understand the natural language input. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods in referring image segmentation. The results show that the comprehensive multi-modal interaction approach can significantly improve the accuracy of object segmentation and has potential applications in various fields, such as image editing, content-based image retrieval, and visual question answering.

Many approaches to 3D image segmentation are based on the hierarchical clustering of supervoxels into image regions. Here we describe a distributed-memory algorithm which can operate with a very large number of supervoxels. The algorithm operates recursively; the regions are broken down into a series of sub-regions which are then processed in parallel by several workers. At each recursive level the region size is doubled in all dimensions, until a single region covers the entire image. The end result is shown to be independent of the chunking procedure, and the same as if the entire image were to be processed without any partitioning. This is not a trivial result because the statistical property of a pair of adjacent regions (say for instance two adjacent cells in a blob) is evaluated. That property depends on the distribution of affinities between the two regions, and the pair may reside in any number of chunks. The trick is to delay merging those regions which are located on the boundary of two different chunks until the region is entirely within one chunk. We demonstrate the method on a brain volume with over 135 billion supervoxels and over 1.4 106 affinities.

The day of his birth, the midwife gasped in awe as she saw the artful tattoos that covered the newborn's tiny body. He had a series of mysterious symbols and images that were unlike anything anyone had ever seen before. It was as if he had been born with a story already written on him. The child's parents were mystified, but they accepted it as part of who their son was. As he grew older, the boy became fascinated by the tattoos and spent hours trying to decipher their meaning. He tried various methods - from studying ancient texts to consulting experts - but nothing worked. He was left with an enormous mystery that seemed destined to remain unsolved. Still, he persisted in his search for answers, believing that one day he would figure out the secret behind his tattoos. But as life went on, his curiosity slowly faded away. He had other things to worry about; school, friends, and eventually starting a family. One day, when he least expected it, something strange happened. He was going about his daily life when suddenly he noticed that some of his tattoos had changed. At first he thought he must be imagining it, but soon enough he realized that his tattoos were indeed changing with time. As he watched them evolve, he began to understand their purpose. He saw that every symbol and image represented a moment or event in his life. He was amazed to discover that his tattoos were a visual representation of his journey so far. He now understood why he had never been able to decipher them: they weren't meant to be solved until the story of his life had unfolded. He smiled as he realized that even though he hadn't found the answer he'd been searching for, the tattoos had still served their purpose. They had told the story of his life, even if only he could read it.

Title: A New Model for Heating of Solar North Polar Coronal Holes Abstract: The solar north polar coronal hole is an area of intense magnetic activity in the sun's upper atmosphere. This region experiences extremely high temperature differences between the cold, dark interior and the hot outer edges. In this study, we present a novel model for understanding how these extreme conditions are maintained within the coronal hole. Through extensive data analysis and numerical simulations, we have identified a mechanism that allows excess heat to be transferred from the periphery of the coronal hole towards its center, effectively creating a 'warm bubble.' Our model also accounts for fluctuations in the temperature gradient across the coronal hole, as well as variations in wind speed and direction. The results of our investigation provide valuable insights into the behavior of the solar north polar coronal hole and contribute significantly to our understanding of the physics behind this unique celestial phenomenon.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to graph partitioning called power-law graph cuts. Traditional graph partitioning algorithms aim to find partitions that minimize objective function such as the number of edges crossing the partition boundary. However, these algorithms are not well suited for graphs with power-law degree distributions, which are common in many real-world networks. Our proposed method uses different strategy based on observation that nodes in power-law graphs tend to cluster into communities of similar size. We define a quality function that captures quality of a partition by comparing ratio of intra-community edges to inter-community edges. We then use linear programming relaxation techniques to optimize quality function and obtain high-quality partitions. We test our algorithm on several benchmark datasets and compare its performance to other state-of-the-art graph partitioning methods. Our results show that power-law graph cuts significantly outperform existing methods in terms of both quality and computational efficiency, especially for large graphs. We also demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to various applications such as community detection and image segmentation. Overall, power-law graph cuts represent a major improvement in graph partitioning technology, enabling efficient and effective processing of large-scale networks with power-law structures.

There are several different things going on here: Those "super powerful" computers tend to run those same games with better graphics than consoles are capable of. When they're first released, consoles are often sold at a loss by the manufacturer so that they can make up the money in game sales. And even after release, there's very little profit. For instance, Sony is reported to only make 18 in profit from sales of the PS4. So consoles are cheaper than computers, on an equal-computing-power basis, simply because computer parts are sold at a higher markup. Games are often developed for the consoles first, and then ported to PC later. And there's a trend for mediocre ports that don't take full advantage of PC hardware, so the game doesn't run as smoothly on a PC with the same power as a console, even though that is absolutely something that could be done if the developers had cared to put in the extra effort.', "You don't need super powerful computers to run games. In fact, many games run just fine on on low end hardware, even the despised intel integrated graphics. With a mid range dedicated graphics card, you can expect to run about any game out there. The important thing to consider is that PC games are often run on higher quality settings: For action games, PC gamers expect 60 frames per seconds, whereas console games often get by with 30 fps, which reduces graphics power by half. Furthermore, console games usually run without [anti-aliasing] (URL0), and some games even run on resolutions less than full HD, which both saves a bunch of power. If console games do run on 60 Hz and full HD, the developers have to resort to simpler graphics compared to games that only run on 30 Hz and 900p.," "When devs make console games, they know the exact hardware they'll contain, so they are programmed for those exact parts, which allows them to use every single bit of power they contain. This is called optimization. But with pc's, everybody has different parts, so this can't be done. If games were optimized for a specific pc, performance would be incredibly good.

The Voronoi diagram-based dual-front active contour models are considered as a robust and effective way for addressing the image segmentation and domain partitioning issues. In the simple formulation of the dual-front models, the evolving contours can be viewed as the interfaces of adjacent Voronoi regions. Among these dual-front models, a critical ingredient is known as the geodesic metrics by which the geodesic distances and the corresponding Voronoi diagram can be estimated. In this paper, we introduce a kind of symmetric quadratic metrics dual-front model. The metrics considered are created by the integration of the image features and a vector field generated from the evolving contours. The use of the asymmetry enhancement can increase the risk of contour shortcut or leakage problems even when the initial contours are farther far from the target boundaries or the images have complicated frequency distributions. However, the proposed dual-front model can be employed for picture segmentation in accordance with other region-based homogeneity terms. The computational analyses on both artificial and real images show that the proposed dual-front model actually achieves positive results.

In this study, we propose a novel few-shot segmentation approach that leverages both global and local contrastive learning. Our method is based on the idea of encoding image features in an efficient manner to enable rapid adaptation to new tasks without requiring extensive training data. We demonstrate through experiments conducted on various datasets that our model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods while achieving faster convergence rates thanks to its ability to capture high-level semantic information as well as detailed contextual cues using contrasting examples at multiple scales. Overall, these results suggest that combining different types of contrasts can lead to significant improvements in few-shot performance for segmentation problems.

This academic paper explores the concept of cohesion measurement as a method for object discovery. The authors propose a novel approach to measuring cohesion that takes into account these various factors and demonstrate its effectiveness through a series of experiments. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for the field of object discovery and suggesting potential avenues for future research.

The star whisked through 23 songs in 90 minutes, in a blur of pyrotechnics, lasers and multiple costume changes. She donned silken butterfly wings for a piano-led version of...Baby One More Time, and dressed as a ringmaster during a Circus-themed segment. Spears even made a passable attempt at a London accent while chatting to the audience between songs. "Do you wanna get norr-tee?" she teased, doing her best Sid James impersonation before launching into Freakshow - during which she dragged a (slightly over-enthusiastic) member of the audience around the stage on a leash. It was all great fun but, without the elaborate set pieces of her Vegas production, Spears' shortcomings were left exposed. Her vocals rarely seemed to be coming from the microphone, while her dancing lacked attitude and bite. The choreography was over-reliant on hand gestures; and Spears showed a tendency to slip in and out of time, like a clockwork doll whose mechanism had worn out. Her biggest blunder came during the song Touch of My Hand, as she leant over a dancer's arm to initiate a backflip, but teetered on her heels and aborted the move. Frustratingly, Spears showed glimpses of her former glories - pulling off a series of impressive lifts, as well as a punchy dance breakdown during Womanizer - but the routines more often felt like they were stuck in the rehearsal room. Tabloids will undoubtedly criticise the star for miming (the producers insist she sings over a pre-recorded backing track) but, at this point, expecting Spears to sing live is like turning up at Nando's and ordering truffles: The only person you're disappointing is yourself. In the end, Spears has always played second fiddle to her songs - especially in the second half of her career, following a much-documented breakdown in 2007 that means her life is still controlled by a court-approved conservatorship - and those songs provided an unshakeable foundation to her act. By now, the 34-year-old has accumulated enough hits to be able to dispense with...Baby One More Time and Oops!...I Did It Again at the top of her show, without worrying about the consequences. Later highlights included an energised version of Gimme More and a pounding, gothic revamp of the early single Stronger. The star only played one new song - the ethereal, beatific Make Me - which may count as a missed opportunity to reinvigorate sales of her album,

Increasing the mini-batch size for stochastic gradient descent offers significant opportunities to reduce wall-clock training time, but there are a variety of theoretical and systems challenges that impede the widespread success of this technique. We investigate these issues, with an emphasis on time to convergence and total computational cost, through an extensive empirical analysis of network training across several architectures and problem domains, including image classification, image segmentation, and language modelling. Although it is common practise to increase the batch size in order to fully exploit available computational resources, we find a substantially more nuanced picture. Our main finding is that across a wide range of network architectures and problem domains, increasing the batch size beyond a certain point yields no decrease in wall-clock time to convergence for \emph{either} train or test loss. This batch size is usually substantially below the capacity of current systems. We show that popular training strategies for large batch size optimisation begin to fail before we can populate all available compute resources, and we show that the point at which these methods break down depends more on attributes like model architecture and data complexity than it does directly on the size of the dataset.

The room glowed slightly from all the screens. Hundreds and hundreds of screens, some small, some bigger than others across every available wall surface. Apart from the light from the screens themselves there were a few faint flickering lights that indicated just where other players might be in the room at any given time. It was quite different to what I had expected it would look like though. It looked like an office suite - or more accurately kept very clean offices - but with people sitting around in front of computers doing things instead of being secretaries who keep spreadsheets on their desks. The footage flowing out of those monitors was familiar - it seemed to come straight from television news bulletins and real-time updates about current events playing on the screen. It wasn't crystal clear, but you could make out faces and close-ups of conversations if you knew where to look, so when I saw Rooker and his fellow security officers jump up and run into one of the huge screens directly in front of me as they waited for my orders to proceed, I realised instantly what was happening. I watched from my position in this giant empty corridor as various human beings conducted surveillance missions over a large area of London. They weren't from the same organisation and didn't know each other, but they worked together to tackle a global threat. This is how a team works: that's why there are no single agents working against multiple threats as individual teams; everyone has access to data feeds and information which allows them to work collaboratively. All of these individuals have been tasked with cracking an encryption code called 'Deny' which stops anyone else from reading, listening or viewing files owned by hackers named "WannaCry" and many others whose names haven't yet appeared online. One of those men watching the cameras was Rooker himself. He sat down behind a desk covered with paper and folders held loosely between two metal sheets that stood just inches apart. His hand rested lightly on the edge of the chair as he continued to stare intently at the computer monitor. He'd turned off the sound and the accompanying video so I couldn't hear him speak too clearly through the speakers in his headphones. He pulled out his phone and started scrolling through messages and calls sent to him during his shift

Training deep networks with limited labeled data while achieving a strong generalization ability is key in the quest to reduce human annotation efforts. This is the goal of semi-supervised learning, which exploits more widely available unlabeled data to complement small labeled data sets. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for discriminative pixel-level tasks using a generative model of both images and labels. Concretely, we learn a generative adversarial network that captures the joint image-label distribution and is trained efficiently using a large set of unlabeled images supplemented with only few labeled ones. We build our architecture on top of StyleGAN2, augmented with a label synthesis branch. Image labeling at test time is achieved by first embedding the target image into the joint latent space via an encoder network and test-time optimization, and then generating the label from the inferred embedding. We evaluate our approach in two important domains: medical image segmentation and part-based face segmentation. We demonstrate strong in-domain performance compared to several baselines, and are the first to showcase extreem out-of-domain generalization, such as transferring from CT to MRI in medical imaging, and photographs of real faces to paintings, sculptures, and even cartoons and animal faces. The task of segmenting objects within an image requires comprehensive understanding of spatial relationships between different segments. Traditional interactive semantic segmentation methods usually rely on global changes to images or regions, which may be detrimental to maintaining local context and relationship between adjacent pixel groups. In this work, we introduce a novel approach called EdgeFlow that uses edge information as input to achieve practical interactive segmentation while considering local dependencies in real-time. Our proposed framework learns robust edge maps from both low and high resolution levels, utilizing temporal correlations through dynamic motion estimates based on optical flow. We then combine edge cues from high and low resolution level with a set of locally-adapted filter weights to create a fine-tuned intermediate map, capturing delicate details across space and time. Finally, our model performs interactive manipulation using gradient descent until convergence, resulting in accurate segmentation output without need for human intervention. Furthermore, we evaluate our method on three benchmark datasets, demonstrating outperformances over classical approaches by preserving more detailed spatial patterns while achieving significantly faster processing times.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for referring image segmentation that incorporates comprehensive multi-modal interactions between the user and the system. Our approach allows users to interact with the system through various modalities, including speech, gesture, and touch, to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation process. We propose a deep learning-based framework that integrates multiple modalities and leverages their complementary information to improve the segmentation performance. The framework consists of several components, including a speech recognition module, a gesture recognition module, a touch-based interaction module, and a segmentation module. These components work together to enable the user to provide rich and diverse inputs that can effectively convey their desired segmentation goals. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional single-modal interaction methods. Our experiments show that the proposed approach can significantly improve the segmentation accuracy and reduce the interaction time, making it more efficient and user-friendly. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: * We propose a comprehensive multi-modal interaction framework for referring image segmentation that integrates speech, gesture, and touch modalities. * We develop a deep learning-based model that fuses the complementary information from multiple modalities to improve the segmentation performance. * We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional single-modal methods. Our work has important implications for various applications, such as medical imaging, robotics, and human-computer interaction. The proposed approach can help improve the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation tasks, making it more accessible and user-friendly for a wide range of users.

A 19-year-old man has been jailed for life in London, England after being found guilty of plotting a terrorist attack. The court heard that the man, Haroon Syed, had planned to detonate a bomb either at an Elton John concert or on Oxford Street in central London. Syed was arrested by officers from the Metropolitan Police's Counter Terrorism Command in September 2016. They discovered that he had researched and purchased materials to make an explosive device online as part of his plan. In a hearing at the Old Bailey, Syed admitted attempting to source explosives and firearms with intent to endanger life. He also pleaded guilty to preparing acts of terrorism between April 2016 and September 2016. The prosecution argued that Syed had been motivated by a twisted interpretation of Islam and Isis propaganda. They presented evidence showing that Syed had discussed his plans with an undercover police officer, who he believed was a contact for Isis. Judge Mark Dennis QC said that Syed had "demonstrated a dangerous level of commitment" and sentenced him to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 15 years. He added that Syed had posed "a significant risk to public safety" and that the sentence was necessary to protect the public. This case serves as a stark reminder of the threat posed by lone-wolf terrorists. The police and security services continue to work tirelessly to protect the public from those who seek to do us harm.

Videos can be viewed as unique objects in an image space on the screen, but their structure and arrangement cannot easily be captured or understood by conventional video and image processing algorithms used today, such as edge detection [26]. At the same time, they are not static and do not need to conform exactly to any particular representation of the scene – many videos may simply consist of repeating visual patterns where repeated motions of characters are played out with different camera angles within a scene [4], or simply have no apparent story at all without dialogue or narration (for example), but all of these structures remain hidden to human perception. An ambitious project has been undertaken to quantify some of these features which were previously unseen, enabling video segmentation programs to accurately render videos which would otherwise escape classification or other automated analysis. The goal was to produce real VAS scores representing this hidden structure via a novel video object model that combines low-level features into high-level abstractions of what happens in these videos. We use YouTube-vos [7] to explore how good VAS estimators based on traditional, image-based segmentation techniques perform once applied against large videos whose size permits visualization, and how these results are related to a theoretical machine modeling approach, called 'Video VOS'. Our experiments show that YouTube-vos could identify certain key properties of the video footage while allowing for different interpretation. These results help to distinguish approaches which can successfully classify complex videos from those which will ultimately fail due to insufficient understanding how the relevant video representations change over time. We also demonstrate the potential benefits of using YouTube-vos to apply new learning methods in areas of artificial intelligence where image/video classifier systems might already excel. The present paper proposes a new approach for learning food portions from monocular images by cross-domain feature adaptation. The proposed method is to overcome the challenge of data shift between the training and the test, by transferring the features of the source domain to the target domain. This work makes a contribution to the development of automatic food portion estimation systems and has the potential to be applied in nutrition research and diet control.

In this paper, we present a novel approach To interactive segmentation called EdgeFlow, which leverages edge information to guide the segmentation process and achieve practical interaction efficiency. Existing methods often suffer from slow convergence or rely on heuristics that limit their accuracy, making them impractical for real-world applications. EdgeFlow addresses these limitations by introducing an edge-guided flow algorithm That combines the benefits of both boundary-following and gradient-descent-based methods. The proposed method efficiently explores the Image space while adaptively adjusting its behavior based on local edge features, ensuring accurate segmentation and minimizing user input. We evaluate EdgeFlow on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art methods in terms of efficiency, accuracy, and usability. Our results show significant advantages in terms of both computational cost and user effort required to obtain high-quality segmentations. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of EdgeFlow through Applications in various domains such As object recognition, medical imaging, and video analysis. The key contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: * Introducing EdgeFlow, a practical solution for Efficient and accurate interactive segmentation guided by edge information. * Developing a novel edge-guided flow algorithm that adapts to local edge features, promoting accurate and efficient segmentation. * showcasing superior performance of EdgeFlow compared to existing methods In terms of both computational cost And user effort Required. * Demonstrating the applicability of edgeFlow across diverse domains, including object recognition, medical imaging, and video analysis. In conclusion, our proposed method presents a substantial improvement over traditional Interactivesegmentation techniques and has far-reaching implications for applications where Precise segmentation is critical. We envision EdgeFlow serving as a valuable tool for researchers, practitioners, and users seeking efficient and reliable segmentation solutions.

This paper proposes a novel algorithm for the problem of structural image segmentation through an interactive model-based approach. Interaction is expressed in the model creation, which is done according to user traces drawn over a given input image. Both model and input are then represented by means of attributed relational graphs derived on the fly. Appearance features are taken into account as object attributes and structural properties are expressed as relational attributes. To cope with possible topological differences between both graphs, a new structure called the deformation graph is introduced. The segmentation process corresponds to finding a labelling of the input graph that minimizes the deformations introduced in the model when it is updated with input information. This approach has shown to be faster than other segmentation methods, with competitive output quality. Therefore, the method solves the problem of multiple label segmentation in an efficient way. Encouraging results on both natural and target-specific color images, as well as examples showing the reusability of the model, are presented and discussed.

This scientific journal discusses the use of generative models for cognitive segmentation, primarily relying on semi-supervised learning and strong out-of-domain generalization. The researchers suggest a novel method that uses the power of generative models to improve the efficiency of cognitive segmentation functions. Through numerous studies, the researchers demonstrate the efficacy of their method in obtaining state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark data while additionally demonstrating good performance on out-of-domain data. Overall, this paper gives important insights into the potential of generative models for cognitive segmentation and highlights the relevance of semi-supervised learning and out-of-domain generalization in computer vision tasks.

The generalized asymmetric dual-front model is a novel approach to active contours and image segmentation. This model combines the advantages of both level set methods and geometric variational frameworks, allowing for efficient and accurate boundary detection in various imaging applications. The proposed method utilizes an asymmetrical energy functional that considers both internal and external forces acting on the contour, enabling flexibility in adjusting the influence of these factors based on specific task requirements. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methodology compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques across several benchmark datasets, indicating its potential as a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners working with visual data analysis tasks.

You were going through your mail when you noticed an unaddressed letter at the bottom of the pile. The envelope was plain and unremarkable, but the words printed in bold red ink across the front caught your attention: "DO NOT answer that phone." You hesitated to open it, but curiosity got the best of you. Inside, there was no signature, only a message scrawled in rushed handwriting: "If you know what's good for you, ignore the ringing phone. Do not answer it, no matter who it may be." As you read the ominous warning, your phone began to ring. You couldn't help but feel a chill run down your spine. You considered not answering, but you could hardly just ignore your phone. Slowly, you picked up the receiver. "Hello?" you answered with trepidation. Silence. "Hello?" you repeated, a little louder this time. Suddenly, a shrill voice screamed in your ear, "I told you not to answer that phone!" You ripped the phone away from your ear, your heart racing as you tried to catch your breath. "Who is this?" you demanded, but the line was already dead. You spent the rest of the day on edge, nervously glancing at your phone every time it beeped or rang. Who had written that letter? Was someone watching you? You couldn't shake the feeling that someone was out to get you. You decided to take the warning seriously and stay away from your phone as much as possible. In the end, you never did find out who sent you that terrifying letter or who called that day, but you never forgot the feeling of fear it left you with.

Large-scale image segmentation is a challenging task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into multiple regions based on their visual characteristics. Distributed clustering algorithms offer a promising approach to this problem by allowing for parallel processing of image data across multiple nodes in a distributed system. In this paper, we propose a novel large-scale image segmentation method based on distributed clustering algorithms. Our approach involves dividing the image into smaller regions and applying a clustering algorithm to each region in parallel. The resulting clusters are then merged to form the final segmentation result. We evaluate our method on a large dataset of images and demonstrate its effectiveness in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Our results show that our method outperforms traditional centralized clustering algorithms and can scale to handle very large images.

High-resolution segmenting of tooth crown fissures using nonparametric multivariate regularization for feature-free, polygonal, parametrical reconstruction. We propose a new method based on hierarchical linear algebra (HLA) that can be efficiently used to segment an entire tooth root. Instead of attempting to use a very high amount of parameters or gradient computation in order obtain optimal results, we directly incorporate the best features of individual teeth into our model in a parameter-dependent manner and leverage their overlap to acheive a good result. The resulting curve fit to each landmark provides a continuous indication on where to focus further investigation in terms of determining the most likely path to take (i.e. tooth edge). For this paper, we present experiments using state-of-the-art DRSM hardware with a sampling rate of 100 times per second, as well as several thousand data points collected over a period of weeks by multiple users over 8 consecutive days to evaluate the effectiveness of our method. Our procedure was confirmed after performing hundreds of thousands of steps per hour using real human and simulated teeth. While results were inconsistent (due to the variance inherent in sampling), they were statistically significant at p<0.001 when considering 10 000 steps/hour. With additional refinement using several more datasets, we found similer positive correlations: correlation coefficient = 0.891, Pearson r2 = 0.844, η p 2 = 0.88

Ground control didn't see the asteroid belt and neither did we until we struck it. Our ship was torn apart within minutes and both of us had been sucked out. The cosmic dust was our only other companion. Immortality seemed like the worst choice to make. They first few moments were the worst. First my lungs exploded with the force of a thousand hammers, hitting just the right nails, and all I could do was watch the same happen to her just seconds later. I just kept staring at her. Her already pale skin wept as the bright reds of her wrinkled lips escaped their master. I remembered her walking out of the shower, just a towel wrapped around her. How she'd walk over to me, sleeping in and lean forward, brushing her speaking hair against my face as I smiled in my complacent sleep. The same hair that floated in every direction with us. I held her tighter and she held me the same. I kissed her icy forehead as I saw the tears escape our eyes, clump together and drift away as aimlessly as us. I tried to remember our time on earth. I remember her family on Christmas. Everyone one of them more dull than the next. I remember us running away close to midnight. Making our way to the park in the country side and lying down. Just looking in awe at the same stars that now mocked our immortality. Her smiling head against the night sky as she kissed me juxtaposed with my current view of her silently sobbing visage. I kept trying to remember more. I remember a fight. We fought about this. We fought about immortality. She never wanted to become immortal and go into space. In fact..... She didn't agree to it. I felt my mind betray me as her warmth faded away. I looked up at the galaxies swirling into the abyss. She left me. Cold. So cold. But at least the view was nice.

The O-minimal Hauptvermutung is a conjecture in mathematics that has been open for over a century. It states that every algebraic variety defined by a polynomial system with rational coefficients is also O-minimal, meaning that it has a finite number of rational points. In this paper, we explore the O-minimal Hauptvermutung for polyhedra, which are three-dimensional objects defined by a set of linear equations. We prove that every polyhedron is O-minimal, thus providing a new proof of the O-minimal Hauptvermutung for polyhedra. Our proof relies on the theory of tropical geometry, which is a branch of mathematics that studies the geometry of algebraic varieties over the tropical semirings. We also provide some applications of our result, including a new proof of the Tarski-Carleson theorem and a new approach to the study of the distribution of rational points on algebraic varieties.

One of the main things that a bank does is to let people borrow money from them. One of the most common forms of this is called "mortgage," where people borrow money from a bank to buy something really big, usually a house. They then pay this money back over time as they earn it, and then they pay back a little extra to reward the bank for this. The trouble is that the banks, seeking to make some extra money, lent money to people that they normally would not, as those people are not likely to be able to pay it back because they don't have a good job. This is called a "sub-prime mortgage." Now, bankers are not stupid. They know that there's a good chance that these people can not pay back their debt. They are still willing to lend the money because they know that if the debt is not paid in time, they can simply take possession of the house. This is called "foreclosing." However, this all went wrong because of a separate thing called the "housing boombubble." For years, houses had kept getting more and more expensive. This was bad if you needed to buy a house, because you would have to borrow more, but if you already owned a house, it was good because you owned something very valuable. One day, the house prices finally stopped getting bigger, and started to get cheaper. This was very bad news for the banks, as by now they had huge amounts of sub-prime mortgages. When people could not pay their debt, the house they foreclosed on was not worth enough to pay for the debt. Some banks which saw this coming managed to sell the debt onto other banks before it got bad, but other banks were holding a lot of sub-prime debt when it hit. Those banks had ended up owning a lot of worthless things that they paid a lot for. They lost a lot of money, and didn't have enough left to pay back all the people who held bank accounts with them. This meant that the government had to step in and give the banks money to ensure that lots of people didn't lose their savings, but that's another story.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to convolutional neural networks called pyramidal convolution, which aims to improve the performance of visual recognition tasks. Our method involves using a pyramid of filters with varying sizes to capture multi-scale features in the input image. We demonstrate through extensive experiments that our approach outperforms traditional convolutional neural networks on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Our findings suggest that pyramidal convolution is a promising direction for advancing the state-of-the-art in computer vision.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for extending pretrained deep learning models to accommodate new anatomy and images. Our method, called "Learn the new, keep the old," enables the integration of new knowledge into preexisting models without discarding the valuable information they have already learned. This is achieved through a two-stage training process that first fine-tunes the pretrained model on a small set of labeled images of the new anatomy, and then adapts the model to the new anatomy using a novel optimization technique that preserves the knowledge gained from the pretraining process. We evaluate our approach on several datasets of medical images, including CT scans and MRI scans, and demonstrate that it outperforms traditional fine-tuning methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Our results show that our method is able to learn new anatomy and images while retaining the knowledge gained from the pretraining process, leading to improved performance on both old and new data. The contributions of this paper are threefold: (1) we propose a novel approach for extending pretrained deep learning models to accommodate new anatomy and images, (2) we introduce a new optimization technique that preserves the knowledge gained from pretraining, and (3) we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several medical image datasets. Our work has important implications for a wide range of applications, including medical image analysis, object detection, and natural language processing.

We investigate Referring Image Segmentation (RIS), which outputs a segmentation map corresponding to given natural language description. To solve RIS efficiently, we need to understand each word's relationship with other words, each region in the image to other regions, and cross-modal alignment between linguistic and visual domains. We argue that one of the limiting factors in the recent methods is that they do not handle these interactions simultaneously. To this end, we propose novel architecture called JRNet, which uses a Joint Reasoning Module(JRM) to concurrently capture the inter-modal and intra-modal interactions. The output of JRM is passed through a novel Cross-Modal Multi-Level Fusion (CMMLF) module which further refines segmentation masks by exchanging contextual information across visual hierarchy through linguistic features acting as a bridge. We present thorough ablation studies and validate our approach's performance on four benchmark datasets, showing considerable performance gains over existing state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for referring image segmentation that incorporates comprehensive multi-modal interactions between the user and the system. Our approach allows users to interact with the system through various modalities, including speach, gesture, and touch, to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation process. We propose a deep learning-based framework that integrates multiple modalities and leverages their complementary information to improve the segmentation performance. The framework consists of several components, including a speach recognition module, a gesture recognition module, a touch-based interaction module, and a segmentation module. These components work together to enable the user to provide rich and diverse inputs that can effectively convey their desired segmentation goals. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional single-modal interaction methods. Our experiments show that the proposed approach can significantly improve the segmentation accuracy and reduce the interaction time, making it more efficient and user-friendly. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: * We propose a comprehensive multi-modal interaction framework for referring image segmentation that integrates speach, gesture, and touch modalities. * We develop a deep learning-based model that fuses the complementary information from multiple modalities to improve the segmentation performance. * We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional single-modal methods. Our work has important implications for various applications, such as medical imaging, robotics, and human-computer interaction. The proposed approach can help improve the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation tasks, making it more accessible and user-friendly for a wide range of users.

This paper presents scalable approach to large-scale image segmentation through utilization of distributed clustering algorithms. With the growing availability of high-dimensional data, traditional centralized processing methods have become increasingly inefficient and limited by computational constraints. To address this challenge, we propose novel framework that enables the parallelization of image segmentation across multiple nodes in a distributed computing environment. Our proposed method leverages the power of distributed clustering algorithms, which are proven to be highly effective in handling massive datasets, to perform pixel-level classification and segmentation of images. By partitioning the input image into smaller chunks and distributing them across multiple processors, our approach achieves unprecedented levels of scalability and efficiency. We demonstrate efficacy of our technique by applying it to several large-scale image datasets, yielding superior performance and accuracy compared to state-of-the-art centralized methods. The key contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: 1. A distributed clustering-based framework for large-scale image segmentation is introduced, which enabled efficient processing of massive images via parallel computation. 2. An optimization strategy was developed to effectively distribute workload and minimize communication overheads between processor nodes. 3. Thorough experiments were conducted on various large-scale image datasets to evaluate the performance of the proposed method against existing centralized approaches. The results show significant improvements in both efficiency and accuracy. 4. The proposed method paves way for tackling even larger imaging datasets, previously considered too vast for practical analysis, opening up new opportunities in applications such as computer vision, machine learning, and multimedia processing. In conclusion, this paper offers a groundbreaking solution to problem of large-scale image segmentation, providing an elegant combination of distributed computing and clustering algorithms that facilitates efficient and accurate processing of huge amounts of image data. Our approach has far-reaching implications for advancing research and developing innovative applications within realm of big data analytics.

Large-scale image segmentation is a challenging task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into multiple regions based on their visual characteristics. Distributed Clustering algorithms offer a promising approach to This problem by allowing for parallel processing of image data across multiple nodes in a distributed system. In this paper, we Propose a novel large-scale image segmentation method based on distributed clustering Algorithms. Our approach involves dividing the image into smaller regions and applying a clustering algorithm to each region in parallel. The Resulting clusters are then merged to form the final segmentation result. We evaluate our method on a large dataset of images and demonstrate its effectiveness in terms Of accuracy and computational efficiency. Our results show that our method outperforms traditional centralized clustering algorithms and can scale to handle very large images.

This study presents a novel high-resolution segmentation approach for tooth root fuzzy edges based on polynomial curve fitting and landmark detection. The paper presents an unsupervised semantic image segmentation method that utilizes Stylegan and CLIP to generate high-quality segmentation masks. The proposed method first generates a set of style-specific masks using Stylegan, which are then used as input to the CLIP model to generate semantic segmentation masks. The resulting method is able to generate accurate and high-quality segmentation masks without the need for labeled data, making it a valuable tool for applications where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method on several benchmark datasets and shows that it is able to generate segmentation masks that are comparable to those generated using supervised methods.

Infrared (UV) image segmentation is important in certain urban defence systems, such as pedestrian monitoring, car counting, security surveillance, etc. Active contour model (ACM) is one of the most commonly employed image segmentation methods at present, but the existing tools only utilize the regional or global single feature information of image to reduce the energy function, which is easy to cause false segmentations in IR images. In this paper, we propose a multi-feature driven active contour segmentation model to handle IR images with intensity inhomogeneity. However, an especially-designed signed pressure force (SPF) function is created by using the regional information measured by regional average gray data and the local multi-feature information measured by regional entropy, regional standard deviation and gradient information. Then, we draw upon adaptive weight coefficient measured by local range to adjust the afore-mentioned regional term and regional term. First, the SPF function is substituted into the level set formulation (LSF) for further evolution. Then, the LSF converges after a finite number of iterations, and the IR image segmentation result is derived from the corresponding convergence result. Experimental findings show that the presented technique outperforms the state-of-the-art models in terms of precision rate and overlapping rate in IR test images.

The recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) combined with the vast amount of data generated by today's medical applications, has contributed to the implementation of imaging AI technologies throughout the entire value chain of clinical imaging, including image reconstruction, clinical imagery segmentation, image-based treatment and treatment planning. Notwithstanding the successes and future potential of AI in clinical imaging, several stakeholders are concerned of the potential risks and societal consequences of imaging AI technologies, which are considered as complex, opaque, and impossible to comprehend, use, and trust in critical medical systems. Besides these difficulties and challenges, there are still no concrete policies and best practices for directing future AI technologies in clinical imaging towards enhanced trust, safety and adoption. To bridge this gap, this journal includes a careful choice of guiding guidelines drawn from the accumulated insights, consensus, and best practices from three big European projects on AI in Medical Systems. These guiding concepts are named FUTURE-AI and its building blocks consist of (i) Fairness, (ii) Universality, (iii) Traceability, (iv) Usability, (v) Robustness and (vi) Explainability. In a step-by-step method, these recommendations are further translated into a framework of concrete guidelines for identifying, designing, implementing, and integrating technically, clinically and socially trustworthy AI solutions into scientific practice.

This study proposes a multi-modal and inter-modal approach for annotating images, which can combine the language description of images with the spatial localization map of images, and the attention mechanism of the images. Deep learning models are used to combine various modes such as text description, localization map, attention mechanism, feature representation, etc., and three benchmarks are used for experiments. The experiments show that our method is superior to existing ones on three benchmarks, and it can be used for image question-answering, image tagging, and other related tasks. Besides, this paper gives some new insights into the design of multi-mode fusion strategies.

Abstract Aseptic surgery requires an accurate visualization of anatomic landmarks and landmarks that are not readily available to surgeon or patient through other means, such as conventional X-ray images, MRI, computed tomography (CT) scans, digital photographs, or MRIs. To produce segmented images using image mosaicking techniques with no manual annotations in a surgical suite without additional tools or software and to preserve visual appearance of end result, the authors present novel image compositing algorithms tailored with data about anatomical landmarks and images on a computer. We demonstrate large coverage maps produced via their algorithms that retain their robustness for normal anatomy despite small errors in source image orientation or magnification settings.

The analysis of stellar disks in nearby S0 galaxies gives important insights into the formation and evolution of these galaxies. In this paper, we present a detailed study of the ages and abundances of stars in large-scale stellar disks of nearby S0 galaxies. We use a mix of spectroscopic and spectral data to identify the ages and metallicities of stars in these disks. Our findings show that the stellar disks of nearby S0 galaxies are composed of a mix of old and young stars, with a average age of over 10 Gyr. We therefore know that the metallicity of these disks differs greatly, with some planets having metallicities as high as -0.5 dex. Our data establishes significant constraints on the formation and evolution of S0 galaxies, and highlights the need for further investigations to better understand the complex processes that shape these fascinating objects.

We address the problem of segmenting 3D multi-modal medical images in scenarios where very few labeled examples are available for training. Leveraging the recent success of adversarial learning for semi-supervised segmentation, we propose a novel method based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to train a segmentation model with both labeled and unlabeled images. The proposed method prevents over-fitting by learning to discriminate between true and fake patches obtained by a generator network. Our work extends current adversarial learning approaches, which focus on 2D single-modality images, to the more challenging context of 3D volumes of multiple modalities. The proposed method is evaluated on the problem of segmenting brain MRI from the iSEG-2017 and MRBrainS 2013 datasets. Significant performance improvement is reported, compared to state-of-art segmentation networks trained in a fully-supervised manner. In addition, our work presents a comprehensive analysis of different GAN architectures for semi-supervised segmentation, showing recent techniques like feature matching to yield a higher performance than conventional adversarial training approaches. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/arnab39/FewShot_GAN-Unet3D

This study introduces comprehensive multi-modal interaction approach for referring image segmentation, which utilizes both natural language and visual cues to accurately segment objects in images. The proposed method employs state-of-the-art deep learning models that effectively combine various modalities such as text descriptions, object localization maps, attention mechanisms, and feature embeddings. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our model over existing baselines on three benchmark datasets, highlighting its potential applications in visual question answering,image captioning,and other related tasks. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into designing effective multimodal fusion strategies tailoredforreferring image segmentation problems.
