The field of underwater sound technology has seen a significant evolution in recent years with research focused on using sonar imageing to increase our understanding of marine environments. This study presents an iterative, deep, and unsupervised synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) image segmentation methodology that allows accurate and efficient classification of seafloor topography, sediment texture, and other marine organisms within sonar images. The proposed method is based on two key components: feature extraction followed by an iterative neural network approach to segmentation. Feature extraction involves extracting specific information from the sonar images, such as texture, edge strength, and intensity at various frequency bands. The resulting extracted features are then fed into an unsupervised autoencoder that learns to represent each area in a sonnet-like sequence. The output generated is then used in conjunction with an additional neural network architecture to perform multi-layer perceptron (MLP)-based synthesis to produce high-resolution segmented versions of the sonar images. Experimental results indicate improved accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional methods. The iterative, deep, and unsupervised SAS image segmentation technique developed provides a useful tool for researchers working towards more effective monitoring and management of ocean habitats, allowing them to identify changes over time and detect critical indicators of ecosystem health.

DeepLab is a state-of-the-art technique for semantic image segmentation that uses deep convolutional nets, atrous convolution, and partially connected conditional random fields (CRFs). The technique ensures low precision and reliable algorithms by combining a deep neural network with atrous convolution to capture multi-scale context and a partially connected CRF to model temporal dependencies between neighboring pixels. The paper provides an extensive review of DeepLab on many benchmark datasets, highlighting its dominance over other tools in terms of both precision and speed. Overall, DeepLab demonstrates a major advance in the field of semantic image segmentation and has the potential to provide a broad variety of applications in computer vision.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to semantic image segmentation using deep convolutional neural networks, atrous convolution, and fully connected conditional random fields (CRFs). Our proposed method, called DeepLab, leverages the strengths of both CNNs and CRFs to improve accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation. We begin by using deep CNN to extract features from input image. We then employ atrous convolution to increase the resolution of feature maps, allowing us to capture finer details in the image. Next, we apply a fully connected CRF to refine segmentation results, using the feature maps as input. The CRF allows us to model the spatial relationships between pixels and enforce label consistency, leading to improved segmentation accuracy. We evaluate DeepLab on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes. Our experiments show that DeepLab outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation methods, achieving an mIoU of 81.7% on PASCAL VOC 2012 and 77.6% on Cityscapes. Additionally, we demonstrate that DeepLab is computationally efficient, with faster runtime than other state-of-the-art methods. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: * We propose novel approach to semantic image segmentation using deep convolutional neural networks, atrous convolution, and fully connected CRFs. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of DeepLab on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and efficiency. * We show that DeepLab can be used for variety of applications, including object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation. Overall, DeepLab represents a significant advancement in the field of semantic image segmentation, and we believe it has potential to be widely adopted in variety of domains.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to few-shot segmentation, which leverages both global and local contrastive learning to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Our proposed method, called FSGL (Few-Shot Segmentation with Global and Local Contrastive Learning), combines the strengths of global contrastive learning and local contrastive learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of few-shot segmentation. Global contrastive learning is used to learn high-level features that are robust across different datasets and tasks, while local contrastive learning is employed to learn task-specific features that are important for segmenting specific objects or regions in an image. By combining these two types of contrastive learning, our model can learn both generalizable and task-specific knowledge, leading to improved performance on few-shot segmentation tasks. FSGL consists of two main components: a global feature extractor and a local feature refiner. The global feature extractor uses a self-supervised loss function to learn high-level features from a large dataset, while the local feature refiner uses a supervised loss function to fine-tune the learned features for a specific segmentation task. We also propose a novel technique called multi-scale dense connections to integrate the global and local features effectively. Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets show that FSGL outperforms existing state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods by a significant margin. Notably, FSGL achieves an average IoU score of 86.5% on PASCAL VOC, which is 10.2% higher than the previous state-of-the-art method. Moreover, FSGL requires only 320k parametres, making it much more efficient compared to other state-of-the-art models. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating both global and local contrastive learning into few-shot segmentation models. The proposed FSGL model has important implications for real-world applications where accurate segmentation is required, such as autonneomous driving, robotics, and medical imageing.

As we walked in, three or four people were waiting around a table - but which one, I wondered, was the father of Bitcoin? Then I realised that one man was staring intensely at a very chunky laptop - this was Dr Craig Wright. He carried on working, apparently unaware that we had entered the room. Once we had been introduced he gradually warmed up - especially when it came to performing the demonstration that showed that he did have access to the cryptographic keys used by Satoshi when he made the first Bitcoin transaction in 2009. We had arrived wondering just how convincing a case would be made that the almost mythical creator of Bitcoin was at last stepping out of the shadows. What we saw seemed impressive - though it would need a far higher level of expertise than we possess to be certain. But Jon Matonis, a senior figure in the Bitcoin world, was in the room watching, having had his own demonstration some time before. And the news that Gavin Andresen, chief scientist at the Bitcoin Foundation, was also convinced provided more reassurance. Now Craig Wright has published his evidence on his blog, it will be examined in minute detail for any chink in his case. But put aside the question of whether you believe him or not - and he told me he didn't care either way - there were still plenty of questions we wanted to put to the fascinating, if somewhat prickly Dr Wright. Why keep his secret so long? Why come out now? What about that run-in with the Australian tax authorities? And is he fabulously rich, with a huge stock of Bitcoin? At our first meeting - without a television camera - we roamed freely over all sorts of territory. We learned that he ran a substantial business in London, employing quite a few people here in what seemed to be some kind of Bitcoin trading and consultancy operation. We challenged him about that tax investigation - he conceded that there was what he called an "audit" underway in Australia but insisted that this was mainly due to the tax authorities there not really understanding Bitcoin. We asked where the pseudonym had come from - he mentioned a 17th century libertarian philosopher called Nakamoto but said he'd keep the Satoshi bit to himself. Many approaches to 3D image segmentation are based on hierarchical clustering of supervoxels into image regions. Here we describe a distributed algorithm capable of handling a tremendous number of supervoxels. The algorithm works recursively, the regions are divided into chunks that are processed independently in parallel by multiple workers. At each round of the recursive procedure, the chunk size in all dimensions are doubled until a single chunk encompasses the entire image. The final result is provably independent of the chunking scheme, and the same as if the entire image were processed without division into chunks. This is nontrivial because a pair of adjacent regions is scored by some statistical property (e.g. mean or median) of the affinities at the interface, and the interface may extend over arbitrarily many chunks. The trick is to delay merge decisions for regions that touch chunk boundaries, and only complete them in a later round after the regions are fully contained within a chunk. We demonstrate the algorithm by clustering an affinity graph with over 1.5 trillion edges between 413 billion supervoxels derived from a 3D electron microscopic brain image.

> Image segmentation is a fundamental problem in computer vision. It has been studied for decades and has been applied to a wide range of applications. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey of image segmentation and cosegmentation. We first review the bottom-up approaches, which are based on the assumption that the image can be decomposed into a set of parts. We then review the top-down approaches, which are based on the assumption that the image can be decomposed into a set of objects. We also review the semantic segmentation approaches, which are based on the assumption that the image can be decomposed into a set of semantic concepts. Finally, we review the cosegmentation approaches, which are based on the assumption that the image can be decomposed into a set of co-occurring objects. We hope that this survey will provide a useful reference for researchers working in this field. The paper is available here.

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is first cause of death in many countries. CRC originates from small clump of cells on lining of the colon called polyps, which over time might grow and become malignant. Early detection and removal of polyps are therefore necessary for the prevention of colon cancer. In this paper, we introduce an ensemble of medical polyp segmentation algorithms. Based on an observation that different segmentation algorithms will perform well on different subsets of examples because of the nature and size of training sets they have been exposed to and because of method-intrinsic factors, we propose to measure confidence in the prediction of each algorithm and then use an associate threshold to determine whether the confidence is acceptable or not. An algorithm is selected for ensemble if the confidence is below its associate threshold. The optimal threshold for each segmentation algorithm is found by using Comprehensive Learning Particle Swarm Optimization (CLPSO), swarm intelligence algorithm. The Dice coefficient, a popular performance metric for image segmentation, is used as fitness criteria. Experimental results on two polyp segmentation datasets MICCAI2015 and Kvasir-SEG confirm that our ensemble achieves better results compared to some well-known segmentation algorithms.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to constructing prediction sets that are distribution-free and risk-controlling. Existing methods for constructing prediction sets typically rely on assuming a specific distribution for the data, which can be limiting in many real-world applications where the underlying distribution is unknown or complex. Our proposed method, on the other hand, does not require any distributional assumptions and instead relies on a robust optimization framework to construct prediction sets with guaranteed coverage probabilities. Additionally, our approach allows for controlling the risk of the prediction set, ensuring that the error probability is upper bounded by a specified level. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through simulations and real-data experiments, showcasing its ability to provide accurate predictions while maintaining rigorous control over the risk level. We also compare our approach with existing state-of-the art methods, and show that it provides better performance in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Moreover, we discuss the implementation details of our algorithm and illustrate how it can be applied to various machine learning models, including neural networks and decision trees. Our main contribution is thus a powerful tool for constructing reliable prediction sets that do not impose any distributional assumptions, enabling their application in diverse domains such as medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and autonomous systems, among others. By providing a principled way to balance accuracy and risk, our work advances the field of uncertainty quantification and decision making under uncertainty.

This paper proposes a novel approach for greenhouse segmentation in high-resolution optical satellite imagery, utilizing deep learning techniques. Greenhouses are an essential component of modern agriculture, and accurate identification and segmentation of these structures is crucial for crop monitoring, yield prediction, and precision farming. Existing methods for greenhouse segmentation have limitations, including low accuracy and efficiency, particularly when dealing with large areas or complex scenes. To address these challenges, this study employs a deep learning framework based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to perform greenhouse segmentation. The proposed method is trained and validated using a dataset of high-resolution optical satellite images, captured by various sensors such as QuickBird and GeoEye-1. We investigate the effectiveness of different CNN architectures, including U-Net, FCN, and fully convolutional network (FCN)-based models, in extracting greenhouses from satellite images. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed deep learning-based approach achieves higher accuracy and faster processing times compared to traditional computer vision techniques. We also explore strategies to enhance the performance of the model, such as transfer learning, data augmentation, and feature pyramid networks (FPN). Additionally, we assess the impact of varying spatial resolutions, image contrast, and weather conditions on the accuracy of greenhouse segmentation. Our results show that the proposed method can accurately identify and segment greenhouses even in complex scenarios with multiple structures, shadows, and vegetation. The main contributions of this research include: * A novel deep learning-based approach for greenhouse segmentation in high-resolution optical satellite imagery * An extensive evaluation of different CNN architectures and their performance in greenhouse segmentation tasks * Investigation of techniques to improve model accuracy and efficiency, including transfer learning, data augmentation, and FPN * Analysis of the effects of various environmental factors on greenhouse segmentation accuracy This study has significant implications for precision agriculture, environmental monitoring, and sustainability management. The developed technique can be employed for timely detection of greenhouses, optimization of irrigation systems, and estimation of crop yields.

The generalised asymmetric dual-front model is a novel approach to active contours and image segmentation. This model combines the advantages of both level set methods and geometric variational frameworks, allowing for efficient and accurate boundary detection in various imageing applications. The proposed method utilises an asymmetrical energy functional that considers both internal and external forces acting on the contour, enabling flexibility in adjusting the influence of these factors based on specific task requirements. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methodology compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques across several benchmark datasets, indicating its potential as a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners working with visual data analysis tasks.

" I don't owe you a fair fight. " Invisible fingers seized Erika's lips and pulled. She smiled like her mother taught her, sharp and full of benign hatred. She was about to give up when the snapping sound stopped again; this time it came from behind. Erika spun around to find herself face-to-face with a large man in black leather pants, boots and a wide brimmed hat. He had no shirt on except for an open collarless jacket that he wore over his black vest and carried a longsword that could be seen under his left arm. His hands were covered by thick gloves that held a thin sheath of steel at each end. He made a loud noise as he lunged toward Erika and Erika shrieked, dropping her weapon and fumbling for the knife attached to it. The man's fist slammed into the blade of the knife, sending it flying across the room. The crossbow bolt bounced off the wall next to Erika before entering through one side and landing near the edge of a bed. It also ricocheted off another wall, narrowly missing Erika's head but still grazing her leg. Her hand went numb right above the elbow. For a moment she thought she might die. The man grabbed Erika and lifted her to stand just outside the door of their chamber. She tried to smile as she saw him standing there looking confused. Then she recognized the sword. Oh my God! This is my father! She tried to explain what happened without frightening him or arousing suspicion. But after a minute's silence he nodded and said "Did something happen here?" "Yes," she told him calmly "I'm sorry." At that point her father stepped closer. "Are you feeling all right?" She looked down at himself, then back up at Erika who stood trembling beside them. "No..." "You look pale and tired." "That's because we traveled far today and I haven't eaten much since yesterday morning." She reached behind her and took out a small bag from within the pocket where she kept her medicine. "I'm fine now though." Her father examined the small gold pill inside and found it to be just the drug she'd taken earlier and gave it to her. "Thank you."

Training deep networks with limited labeled data while achieving strong generalization ability is key in quest to reduce human annotation efforts. This is goal of semi-supervised learning, which exploits more widely available unlabeled data to complement small labeled data sets. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for discriminative pixel-level tasks using a generative model of both images and labels. Concretely, we learn a generative adversarial network that captures the joint image-label distribution and is trained efficiently using a large set of unlabeled images supplemented with only few labeled ones. We build our architecture on top of StyleGAN2, augmented with a label synthesis branch. Image labeling at test time is achieved by first embedding the target image into joint latent space via encoder network and test-time optimization, and then generating the label from inferred embedding. We evaluate our approach in two important domains: medical image segmentation and part-based face segmentation. We demonstrate strong in-domain performance compared to several baselines, and are first to showcase extreme out-of-domain generalization, such as transferring from CT to MRI in medical imaging, and photographs of real faces to paintings, sculptures, and even cartoons and animal faces. While deep convolutional neural systems achieved remarkable progress in medical image computing and research, its paradigm of supervised learning demands a huge number of annotations for training to reduce overfitting and achieving promising outcomes. In scientific practices, large semantic annotations are easy to obtain in some circumstances where specialized biomedical expert expertise is needed, and it is not a common condition where only few annotated classes are available. In this work, we proposed a novel technique for few-shot medical picture segmentation, which allows a segmentation model to fast generalize to an unseen class with few training images. We construct our few-shot image segmentor using a deep convolutional network trained episodically. Motivated by the temporal accuracy and consistency in medical images, we developed an efficient global correlation module to capture the similarity between a support and query image and incorporate it into the deep network called global correlation network. Specifically, we enhance discriminability of deep embedding to encourage clustering of the feature domains of the same class while keep the feature domains of multiple organs farther away. Ablation Study showed the validity of the proposed global correlation module and discriminative embedding loss. Numerous studies on anatomical abdomen images on both CT and MRI techniques are performed to establish the state-of-the-art efficiency of our proposed model.

In this paper, we explore the connection between S-folds and 4d N=3 superconformal field theories. We begin by reviewing concept of S-folds and their role in the context of string theory. We then examine properties of 4d N=3 superconformal field theories and their relationship to S-folds. Using combination of theoretical and numerical techniques, we demonstrate that S-folds can be used to engineer 4d N=3 superconformal field theories. We show that S-fold structure encodes information about the gauge group, matter content, and superconformal symmetries of the field theory. We also discuss relationship between S-folds and other approaches to engineering superconformal field theories, such as brane configurations and quiver gauge theories. Our results provide new insights into the structure of 4d N=3 superconformal field theories and their connection to string theory. They also demonstrate power of S-folds as tool for studying superconformal field theories and their applications to condensed matter physics and other areas of physics. Overall, this paper represents a significant advance in our understanding of the connection between S-folds and 4d N=3 superconformal field theories, and opens up new avenues for exploring the landscape of superconformal field theories.

He crossed his hands above his head as he finished the race - a gesture made by Ethiopia's Oromo people who have suffered brutal police crackdowns. He says he may be killed if he goes home but Ethiopia's government says he will be welcomed as a hero. However, state media is not showing photos of him crossing the line. There has been a wave of protests in Ethiopia in recent months over a series of frustrations, including attempts by the governments to reallocate land in the Oromo and Amhara regions. US-based Human Rights Watch says security forces have killed more than 400 Oromo protesters, a figure the government disputes. Rule 50 of the Olympic charter bans political displays or protests and the IOC say they are gathering information about the case. The BBC's Emmanuel Igunza in neighbouring Kenya says Mr Feyisa is being described by some as the bravest Olympian at the Rio Games for his anti-government protest, but he now faces the prospect of a life in exile. Within hours of his protest, a crowd-funding page was set up, saying the runner had displayed "extraordinary heroism" and that he had become an "international symbol" for the Oromo protests. The California-based organiser had initially set a target of 10,000 but it was exceeded within an hour. "We raised the bar to 25,000 and that too was exceeded in a few hours," Solomon Ungashe wrote on Facebook. After the race, Mr Feyisa explained why, as an Oromo, he supported the protests about land and resources. "The Ethiopian government is killing my people so I stand with all protests anywhere as Oromo is my tribe. My relatives are in prison and if they talk about democratic rights they are killed," he said. A legal team hired by Ethiopians in US is headed to Rio to try and help Mr Feyisa, who has a wife and two children in Ethiopia, with a request to seek asylum in the US. But Information Minister Getachew Reda told the BBC the government had no reason to arrest him and it respected his political opinion. He also said none of Mr Feyisa's relatives had been jailed over the Oromo protests. Ethiopian state-owned television station EBC Channel 3 covered the race live, including the finish, but did not repeat the clip in subsequent bulletins - focussing instead on the winner Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge.

The general consensus with frame rates greater than 24 or 30 fps in live action work is that it sucks. The illusion of a flickery alternate world breaks down when the frame rate is too smooth. The main problem with higher frame rates in live action work is that it tends to look unnatural and sterile. Generally, high frame rates make things look incredibly smooth and realistic, but this can be too much when applied to a live action setting. This leads to an artificial look that can make the footage feel slightly uncanny or off-putting. It also tends to reduce the cinematic quality of the footage, making it appear less immersive. Additionally, high frame rates require more computing power to process, which can be an issue for filmmakers who are working on tight budgets. This can lead to longer render times and additional costs associated with the production. That being said, higher frame rates do have their uses in certain situations. High frame rates can be useful in sports broadcasting or when filming fast action scenes, as they can help capture more detail in a shorter amount of time. Another use for higher frame rates is in 3D filmmaking, where smoother movements can create a more lifelike effect. Ultimately, it's up to filmmakers to decide whether the benefits of higher frame rates outweigh the potential drawbacks. While some filmmakers may choose to embrace the more realistic look of higher frame rates, others may prefer the classic cinematic look of 24 or 30 fps.

Styrofoam coffee cups simply melt in a microwave. I hope it's obvious why this isn't a good thing. Finally, it's a legal thing. Cups aren't dangerous, microwaving liquids inside until they are way too hot is the only reasonable way to hurt someone or something. Efficient generation of cluster states is crucial for engineering large-scale measurement-based quantum computers. Hybrid matter-optical systems offer a robust, scalable path to this goal. Such systems have ancilla which acts as a bus connecting the qubits. We show that by generating smaller cluster "Lego bricks", reusing one ancilla per brick, the cluster can be produced with maximal efficiency, requiring fewer than half the operations compared with no bus reuse. By reducing the time required to prepare sections of cluster, bus reuse more than doubles size of computational workspace that can be used before decoherence effects dominate. A row of buses in parallel provides fully scalable cluster state generation requiring only 20 CPhase gates per bus use.

The room glowed slightly from all the screens. Hundreds and hundreds of screens, some small, some bigger than others across every available wall surface. Apart from the light from the screens, it was dark. Electricity is expensive after all when reindeer power the generator. In the midst of the screens was a chair and a small desk, empty except for three telephones. In the chair sat a visibly disheveled man. Watching, always watching the thousands and thousands of screens. The man couldn't remember the last time he had slept. Ever since selling this mainframe to the US government he had been required to monitor it constantly. This was not the issue though, because he had monitored it since the beginning of time. The issue was that they demanded to know things they shouldn't. It taxed the old man. He was the keeper of secrets, the decider of good and bad. Not them. Not them. What the NSA didn't know was that the old man had made similar sales to other customers, each believing that they alone had purchased this amazing technology. The Chinese had bought his services first, then the Russians. It wasn't until trade deals began being sabotaged and national secrets began leaking that the Americans had finally made the purchase. Because the old man was the only one who could operate this system, each had no reason to believe that any other nation had access. A phone rang, and the old man answered. A look of concern flashed across his face before he slammed the phone down and looked at the floor. Who were they to ask such a thing? The old man thought for a moment, breaking from watching the screens for what seemed the first time in a thousand years. Then he had an idea. he picked up the phone that had just rung, and without hesitation said the only words that maybe, just maybe, would end his torment. 'The Russians are launching their nukes." Then he had similar conversations with the other two phones. The old man smiled. An enormous weight lifted from his shoulders. Across the globe chaos and death would be unfolding in the next few seconds. He leaned back in his chair and muttered to himself: "Christmas is cancelled this year."

What didn't happen you say? Well, I'll tell you. Everything happened I supposed, from the beginning. The world was warm and bright, while a little cold at some times. It was a rich, a dirt pile with enough soil for the worms to eat, enough worms for the birds to eat, enough birds for the cats to eat, enough cats for the wolves to eat, then enough bears for man, the greatest of the worms, to eat. But then nothing happened. It didn't stop. It simply didn't happen. Nothing was there. No lights, no sounds. Not even the person you are sitting next to happened. There wasn't even an empty void. For how can you have a void of nothing when nothing happened? Time never happened. The universe never happened. You never happened. All thanks to a vengeful god, the last of his species, who survived the battle of the heavens and was it's greatest killer. Whose mind dove into the wild and fire of insanity until he was nothing more than a beast. And he too was nothing.

In this study, we investigate the time complexity of synchronizing collection of discrete pulse-coupled oscillators (PCOs) operating on a tree topology. PCO networks have long been used to model and control biological systems, such as heartbeat regulation and animal locomotion. However, their effectiveness is heavily dependent on the ability to synchronize individual oscillators, which remains open research challenge. Despite extensive work in this area, it has not yet been established what determines the efficiency of different algorithms in accomplishing this task. In this context, we analyze two popular algorithms for synchronization: the Kuramoto algorithm and its variants based on spectral theory. Both these algorithms are known to operate with linear time complexity, which implies that they can be easily scaled up to handle large numbers of coupled oscillators. We demonstrate how their convergence properties depend on various parameters of system (such as coupling strength and initial conditions), using both numerical simulations and theoretical analyses. Our results suggest that efficient operation of these algorithms requires careful tuning of these parameter values. Additionally, we observe that certain structural characteristics of the network (e.g., clustering coefficients and path lengths) also play crucial role in determining their performance.

A video can be regarded as an object in the image space of the screen, but its structure and arrangement cannot easily be captured or understood by the usual image and movie processing tools, such as edge detection. And at the same time, a video does not need to fit into any precise representation of a scene. A number of videos, for example, are just repeated visual patterns, with actors repeating motions, a scene with no apparent story, without dialogue, without narration, but all these structures are hidden from human observation. An ambitious project is underway to recognize some of these hidden characteristics, so as to enable segmentation of a video which otherwise would escape automatic analysis and classification. A new type of mathematical representation of a video object is being devised, which combines low-level features into high-level abstractions of what is happening in a video. We use the program YouTube-Vos [7] to examine how well the excellent features based on image-based segmentation can perform when applied to a large movie, and to test these results against a theory of machine modelling of a scene called “Video VOS”. Our experiments show that youtube-Vos can detect a number of important features of the movie, but not without some subjectivity in interpretation. These results help us to identify approaches that are able to successfully classify complex movies, and those that will fail, because they do not understand the complexity of the movie and the temporal sequences of its features. We also show the potential benefits of using youtube-Vos for new types of learning methods in a field of artificial intelligence where current methods are already successful. In this research, a novel voxel-level Siamese representation learning methodology is proposed towards obtaining more realistic abdomen multi-organ segmentation from medical images. The proposed methodology uses the strengths of three Siamese systems simultaneously to learn joint representations from different organs and evaluate the segmentation efficiency without focusing on shared encoder weights or any transferable features. We evaluate our method using CT scans with two segmented abdominal organs obtained by manual labeling. Our findings show that with the use of different Siamese streams, our simulation produces competitive results compared to recently published deep learning models while providing relatively simple network design, featuring only few partially connected layers.

> "We introduce an unsupervised learning method that can achieve semantic segmentations on 90+ ImageNet classes given only a small target domain training set -- no class labels, object bounds or auxiliary data required. First we build a teacher-student pipeline using adversarial learning to ensure strong perceptual fidelity of synthesized images (a challenging dataset constraint). Next, to improve synthesis accuracy by incorporating external knowledge about fine details like natural colors & shapes across various contexts, instead of supervision we incorporate contrastive embeddings between source domains images as additional discriminative information loss terms during GAN training. Since our student network captures global and regional style factors while preserving the shape content from both real and synthetic sample sets together, this framework provides superior semantic masks over prior methods."

Russia's plan for "de-escalation" zones was backed by Iran at talks in Kazakhstan. Both countries support Syrian president Bashar al-Assad. Turkey, which supports rebel groups, also agreed to act as a guarantor. But some delegates from the rebel forces angrily rejected the plan. As the three countries were invited to sign the document on Thursday in the Kazakh capital, Astana, rebel delegates angrily shouted that they did not accept it and walked out. Reporters at the talks said the rebels were unhappy about Iran's involvement in the deal as a guarantor. The US also expressed concern over Iran, saying the country had "only contributed to the violence, not stopped it." The Syrian government is not a signatory, but its state news agency said it supported the plan. The talks were meant to shore up an oft-violated ceasefire which was originally agreed in December. A partial cessation of hostilities was declared at the end of last year, but violence has continued on several fronts. Under the Russian plan, safe zones would be established in rebel-held territory in the north-western province of Idlib, in parts of Homs province in the centre, in the south, and in the opposition enclave of Eastern Ghouta near Damascus, the AFP news agency reported. Syrian and Russian warplanes would stop bombing rebel positions while opposition groups would halt attacks inside the "de-escalation zones." The objective is to "put an immediate end to the violence" and "provide the conditions for the safe, voluntary return of refugees" in addition to the speedy provision of relief supplies and medical aid. The safe zones would remain in place for six months, the Kremlin has said. They would be surrounded by checkpoints manned by rebels and government troops, and foreign troops could also be deployed in observer roles, according to AFP. The UN's envoy for Syria, Staffan de Mistura, called the agreement a step in the right direction. Syria's envoy to the UN Bashar al-Jaafari said he hoped Russia and Iran would discuss the plan's details with the Syrian government as soon as possible. Syria's war has claimed more than 300,000 lives since it erupted in 2011.

Artificial intelligence (AI), and particularly machine learning, has become increasingly prevalent within healthcare as diagnostic support technology known as artificial intelligence medical systems, with applications spanning multiple areas including radiology and pathology imaging data interpretation but also genomics to facilitate precision medicine efforts. In response to this rapid innovation dynamic, we seek to help ensure that AI within all contexts of health care are trustworthy through the lens of human-machine collaboration. Toward these ends, experts representing a diversity of disciplines engaged across government agencies, academic institutions, industry leaders, and patient advocacy group representatives gathered at an international workshop entitled FUTURE-AI. A major goal was to elucidate how best practices could be developed toward achieving trustworthiness of AI systems utilized throughout radiological clinical practice workflows from pre-training inputs through validation methodologies to final deployment and ongoing use assessment frameworks. More specifically, during sessions over five days participants identified key principles pertinent to designing machine intelligence technologies in conjunction with humans on which future guidance documents can be built. Topics included definitions of terms such as explainability, fairness and bias, transparency and accessibility; ethical considerations around human factors involved in the design of intelligent machines especially when applied clinically; and approaches to training, testing, validating and deploying models in realistic clinical environments for diverse patient populations. Participants also assessed gaps in existing AI standards and made suggestions regarding necessary improvements or updates currently lacking in order to promote future safe system development and implementation, ultimately leading to recommendations for moving forward along established guidelines. Through this consensus process, we hope to inform best practices for using advanced computer science analytics towards helping physicians deliver optimal patient outcomes.

In this paper we study the phenomenon of the formation of localized states in one-dimensional elastomers. The phenomenon of localization, in general, is the occurrence of exponentially localized states in systems with internal disorder, the presence of randomness or imperfections causing the inhibition of wave propagation and the formation of stationary waves confined to certain regions of the system. Using numerical experiments on a typical one-dimensional elastomer, we show that the phenomenon of localization is present. As is the case in many such systems, the presence of small amounts of disorder can lead to a strong inhibition of wave propagation, the emergence of localized modes, which are not explained by the conventional analyses of the geometry or periodicity of the system. We also study the influence of the various system parameters on the localization phenomenon. Our results show that there is an optimum amount of disorder for which the localization effects are most pronounced, and the system's scaling with respect to these system parameters is well in agreement with theoretical expectations. This paper demonstrates the importance of the localization phenomenon in explaining many experimental observations on the properties of materials and also provides new insights into the role of disorder in controlling their properties. This has important implications for the design of new materials and structures with unusual wave propagation properties, which could be used in many different areas of application such as vibration damping, impact attenuation, and sensing.

Abstract Non-automated image segmentation for facial refrence identification is extremely challenging even with large data sets, especially when there are multiple eyes and/or nose pointing to a given face in an array representation. In this work we present such a scalable automatic system for automated multi-modality image segmentations based both on the similarity between two images taken at high resolution and their relative orientation similarity at all pixel resolutions (e.g., depth). The resulting classification results are compared at various refrence types for human or robot recognition tasks: facial, occlusion and hair matching. Compared to previous state-of-the-art approaches, our approach uses more sparse feature representations from higher resolutions while maintaining good performance for different training images at the same spatial resolution (i.e., ~400×500). Our algorithm has excellent localization accuracy with very low error rate under similer test conditions using a variety of object attributes including depth, face shape parameters, orientation and texture data. We demonstrate our method's robustness by applying it to five widely used object data formats that make up a wide range of real world applications, yielding successfull model learning for facial match, occlusion detection and partial occlusion classifying as well as hair type matches. Furthermore, the overall improvement over previously published methods on several categories is considerable. Overall, these results suggest that our methodology is effective enough during general task requirements and that it could be further developed through tuning its framework for faster iteration times. Additionally, our method may also have application in robotics where human-robot interactions involve pose sensing since many activities might require accurate recognition of the subject's facial appearance. In conclusion, we apply our comprehensive multi-modality inference technique for image segmentation towards building robust automatic referance object segmentation systems using a diverse set of diverse domain attires and thereby improve the quality of personal assistant application input features. Our initial research aims at testing wether our deep convolutional neural networks can be built into future generation intelligent assistants that use image capture without requiring humans to manually define context or select suitable objects. This study aimed to develop a robust general medical image segmentation algorithm. A comprehensive review of existing techniques was conducted, and an innovative approach combining deep learning with traditional machine learning methods was proposed. The effectiveness of the method was demonstrated through extensive experiments on multiple datasets covering various anatomical structures and imaging modalities. Results showed that the proposed methodology significantly improved segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the art models, making it a promising tool for clinicians and researchers in the field of medical imaging.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to domain adaptation called scribble-based domain adaptation via co-segmentation. Our method leverages the power of manual annotation to adapt machine learning models to new domains in way that is efficient, effective, and robust. Existing domain adaptation methods often rely on large amounts of labeled data from target domain, which can be difficult or expensive to obtain. In contrast, our approach requires only small number of annotated examples from source domain and a set of scribbles, or rough segmentations, provided by expert oracle. These scribbles indicate location of the object or feature of interest in images, but do not require precise segmentation masks. We introduce new algorithm that uses these scribbles to learn domain-adaptive representation space through a process of co-segmentation. The key idea is to iteratively align source and target domains while simultaneously refining the scribbled bounding boxes to improve their accuracy. This allows us to transfer knowledge between domains effectively even when there are significant differences in image distribution or object placement. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, achieving state-of-the-art performance on several challenging benchmark datasets including VisDA2017, CIFAR10, and SYTHIA. We also perform comprehensive ablation studies to analyze the contributions of different components of our method, providing insights into its strengths and limitations. Overall, our work offers a promising solution to the problem of domain shift, enabling machine learning models to generalize across diverse environments with minimal additional training data. This has important implications for real-world applications such as robotics, autonomous driving, and medical imaging, where domain shifts are common and annotated data is scarce.

The Voronoi diagram-based dual-front active contour models are known as a powerful and efficient way for addressing the image segmentation and domain partitioning problems. In the basic formulation of the dual-front models, the evolving contours can be considered as the interfaces of adjacent Voronoi regions. Among these dual-front models, a crucial ingredient is regarded as the geodesic metrics by which the geodesic distances and the corresponding Voronoi diagram can be estimated. In this paper, we introduce a type of asymmetric quadratic metrics dual-front model. The metrics considered are built by the integration of the image features and a vector field derived from the evolving contours. The use of the asymmetry enhancement can reduce the risk of contour shortcut or leakage problems especially when the initial contours are far away from the target boundaries or the images have complicated intensity distributions. Moreover, the proposed dual-front model can be applied for image segmentation in conjunction with various region-based homogeneity terms. The numerical experiments on both synthetic and real images show that the proposed dual-front model indeed achieves encouraging results.

This academic paper investigates the existence and behavior of traveling wave solutions for a bistable equation with nonlocal-diffusion. The bistable equation is a mathematical model that describes systems that can exist in two stable states, and the nonlocal-diffusion term accounts for long-range interactions between particles. The paper employs analytical and numerical methods to study the properties of these traveling waves, including their speed, stability, and dependence on the parameters of the model. The results provide insights into the role of nonlocal-diffusion in shaping the dynamics of bistable systems and have implications for a range of applications in physics, biology, and other fields.

First, we describe a biophysics-based domain adaptation approach. second, we propose an automatic procedure to segment black and black matter, and spinal fluid, in addition to tumorous tumor. Regarding our next innovation, we use a domain adaptation methodology that combines a novel multispecies biological tissue development model with a generative adversarial model to produce realistic looking synthetic multimodal MR images with known segmentation. Regarding our next innovation, we propose an automatic method to enrich available segmentation data by computing the segmentation for healthy tissues. This segmentation, which is done using diffeomorphic image registration between the BraTS training data and a set of prelabeled atlases, gives more information for training and reduces the class imbalance problem. Our overall method is not relevant to any specific neural network and can be applied in accordance with existing technologies. We demonstrate the performance improvement using a 2D U-Net for the BraTS'18 segmentation challenge. Our biophysics based domain adaptation produces better results, as compared to the existing state-of-the-art GAN model designed to provide synthetic data for training.

CRNet: Cross-Reference Networks for Few-Shot Segmentation Segmenting objects from images is a fundamental task in computer vision, but traditional methods require large amounts of annotated data to acheive good performance. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called CRNet (Cross-Reference Network), which leverages cross-reference information between images to improve few-shot segmentation accuracy. CRNet consists of two main components: a referance encoder and a target decoder. The refrence encoder extracts features from a set of referance images, while the target decoder segments the object of interest in a target image using the extracted features. We introduce a novel cross-referencing module that compares the similarity between the referance and target feature maps, enabling the model to focus on the most revelant regions for segmentation. We evaluate CRNet on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and COCO, and demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods. Our experiments show that CRNet can accurately segment objects with only a few labeled examples per class, outperforming previous approaches that rely solely on within-image annotation. Additionally, we perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components in CRNet and provide insights into the working mechanism of our proposed method. The main contributions of this paper are: 1. Introduction of Cross-Reference Networks (CRNets) for few-shot segmentation, which utilize cross-image information to improve segmentation accuracy. 2. Design of a novel cross-referencing module that compares referance and target feature maps, allowing the model to focus on revelant regions for segmentation. 3. Experimental validation of CRNets on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating their superiority over existing few-shot segmentation methods. 4. Ablation studies providing insights into the functioning of CRNets and identifying key components that contribute to their success. Overall, CRNet presents a significant step forward in few-shot segmentation research, offering a promising direction for future investigations in this area.

In this paper, we study medical image (MI) segmentation and use the knowledge of the human subject domain in self-supervised training to improve the quality of MI segmentation. We have two reasons for this approach: First, since in the vast majority of real data there are only one or a few domain experts available, the use of these annotations as supervisory signals to perform semantic information extraction can extract more complete scene context than purely unsupervised learning. Second, from the neuro-scientific research on visual perception, people's visual perception is mainly based on the previous information they receive through multi-sense input, including visual input. [1] and non-visual input. Based on this observation, our method is not based on raw R, G and B features, and it is constructed by high-level semantics based on external information, a spatial guidance network and a local feature aggregator. The whole is called a "prior guidance network". By using the knowledge of the subject to guide the training process, the prior guidance network is able to infer accurate perceptual clues, which can be used for image segmentation, and is superior to single-shot learning methods that only rely on visual input. Furthermore, our method is combined with the encoder network, which is well-known for its ability to compress deep convolutional networks., the initial weights of which are obtained by this deep convolutional network, so as to avoid the high initialization cost of such deep convolutional networks, which often have millions of trainable parameters. The experimental results show that the classification accuracy of our method is superior to that of previous methods, especially in the case of challenging samples, which have a high proportion of ambiguous samples in the object boundary, and even difficult for people to distinguish the two classes. Automated weed detection is a crucial task for efficient crop management, especially in precision agriculture. This research proposes an automatic approach to detect weeds based on deep learning techniques that utilize contextual information from aerial imagery. The proposed method uses convolutional neural networks (CNN) combined with attention mechanisms that allow the model to focus on informative regions of interest and extract vital features that distinguish weeds from other crops. The CNNs are trained using large-scale datasets containing diverse types of weeds and crops under varying environmental conditions. The results show that the proposed technique exhibits high accuracy and robustness across different scenarios while outperforming state-of-the-art methods. This work paves the way towards advancements in automated farming practices by providing a reliable tool for weeding optimization without relying on human intervention or extensive manual labor.

In this study, we propose a novel few-shot segmentation approach that leverages both global and local contrastive learning. Our method is based on the idea of encoding image features in an efficient manner to enable rapid adaptation to new tasks without requiring extensive training data. We demonstrate through experiments conducted on various datasets that our model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods while achieving faster convergence rates thanks to its ability to capture high-level semantic information as well as detailed contextual cues using contrasting examples at multiple scales. Overall, these results suggest that combining different types of contrasts can lead to significant improvements in few-shot performance for segmentation problems.

In this study, we provide large scale image segmentation using high-dimensional distributions as a function of spatial and temporal resolution: it maps small to large images with similer pixel contents but different features, like color, location, depth and shape. The use of multidimensional local distribution (MDL) methods results in more information being extracted. We compare our experiments on a large dataset of 1000 images and show that we can reduce reconstruction time by two orders of magnitude compared to state of art methods, such as SIFT or SVM classification. Furthermore, many MDL approaches have been proposed for different problem domains. For example, our implementation performs significantly better than those of Gaussians as described in previous work and supports multiple classification tasks including regression classification and machine translation. To demonstrate image segmenting, three datasets were used, one at 12.5cm x 12.5cm, 20cm x 20cm and 90 metres x 90 meters, measured diagonally with a 3D scanner. A total sample size of 1,000 was sampled each time to verify good performance across dimensions. Figure 2 shows an extreem case where a dense mask (15 pixels wide at 180° and 10×20 rectangles horizontally on 3D imaging plane), resulting in nearly 300 x 30 × 40 data points per mesh area, was utilized while performing Image Reshaping and Segmentation using Deep Learning (IRSE). This has shown that IRSE achieves significant performance improvements over preprogrammed deep net architectures, even though its training procedure requires more computation on image creation. In short, the results are encouraging and may be readily implemented with existing technology in order to adress current photo-sharing and search problems.

In this study, we proposed a high-resolution segmentation method to extract tooth root edge in radiographic images. Our approach combined polynomial curve fitting and landmark detection techniques. Firstly, we located 10 significant landmarks of each root using image processing techniques including template matching, edge detection and contour analysis. Then the remaining root edges were extracted by applying polynomial curve fitting algorithm, obtaining smooth and continuous functions that represented root edges' distribution patterns. Finally, the fuzzy connectivity among these curves was adjusted through membership function calculation and distance between roots' surfaces computation methods. The performance evaluation showed our proposed method outperformed other state of the art algorithms based on quantitative assessment metrics indicating accuracy and computational complexity. This work could provide valuable information in developing efficient automation tools for dental professionals to improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce patient exposure time from complex radiographs.

We investigate Referring Image Segmentation (RIS), which outputs a segmentation map corresponding to the given natural language description. To solve RIS efficiently, we need to understand each word's relationship with other words, each region in the image to other regions, and cross-modal alignment between linguistic and visual domains. We argue that one of the limiting factors in the recent methods is that they do not handle these interactions simultaneously. To this end, we propose a novel architecture called JRNet, which uses a Joint Reasoning Module(JRM) to concurrently capture the inter-modal and intra-modal interactions. The output of JRM is passed through a novel Cross-Modal Multi-Level Fusion (CMMLF) module which further refines the segmentation masks by exchanging contextual information across visual hierarchy through linguistic features acting as a bridge. We present thorough ablation studies and validate our approach's performance on four benchmark datasets, showing considerable performance gains over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

As the most economical and routine auxiliary examination in the diagnosis of root canal treatment, oral X-ray has been widely used by stomatologists. It is still challenging to segment the tooth root with a blurry boundary for the traditional image segmentation method. To this end, we propose a model for high-resolution segmentation based on polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection (HS-PCL). It is based on detecting multiple landmarks evenly distributed on the edge of the tooth root to fit a smooth polynomial curve as the segmentation of the tooth root, thereby solving the problem of fuzzy edge. In our model, a maximum number of the shortest distances algorithm (MNSDA) is proposed to automatically reduce the negative influence of the wrong landmarks which are detected incorrectly and deviate from the tooth root on the fitting result. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach not only reduces Hausdorff95 (HD32) by 76.4% and Average Surface Distance (ASD) by 42.1% compared with the state-of-the-art method, but it also achieves excellent results on the minute quantity of datasets, which greatly improves the feasibility of automatic root canal therapy evaluation by medical image computing.

The development of trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) is crucial for the future of medical imaging. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the current state of AI in medical imaging and identifies key challenges and opportunities for future development. The paper also outlines guiding principles and consensus recommendations for ensuring the safety, reliability, and ethical use of AI in medical imaging. These principles include transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy, and security, as well as the need for ongoing monitoring and evaluation of AI systems. The paper concludes by emphasizing the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and stakeholder engagement in developing and implementing trustworthy AI in medical imaging.

Other approaches to 3D image segmentation are based on hierarchical clustering of supervoxels into image regions. Here we describe a distributed algorithm capable of handling a huge number of supervoxels. The algorithms works recursively, the regions are separated into chunks that are processed simultaneously in parallel by different workers. At each round of the recursive process, the chunk size in all dimensions are doubled until a second slice covers the whole image. The final result is provably independent of the chunking scheme, and the same as if the whole image were processed without division into portions. This is nontrivial because a pair of adjacent regions is scored by some mathematical property (e.g. mean or average) of the affinities at the interface, and the interface can extend over arbitrarily different chunks. The trick is to delay merge decisions for areas that touch chunk boundaries, and only complete them in a later round after the areas are completely contained within a slice. We demonstrate the algorithm by clustering an affinity graph with over 1.5 billion edges between 135 trillion supervoxels obtained from a 3D electron microscopic brain image.

This academic paper presents an iterative deep unsupervised approach to synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) image segmentation. Overall, this novel technique offers significant potential for enhancing object detection and classification tasks in SAS imaging applications.

The paper presents a novel method for high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy edges based on polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection. The proposed method uses a combination of landmark detection and polynomial curve fitting to accurately segment tooth root fuzzy edges. The landmark detection algorithm is used to identify the key points on the tooth root surface, while the polynomial curve fitting algorithm is used to model the fuzzy edges between these key points. The resulting segmentation is highly accurate and can be used for a variety of applications in dental imageing and analysis. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through a series of experiments and comparisons with other state-of-the-art methods.

The economic research institute questioned 320 businesses following the vote on leaving the EU. The survey found more than 60 of Scottish firms believe Brexit would have a "negative impact" on them. However, the institute said there was little evidence of companies cancelling investment or recruitment outright. The Fraser of Allander Institute, an independent research body based at the University of Strathclyde, carried out the survey between 5 July and 12 July, in the aftermath of the EU referendum. Just over 60 of Scottish firms surveyed said they believed Brexit will have a negative impact on their business, while only 19 said it would have a positive impact. One third said the impact would be "very negative." About 40 believe that leaving the EU could lead to a decrease in their investment and expansion plans, and 34 said that they could cut back on recruitment. More than 70 of firms surveyed as part of the research had done no preparation for the UK exiting the EU. Two-thirds of businesses said resolution of the uncertainty in the economy was a key issue in the negotiation of the UK's exit from the European Union, while 49 of firms cited access to the single market as a key issue. However, the survey found little evidence of companies actually cancelling investment or recruitment plans. A quarter of firms said they had made a decision to change their investment and recruitment plans, though the vast majority - 95 - said that decisions had been postponed rather than cancelled entirely. Prof Graeme Roy, director of the institute, said: "This is the first hard survey evidence post-referendum of what businesses in Scotland are thinking and how they are responding to the unexpected EU referendum result. "A clear majority believe that the impact - certainly in the short to medium term - will be negative. The survey offers some evidence that investment and recruitment plans may be being put on hold. "Resolving the current political and economic uncertainty must now be the key priority. The longer the period of uncertainty continues, the more damaging the impact will be on the economy."

Large-scale image segmentation is a critical task in computer vision applications. In this work, we present a novel technique to perform image partitioning utilizing distributed clustering algorithms such as K-means and hierarchical clustering. Our approach aims at addressing the challenges of large data processing by dividing the image into smaller subimages that can be processed independently and then combining their results to derive a final output. We also propose an adaptive method to rearrange the partitions of small clusters with minimum communication overhead, which improves scalability. The algorithm converges faster than conventional techniques by leveraging MPI (Message Passing Interface) for parallel communication between nodes. Results show that our proposed method outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior accuracy with reduced computational time and communicative cost.

Reinforcement learning requires manual specification of a reward function to learn a task. While in principle this reward function only needs to specify the task goal, in practice reinforcement learning can be very time-consuming or even infeasible unless the reward function is shaped so as to provide a smooth gradient towards a successful outcome. This shaping is difficult to specify by hand, particularly when the task is learned from raw observations, such as images. In this paper, we study how we can automatically learn dynamical distances: a measure of the expected number of time steps to reach a given goal state from any other state. These dynamical distances can be used to provide well-shaped reward functions for reaching new goals, making it possible to learn complex tasks efficiently. We show that dynamical distances can be used in a semi-supervised regime, where unsupervised interaction with the environment is used to learn the dynamical distances, while a small amount of preference supervision is used to determine the task goal, without any manually engineered reward function or goal examples. We evaluate our method both on a real-world robot and in simulation. We show that our method can learn to turn a valve with a real-world 9-DoF hand, using raw image observations and just ten preference labels, without any other supervision. Accuracy has been the goal of recent years in Machine Learning, but a reliable decision-making only requires uncertainty. Using learning systems in real life conditions also requires the calibration and communication of the uncertainty of the predictions. To represent uncertainty for individual predictions, we show how to generate set-valued predictions from a black box predictor which reduce the expected loss on future test points at the level desired by the user. Our approach provides an explicit loss bound for every problem on a dataset by calibrating the size of the prediction set on a holdout sample. This framework allows simple and distribution-free error control and is illustrated by five large-scale machine learning problems: (1) classification problems with a cost of errors, (2) multi-label classification, where each observation has a number of associated labels, (3) hierarchical classification, (4) image segmentation, where one tries to predict a set of pixels in an image that contains a given object, and (5) prediction of the structure of a protein. Finally, we discuss extensions to uncertainty quantification for ordering, metric learning and distributionally robust learning.

Studies on income inequality and growth have sometimes found evidence confirming the Kuznets curve hypothesis, which states that with economic development, inequality first increases, then decreases. Economist Thomas Piketty challenges this notion, claiming that from 1914 to 1945 wars and "violent economic and political shocks" reduced inequality. Moreover, Piketty argues that the "magical" Kuznets curve hypothesis, with its emphasis on the balancing of economic growth in the long run, cannot account for the significant increase in economic inequality throughout the developed world since the 1970s.

With the Widespread success of deep learning in biomedical image segmentation, domain shift becomes a critical and challenging problem, As the gap between two domains can severely affect Model performance when deployed to unseen data with heterogeneous features. to alleviate this problem, we present a novel unsupervised domain adaptation network, for generalizing models learned from the labeled source domain to the unlabeled target domain for cross-modality biomedical image segmentation. Specifically, our approach consists of two key modules, a conditional domain discriminator~(CDD) and a category-centric prototype aligner~(CCPA). The CDD, extended from conditional domain adversarial networks in classifier tasks, is effective and robust in handling complex cross-modality biomedical images. the CCPA, improved from The graph-induced prototype alignment mechanism in cross-domain object detection, can exploit precise instance-level features through an elaborate prototype representation. In addition, it can address the negative effect of Class imbalance Via entropy-based loss. Extensive experiments on a public benchmark for the cardiac substructure segmentation task demonstrate that our method significantly improves performance on the target domain.

We present an approach to training deep generative models that learns large sparse non-stationary distributions for the input features in image processing problems. To solve these problem we employ coarse-and-fine convolutional neural network. The model consists of two layers with separate hidden states; one layer generates the high-dimensional features while the other provides the low-dimensional perceptrons on top of which the high-resolution feature is computed. This allows us to train a large network whose structure consists of two recurrent connections to each hidden node through an arbitrary multilayer feedforward process (such as forward pass followed by back propagation). Our main inspiration was inspired by the famous Krizhevsky–Lehoux architecture of VGG. We show how our algorithm can be used to learn efficient and scalable multi-scale philtres at scales greater than even the computational power available today. (Image courtesy of Wikipedia Commons)

This research aims to develop a comprehensive multi-modal interaction system for referring image segmentation. Such a system enables users to input reference words in two modes, visual and textual, thereby enhancing accuracy and efficiency in performing semantic labelling tasks. A series of experimental investigations were conducted on different benchmark datasets using various state-of-the-art models, including visual CNNs and language-based transformer networks. The findings suggest that fusing both mode's attention mechanisms leads to better model performance than adopting either modal individually. Thus, this study highlights the importance of leverageing multi-modality for more sophisticated referring image segmentation systems.

Edge detection is a fundamental task in image processing and computer vision, and has been extensively studied in the past few decades. Recently, deep learning-based methods have gained popularity for their ability to learn complex features and achieve state-of-the-art performance. However, these methods often require large amounts of labelled data and computational resources, which can be limiting for real-world applications. In this paper, we propose a novel deep neural network architecture inspired by traditional edge detection methods, which can be efficiently deployed on resource-constrained devices at the edge of the network. Our approach leverages the strengths of traditional methods, such as the Sobel operator and Canny edge detector, to extract robust features that are less sensitive to noise and artefacts. We combine these features with a deep neural network to learn a hierarchical representation of the image, which enables accurate edge detection and segmentation. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art edge detection methods. Our results show that our proposed method outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, while also providing better interpretability and robustness. We also demonstrate the feasibility of deploying our method on resource-constrained devices, such as smartphones and smart cameras, which is not feasible with existing deep learning-based methods. Our work has important implications for edge computing and IoT applications, where real-time processing and low latency are critical. By leverageing traditional methods and deep learning techniques, we can develop efficient and accurate edge detection systems that can be deployed in a variety of real-world scenarios.

Before the Marian reforms, the Roman military forces were exclusively made up of citizens people of property (3500 sesterces, say about 1750 loaves of bread) and capable of supplying their troops in a war situation. The soldiers' pay was called manus - literally "hand" - because it consisted of money handed to them by hand-picked citizen recruits at battle. To go into battle on campaign or for training purposes, they would have been given extra rations or other refreshments as well. They received this payment only after fulfilling certain requirements: service to one's army unit, good conduct while serving (including not stealing), bearing arms, etc., usually until retirement. Because the poor could not afford weapons and armour, many became mercenaries who fought for whoever paid more. This brought concerns over state sovereignty, since these individuals had no loyalty to any state but rather to themselves; in particular, cavalrymen often went rogue and joined with outlaws or revolting populations. Such brigands included the famous Gens Lepida (The Pious Ones), led by Publius Decimus Brutus Meserve during Caesar Augustus' civil wars. In addition, some citizen armies formed via popular assemblies from large numbers of volunteers also caused problems when used against noncitizens.[4] In such cases, citizenship might be required before allowing enlistment; if so, those excluded would sometimes form militias out of former members of city militias (i.e. formerly enrolled citizens). Military units generally did not use serfs as conscripts, preferring poorer free men whose loyalties may have been less settled than that of a slave. During times of peace, the majority of disciplined Roman soldiers probably worked civilian jobs, and had no interest in fighting. When towns needed warriors for defense or auxiliary troop gathering, they would usually hire troops drawn from neighboring tribes or states. These mercenary bands then provided an alternate source of tension between Rome and its neighbors, particularly Carthage. When Elagabalus attempted to placate his own disgruntled populace through greater dedication to Rome and less towards Carthage, he ultimately earned himself widespread support but incurred the wrath of Hamilcar Barca. Barcas son Hasdrubal murdered him and usurped power. He quickly lost favor both with Rome itself, and among most Punic groups outside the Seleucid Empire due to his unpopularity. His inability to maintain control meant that he had little choice but to convince Rome again to send troops, which she eventually did under her new governor Aulus

We propose a new framework to assess the robustness of general medical image segmentation systems. Our contributions are two-fold: (i) we propose a new benchmark to evaluate robustness in the Context Of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) by extending the recent AutoAttack natural image classification framework to the domain of volumetric data Segmentation, and (ii) we present a novel lattice architecture for RObust Generic medical image segmentation (ROG). our results show that ROG is capable of generalizing across different tasks of the MSD and largely Surpasses the state-of-the-art under sophisticated adversarial attacks.

In this work, we use LHCb to probe what happens in the fissile material that initiates a nuclear chain reaction or a "hot fusion." The experiment includes two major parts that lead to a detection of spontaneous thermal X-ray emission and the detection of the decay products with no radioactive isotope contributions. This allows us to obtain the first realistic snapshot at high particle energies (30 TeV). These two observations are related because these hot atoms produce a high concentration of energetic neutrinos as they collapse under their own weight into stable atoms, leading to their rapid disintegration (i.e., fission) within seconds after being created. Thus we find in one second between 100 and 1000 collisions on one half of the proton–proton beam axis, representing less then 0.1% of all possible collisions over the lifetime of the experiment. In addition there will be many random events which do not contribute to any detection and therefore have negligible impact on the results, due to its short run duration and sensitivity to collisions on different experimental scales. We demonstrate that it is indeed possible to detect spontaneous thermal X-rays from the high-energy decay of heavier fermions in an environment where the majority of neutrons are produced during nuclear fission by fusing nucleons of lower energy. For the purposes of our analyses, this "fission chain reaction" requires a high degree of accuracy in tracking fast neutrons—a problem that cannot be solved without additional data. Using the available resources and computing power of the LHCb machine combined with improved methods for dealing with noise as well as the advent of very accurate spectroscopy using FET detectors [28], we can now monitor extremely sensitive processes on a much larger scale than even that envisaged in the recent large experiments such as SNIC or Fermilab's ATLAS [3], both located more than 40 kilometers away from LHCb.
