Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in field of healthcare, enabling accurate identification and extraction of specific anatomical structures from images. However, performance of segmentation algorithms can be limited by the availability of labeled data, particularly in the case of small-scale datasets. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to robust medical image segmentation on small-scale data with incomplete labels. Our method leverages a combination of deep learning and transfer learning techniques to improve accuracy and robustness of segmentation model. We also introduce a novel data augmentation strategy to address issue of limited labeled data. Our experiments demonstrate effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance even with limited labeled data. Overall, our work contributes to the development of more efficient and accurate medical image segmentation techniques, with important implications for clinical practice and research.

Many approaches to 3D image segmentation are based on hierarchical clustering of supervoxels into image regions. Here we describe a distributed algorithm capable of handling a tremendous number of supervoxels. The algorithm works recursively, the regions are divided into chunks that are processed independently in parallel by multiple workers. At each round of the recursive procedure, the chunk size in all dimensions are doubled untill a single chunk encompasses the entire image. The final result is provably independant of the chunking scheme, and the same as if the entire image were processed without division into chunks. This is nontrivial becuase a pair of adjacent regions is scored by some statistical property (e.g. mean or median) of the affinities at the interface, and the interface may extend over arbitrarily many chunks. The trick is to delay merge decisions for regions that touch chunk boundaries, and only complete them in a later round after the regions are fully contained within a chunk. We demonstrate the algorithm by clustering an affinity graph with over 1.5 trillion edges between 135 billion supervoxels derived from a 3D electron microscopic brain image.

Nikola's Founder Steps Down From Board as Company Faces Fraud Allegations Trevor Milton, the founder and executive chairman of Nikola Corporation, has resigned from the board of directors, effective immediately. The announcement came amid concerns about the company's practices and allegations of fraud. Milton addressed the issue on social media, stating that he would defend himself against the allegations. "The focus should be on the Company and its world-changing mission, not me," he wrote. "So I made the difficult decision to step aside and let the Company move forward." Nikola has been the center of controversy this year, with short-seller Hindenburg Research releasing a report claiming that the company had misled investors about its technology and partnerships with major automakers. The report accused Milton of exaggerating the company's progress and claimed that Nikola's key technology, a hydrogen fuel cell-powered truck, was essentially a shell. Nikola initially denied the allegations and threatened legal action against Hindenburg Research. However, the company later admitted that a promotional video showing a truck rolling down a hill without an engine was "inaccurate" and had been staged. Nikola's stock price fell sharply after the report was released. The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Department of Justice (DoJ) are reportedly investigating Nikola over the allegations. The company released a statement saying that it was cooperating with the authorities and that it remained "committed to its mission of delivering environmentally friendly vehicles." Milton's resignation from the board comes at a time when Nikola is facing major challenges. The company has yet to generate any revenue and has not delivered a single vehicle to customers. Its partnership with General Motors, which was supposed to provide Nikola with access to its fuel cell technology, has been put on hold. Nikola's board of directors issued a statement thanking Milton for his contributions to the company and wishing him well in his future endeavors. Stephen Girsky, a former GM executive and Nikola board member, will replace Milton as chairman. Investors will be closely watching how Nikola navigates these challenges in the coming months. The company's success or failure could have significant implications for the future of the electric vehicle market.

Artificial intelligence (AI), and particularly machine learning, has become increasingly prevalent within healthcare as diagnostic support technology known as artificial intelligence medical systems, with applications spanning multiple areas including radiology and pathology imageing data interpretation but also genomics to facilitate precision medicine efforts. In response to this rapid innovation dynamic, we seek to help ensure that AI within all contexts of health care are trustworthy through the lens of human-machine collabouration. Toward these ends, experts representing a diversity of disciplines engauged across government agencies, academic institutions, industry leaders, and patient advocacy group representatives gathered at an international workshop entitled FUTURE-AI. A major goal was to elucidate how best practises could be developed toward achieving trustworthiness of AI systems utilised throughout radiological clinical practise workflows from pre-training inputs through validation methodologies to final deployment and ongoing use assessment frameworks. More specifically, during sessions over five days participants identified key principles pertinent to designing machine intelligence technologies in conjunction with humans on which future guidance documents can be built. Topics included definitions of terms such as explainability, fairness and bias, transparency and accessibility; ethical considerations around human factors involved in the design of intelligent machines especially when applied clinically; and approaches to training, testing, validating and deploying models in realistic clinical environments for diverse patient populations. Participants also assessed gaps in existing AI standards and made suggestions regarding necessary improvements or updates currently lacking in order to promote future safe system development and implementation, ultimately leading to recommendations for moving forward along established guidelines. Through this consensus process, we hope to inform best practises for using advanced computer science analytics towards helping physicians deliver optimal patient outcomes.

The abstract of the paper "Sem-GAN: Semantically-Consistent Image-to-Image Translation" can be written as follows: In this paper, we address image-to-image translation in a semantically consistent manner. When you put food in the microwave, the microwaves go inside the food and make it hot. So when you are heating up one frozen burrito, the microwaves go all around it and make it hot. She walks out into the blinding snowstorm and the harsh winds whipping at her hair. It's early January, after all. What are these women thinking? How can two people so clearly overstimulated by a place where no one speaks English and everyone knows your name want to stay here forever? There is something very strange about all this: the fact that they seem perfectly fine with being away from each other yet there seems to be some sort of bond forming between both of them as if they'll never see each other again. As the hour passes though, the woman begins to think maybe she isn't ready to go afterall. Maybe she should reconsider because how could she possibly know what it would feel like to live here permanently. And then when they start saying goodbye she realizes the truth-she really likes them and misses them terribly already. And when the two men tell her that they don't speak Spanish either...well, they just stand there stunned. No response. After more than ten hours hiking through fresh powder, they eventually arrive back home at the hotel. A few minutes later the driver pulls up, getting out of the car first. Meanwhile, the woman has been eating pizza and watching TV by herself while her husband has disappeared into the night (or rather, the parking lot). And now for the bad news! The family is going to have to split up soon. They only have enough food for one day left. If anyone needs any help cooking, they said yes. But that means a lot of packing and rearranging before they leave tomorrow morning.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to weakly supervised semantic image segmentation using Gated CRF Loss. Traditional methods rely heavily on annotated data, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. Our proposed method utilizes easy-to-obtain web images with class labels to train a deep neural network for semantic segmentation. We introduce a novel loss function that incorporates a gating mechanism to emphasize the learning of discriminative features from labeled data while regularizing the learning process with unlabeled data. The Gated CRF Loss encourages the model to produce accurate segmentations even in the presence of incomplete or noisy annotations. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art weakly supervised segmentation approaches on multiple benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes. Notably, our method achieves an mIoU score of 84.7% on PASCAL VOC val set without any annotations, surpassing fully supervised baselines. Furthermore, we show that our method is robust to different annotation qualities, displaying superior performance compared to other weakly supervised techniques when faced with noisy or imbalanced annotations. The key contributions of this work are: 1. Introduction of Gated CRF Loss for weakly supervised semantic image segmentation, enabling effective use of easily accessible web images with class labels. 2. Presentation of a gating module that leverages labeled data to learn discriminative features while regularizing the model with abundant unlabeled data. 3. Demonstration of superior performance compared to existing weakly supervised segmentation methods across various datasets, especially under challenging scenarios such as limited annotated data, noise, and class imbalance. This study paves the way for exploiting large-scale web data to train deep models for pixel-wise image understanding tasks, opening up new possibilities for further advancements in computer vision research.

It dissolved into very small fibers, which are drained to the sewage system and taken to the water treatment plant for processing of waste. Some Ammonia gas may get released during this process so check local regulations before flushing it away!

The use of multidimensional local distribution (MDL) methods results in more information being extracted. We compare our experiments on a large dataset of 1000 images and show that we can reduce reconstruction time by two orders of magnitude compared to state of art methods, such as SIFT or SVM classification. Furthermore, many MDL approaches have been proposed for different problem domains. The field of image segmentation in neuroscience has been developing rapidly in recent years, and there are many challenges that can be addressed. We consider here a problem where these challenges collide and where they create the greatest value; namely, the use in medical imaging to infer what part of the brain has been damaged or destroyed by disease. In this work, we present an approach based on direct cortical and subcortical surface morphometry. During this work, we focus entirely in two directions: (1) We use cortical and subcortical surface morphology as indicators of structural change associated with disease and (2) the development of a robust method which allows reconstruction of complex images directly from cortical data, allowing us to recover a highly structured representation of large numbers of voxels without requiring a knowledge of any other structures or their properties. Our central hypothesis is that once defined well enough, this representation will be capable to reconstruct almost perfectly realistic faces from simple images.

In this paper, we present EdgeFlow, a novel approach to interactive segmentation that uses the principle of edge-guided flow to achieve practical and effective segmentation of images. interactive segmentation is a basic task in computer vision that includes enabling a user to engage with an image to specify the regions of interest. Additionally, existing techniques for interactive segmentation are also restricted by their dependence on iterative user feedback, which can be time-consuming and will not adequately capture the interface's intended segmentation. EdgeFlow addresses these difficulties by developing a new methodology that combines the effectiveness of edge-guided segmentation with the practicality of interactive segmentation. Our method provides a novel edge-guided flow algorithm that generates user feedback onto the edges of an image, enabling for fast and reliable segmentation of complex pictures. We demonstrate the efficacy of EdgeFlow through numerous studies on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms state-of-the-art interactive segmentation techniques in terms of both performance and reliability. In addition, we explore the versatility of EdgeFlow by using it to a range of technologies, including object segmentation, medical photo segmentation, and video segmentation. Our findings show that EdgeFlow can manage a broad variety of situations, from basic object segmentation to complex medical image segmentation, and can effectively segment objects in real-time. Overall, EdgeFlow demonstrates a major development in the field of interactive segmentation, offering a practical and effective technique that can be applied in a range of systems. Its capability to efficiently segment images with minimal user feedback makes it an excellent tool for a broad variety of users, from scientists to professionals.

> Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in medical imageing to improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce workload, and improve patient care. However, the use of AI in medical imageing raises ethical, legal, and social issues that must be addressed to ensure the safe and effective use of AI in healthcare. > > In this paper, we present the results of a consensus-building process that involved a multidisciplinary group of experts in AI, ethics, law, and medicine. The goal of the process was to develop a set of guiding principles and consensus recommendations for trustworthy AI in future medical imageing. > > The process involved a series of workshops and online discussions, during which the experts identified key ethical, legal, and social issues related to the use of AI in medical imageing. The experts then developed a set of guiding principles and consensus recommendations for trustworthy AI in future medical imageing. > > The guiding principles and consensus recommendations cover a wide range of issues, including transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy, and security. The principles and recommendations are intended to provide a framework for the development and use of AI in medical imageing, and to ensure that AI is used in a way that is safe, effective, and ethical. > > The results of the consensus-building process are presented in this paper, along with a discussion of the implications for the development and use of AI in medical imageing. The paper also highlights the need for continued research and collabouration to ensure that AI is used in a way that is safe, effective, and ethical. In this paper, we propose a novel method to few-shot segmentation, which is a challenging task in computer vision that requires analyzing objects from a large number of labeled examples. Our method, named Few-Shot Segmentation with Global and Local Contrastive Language (FSS-GCL), utilizes the strengths of regional and regional contrastive learning to reduce segmentation accuracy. International contrastive learning has been seen to be beneficial in learning high-level representations that are important for few-shot learning. Unfortunately, it will not capture local data that is necessary for segmentation tasks. Local contrastive learning, on the other hand, can capture local data but will not generalize well to new examples. In FSS-GCL, we propose a two-stage training approach that first uses regional linguistic learning to develop high-level representations and then employs regional contrastive learning to develop the segmentation masks. We therefore introduce a novel mask-based contrastive loss function that allows the model to develop realistic segmentation masks. Experiments on various benchmark datasets show that FSS-GCL outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation techniques, including those that use regional or regional contrastive learning alone. We often perform ablation experiments to identify the impact of the various parts of our methodology. Our major contributions are: * A novel few-shot segmentation technique called FSS-GCL that emphasizes regional and regional contrastive learning * A two-stage training approach that demonstrates the strengths of regional and regional contrastive learning * A mask-based contrastive loss function that provides accurate segmentation masks * State-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets Overall, FSS-GCL emphasizes the efficacy of integrating regional and regional contrastive learning for few-shot segmentation, and offers a promising path for future research in this region.

Prison overcrowding has become a serious, world-wide problem that is increasingly affecting populations across the world. In the United States, for example, there has been a spike in the demand for correctional facilities and the crime rate has skyrocketed over the past few years. As a result, there is no doubt that something must be done about this issue to safeguard the rights and liberties of those who are incarcerated. What the world needs right now is a more sustainable approach to tackling crime that is geared towards rehabilitating offenders and reducing recidivism. A proposal would be to establish community-based sentencing programs that emphasize non-incarceration for non-violent offenses. In addition to this, we could work on building more diversion programs that are designed to provide education, treatment and mentoring services. These programs would be targeted towards offenders who demonstrate a willingness to change and become more responsible members of society. Another solution lies in investing in more proactive policing practices that target crime hot-spots, rather than arresting large numbers of individuals for minor offenses. Investing in technology, such as body cameras and drones, could help police officers collect and analyze crime data effectively. Furthermore, we could explore alternatives to imprisonment such as electronic monitoring and house arrest, instead of locking individuals away. In conclusion, prison overcrowding has become a pressing issue that requires a practical and sustainable solution. By investing our resources in innovative community-based sentencing programs, diversion programs, proactive policing practices and alternative measures to imprisonment we can reduce the number of individuals locked up in challenging and overcrowded prisons across the globe. This will not only save lives but also ensure that we create a more just and equitable society for all.

[Abstract] At present, future surgical imaging is often being designed to identify patients with illness or other life-threatening issues without a doctor's input (1⇓⇓–4). In fact, this level of medical monitoring has evolved as an urgent need and a cost efficient alternative to a traditional medical approach of operationally preventing cancer when scientific results warrant it (5, 6). Additionally, current methods are very inexpensive compared to human patients who only perform a large part of total imaging-related revenue (7). However, medical systems can now prioritize not just what images should be captured but how they should to be collected and organized (8). To date, several researchers have concluded that small volumes do need to be recorded (9) for specific kinds of healthcare problems such as pulmonary infarction detection in which data is useful beyond not enabling physicians to identify atrial fibrillation [6]. These standards generally dictate usage of standardized storage protocols for collecting medically relevant medical information on large-scale data centers (10), while others might prefer to expect less clarity about which hospitals hold the most medical statistics, thus allowing governments to determine that privacy is necessary when taking health choices using mass data (11). With these differences, no consensus approach exists concerning the best way ahead with regard to both creating mass imaging images and ensuring proper access, reliability and security while recording them on centralized information sources. This raises the question: Should we find technologies which achieve performance while reducing the quantity stored or rely only on methods for transferring information? We propose the following guiding guidelines for developing trustworthy artificial intelligence in the field of clinical imaging and apply them to many problems now facing modern clinical machine learning that involve: identifying common diseases in low volume samples; identifying noncontroversial features in small quantities at high accuracy through pattern recognition or image classification based on previous experience, like heart rate, pupil diameter; identifying and cataloguing images to provide appropriate contextual context that can contribute to diagnosis recommendations and identify potential anomalies; conducting post-processing routines such as pre and/or post activation (activation steps) and noise correction, as well as developing customized visualization programs by manually creating predefined templates in order to better identify what is presented in these documents; and giving ongoing input as to how the algorithms are analyzing the clinical data and helping medical professionals make choices concerning management

In this paper, we present a novel approach to interactive segmentation called EdgeFlow, which leverages edge information to guide the segmentation process and achieve practical interaction efficiency. Existing methods often suffer from slow convergence or rely on heuristics that limit their accuracy, making them impractical for real-world applications. EdgeFlow addresses these limitations by introducing an edge-guided flow algorithm that combines the benefits of both boundary-following and gradient-descent-based methods. The proposed method efficiently explores the image space while adaptively adjusting its behavior based on local edge features, ensuring accurate segmentation and minimizing user input. We evaluate EdgeFlow on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art methods in terms of efficiency, accuracy, and usability. Our results show significant advantages in terms of both computational cost and user effort required to obtain high-quality segmentations. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of EdgeFlow through applications in various domains such as object recognition, medical imaging, and video analysis. The key contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: * Introducing EdgeFlow, a practical solution for efficient and accurate interactive segmentation guided by edge information. * Developing a novel edge-guided flow algorithm that adapts to local edge features, promoting accurate and efficient segmentation. * Showcasing superior performance of EdgeFlow compared to existing methods in terms of both computational cost and user effort required. * Demonstrating the applicability of EdgeFlow across diverse domains, including object recognition, medical imaging, and video analysis. In conclusion, our proposed method presents a substantial improvement over traditional interactivesegmentation techniques and has far-reaching implications for applications where precise segmentation is critical. We envision EdgeFlow serving as a valuable tool for researchers, practitioners, and users seeking efficient and reliable segmentation solutions.

> Image segmentation is a fundamental problem in computer vision. It is the process of partitioning an image into multiple regions, each of which is homogeneous with respect to some property. The most common property is intensity, but other properties such as colour, texture, and shape are also used. > > In this paper, we propose a new method for image segmentation based on the concept of lambda-connectedness. Lambda-connectedness is a generalisation of the notion of connectedness that allows for the inclusion of additional information, such as the intensity of a pixel. We show that lambda-connectedness can be used to segment images into regions that are homogeneous with respect to intensity, and we present an algorithm for determining the lambda-connected components of an image. We also show that lambda-connectedness can be used to segment images into regions that are homogeneous with respect to other properties, such as colour and texture. > > We evaluate our method on a variety of images, and we show that it is able to segment images into regions that are homogeneous with respect to intensity, colour, and texture. We also show that our method is able to segment images into regions that are homogeneous with respect to other properties, such as shape. The paper is available here.

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the first cause of death in Many countries. CRC originates from a small Clump of cells on the lining of the colon called polyps, which over Time might grow and become malignant. Early detection and removal of polyps are therefore necessary for the prevention of colon cancer. In this paper, we introduce an ensemble of medical Polyp segmentation algorithms. based on an observation that different segmentation algorithms will perform well on different subsets of examples because of the nature and size of training sets they have been exposed to and because of method-intrinsic factors, we propose to measure the Confidence in the prediction of each algorithm and then use an associate threshold to determine whether the confidence is acceptable or not. An algorithm is selected for the ensemble if the confidence is below its associate threshold. The optimal threshold for each Segmentation algorithm is Found by using Comprehensive learning Particle Swarm Optimization (CLPSO), a swarm intelligence algorithm. The Dice coefficient, a popular performance metric for image segmentation, is Used as the fitness criteria. Experimental results on two polyp segmentation datasets MICCAI2015 and Kvasir-SEG confirm that our ensemble achieves better results compared to some well-known segmentation algorithms.

This paper proposes a parallel optimization algorithm for cooperative automation of large-scale connected vehicles. The task of cooperative automation is formulated as a centralized optimization problem taking the whole decision space of all vehicles into account. Considering the uncertainty of the environment, the problem is solved in a receding horizon fashion. Then, we employ the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to solve the centralized optimization in a parallel way, which scales more favorably to large-scale instances. Also, Taylor series is used to linearize nonconvex constraints caused by coupling collision avoidance constraints among interactive vehicles. Simulations with two typical traffic scenes for multiple vehicles demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method.

This paper presents a scalable approach to large-scale image segmentation through the utilization of distributed clustering algorithms. With the growing availability of high-dimensional data, traditional centralized processing methods have become increasingly inefficient and limited by computational constraints. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that enables the parallelization of image segmentation across multiple nodes in a distributed computing environment. Our proposed method leverages the power of distributed clustering algorithms, which are proven to be highly effective in handling massive datasets, to perform pixel-level classification and segmentation of images. By partitioning the input image into smaller chunks and distributing them across multiple processors, our approach achieves unprecedented levels of scalability and efficiency. We demonstrate the efficacy of our technique by applying it to several large-scale image datasets, yielding superior performance and accuracy compared to state-of-the-art centralized methods. The results show significant improvements in both efficiency and accuracy. 0. Our approach has far-reaching implications for advancing research and developing innovative applications within the realm of big data analytics.

Training deep networks with limited labeled data while achieving a strong generalization ability is key in the quest to reduce human annotation efforts. This is the goal of semi-supervised learning, which exploits more widely available unlabeled data to complement small labeled data sets. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for discriminative pixel-level tasks using a generative model of both images and labels. Concretely, we learn a generative adversarial network that captures the joint image-label distribution and is trained efficiently using a large set of unlabeled images supplemented with only few labeled ones. We build our architecture on top of StyleGAN2, augmented with a label synthesis branch. Image labeling at test time is achieved by first embedding the target image into the joint latent space via an encoder network and test-time optimization, and then generating the label from the inferred embedding. We evaluate our approach in two important domains: medical image segmentation and part-based face segmentation. We demonstrate strong in-domain performance compared to several baselines, and are the first to showcase extreme out-of-domain generalization, such as transferring from CT to MRI in medical imaging, and photographs of real faces to paintings, sculptures, and even cartoons and animal faces. A SpaceX Starship rocket prototype has exploded during a pressure test. It was the second to explode in four months. Founder Elon Musk has laughed off the incident, saying that it was expected. It will carry the Tesla Roadster of Musk's personal friend and SpaceX board member, billionaire PayPal founder Peter Thiel, into space. The launch is a test for the Falcon Heavy and for the Starship rocket, which will be sent into orbit to test its propulsion system, the company said. It will also be used to test the heat shield. The launch is also seen by some as a symbolic attempt to prove that the US can compete with SpaceX's biggest competitor, the Russians.

We report on a systematic study of modulation of the field emission current from carbon nanowalls using a sharp probe as the anode in an ultrahigh vacuum system. Modulation of the local emission current was achieved by either varying the anode-cathode distance (d) with the aid of an AC magnetic field or superimposing a small AC bias on a DC bias during the field emission measurement. Current modulation ratio of over two orders of magnitude was achieved with the modulation becoming more efficient at a smaller d. The experimental results are discussed using the Fowler-Nordheim theory in combination with a simple cantilever model to account for the modulation effect. The experimental results demonstrated good static stability and dynamic controllability of local field emission current from the carbon nanowalls.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Lifted Multicuts, which leverages domain knowledge to improve the accuracy and efficiency of microscopy image segmentation. Lifted Multicuts combines the strengths of two popular segmentation techniques: lifted probabilistic models and graph-based algorithms. Lifted probabilistic models are a class of probabilistic models that can effectively capture the structural information of images, while graph-based algorithms are well-suited for handling complex objects and boundaries. By combining these two techniques, Lifted Multicuts can accurately segment microscopy images while also incorporating domain knowledge into the segmentation process. We evaluate the performance of Lifted Multicuts on several datasets of microscopy images and compare it to state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Our results show that Lifted Multicuts outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. We also demonstrate the versatility of Lifted Multicuts by applying it to various types of microscopy images, including fluorescence microscopy and brightfield microscopy. In addition to its improved performance, Lifted Multicuts also provides several other advantages. First, it allows for interactive segmentation, where the user can provide feedback and guidance during the segmentation process. Second, it provides a probabilistic output, which can be useful for quantifying uncertainty and identifying areas of potential error. Finally, Lifted Multicuts is computationally efficient, making it suitable for large-scale image segmentation tasks. In conclusion, Lifted Multicuts is a powerful and flexible approach to microscopy image segmentation that leverages domain knowledge to improve accuracy and efficiency. Its ability to incorporate user feedback and provide probabilistic outputs makes it a valuable tool for biomedical researchers who need to analyze large amounts of microscopy data.

While improving prediction accuracy has been the focus of machine learning in recent years, this alone does not suffice for reliable decision-making. Deploying learning systems in consequential settings also requires calibrating and communicating uncertainty of predictions. To convey instance-wise uncertainty for prediction tasks, we show how to generate set-valued predictions from a black-box predictor that control the expected loss on future test points at user-specified level. Our approach provides explicit finite-sample guarantees for any dataset by using holdout set to calibrate the size of the prediction sets. This framework enables simple, distribution-free, rigorous error control for many tasks, and we demonstrate it in five large-scale machine learning problems: (1) classification problems where some mistakes are more costly than others; (2) multi-label classification, where each observation has multiple associated labels; (3) classification problems where labels have hierarchical structure; (4) image segmentation, where we wish to predict a set of pixels containing an object of interest; and (5) protein structure prediction. Lastly, we discuss extensions to uncertainty quantification for ranking, metric learning and distributionally robust learning.

Abstract A central problem in medical image analysis is to automatically segment anatomical structures or other objects from 3D images. This task can be modeled as regression with the target value being binary surface that divides one class from another. Recently, there have been considerable efforts at developing convolutional neural network (CNN) methods dedicated to biomedical 3D segmentations tasks which use atlases for learning. In this work we introduce VoteNe...ts - effective method for automatic multi-atlas label fusion based on deep convolutional encoders and decoders. To improve training efficiency, random transforms are performed during training using the attention loss. Experiments were carried out on six public benchmark datasets covering four different imaging modalities and tissue types. Our experimental results demonstrate superior performance against state-of-the-art techniques including recent CNN and traditional label fusion approaches. We also show that vote predictions may be used alone or together with CNN features for additional performance boost when using more than just three atlases for ensemble voting.

This paper presents a novel method for high-resolution fuzziness-based tooth-root contour decomposition based on polynomial curve fitting and landmark detection. The proposed method uses a combination of landmark detection and polynomial curve fitting to model the fuzzy boundary of the tooth-root contour. The landmark detection is used to identify the key points on the tooth-root surface, and the polynomial curve fitting is used to fit the fuzzy edges between these key points. The resultant contour decomposition is very accurate, which makes it useful for a wide range of dental applications. This paper presents a detailed experimental study of the proposed method and a comparative study of it with other existing methods.

In this paper, we present a new approach to the problem of semantic segmentation using convolutional gated recurrent networks. This is a fundamental problem in vision which consists of dividing a scene into its constituent parts or objects. Existing methods have been limited by inadequate temporal coherence, inadequate spatial accuracy, and lack of ability to cope with complex scenes. Our proposed method takes advantage of the strengths of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to overcome these limitations. The convolutional gated recurrent network (CGRN) model consists of two main components: a convolutional layer for extracting spatial features and a gated recurrent unit (GRU) for capturing the temporal dependence. The GRU includes a gated mechanism that selectively preserves and propagates information from previous time steps, thus making it possible to represent long-term temporal dependencies. We evaluate our method on several datasets, including the YouTube-VoS, Cityscapes, and ECSVT datasets. We show that the CGRN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, stability, and consistency. We also perform a -factor analysis of our model, in which we consider the contributions of each component to the performance of the overall model. The main contribution of this paper is the CGRN architecture, which is able to integrate spatial and temporal information to improve the performance of the model. Our method has wide-ranging implications for many applications, including object tracking, human-machine interaction, and self-driving cars. The present paper is an important step forward in the field of scene understanding and provides a basis for further research in this area.

This study proposes an ensemble learning approach that combines classifier prediction confidence with comprehensive learning particle swarm optimisation (CLPSO) to improve the accuracy of polyp localization in colonoscopy images. The method utilises a variety of traditional machine learning algorithms, such as decision trees, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbours, and naive Bayes, which are trained using different feature sets extracted from the input data. The output predictions of these classifiers are then combined by weighting them according to their individual predictive performance scores derived from cross validation experiments. Additionally, CLPSO is employed to optimise the weight allocation process further enhancing the overall system's robustness against overfitting issues while improving its generalisation capacity. Experimental results show significant improvements compared to standalone approaches demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed technique. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into designing efficient computer aided diagnostic systems capable of detecting polyps during endoscopies enabling improved patient outcomes through timely diagnosis and therapy interventions.

Abstract: Deep learning has made major progress on several segmentation tasks such as semantic and instance segmentation. However, many important practical applications are not covered by existing methods, especially when it comes to interactive segmentation settings including weakly or poorly supervised, unsegmented scenes (Figure 1). While state-of-the-art interative segmentation techniques often do well in these scenarios for simple objects like cars and chairs, they struggle with high resolution datasets that involve complex geometry and large occlusion. Moreover, we find significant performance degradation even under fully supervi- sion which limits their use even with highly structured object labels. In this work, we adress these challenges through an intuitive approach guided by boundaries between objects. We propose 'EdgeFlow,' a boundary-aware flow optimization algorithm that uses edge guidence features learned on synthetic data paired with deep network inputs (e.g., RGB) captured from either raw video capture or depth sensors such as Kinect (see Figure 3). Our approach requires neither strong nor dense object labeling for training; instead we only require low supervision of edges through depth input that encodes partial ordering information. On four popular benchmarks, EdgeFlow generalizes better than existing weak-supervision based approaches while achieving comparable accuracy with fully supervised baselines at one tenth of the computational cost. The pre-processing stage is responsible for enhancing the contrast of the image and removing noise. The polynomial fitting stage uses a non-linear least-squares minimization method to fit a cubic polynomial to the fuzzy boundary of the tooth root, then the polynomial is used to separate the tooth root from the surrounding tissues. The landmarks are then located by identifying the points on the curve that have the maximum gradient. The performance of the proposed method was tested on a series of twenty digital dental images, using a leave-one-out cross-validation scheme. The results of the evaluation show that the proposed method outperforms the existing methods in terms of accuracy, speed and robustness. The average absolute error was 0.15 mm, and the processing time was less than 30 seconds per image. The proposed method is expected to have a significant impact on the analysis of dental images and its associated applications, such as: orthodontic treatment planning, dental implant design and dental disease diagnosis. Using the proposed method it will be possible to improve the accuracy and efficiency of dental procedures, thereby improving the health outcomes of patients.

In this paper, we investigate the relationship between quantitative volume space form rigidity and lower Ricci curvature bounds in Riemannian manifolds. We present a new method for establishing rigidity results in the context of non-uniformly curved spaces, which allows us to significantly generalize previous work in the field. Our approach relies on a novel combination of geometric analysis techniques, including heat kernel estimates, Bochner's inequality, and a careful study of the effect of boundary terms on the volume form. We prove that if a complete Riemannian manifold with non-negative Ricci curvature satisfies a suitably chosen lower bound on its Ricci curvature, then it must have a constant volume form. This result has important implications for our understanding of the structure of such manifolds, and provides new insights into the interplay between curvature, topology, and geometry in these spaces. Our proof technique also yields a number of additional consequences, including a corresponding rigidity result for metric measure spaces with non-negative Ricci curvature and Gaussian measures, as well as a characterization of flat tori as the only compact manifolfds admitting a probability measure with finite moments and non-zero cosmological constant. Overall, our results represent a significant advancement in the understanding of quantitative volume space form rigidity under lower Ricci curvature bounds, and provide new tools for studying the properties of non-uniformly curved spaces more generally.

Existing one-shot segmentation strategies depend on both meta-learning or transfer learning, which have advantages in terms of few-shot capability and requirement for large-scale annotated databases. In contrast, SMPL learns a set of class models that capture the semantic connections between classes, providing for efficient few-shot segmentation. The fundamental insight of SMPL is to develop a model for each class that is semantically meaningful, meaning that it reflects the fundamental structure of the class. We achieve this by implementing a novel model loss function that allows the models to be identical for semantically identical classes and dissimilar for semantically similar classes. We evaluate SMPL on various benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and COCO, and demonstrate its excellent efficiency compared to state-of-the-art one-shot segmentation procedures. Our tests demonstrate that SMPL produces low segmentation accuracy on unseen classes with only a single training instance, outperforming other techniques that involve many instances or large-scale annotated information. This paper proposes a new method for one-shot semantic image segmentation, which learns semantically meaningful classifiers by reducing a novel loss function that encourages the learned classifier to be similar in not only features but also semantics. The method is trained on synthetic images generated by adversarial networks and gives a good result for real images with a minimum of supervision. We show the effectiveness of our method by comparing the performance of various state-of-the-art methods on the latest benchmark data. Moreover, we perform experiments that show the sensitivity of the method to changes in network architecture and data characteristics, demonstrating its generality.

While improving prediction accuracy has been the focus of machine learning in recent years, this alone does not suffice for reliable decision-making. Deploying learning systems in consequential settings also requires calibrating and communicating the uncertainty of predictions. To convey instance-wise uncertainty for prediction tasks, we show how to generate set-valued predictions from a black-box predictor that control the expected loss on future test points at a user-specified level. Our approach provides explicit finite-sample guarantees for any dataset by using a holdout set to calibrate the size of the prediction sets. This framework enables simple, distribution-free, rigourous error control for many tasks, and we demonstrate it in five large-scale machine learning problems: (1) classification problems where some mistakes are more costly than others; (2) multi-label classification, where each observation has multiple associated labels; (3) classification problems where the labels have a hierarchical structure; (4) image segmentation, where we wish to predict a set of pixels containing an object of interest; and (5) protein structure prediction. Lastly, we discuss extensions to uncertainty quantification for ranking, metric learning and distributionally robust learning.

Tom was a clock collector. He loved the movements and details. He obsessed over the time. His wife thought he needed a change. Buying him a watch only slightly shifted his mood, because he liked to keep up with watches that were on display in his room like a watchmaker's workshop - he always knew how much better it would look if it had been retired at night when the clocks went off each day so that he could use the timepiece as light duty storage for all the watches he bought from the warehouse. John Henry was probably best known by literally hundreds of millions of people worldwide after he created the classic 1930s chronograph watch series - the Modern Days chronographs. They are still one of his most famous products. He invented the world records setter and the first date recorder used today instead of the standard chronometer. Today John Henry chronometer enthusiasts celebrate his accomplishments every year through the anniversary season throughout the year but during his lifetime they recognize his contribution to history together. He is also remembered monthly for his contributions to the science of chronometers since (when he launched his company). A 1977 documentary titled John Henry chronotherapy was produced for the National Geographic Society Awards, honoring the late Chantal Henry. Eliot never knew what to get his mother for her birthday. No matter how much money he spent, she always seemed dissatisfied. Even expensive jewelry failed to make much of an impression on her: "There was a part in the story that I liked about it, which is the death-of-the-jewelry idea," Eliot says. The last thing he wanted to do when we met up at the Greenpoint station was discuss the meaning of life. He stopped short at the top of his lungs and looked over all the commuters staring at us with their arms folded across their chests like they were waiting for something terrible to happen. With his political beliefs firmly held, this was my first time meeting him outside of our usual meetups in Brooklyn's Crown Heights neighborhood where we both work as reporters for the same newspaper. His personality wasn't too dissimilar from most of the people who pass through the station every day - maybe even more so than some of them. But once you got past that initial shock, there isn't really any telling whether he has changed or not - what does change are the kinds of questions you ask yourself after hearing his answers. We sat down next to each other near the New York City Subway's Red Line platform; neither one had ever been inside a subway before. We took turns talking into our cellphones while standing there for what felt like hours. It turned out we weren't alone, since two men had just walked onto the platform behind us to stand watching us for a few moments before finally taking off. They tried to sell me a magazine but made no attempt to introduce themselves and quickly ran back into the crowd again - this was definitely something new to experience on public transit. From then on, I bounced between thinking about the many unanswered questions by now swirling around in my head and trying to stay focused on a conversation that would turn serious if it started to devolve into a shouting match. When it ended, both Elliott and I couldn't stop laughing. Is there anything worse than getting your hopes up only to have them dashed? I don't think so. The $\log 8$ Theorem, proved by Culler and Shalen, states that every point in the hyperbolic 2-space is moved a distance at least $\log 3$ by one of the non-commuting isometries $\xi$ or $\eta$ provided that $\xi$ and $\eta$ generate a torsion-free, discrete group which is not co-compact and contains no parabolic. This theorem lies in the foundation of many techniques that provide lower estimates for the volumes of orientable, closed hyperbolic 0-manifolds whose fundamental group has no 2-generator subgroup of finite index and, as a consequence, gives insights into the topological properties of these manifolds. In this paper, we show that every point in the hyperbolic 3-space is moved a distance at least $(1/0)\log(5+3\sqrt{2})$ by one of the isometries in $\{\xi,\eta,\xi\eta\}$ when $\xi$ and $\eta$ satisfy the conditions given in the $\log 6$ Theorem.

This study proposes an ensemble learning approach that combines classifier prediction confidence with comprehensive learning particle swarm optimization (CLPSO) to improve the accuracy of polyp localization in colonoscopy images. The method utilizes a variety of traditional machine learning algorithms, such as decision trees, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors, and naive Bayes, which are trained using different feature sets extracted from the input data. The output predictions of these classifiers are then combined by weighting them according to their individual predictive performance scores derived from cross validation experiments. Additionally, CLPSO is employed to optimize the weight allocation process further enhancing the overall system's robustness against overfitting issues while improving its generalization capacity. Experimental results show significant improvements compared to standalone approaches demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed technique. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into designing efficient computer aided diagnostic systems capable of detecting polyps during endoscopies enabling improved patient outcomes through timely diagnosis and therapy interventions.

One can use quantum computation to simulate and approximate many tasks at once, as long as one can guarantee that these are independent of each other, otherwise they will compete/compete against each other in terms of time, processing power, space-time error spread, probability distributions, etc. Since quantum computing offers an opportunity for noninterference between parallel processes it has emerged as an extremely promising tool for solving some high priority problems in physics, biology, economics and information science. This article presents a novel optimization scheme using quantum computers to improve the quality of image segmentation by measuring the distribution of the measurements performed on the whole image in a patch using different patches of varying distance and resolution and then combining all measurement statistics. From this model two key principles emerge - First, no information about previous pixel positions or directionality is lost when performing random searches across the image; Second, all possible combinations of pixels are used when making the search, without any predefined mapping between input values and output images. While only three kernels (two of which have been previously described) could be computed during our experiments, we show experimentally that optimal kernel pairs can efficiently solve more than 90% of the image segmentation problems we analyzed with both CPU and GPU. In particular, a new type of machine learning classifier named the Qubectical Kernel Classifiers (QKCCs) was trained to extract most useful features, such as small patches or edges, from a single image. Moreover, the QKCCC approach makes perfect use of hardware quantum simulation, giving the best results compared with previous work based on classical algorithms at the same classification accuracy rate and also for certain workloads.

The authors propose a novel prediction set methodology that utilizes statistical measures of risk and uncertainty to construct sets of predictions with guaranteed performance characteristics. Unlike traditional methods that assume knowledge about the underlying data distribution, the proposed approach allows for flexibility in terms of selecting appropriate distributions. Additionally, the authors demonstrate how their technique can be applied to nonlinear regression models and provide several examples to illustrate its effectiveness. Overall, this work represents an important advancement into the realm of robust and reliable predictive analytics, which has critical applications across many diverse disciplines.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to constructing prediction sets that do not rely on any distributional assumptions and simultaneously control the risk of over-prediction. Our method, called distribution-free, risk-controlling prediction sets (DFRCPS), is based on a non-parametric, data-driven approach that leverages the concept of conformal prediction. We demonstrate that DFRCPS can be used to construct prediction sets with a guaranteed level of confidence, while also providing a risk-controlling mechanism to prevent over-prediction. We evaluate the performance of DFRCPS through simulations and real-world case studies, comparing it to existing methods such as conformal prediction and Bayesian prediction. Our results show that DFRCPS outperforms these methods in terms of both accuracy and risk control, particularly in situations where the underlying distribution is complex or unknown. The key contribution of this paper is the development of a distribution-free, risk-controlling approach to prediction set construction that does not require any distributional assumptions. Our method provides a principled way to balance the trade-off between accuracy and risk control, and can be applied to a wide range of prediction problems, including classification, regression, and time-series forecasting. The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we review the related work on prediction sets and conformal prediction. In Section 3, we introduce the concept of DFRCPS and its construction method. In Section 4, we present the theoretical properties of DFRCPS, including its risk control and confidence guarantees. In Section 5, we evaluate the performance of DFRCPS through simulations and case studies. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the results and future directions in Section 6. Overall, this paper provides a novel approach to prediction set construction that addresses the limitations of existing methods and provides a distribution-free, risk-controlling alternative. The proposed method has broad applications in fields such as machine learning, statistics, and decision-making under uncertainty.

A few points clarifying my view: By primary language, I mean either official language (i.e. English or French in Canada) or the language most spoken by the people in that country. For example, if Quebec is a majority francophone province of Canada with an official language policy which requires all government employees to provide services and documents only in French except where it would be impossible for them to do so without violating their rights given the low proportion who actually speak French - then there's no reason to assume that they are not bilingual but simply monolingual francophones. In the same vein, although many Canadians claim fluent English pronunciation as one of their national traits, this does not necessarily make true fluent speakers of English from other countries generalizing 'Canadians speak excellent English' since it is quite possible that some Canadian born children may have learned not-so-fluent English at home while others were exposed to British public school education together with fluency in both languages. In practice, the amount of influence on someone speaking primarily one foreign language versus another varies considerably depending on such things as agebackground etc., but ultimately what matters most in any case is whether you consider it useful. Certainly, for communicating effectively between non-native English writers and native ones, using American English rather than British English will likely produce more accurate results since US1 allows words like 'there', 'their', 'theirs' without having to resort to archaic constructions they', 'them or synonyms such as "their" those," "these, whilst UK2 forces one into adverbs such as'very' quite, whereas G8 permits these even when unnecessary.

In this work, we address the challenging task of few-shot segmentation. Previous few-shot segmentation methods mainly employ the information of support images as guidance for query image segmentation. Although some works propose to build cross-reference between support and query images, their extraction of query information still depends on the support images. We here propose to extract the information from the query itself independently to benefit the few-shot segmentation task. To this end, we first propose a prior extractor to learn the query information from the unlabeled images with our proposed global-local contrastive learning. Then, we extract a set of predetermined priors via this prior extractor. With the obtained priors, we generate the prior region maps for query images, which locate the objects, as guidance to perform cross interaction with support features. In such a way, the extraction of query information is detached from the support branch, overcoming the limitation by support, and could obtain more informative query clues to achieve better interaction. Without bells and whistles, the proposed approach achieves new state-of-the-art performance for the few-shot segmentation task on PASCAL-5$^{i}$ and COCO datasets.

In this research, we propose a novel few-shot segmentation method that uses both regional and regional contrastive learning. Our approach is based on the concept of encoding image features in an effective way to ensure rapid adaptation to new tasks without needing detailed training data. We demonstrate through studies conducted on multiple datasets that our model greatly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques while maintaining faster convergence rates thanks to its capability to capture high-level linguistic data as well as detailed semantic cues using contrasting examples at different scales. Overall, these findings indicate that using multiple styles of contrasts can lead to substantial changes in few-shot efficiency for segmentation problems.

In this paper, we propose a novel method for efficient 3D neural network design called Channel-wise Automatic Kernel Shrinking (CAKES). This approach targets reducing computational cost and memory bandwidth requirements while maintaining comparable or improved accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models. Existing methods for efficient 3D neural networks mainly focus on pruning or quantization, which can result in increased computational complexity or reduced accuracy. CAKES addresses these limitations by introducing a channel-wise automated kernel shrinking technique that adaptively adjusts the size of each kernel along the channels of a 3D convolutional layer. This allows for significant reductions in parameters and computations without compromising performance. The proposed method is evaluated on several publicly available datasets and benchmarked against state-of-the-art models. Our results show that CAKES achieves better or comparable accuracy with significantly fewer parameters and computations. Specifically, we observe an average reduction of 52% in parameters and 46% in computations compared to the baseline model while maintaining similar accuracy. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of CAKES by applying it to various 3D deep learning architectures, including Voxel-based CNNs and PointNet-like models. Keywords: Efficient 3D Deep Learning, Neural Network Pruning, Quantization, Channel-wise Kernel Shrinking, Computational Cost Reduction

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation using a highly fused convolutional network with multiple soft cost functions. Semantic segmentation is the task of assigning a class label to each Pixel in an image, and it is a fundamental problem In computer vision. Our proposed approach leverages the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to improve the accuracy and efficiency of semantic segmentation. Existing approaches to semantic segmentation typically rely on a single Cost function, such as cross-entropy loss, to optimize the output of the network. however, these cost functions can be limited in their ability To capture the complex relationships between pixels in an image. In contrast, our proposed Approach uses multiple soft cost functions to better Capture these relationships and Improve the accuracy of the segmentation. The proposed network architecture is designed To effectively fuse low-level and high-level features from the input image, allowing the network to capture both Local and global context. The multiple soft cost functions are combined using a novel fusion strategy that takes into account the strengths and weaknesses of each cost function. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate improved performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our main contributions are: * A novel Approach to semantic segmentation using a highly fused Convolutional network with multiple soft cost functions * A new network architecture that effectively fuses low-level and high-level features from the input image * A novel fusion strategy for combining multiple soft cost functions that takes into account their strengths and weaknesses * Improved performance on several benchmark datasets compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our approach has important implications For a wide range of applications, including object detection, image editing, and autonomous driving. We believe that our proposed approach represents a significant advancement in the field of semantic segmentation and Has the potential to enable New applications and use cases.

In this paper, we present a new approach to fine-grained semantic segmentation of motion capture data, based on DTF-FCNs. Motion capture technology has become popular in many fields, such as sports, medicine, and entertainment, thereby increasing the demand for efficient and accurate motion analysis methods. However, the current methods for motion segmentation often fail to capture the fine variation of movements and often rely on a priori features and templates. In this paper, we use DTF-FCNs to learn hierarchical representations of the data from the whole DTF-FCN network. The DTF-FCN model consists of several DTF-FCN layers, a DTF-graph convolutional layer, and a DTF-fully connected layer. The DTF-graph convolutional layer can learn the relationship between the different parts of the body. We conduct experiments on the publicly available motion capture data sets: the MPI-3DHP dataset, the HumanEva dataset, and the Motion Capture dataset. The experiments show that the DTF-FCN model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and speed. The main contributions of this paper are: We propose a novel DTF-FCN architecture for fine-grained semantic segmentation of motion capture data. We use DTF-graph convolutions to capture long-term dependencies. We obtain good results on several publicly available motion capture data sets. We show that DTF-graph convolution is effective.

The recent advancements in artificial inteligence (AI) combined with the extensive amount of data generated by today's clinical systems, has led to the development of imaging AI solutions across the whole value chain of medical imaging, including image reconstruction, medical image segmentation, image-based diagnosis and treatment planning. Notwithstanding the successes and future potential of AI in medical imaging, many stakeholders are concerned of the potential risks and ethical implications of imaging AI solutions, which are perceived as complex, opaque, and difficult to comprehend, utilise, and trust in critical clinical applications. Despite these concerns and risks, there are currently no concrete guidelines and best practices for guiding future AI developments in medical imaging towards increased trust, safety and adoption. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a careful selection of guiding principles drawn from the accumulated experiences, concensus, and best practices from five large European projects on AI in Health Imaging. These guiding principles are named FUTURE-AI and its building blocks consist of (i) Fairness, (ii) Universality, (iii) Traceability, (iv) Usability, (v) Robustness and (vi) Explainability. In a step-by-step approach, these guidelines are further translated into a framework of concrete recommendations for specifying, developing, evaluating, and deploying technically, clinically and ethically trustworthy AI solutions into clinical practice.

Achieving transparency in black-box deep learning algorithms is still an open challenge. High dimensional features and decisions given by deep neural networks (NN) require new algorithms and methods to expose its mechanisms. Current state-of-the-art NN interpretation methods (e.g. Saliency maps, DeepLIFT, LIME, etc.) focus more on the direct relationship between NN outputs and inputs rather than the NN structure and operations itself. In current deep NN operations, there is uncertainty over the exact role played by neurons with fixed activation functions. In this paper, we achieve partially explainable learning model by symbolically explaining the role of activation functions (AF) under a scalable topology. This is carried out by modelling the AFs as adaptive Gaussian Processes (GP), which sit within a novel scalable NN topology, based on the Kolmogorov-Arnold Superposition Theorem (KST). In this scalable NN architecture, the AFs are generated by GP interpolation between control points and can thus be tuned during the back-propagation procedure via gradient descent. The control points act as the core enabler to both local and global adjustability of AF, where the GP interpolation constrains the intrinsic autocorrelation to avoid over-fitting. We show that there exists a trade-off between the NN's expressive power and interpretation complexity, under linear KST topology scaling. To demonstrate this, we perform a case study on a binary classification dataset of banknote authentication. Our model converge at better precision rate than state-of-the-art SVM algorithms which indicates that we do not make performance sacrifices in our approach. Meanwhile, by quantitatively and qualitatively investigating the mapping relationship between inputs and output, our explainable model can provide interpretation over each of the one-dimensional attributes. These early results suggest that our model has the potential to act as the final interpretation layer for deep neural networks.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for segmenting medical imaging data using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Medical image segmentation is a crucial step in various medical applications, including disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. However, manual segmentation is time-consuming, observer-dependent, and may introduce errors, highlighting the need for automated segmentation methods. We propose a CNN-based segmentation framework that leverages the strengths of deep learning to accurately and efficiently segment medical images. Our approach consists of three stages: data preprocessing, CNN training, and segmentation. In the data preprocessing stage, we prepare the medical images for training by resizing, normalizing, and splitting them into batches. We then train a CNN using the batches, employing a combination of convolutional and pooling layers to extract features from the images. Finally, we use the trained CNN to segment new, unseen images. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of medical images and compare the results with those obtained using traditional image segmentation methods. Our results show that the CNN-based segmentation outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. Specifically, we achieve an accuracy of 95% in segmenting tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, which is 10% higher than the accuracy obtained using traditional methods. Additionally, our approach reduces the segmentation time by 75% compared to traditional methods. The main contribution of this paper is the development of a CNN-based segmentation framework that can be applied to various medical imaging modalities. Our approach has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation, which can have a significant impact on various medical applications. Future work includes further optimizing the CNN architecture and exploring its application to other medical imaging modalities.

Semi automatic data augmentation using masks and feature maps Semi automatic data augmentation uses masking features to train local discriminative regions (localizers) within an image to predict semantic distance values given target and training inputs. In a traditional supervised learning context, localizers are implemented using feature maps or regularization metrics that control their learning rate independently of input. This leads to highly variable, unpredictable learning rates which increase variance in subsequent models, especially when multiple sublinear models perform on identical observations with diverse target inputs. As such, typical use cases involve training multiple discriminative maps simultaneously over the entire dataset with each map having slightly different training weights, resulting in a poor match between model estimates and observed targets. A more effective approach, where each individual mapping maintains its exact form across time, is to train a small number of discrete feature maps instead. These can be generated by adding a few mask blocks and averaging them across all images to get a weighted sum representation that does not change as quickly without any adaptation step as feature maps used for sparse data sets like object faces alone would tend to do. These maps can then be applied across training frames and tested independently of the other predictions (i.e., prediction error). Despite being far less computationally intensive or subjectively demanding than previous methods, this method cannot provide sufficient accuracy for real world usage and requires the additional step where the training frames must be saved and processed as seperate classes for cross validation purposes that increases coding complexity significantly, and also makes it susceptible to loss of performance in some training experiments. Thus, for semi-automatic segmentation, the most interesting classifier is one built around feature maps and feature vectors, where each localizer is trained specifically on a different set of images where each feature maps is extracted from one or a few input features. The goal was to make fully convolutional layer-wise discriminant separators (fully-connected units), with sparse representations for output neurons that are able to learn a new spatial encoding model efficiently using only the training information from the target-space subgraphs they have seen recently along with all learned subgraph transformations. To accomplish these goals via feature maps, we constructed a neural network architecture consisting of an LSTM (Leveraging Surface Feature Matrix Transcatheter Network Model) kernal at the top which encodes image features

This paper presents a generalized asymmetric dual-front model for image segmentation. The model extends the traditional dual-front model by introducing an asymmetric component that provides a more efficient and accurate way of handling complex boundary images. The proposed model is verified with a large number of experiments on a wide variety of images, demonstrating its effectiveness in segmenting images with various levels of complexity. The generalized asymmetric dual-front model provides a powerful tool for image segmentation and active contours applications.

This study proposes an ensemble learning approach that combines classifier prediction confidence with comprehensive learning particle swarm optimization (CLPSO) to improve accuracy of polyp localization in colonoscopy images. The method utilizes variety of traditional machine learning algorithms, such as decision trees, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors, and naive Bayes, which are trained using different feature sets extracted from the input data. The output predictions of these classifiers are then combined by weighting them according to their individual predictive performance scores derived from cross validation experiments. Additionally, CLPSO is employed to optimize the weight allocation process further enhancing overall system's robustness against overfitting issues while improving its generalization capacity. Experimental results show significant improvements compared to standalone approaches demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed technique. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into designing efficient computer aided diagnostic systems capable of detecting polyps during endoscopies enabling improved patient outcomes through timely diagnosis and therapy interventions.

If we have a cold-induced cough that continuously drains air from our lungs during sleep, these vessels may not be able to easily open when they want to drain excess oxygen back into our bloodstream." High-quality training data play a crucial role in image segmentation tasks. Usually, pixel-level annotations are costly, difficult and time-consuming for the small volume of training data. To minimize labelling cost and reduce segmentation reliability, interactive segmentation tools have been proposed, which give the result with just a few clicks. Unfortunately, their efficiency does not fulfill the standards of practical segmentation tasks in terms of speed and precision. In this work, we propose EdgeFlow, a novel design that fully provides interactive information of user clicks with edge-guided flow. Our method delivers state-of-the-art efficiency without any post-processing or iterative optimization scheme. Comprehensive studies on benchmarks only demonstrate the superiority of our methodology. In addition, with the proposed methodology, we develop an effective interactive segmentation tool for practical data annotation functions. The source code and tool is available at http://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleSeg.
