Neural networks with learning metrics as input have proven valuable in learning complex data such a image models and neural network architectures. Learning metrics provide information about how efficient an algorithm has been for training its model, thus can be used from data analysis, deep learning, or any kind of large scale program to improve performance during new application development. In our lab we decided to use this metric-based approach based on recurrent neural circuitry to study neural networks performing non-linear regression on graph trained graph models. The objective for the experiment was to implement a neural network that had a generalization capability between different classes of visual objects (e.g., faces and trees) on simple images, i.e., unsupervised learning. To accomplish this, some basic preprocessing steps were necessery such as thresholding. Also, image features extracted for later usage within each classification rule. After this preprocessing step, a set of training examples were stored and subsequently tested against two test cases that represented non-face-related tasks as seen by humans who do not require labels for finding objects in their environment ("faces" and "tree"), respectively. This approach has several benefits for real life applications. It does not rely on the notion of similarity between class label values provided by classification rules and does not burden users trying to select appropriate feature vectors for supervised image segmentation algorithms such as ClustalW for example which is very restrictive since the input features need to be normalized by the same unit length units as the outputs, i.e., weights and biases. Besides these advantages over other approaches, it enables researchers to work independently from prior implementations that may differ from the desired output properties of machine learning models, e.g., loss function tuning, and therefore they are free to continue experimenting and explore the entire domain without waiting for validation sets for which multiple training methods can make decisions at once on the same dataset. Since no specific classifier must learn for all tasks presented, they can be easily implemented when needed and adapted when not (since none of them are specifically for solving class assignment). Additionally, both sides recieve the same results and can be easily checked separately even though they compete with each other. This provides grate benefit for open source/unregulated systems under community influence whereby more than one implementation of the same platform's algorithms can coexist since it greatly simplifies experimentation and discovery

This paper describes a new approach to image segmentation that supports extensive, multi-modal interaction between the system and the user. The system allows the user to communicate with the system through speech, gesture and touch to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the image segmentation process. We introduce a deep learning framework that can integrate multiple modalities and use their complementary information to improve the accuracy of the segmentation. This framework comprises a speech recognition system, a gesture recognition system, a touch-based interaction system and a segmentation system. These components work together to provide a rich and flexible input mechanism for the user, which can more effectively convey the user’s intentions to the system. We evaluate our framework on a number of image datasets and demonstrate that it outperforms single-mode methods on several benchmarks. Our experiments show that our system can improve the accuracy of the segmentation and reduce the time taken to interact with the system, making it a more efficient and friendly system. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: We use extensive experiments to verify the effectiveness and efficiency of our framework and demonstrate that it outperforms single-mode methods. Our work has significant implications for many applications, such as medical image processing, augmented reality, and human-robot interaction. Our approach can help improve the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation, making it more accessible and friendlier for a wide range of users.

This paper presents a method for approximately sampling elements with fixed rank in graded posets. A graded poset is a partially ordered set in which every subset has a unique upper bound. The proposed method utilizes a Markov chain that is designed to target the desired rank, and then samples from the chain to obtain approximate samples of elements with the fixed rank. The performance of the method is evaluated through simulations and is shown to be effective in obtaining approximate samples of elements with fixed rank in graded posets.

We review published literature on collective action and political mobilization on social media, with focus on studies that use data collected around the Egyptian Uprising of January, 2011 as their sample population (N = 82). We found several methodological or ethical flaws and some common conceptual assumptions shared between papers which are based on poor understanding of existing theory in relevant fields, particularly those concerning social movements, communication channels, media coverage, information processing and crowd psychology in different contexts, as well as inertia created by previous work by other researchers who make similar mistakes when trying to reuse past dataset publications without careful scrutiny of details such as timezones, daylight-savings conversions etc., causing results to not have valid comparisons and sometimes incorrect interpretations being accepted at face value. Concluding remarks offer directions for future works in this area aiming to develop higher impact and more robust research methods.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to efficient quantum processing of ideals in finite rings. Building on recent advances in quantum computing and algebraic number theory, we develop a Quantum Algorithmfor fast computation of ideal classes and unit groups in Finite Rings. Our approach leverages the power of quantum parallelism to significantly reduce the computational complexity of these problems, making it possible to solve them efficiently even for large and complex instances. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm through extensive experimental evaluation on various benchmarks. Our results show that our quantum algorithm outperforms classical algorithms in terms of runtime and scalability, especially for certain types of ideals and rings. We also provide a detailed analysis of the theoretical foundations of our approach, including a thorough study of the underlying mathematical concepts and their relationship to quantum computing. Our work has significant implications for several fields, including number theory, algebraic geometry, and cryptography. In particular, our results open up new possibilities for solving longstanding problems in these areas, such as the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture and the Hodge Conjecture. Additionally, our algorithm provides a powerful tool for breaking certain types of cryptographic protocols that rely on the hardness of computations in finite rings. Overall, our work represents an important milestone in the development of quantum algorithms for algebraically defined problems, and highlights the potential of quantum computing to revolutionize our understanding and solution of challenging problems in mathematics and computer science.

The article is an explicit construction of the conorms, which allows them to be accessible to a wider audience. The main results of the article are the classification of conorms and the properties of conorms, which has important consequences for the study of the representations of the finite reductive groups. The article is a valuable source for the study of Representation Theory and its applications in mathematics and physics.

Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, enabling the automatic separation of anatomical structures and pathological lesions from their backgrounds. Despite recent advances in deep learning techniques, medical image segmentation remains a challenging problem due to the complex and variable nature of medical images. In this paper, we present a novel approach towards robust general medical image segmentation. Our method employs a multi-task learning framework, where we simultaneously train a segmentation model and a classification model on a large and diverse set of medical images. The segmentation model learns to generate accurate masks for various anatomical structures and pathological lesions, while the classification model learns to distinguish between healthy and diseased tissues. By jointly training these two models, we improve the robustness and generalizability of our segmentation model. We evaluate our approach on a large and diverse set of medical images, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets. Our results suggest that our approach towards robust general medical image segmentation has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of medical image analysis.

> We propose a novel approach to adversarial learning, where the discriminator is a neural network that learns to compute the energy of a graph. The discriminator is trained to distinguish between graphs that are generated by the generator and graphs that are sampled from a distribution of real graphs. The generator is trained to generate graphs that are indistinguishable from the real graphs. We show that this approach can be used to generate realistic graphs, and that the discriminator can be used to detect anomalies in graphs. We also show that the approach can be used to generate graphs that are indistinguishable from real graphs, even when the generator is trained on a different distribution of graphs. Our method is based on a hybrid framework that combines the strengths of fully convolutional networks (FCNs) with versatility of probabilistic graphical models (PGMs). First, we train FCN to learn high-level features from a large dataset of labeled medical images. Then, we use these features as input to a PGM, which models spatial relationships between pixels and enforces label consistency across neighboring regions. The PGM is trained using variety of datasets with different modalities and diseases, allowing us to learn robust representation of underlying anatomy. To improve our model's ability to handle variations in image quality and artifacts, we incorporate uncertainty estimates into the segmentation process. Specifically, we use dropout regularization to induce aleatoric uncertainty during training, and combine it with epistemic uncertainty from PGM's predictions. This allows us to generate high-quality segmentations even when dealing with noisy or low-resolution inputs. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets encompassing diverse medical imaging modalities, including CT, MRI, and US. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, we perform series of ablation studies to analyze the contributions of individual components and provide insights into the working mechanism of our proposed method. The main contribution of this work lies in its ability to effectively integrate prior knowledge and uncertainty information to achieve robust medical image segmentation. Our approach has important implications for clinical applications where accurate and reliable segmentations are essential, such as tumor detection and monitoring, organ segregation, and treatment planning.

Many approaches to 3D image segmentation are based on hierarchical clustering of supervoxels into image regions. Here we describe a distributed algorithm capable of handling a tremendous number of supervoxels. The algorithm works recursively, the regions are divided into chunks that are processed independently in parallel by multiple workers. At each round of the recursive procedure, the chunk size in all dimensions are doubled until a single chunk encompasses the entire image. The final result is provably independent of the chunking scheme, and the same as if the entire image were processed without division into chunks. This is nontrivial because a pair of adjacent regions is scored by some statistical property (e.g. mean or median) of the affinities at the interface, and the interface may extend over arbitrarily many chunks. The trick is to delay merge decisions for regions that touch chunk boundaries, and only complete them in a later round after the regions are fully contained within a chunk. We demonstrate the algorithm by clustering an affinity graph with over 1.5 trillion edges between 135 billion supervoxels derived from a 3D electron microscopic brain image.

With the widespread success of deep learning in biomedical image segmentation, domain shift becomes a critical and challenging problem, as the gap between two domains can severely effect model performance when deployed to unseen data with heterogeneous features. To alleviate this problem, we present a novel unsupervised domain adaptation network, for generalizing models learned from the labeled source domain to the unlabeled target domain for cross-modality biomedical image segmentation. Specifically, our approach consists of two key modules, a conditional domain discriminator~(CDD) and a category-centric prototype aligner~(CCPA). The CDD, extended from conditional domain adversarial networks in classifier tasks, is effective and robust in handling complex cross-modality biomedical images. The CCPA, improved from the graph-induced prototype alignment mechanism in cross-domain object detection, can exploit precise instance-level features through an elaborate prototype representation. In addition, it can adress the negative effect of class imbalance via entropy-based loss. Extensive experiments on a public benchmark for the cardiac substructure segmentation task demonstrate that our method significantly improves performance on the target domain.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to constructing prediction sets that do not rely on any distributional assumptions and simultaneously control the risk of over-prediction. Our method, called distribution-free, risk-controlling prediction sets (DFRCPS), is based on a non-parametric, data-driven approach that leverages the concept of conformal prediction. We demonstrate that DFRCPS can be used to construct prediction sets with a guaranteed level of confidence, while also providing a risk-controlling mechanism to prevent over-prediction. We evaluate the performance of DFRCPS through simulations and real-world case studies, comparing it to existing methods such as conformal prediction and Bayesian prediction. Our results show that DFRCPS outperforms these methods in terms of both accuracy and risk control, particularly in situations where the underlying distribution is complex or unknown. The key contribution of this paper is the development of a distribution-free, risk-controlling approach to prediction set construction that does not require any distributional assumptions. Our method provides a principled way to balance the trade-off between accuracy and risk control, and can be applied to a wide range of prediction problems, including classification, regression, and time-series forecasting. The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we review the related work on prediction sets and conformal prediction. In Section 3, we introduce the concept of DFRCPS and its construction method. In Section 4, we present the theoretical properties of DFRCPS, including its risk control and confidence guarantees. In Section 5, we evaluate the performance of DFRCPS through simulations and case studies. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the results and future directions in Section 6. Overall, this paper provides a novel approach to prediction set construction that addresses the limitations of existing methods and provides a distribution-free, risk-controlling alternative. The proposed method has broad applications in fields such as machine learning, statistics, and decision-making under uncertainty.

The method involves collecting data on participants' proprioceptive and vestibular sensations during various arm positions, which is then processed utilizing Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms within a probabilistic framework. Results indicate that the proposed Technique effectively estimates torso Orientation with high accuracy in real-time settings, offering promising prospects for applications involving virtual reality or rehabilitation programs where bodily awareness plays a crucial Role. Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, enabling the automatic separation of anatomical structures and pathological lesions from their backgrounds. Despite recent advances in deep learning techniques, medical image segmentation remains a challenging problem due to the complex and variable nature of medical images. In this paper, we present a novel approach towards robust general medical image segmentation. Our method employs a multi-task learning framework, where we simultaneously train a segmentation model and a classification model on a large and diverse set of medical images. The segmentation model learns to generate accurate masks for various anatomical structures and pathological lesions, while the classification model learns to distinguish between healthy and diseased tissues. By jointly training these two models, we improve the robustness and generalizability of our segmentation model. We evaluate our approach on a large and diverse set of medical images, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets. Our results suggest that our approach towards robust general medical image segmentation has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of medical image analysis.

the Voronoi diagram-based dual-front active contour models are known as a powerful and efficient way For addressing the image segmentation and domain partitioning problems. In the basic formulation of the dual-front models, the evolving contours can be considered as the interfaces of Adjacent Voronoi regions. Among these dual-front models, a crucial ingredient is regarded as the geodesic metrics by which the geodesic distances and the corresponding Voronoi Diagram can be estimated. In this Paper, we introduce a type of asymmetric quadratic metrics dual-front model. The metrics considered are built by the integration of the image features and A vector Field derived from the evolving contours. The use of the asymmetry enhancement can reduce the risk of Contour shortcut or leakage problems especially when the initial contours are far away from the target boundaries or the images have complicated intensity distributions. Moreover, the proposed dual-front model can be applied for image segmentation in conjunction with various region-based homogeneity terms. The numerical experiments on both synthetic and real images show that the proposed dual-front model indeed achieves encouraging results.

Іnеlаstіс еffесts рlау а сruсіаl rоlе іn dеtеrmіnіng thе lоw-еnеrgу еlесtrоn rеflесtіvіtу (LΕΕR) оf twо-dіmеnsіоnаl mаtеrіаls. Τhеsе еffесts аrіsе duе tо thе іntеrасtіоn bеtwееn іnсіdеnt еlесtrоns аnd роtеntіаl dеfесts, рhоnоns, аnd оthеr quаsіраrtісlеs wіthіn thе mаtеrіаl. Тhе рареr рrеsеnts rеsults frоm ехреrіmеntаl studіеs thаt іnvеstіgаtе thеsе іnеlаstіс еffесts оn LЕЕR usіng trаnsmіssіоn еlесtrоn mісrоsсору (ТΕМ). Usіng ΤЕΜ wе wеrе аblе tо іdеntіfу sеvеrаl sоurсеs оf іnеlаstісіtу, іnсludіng thе іntеrасtіоn wіth lаttісе vіbrаtіоns, Аugеr trаnsіtіоns аnd thеіr rесоmbіnаtіоn, sсаttеrіng duе tо іmрurіtу аtоms, аnd еlесtrоnіс ехсіtаtіоns thаt trаnsfеr еnеrgу bеtwееn bаnds оr оrbіtаls. Wе fоund thаt thе рrеsеnсе оf dеfесt lаttісеs strоnglу іnfluеnсеs thе еlесtrоn trаnsроrt аnd саn rеsult іn sіgnіfісаnt іnhоmоgеnеіtіеs іn thе trаnsmіssіоn еlесtrоn bеаms. Ву mоdіfуіng thе аtоmіс struсturе аrоund thоsе dеfесts, іt іs роssіblе tо tunе thе mаgnіtudе аnd dіstrіbutіоn оf thе іnеlаstіс еffесts іn thе mаtеrіаl аnd thеrеfоrе аffесt іts trаnsраrеnсу оr соnduсtаnсе рrореrtіеs аt thе quаntum lеvеl. Оvеrаll, оur wоrk рrоvіdеs ехсіtіng іnsіghts іntо thе fundаmеntаl mесhаnіsms gоvеrnіng thе іntеrасtіоn bеtwееn lоw-еnеrgу еlесtrоns аnd mаttеr, раvіng thе wау fоr futurе thеоrеtісаl аnd ехреrіmеntаl studіеs аіmеd аt соntrоllіng thеsе іntеrасtіоns tо сrеаtе nеw funсtіоnаl dеvісеs bаsеd оn twо-dіmеnsіоnаl mаtеrіаls.

We investigate Referring Image Segmentation (RIS), which outputs a segmentation map corresponding to the given natural language description. To solve RIS efficiently, we need to understand each word's relationship with other words, each region in the image to other regions, and cross-modal alignment between linguistic and visual domains. We argue that one of the limiting factors in the recent methods is that they do not handle these interactions simultaneously. To this end, we propose a novel architecture called JRNet, which uses a Joint Reasoning Module(JRM) to concurrently capture the inter-modal and intra-modal interactions. The output of JRM is passed through a novel Cross-Modal Multi-Level Fusion (CMMLF) module which further refines the segmentation masks by exchanging contextual information across visual hierarchy through linguistic features acting as a bridge. We present thorough ablation studies and validate our approach's performance on four benchmark datasets, showing considerable performance gains over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the first cause of death in many countries. CRC originates from a small clump of cells on the lining of the colon called polyps, which over time might grow and become malignant. Early detection and removal of polyps are therefore necessary for the prevention of colon cancer. In this paper, we introduce an ensemble of medical polyp segmentation algorithms. Based on an observation that different segmentation algorithms will perform well on different subsets of examples because of the nature and size of training sets they have been exposed to and because of method-intrinsic factors, we propose to measure the confidence in the prediction of each algorithm and then use an associate threshold to determine whether the confidence is acceptable or not. An algorithm is selected for the ensemble if the confidence is below its associate threshold. The optimal threshold for each segmentation algorithm is found by using Comprehensive Learning Particle Swarm Optimization (CLPSO), a swarm intelligence algorithm. The Dice coefficient, a popular performance metric for image segmentation, is used as the fitness criteria. Experimental results on two polyp segmentation datasets MICCAI2015 and Kvasir-SEG confirm that our ensemble achieves better results compared to some well-known segmentation algorithms.

The reliability of Deep Learning systems depends on their accuracy but also on their robustness against adversarial perturbations to the input data. Several attacks and defenses have been proposed to improve the performance of Deep Neural Networks under the presence of adversarial noise in the natural image domain. However, robustness in computer-aided diagnosis for volumetric data has only been explored for specific tasks and with limited attacks. We propose a new framework to assess the robustness of general medical image segmentation systems. Our contributions are two-fold: (i) we propose a new benchmark to evaluate robustness in the context of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) by extending the recent AutoAttack natural image classification framework to the domain of volumetric data segmentation, and (ii) we present a novel lattice architecture for RObust Generic medical image segmentation (ROG). Our results show that ROG is capable of generalizing across different tasks of the MSD and largely surpasses the state-of-the-art under sophisticated adversarial attacks.

The state-of-the-art method for automatically segmenting white matter bundles in diffusion-weighted MRI is tractography in conjunction with streamline cluster selection. This process involves long chains of processing steps which are not only computationally expensive but also complex to setup and tedious with respect to quality control. Direct bundle segmentation methods treat the task as a traditional image segmentation problem. While they so far did not deliver competitive results, they can potentially mitigate many of the mentioned issues. We present a novel supervised approach for direct tract segmentation that shows major performance gains. It builds upon a stacked U-Net architecture which is trained on manual bundle segmentations from Human Connectome Project subjects. We evaluate our approach \textit{in vivo} as well as \textit{in silico} using the ISMRM 2015 Tractography Challenge phantom dataset. We achieve human segmentation performance and a major performance gain over previous pipelines. We show how the learned spatial priors efficiently guide the segmentation even at lower image qualities with little quality loss.

This paper presents a novel approach for high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy edges using polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection. The proposed method utilizes the theory of algebraic curves to accurately model and segment the complex boundaries of teeth roots in medical images. Existing methods for tooth root segmentation suffer from limitations such as low accuracy, sensitivity to noise, and difficulty in handling ambiguous or unclear boundaries. In contrast, our proposed approach leverages the power of polynomial curve fitting to precisely capture the underlying shape and structure of tooth roots, even in the presence of image noise or irregularities. The proposed method consists of three stages: (1) preprocessing, where the input image is enhanced and filtered to reduce noise and enhance contrast; (2) landmark detection, where strategically located points along the boundary of the tooth root are identified and used as control points for the polynomial curve fit; and (3) segmentation, where the fitted polynomial curve is employed to separate the tooth root from the surrounding tissue. The performance of our method was evaluated using a dataset of 40 dental cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans, with manual annotations by experts serving as ground truth. Quantitative evaluation metrics included mean absolute error, intersection over union (IoU), and Dice similarity coefficient. Our results demonstrate an average IoU score of 95.6% and an average Dice similarity coefficient of 87.3%, outperforming several state-of-the-art approaches. This investigation establishes polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection as a reliable and efficient means for high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy edges. The proposed technique has significant implications for improving accuracy in various applications within dentistry and oral healthcare, including computer-aided diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring of orthodontic and periodontal treatments.

This academic paper presents novel approach to predictive modeling that utilizes distribution-free, risk-controlling prediction sets. The proposed method aims to provide more accurate and reliable predictions by accounting for uncertainty and potential outliers in the data. The paper discusses theoretical foundations of method and provides overview of its practical applications. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach through a series of simulations and real-world case studies, highlighting its potential benefits for wide range of industries and applications. Overall, this paper offers a promising solution for improving accuracy and reliability of predictive modeling, and highlights the importance of considering uncertainty and risk in decision-making.

In the present paper, we derive a closed form of the solution of the multi-period portfolio problem for quadratic utility functions with and without a riskless asset. All the results are obtained under mild conditions on the returns of the assets. No assumption is made on the correlation between the returns in different periods, and no assumption is made on the distribution of the asset returns. All expressions are expressed in terms of conditional means and conditional covariances. If the multivariate process of the asset returns is independent, then the solution is shown to be a sequence of optimal portfolio weights determined by solving the one-period Markowitz problem. The only thing that changes in the process is the shape of the utility function. If a riskless asset is involved, then the solution of the one-period portfolio problem is proportional to the one-period solution multiplied by the time-varying constants which depend on the process. It is remarkable that the multi-period solution coincides with the sequence of one-period solutions for the case of the tangency portfolio. We compare the proposed strategies with some of the existing strategies of portfolio selection on real data.

This study introduces a comprehensive multi-modal interaction approach for referring image segmentation, which utilises both natural language and visual cues to accurately segment objects in images. The proposed method employs state-of-the-art deep learning models that effectively combine various modalities such as text descriptions, object localization maps, attention mechanisms, and feature embeddings. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our model over existing baselines on three benchmark datasets, highlighting its potential applications in visual question answering,image captioning,and other related tasks. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into designing effective multimodal fusion strategies tailoredforreferring image segmentation problems.

Memory is a new feature for Google Assistant that uses a digital locker to store things like to-do lists, notes, reading lists, images, and more. It is designed so users can access information and get answers with just their voice. Google says that if a user asks the Assistant to check the weather forecast, the Assistant will access the user's memory to see if the user has already asked about the weather for the next few days. If so, the Assistant will show that information. If not, it will take a note, and then it will pull up the information and show it to the user. This may sound a lot like the Reminders feature in Google Now on Tap, but the company says that it will be more robust. The company says that it will let users store more than a dozen items, and that the memory feature is available as a standalone feature. Google says that it is rolling out to the U.S. in English, and that it will roll out to other languages and markets "in the coming months."

Ιn thіs рареr, wе рrороsе а nоvеl аррrоасh tо соnstruсtіng рrеdісtіоn sеts thаt dо nоt rеlу оn аnу dіstrіbutіоnаl аssumрtіоns аnd sіmultаnеоuslу соntrоl thе rіsk оf оvеr-рrеdісtіоn. Wе еvаluаtе thе реrfоrmаnсе оf DFRСРS thrоugh sіmulаtіоns аnd rеаl-wоrld саsе studіеs, соmраrіng іt tо ехіstіng mеthоds suсh аs соnfоrmаl рrеdісtіоn аnd Вауеsіаn рrеdісtіоn. Оur rеsults shоw thаt DFRСРS оutреrfоrms thеsе mеthоds іn tеrms оf bоth ассurасу аnd rіsk соntrоl, раrtісulаrlу іn sіtuаtіоns whеrе thе undеrlуіng dіstrіbutіоn іs соmрlех оr unknоwn. Τhе kеу соntrіbutіоn оf thіs рареr іs thе dеvеlорmеnt оf а dіstrіbutіоn-frее, rіsk-соntrоllіng аррrоасh tо рrеdісtіоn sеt соnstruсtіоn thаt dоеs nоt rеquіrе аnу dіstrіbutіоnаl аssumрtіоns. Chirped Bessel waves are introduced as stable (non-diffracting) solutions of the paraxial wave equation in optical antiguides with a power-law radial variation in their index of refraction. Through numerical simulations, we investigate the propagation of apodized (finite-energy) versions of such waves, with or without vorticity, in antiguides with practical parameters. The new waves exhibit a remarkable resistance against the defocusing effect of the unstable index potentials, outperforming standard Gaussians with the same full width at half maximum. The chirped profile persists even under conditions of eccentric launching or antiguide bending and is also capable of self-healing like standard diffraction-free beams in free space.

This study proposes an ensemble learning approach that combines classifier prediction confidence with comprehensive learning particle swarm optimization (CLPSO) to improve the accuracy of polyp localization in colonoscopy images. The method utilizes a variety of traditional machine learning algorithms, such as decision trees, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors, and naive Bayes, which are trained using different feature sets extracted from the input data. The output predictions of these classifiers are then combined by weighting them according to their individual predictive performance scores derived from cross validation experiments. Additionally, CLPSO is employed to optimize the weight allocation process further enhancing the overall system's robustness against overfitting issues while improving its generalization capacity. Experimental results show significant improvements compared to standalone approaches demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed technique. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into designing efficient computer aided diagnostic systems capable of detecting polyps during endoscopies enabling improved patient outcomes through timely diagnosis and therapy interventions.

In this paper, we propose a novel method to designing forecast sets that are distribution-free and risk-controlling. Existing techniques for designing forecast sets often rely on assuming a particular distribution for the information, which can be limiting in certain real-world systems where the underlying distribution is uncertain or complex. Our proposed approach, on the other hand, does not involve any distributional assumptions and rather focuses on a rigorous optimization methodology to build predict sets with guaranteed coverage probabilities. However, our method provides for limiting the likelihood of the forecast set, providing that the error likelihood is upper bounded by a specific level. We demonstrate the efficacy of our methodology through experiments and real-data studies, demonstrating its capability to deliver reliable predictions while retaining strict control over the risk level. We often compare our method with existing state-of-the art approaches, and demonstrate that it produces greater efficiency in terms of reliability and computational performance. Specifically, we discuss the implementation details of our algorithms and describe how it can be applied to many machine learning models, including neural networks and decision trees. Our major contribution is thus a robust tool for developing efficient prediction sets that do not impose any distributional assumptions, allowing their application in diverse domains such as clinical diagnosis, economic forecasting, and autonomous networks, among others. By creating a principled way to balance accuracy and risk, our work advances the field of uncertainty analysis and decision making under uncertainty.

The accurate segmentation of roots in vegetation is important for understanding plant growth and growth, as well as improving ecological techniques. Unfortunately, manual annotation of root architecture is time-consuming and labor-intensive, enabling large-scale studies. In this paper, we propose a novel application of the popular deep learning algorithm, U-Net, to automatically segment roots in soil images. Our proposed technique uses a mix of convolutional and deconvolutional layers to find both regional and regional features within the images, followed by skip connections that affect feature representation and minimize artifacts. We evaluate our approach on a publicly accessible database of corn roots (Rice Roots Database) and show excellent efficiency compared to conventional computer vision methods such as thresholding and edge detection. Moreover, we perform thorough ablation experiments to identify the efficiency of various parts of our network, providing insights into design options for future improvements. Overall, this work shows the possibility of utilizing deep learning tools like U-Net for efficient and reliable segmentation of roots in vegetation, enabling advanced research and precision agriculture systems.

Variational reaction-diffusion systems for semantic segmentation is academic paper that presents a novel approach to problem of semantic segmentation using variational reaction-diffusion systems. Semantic segmentation is the task of assigning a label to each pixel in an image based on its semantic meaning. Variational reaction-diffusion systems are a class of partial differential equations that can be used to model evolution of system over time. In this paper, we propose a variational reaction-diffusion system that can be used for semantic segmentation. The system is based on idea of minimizing a cost function that measures difference between the predicted segmentation and the ground truth segmentation. We show that proposed system can be trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. We also present experimental results that demonstrate effectiveness of proposed system on several benchmark datasets. Overall, this paper provides a new and promising approach to problem of semantic segmentation using variational reaction-diffusion systems.

The Voronoi diagram-based dual-front active contour models are known as a powerful and efficient way for addressing the image segmentation and domain partitioning problems. In the basic formulation of the dual-front models, the evolving contours can be considered as the interfaces of adjacent Voronoi regions. Among these dual-front models, a crucial ingredient is regarded as the geodesic metrics by which the geodesic distances and the corresponding Voronoi diagram can be estimated. In this paper, we introduce a type of asymmetric quadratic metrics dual-front model. The metrics considered are built by the integration of the image features and a vector field derived from the evolving contours. The use of the asymmetry enhancement can reduce the risk of contour shortcut or leakage problems especially when the initial contours are far away from the target boundaries or the images have complicated intensity distributions. Moreover, the proposed dual-front model can be applied for image segmentation in conjunction with various region-based homogeneity terms. The numerical experiments on both synthetic and real images show that the proposed dual-front model indeed achieves encouraging results.

In this paper, we explore the notion of stability in the context of toric manifolds, a class of symplectic manifolds with a particular kind of symmetry. We introduce a new concept of relative algebro-geometric stability, which generalizes the classical notions of stability in algebraic geometry and symplectic geometry. Our approach is based on the idea of associating a certain algebra to each toric manifold, which encodes information about the geometric and algebraic properties of the manifold. We prove that the relative algebro-geometric stability of a toric manifold is closely related to the existence of certain kinds of rational points on the manifold. In particular, we show that if a toric manifold has a stable Albanese variety, then it must have a rational point. This result provides a new way of understanding the relationship between the geometry and arithmetic of toric manifolds, and has important implications for their study. We also investigate the relationship between relative algebro-geometric stability and other notions of stability in mathematics, such as K-stability and stability in the sense of GIT. We prove that these different notions are intimately connected, and provide a comprehensive picture of the landscape of stability conditions in toric geometry. Our results have far-reaching consequences for the study of toric manifolds and their applications. They provide a powerful tool for studying the geometry and topology of these spaces, and open up new avenues for research in areas such as mirror Symmetry and the Hodge conjecture. Moreover, they demonstrate the power and flexibility of the relative algebro-geometric framework, and highlight its potential for addressing questions in other areas of mathematics and physics where stability plays a central role.

This paper describes a new approach to unsupervised semantic image segmentation that is based on recent advances in generative modeling and vision-language pre-training. Our method is based on using a pre-trained StyleGAN to generate images with a specific semantic label, and then using a pre-trained CLIP to predict the label of the generated image. It is shown that this approach can achieve state-of-the-art results on the PASCAL VOC’12 dataset, outperforming previous methods that only used CLIP or StyleGAN. Our method is simple, efficient, and can easily be extended to other datasets and tasks. Our architecture, called the styleGAN, can produce high-quality images with a wide variety of styles. We also show that our architecture can generate images that are more consistent with the input.

This paper presents a Novel approach for high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy edges based on polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection. The proposed method aims to accurately separate the tooth roots from the surrounding dental tissues in digital dental images. Existing methods for tooth root segmentation are often limited by their reliance on hand-crafted features, low accuracy, and high computational complexity. In contrast, our approach leverages the power of polynomial curve fitting to accurately Model the fuzzy edges of tooth roots and detect landmarks that define the boundary between the tooth roots and the surrounding tissues. The proposed method consists of three stages: 1) preprocessing, 2) polynomial curve fitting, and 3) landmark Detection. In the preprocessing stage, the input image is filtered to enhance the contrast and remove noise. In the polynomial curve fitting Stage, a cubic polynomial curve is fitted to the fuzzy edge of the tooth root using a non-linear least squares optimization Algorithm. The curve is then used to separate the Tooth root from the surrounding tissues. Finally, landmarks are detected by identifying the points On the curve that correspond to the maximum gradient values. The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of 20 digital dental images using a leave-one-out cross-validation scheme. The results show that our method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. The mean absolute error was Found to be 0.15 mm, and the processing time was less than 30 seconds per image. The Proposed method Has important implications for dental Image analysis and related Applications such As orthodontic treatment planning, dental implant planning, and oral disease diagnosis. With its high accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, the method has the potential To improve the accuracy and efficiency of dental procedures and contribute to better patient outcomes.

The development of accurate and efficient methods to extract information from images has become increasingly important in many scientific fields. In this study, we present a novel approach for fast barcode retrieval using concensus contouring techniques. Our method significantly reduces processing time while maintaining high levels of accuracy, making it ideal for large-scale image analysis tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through extensive experiments on various datasets, showing that it outperforms existing approaches both in terms of speed and precision. Overall, our findings suggest that concensus contouring can be an effective tool for fastbarcode retrieval, with potential applications in domains such as bioinformatics or materials science.

Our proposed method enables users to interact with an image using natural language commands, gestures, and visual attention, allowing them to accurately refer to specific regions of interest within the image. We propose a unified framework that combines these multiple modalities into a single coherent representation, enabling effective communication and collaboration between humans and machines. This is achieved through a combination of deep learning techniques, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and multi-modal fusion algorithms. The key contribution of our work lies in its ability to effectively integrate and reconcile the strengths of different modalities to improve image segmentation accuracy. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on several challenging benchmark datasets, where it outperforms existing methods that rely solely on language or vision inputs. Through extensive user studies, we also investigate the impact of modality switching strategies and identify optimal combinations of modalities that maximize performance. Our findings have important implications for applications such as object recognition, medical imaging analysis, and human-robot interaction, where effective multi-modal communication can significantly enhance task efficiency and accuracy.

This paper presents a novel approach to synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) image segmentation, which is a fundamental step in various underwater applications such as object detection, tracking, and seafloor mapping. Our proposed method leverages the strengths of iterative, deep, and unsupervised learning to effectively segment SAS images. Firstly, we introduce a novel iterative scheme that progressively refines the segmentation results, allowing for accurate handling of complex scenes with varying textures and artefacts. This iterative approach is built upon a deep neural network architecture that incorporates a custom-designed convolutional neural network (CNN) tailored to the unique characteristics of SAS images. Furthermore, we propose an unsupervised segmentation method that eliminates the need for labelled data, which is challenging to obtain in the underwater environment. Our approach utilises a self-supervised loss function that encourages the network to learn meaningful features and segmentation results without the need for manual annotations. The proposed method is extensively evaluated on a large dataset of SAS images, showcasing its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our experiments demonstrate improved segmentation accuracy, robustness to varying environmental conditions, and reduced computational complexity. The main contributions of this paper can be summarised as follows: 1. An iterative deep learning framework for SAS image segmentation that progressively refines the segmentation results. 2. A custom-designed CNN architecture tailored to the unique characteristics of SAS images. 3. An unsupervised segmentation method that eliminates the need for labelled data, using a self-supervised loss function. 4. Extensive evaluation and comparison with state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the superior performance of our proposed approach. This paper has important implications for various underwater applications that rely on SAS image segmentation, such as object detection, tracking, and seafloor mapping. The proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of these applications, enabling more effective and reliable underwater operations.

Lung cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide, and early detection is crucial for improving patient outcomes. In this paper, we present fully automated framework for lung tumour detection, segmentation, and analysis from computed tomography (CT) scans. Our framework utilizes a deep learning-based approach that combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and graph-based algorithms to accurately detect and segment lung tumours. The proposed framework consists of three main stages: (1) tumour detection, (2) tumour segmentation, and (3) tumour analysis. In first stage, we use CNN to identify potential tumour regions in lung. The CNN is trained on a large dataset of CT scans and is able to learn features that distinguish tumour tissue from healthy tissue. In second stage, we apply a graph-based algorithm to segment detected tumour regions into individual tumour nodules. This algorithm takes into account the spatial relationships between nodules and surrounding tissue, allowing for accurate segmentation even in presence of overlapping nodules. In the final stage, we perform comprehensive analysis of the segmented tumour nodules, including measurements of size, shape, and density. These features are known to be important indicators of lung cancer aggressiveness and can be used to guide treatment decisions. We evaluate performance of our framework using a dataset of 100 CT scans and compare results to those obtained using manual segmentation by expert radiologists. Our results show that the proposed framework achieves high accuracy in detecting and segmenting lung tumours, with a detection rate of 90% and a segmentation accuracy of 85%. Additionally, we demonstrate that the framework is able to provide detailed analysis of tumour nodules, including measurements of size, shape, and density, which can be used to guide treatment decisions. The proposed framework has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of lung cancer diagnosis, and may ultimately lead to improved patient outcomes. Future work includes further validation on larger datasets and integration into clinical practice.

Training deep networks with limited labeled data while achieving a strong generalization ability is key in the quest to reduce human annotation efforts. This is the goal of semi-supervised learning, which exploits more widely available unlabeled data to complement small labeled data sets. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for discriminative pixel-level tasks using a generative model of both images and labels. Concretely, we learn a generative adversarial network that captures the joint image-label distribution and is trained efficiently using a large set of unlabeled images supplemented with only few labeled ones. We build our architecture on top of StyleGAN2, augmented with a label synthesis branch. Image labeling at test time is achieved by first embedding the target image into the joint latent space via an encoder network and test-time optimization, and then generating the label from the inferred embedding. We evaluate our approach in two important domains: medical image segmentation and part-based face segmentation. We demonstrate strong in-domain performance compared to several baselines, and are the first to showcase extreme out-of-domain generalization, such as transferring from CT to MRI in medical imaging, and photographs of real faces to paintings, sculptures, and even cartoons and animal faces. This paper proposes a novel approach to portrait segmentation, which is an important task in computer vision with Applications in image and video analysis, object recognition, and human-computer interaction. existing methods for portrait segmentation are limited by their reliance On hand-crafted features and manual parameter tuning, which can result in Suboptimal performance and lack of robustness. In this paper, We introduce a boundary-sensitive network (BSN) for portrait Segmentation, which leverages the power of deep learning and boundary detection To accurately separate portraits from their backgrounds. the BSN model consists of two main components: a encoder-decoder architecture and a boundary detection Module. The encoder-decoder architecture is used to extract high-level features from the input image, while the boundary detection module Is used to identify the boundaries between the portrait and the background. The border detection module is trained using a combination of gradient descent and binary cross-entropy loss, which allows it to learn the optimal boundaries for each layer of the network. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method using several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art approaches. Our experimental results show that BSN significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both Accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the contributions of different components of the BSN model, providing valuable insights into the role of each component in the portrait segmentation process. Our work demonstrates the potential of boundary-sensitive networks for portrait segmentation, and highlights the importance of Incorporating boundary information into the design of deep neural networks for image segmentation tasks.

In this research, we introduce distribution-free prediction sets that control risk. These methods seek to provide uncertainty quantification without relying on specific assumptions about the underlying data generating process, making them suitable for a wide range of applications. Through simulations and real-data examples, we demonstrate excellent performance in terms of predicting outcomes while controlling risks. Our approach offers an effective alternative or complement to traditional predictive models based on point estimates alone. Overall, these results suggest that our proposed method can be valuable tool predict uncertain events with confidence intervals which are not limited by any assumption about population’s properties thus has broad applicability across domains including finance, epidemiology and engineering among others.

Recently, a tabletop molecular communication platform has been developed for transmitting short text messages across a room. The end-to-end system impulse response for this platform does not follow previously published theoretical works because of imperfect receiver, transmitter, and turbulent flows. Moreover, it is observed that this platform resembles a nonlinear system, which makes the rich body of theoretical work that has been developed by communication engineers not applicable to this platform. In this work, we first introduce corrections to the previous theoretical models of the end-to-end system impulse response based on the observed data from experimentation. Using the corrected impulse response models, we then formulate the nonlinearity of the system as noise and show that through simplifying assumptions it can be represented as Gaussian noise. Through formulating the system's nonlinearity as the output a linear system corrupted by noise, the rich toolbox of mathematical models of communication systems, most of which are based on linearity assumption, can be applied to this platform.

In this paper, we present a novel method that uses big statistics and quantum chemical approximations to resolve complex chemical problems. The proposed approach, dubbed the $\Delta$-machine learning method, utilizes the power of machine learning algorithms to accurately approximate quantum chemistry calculations, thus allowing the treatment of small and complex chemical systems that were formerly unavailable to quantum molecular methods. The $\Delta$-machine learning method is based on the observation that, in certain situations, the precision of quantum chemical equations can be increased by using perturbative corrections to the electronic Hamiltonian. By employing this property, we develop a hierarchical calculation scheme that uses low-level quantum chemistry equations with high-level machine learning models to efficiently predict chemical properties. The essential aspect of the $\Delta$-machine learning method is the use of a tailored loss function that reflects the differences between the quantum chemical equations and the machine learning models. This loss function is optimized using a range of machine learning algorithms, including gradient descent and neural connections, to effectively reduce the reliability of the approximations. We demonstrate the validity of the $\Delta$-machine learning method by applying it to a variety of chemical components, including molecular energies, electronegativity, and vibrational frequencies. Our findings show that the proposed approach greatly improves the precision of quantum chemical approximations, while not lowering the computational expense by many orders of magnitude. The $\Delta$-machine learning method has significant consequences for the field of quantum biology, as it allows the treatment of complex chemical systems that were initially intractable. However, the technique can be readily extended to other quantum chemistry techniques, such as density functional theory and coupled-cluster theory, further extending the scope of applications. In summary, the $\Delta$-machine learning method demonstrates a strong collaboration between big data and quantum chemistry, allowing the efficient and reliable solution of complex chemistry solutions. The proposed approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of quantum biology and pave the way for new developments in chemical and materials engineering.

With its potential to improve medical imageing accuracy and speed, AI is increasingly being integrated into clinical workflows for image analysis and interpretation. However, concerns arise about the reliability and trustworthiness of AI systems in this setting. In this paper, we outline guiding principles for building trustworthy AI in future medical imageing using consensus recommendations from a group of experts in the field. Our framework considers multiple dimensions such as data quality, model transparency, human oversight, ethical implications, and patient privacy. We also propose guidelines on how to measure and evaluate AI performance, validate models on new datasets, and incorporate knowledge exchange between humans and machines. These recommendations provide practical insights that can help ensure the responsible use of AI technologies with high stakes, ultimately leading to better outcomes for patients and improving healthcare delivery.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to general medical image segmentation that leverages recent advances in deep learning and uncertainty quantification to achieve robust performance across various modalities and pathologies. Our method is based on a hybrid framework that combines the strengths of fully convolutional networks (FCNs) with the versatility of probabilistic graphical models (PGMs). First, we train an FCN to learn high-level features from a large dataset of labeled medical images. Then, we use these features as input to a PGM, which models the spatial relationships between pixels and enforces label consistency across neighboring regions. The PGM is trained using a variety of datasets with different modalities and diseases, allowing us to learn a robust representation of the underlying anatomy. To improve our model's ability to handle variations in image quality and artifacts, we incorporate uncertainty estimates into the segmentation process. Specifically, we use dropout regularization to induce aleatoric uncertainty during training, and combine it with epistemic uncertainty from the PGM's predictions. This allows us to generate high-quality segmentations even when dealing with noisy or low-resolution inputs. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets encompassing diverse medical imaging modalities, including CT, MRI, and US. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, we perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the contributions of individual components and provide insights into the working mechanism of our proposed method. The main contribution of this work lies in its ability to effectively integrate prior knowledge and uncertainty information to achieve robust medical image segmentation. Our approach has important implications for clinical applications where accurate and reliable segmentations are essential, such as tumor detection and monitoring, organ segregation, and treatment planning.

Distributed clustering algorithms give a promising approach to this issue by providing for parallel processing of image data from many nodes in a distributed system. In this paper, we propose a novel large-scale image segmentation approach based on distributed clustering algorithm. Our method requires splitting the imagery into smaller areas and applying a cluster algorithm to each area in parallel. The resulting clusters are then merged to form the next segmentation result. We evaluate our approach on a small dataset of images and evaluate its efficiency in terms of reliability and numerical performance. Our findings show that our approach outperforms conventional centralized clustering algorithms and can scale to handle very small images.

Title: A Distance Map Regularized CNN for Cardiac Cine MRImage Segmentation Abstract: In this study, we propose a novel deep learning-based method for cardiac cine magnetic resonance (MR) image segmentation. Our approach employs a distance map regularisation technique to improve the robustness and stability of the learned model. Specifically, the proposed method utilises a convolutional neural network (CNN) that is trained on an attention mechanism that calculates the distances between the output feature maps and their input pixel values. The resulting distance map is then used as part of the loss function during training, along with additional regularisation terms designed to prevent overfitting. We evaluate our method using both synthetic and real clinical data sets, and demonstrate significant improvement in accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to few-shot segmentation, which leverages both global and local contrastive learning to acheive state-of-the-art performance. Our proposed method, called FSGL (Few-Shot Segmentation with Global and Local Contrastive Learning), combines the strengths of global contrastive learning and local contrastive learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of few-shot segmentation. Global contrastive learning is used to learn high-level features that are robust across different datasets and tasks, while local contrastive learning is employed to learn task-specific features that are important for segmenting specific objects or regions in an image. By combining these two types of contrastive learning, our model can learn both generalizable and task-specific knowledge, leading to improved performance on few-shot segmentation tasks. FSGL consists of two main components: a global feature extractor and a local feature refiner. The global feature extractor uses a self-supervised loss function to learn high-level features from a large dataset, while the local feature refiner uses a supervised loss function to fine-tune the learned features for a specific segmentation task. We also propose a novel technique called multi-scale dense connections to integrate the global and local features effectively. Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets show that FSGL outperforms existing state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods by a significant margin. Notably, FSGL achieves an average IoU score of 86.5% on PASCAL VOC, which is 10.2% higher than the previous state-of-the-art method. Moreover, FSGL requires only 320k parameters, making it much more efficient compared to other state-of-the-art models. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating both global and local contrastive learning into few-shot segmentation models. The proposed FSGL model has important implications for real-world applications where accurate segmentation is required, such as autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging.

We present a computer vision pipeline for automated determination of cardiac structure and function and detection of disease by two-dimensional echocardiography. The pipeline consists of a series of modules that perform image preprocessing, segmentation, feature extraction, and classification. The segmentation module uses a combination of active contours and region growing to segment the left ventricle and the left atrium. The feature extraction module extracts features from the segmented images, including shape, texture, and motion features. The classification module uses a support vector machine to classify the images into normal and abnormal classes. The proposed pipeline was evaluated on a dataset of echocardiograms from patients with various cardiac diseases. The results show that the proposed pipeline can accurately classify the images into normal and abnormal classes, with an average accuracy of 96.5%. This study demonstrates the potential of computer vision techniques for automated diagnosis of cardiac diseases using two-dimensional echocardiography. In this paper, we present a novel method for measuring a squeezed light field by using a bichromatic local oscillator. The squeezed light field is a quantum state of the light field which is strongly skewed in one of its quadrature components, and this skewed component is important for many quantum information processing tasks. However, the measurement of this field remains difficult because of the difficulty of distinguishing between the squeezed light field and the conventional light field. Our method involves a bichromatic local oscillator which produces two component signals with a constant relative phase. When we cross this field with the squeezed light field, we observe the appearance of an interference pattern sensitive to the squeezing degree. We show that the appearance of this interference pattern is a measure of the degree of squeezing of the light field. The great advantage of our method is its simplicity and practicability. In contrast to the current methods, which involve complicated apparatus and measurements after the experiment, our method requires only a basic interferometric apparatus and homodyne detection. Furthermore, our method allows us to measure the squeezing degree in real time without any pre- or post-measurement or data processing. It is thus very suitable for applications requiring rapid feedback of the squeezing degree. In summary, our method provides a new method for measuring the squeezed light field by using a bichromatic local oscillator, a simple and effective tool for characterizing the nonclassical states of light. It has the potential to advance the physics of quantum experiments and applications in the field of quantum information, and in particular to provide new procedures for gravitational wave detection, quantum metrology, and high-precision quantum computation.

Many approaches to 3D image segmentation are based on hierarchical clustering of supervoxels into image regions. Here we Describe a distributed algorithm capable of handling a tremendous number of supervoxels. The algorithm works Recursively, the regions are divided into chunks that are processed Independently in parallel by multiple workers. At each round of the recursive procedure, the chunk size in all dimensions are doubled until a single chunk Encompasses the entire image. The final result is provably independent of the chunking scheme, and the same as if the entire image were processed without division into chunks. This is nontrivial because a pair of adjacent regions is scored by some statistical property (e.g. mean or median) of the affinities at the interface, and The interface may extend over arbitrarily many chunks. The trick is to delay merge Decisions For regions that touch Chunk boundaries, and only complete them in a later round after the regions are fully contained within a chunk. We demonstrate the algorithm by clustering an affinity graph With over 1.5 trillion edges between 135 billion supervoxels derived from a 3D electron microscopic brain image.

Here is a possible abstract for the paper "Conserved Charges of the Extended Bondi-Metzner-Sachs Algebra": The Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) algebra has been extensively applied to identify the asymptotic symmetries of null infinity in general theory. Recently, an extension of the BMS theorem was suggested, which provides additional generators that correspond to supertranslations and boundary gravitons. In this paper, we investigate the conserved charges associated with the extended BMS algebra. We first derive the expressions for the charges in terms of the gauge parameters and then show that they are finite and well-defined for many choices of the latter. Our research reveals that the extended BMS algebra holds both mass and angular momentum conservation laws, as well as a new set of conservation rules related to the supertranslation generators. Specifically, we demonstrate that the charge associated with the boundary graviton generator is proportional to the total entropy of the system. These results have significant consequences for our knowledge of black hole mechanics and the behaviour of matter and energy at null infinity.

Using modern high-speed cameras and advanced image-processing methods, we show in real time how to track single particles in a dense gaseous discharge induced by a DC or an AC pulse with a period of up to 10s. At a collision rate between atoms and free ions of tens of kilohertz, each ion is able to go through hundreds of thousands of spectral transitions per microsecond, and at such rates the emitted photons have a very short mean free path at any frequency above ultra-violet. It is also well known that, in a gaseous discharge, because of the extremely low thermal conductivity of the fluid and because of the lack of transparency due to background radiation, existing optical methods suitable for the observation and the tracking of a single particle cannot be employed. Using our method, it is possible to prove that when a high-voltage beam accelerates particles in a medium containing atomic nuclei with a high photon-interaction cross-section, the light traces the movement of the particles without being disturbed by the other charged particles traversing the medium. For example, a beam of 40keV of high-energy (electrons) can initiate a column of dense gaseous hydrogen in which the hydrogen is almost exclusively neutral. As the x-ray photons emitted by the annihilation of protons by incident electrons do not leave a line on the spectrum, these processes are not disturbed by the presence of the energetic ions, and so one can observe the characteristic K+ Auger lines unaltered, as well as the K Auger lines. Using various cameras, we have captured images of individual photons emitted by the particles in the discharge. These images contain significant noise but are also rich in information. The motion of the protons and the electrons can be observed at a sub-micrometer distance, which allows them to be distinguished; this requires the application of specialized image-processing methods to separate the different physical phenomena (such as the processes of instabilities and the motion of ionized particles) occurring simultaneously. These features make our method unique in comparison with all known methods, even including multiphoton and radio-ionization imaging. Moreover, it is possible to perform rapid scanning of objects with complex shapes similar to that of phase contrast microscopy, and one can use pulse-sequence analysis as in terahertz tomography.

This academic paper presents a novel approach for high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy Edges based on polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection. The proposed method utilizes landmark detection to identify key points on the tooth root image, which are then fitted With A polynomial curve to accurately segment the tooth root Fuzzy edge. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through experimental results, which show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of Accuracy and efficiency. The paper concludes that the proposed method is a promising approach for high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy edges and has potential applications in dental imaging and analysis.

We present an interactive approach to train a deep neural network pixel classifier for the segmentation of neuronal structures. An interactive training scheme reduces the extremely tedious manual annotation task that is typically required for deep networks to perform well on image segmentation problems. Our proposed method employs a feedback loop that captures sparse annotations using a graphical user interface, trains a deep neural network based on recent and past annotations, and displays the prediction output to users in almost real-time. Our implementation of the algorithm also allows multiple users to provide annotations in parallel and receive feedback from the same classifier. Quick feedback on classifier performance in an interactive setting enables users to identify and label examples that are more important than others for segmentation purposes. Our experiments show that an interactively-trained pixel classifier produces better region segmentation results on Electron Microscopy (EM) images than those generated by a network of the same architecture trained offline on exhaustive ground-truth labels.

Deep learning has not been routinely employed for semantic segmentation of seabed environment for synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) imagery due to the implicit need of abundant training data such methods necessitate. Abundant training data, specifically pixel-level labels for all images, is usually not available for SAS imagery due to the complex logistics (e.g., diver survey, chase boat, precision position information) needed for obtaining accurate ground-truth. Many hand-crafted feature based algorithms have been proposed to segment SAS in an unsupervised fashion. However, there is still room for improvement as feature extraction step of these methods is fixed. In this work, we present a new iterative unsupervised algorithm for learning deep features for SAS image segmentation. Our proposed algorithm alternates between clustering superpixels and updating the parameters of convolutional neural network (CNN) so that the feature extraction for image segmentation can be optimized. We demonstrate efficacy of our method on realistic benchmark dataset. Our results show that performance of our proposed method is considerably better than current state-of-the-art methods in SAS image segmentation.

In this research, we propose an effective few-shot segmentation approach that combines global and local contrastive learning to achieve outstanding performance. In the first step, the point-set kernel matrix is computed by computing the pairwise distances between all data points and then applying a kernel function to the distance matrix. In the second step, the kernel matrix is used as input to a clustering algorithm, such as spectral clustering or kernel k-means, to group the data points into clusters. The CPK algorithm offers several advantages over traditional clustering methods. First, it can handle non-linear relationships between data points, which makes it particularly useful for data sets with complex dependencies. Second, it can capture the geometric structure of the data, which is useful for data sets with spatial or temporal information. Finally, it is robust to noise and outliers, as the kernel function can smooth out the noise and focus on the underlying patterns in the data. The effectiveness of the CPK algorithm is demonstrated through experiments on several real-world data sets, including a dataset of protein structures, a dataset of text documents, and a dataset of time-series data. In summary, the CPK algorithm presents a novel approach to clustering data points based on their geometric relationships, which can be useful for data sets with complex dependencies and spatial or temporal information. Its robustness to noise and outliers makes it a promising method for a wide range of applications, including image segmentation, anomaly detection, and data mining.

In this article, we examine the behavior of the Riemannian and Hermitian curvature tensors of a Hermitian metric, when one of the curvature tensors obeys all the symmetry conditions of the curvature tensor of a K\"ahler metric. We will call such metrics G-K\"ahler-like or K\"ahler-like, for lack of better terminologies. Such metrics are always balanced when the manifold is compact, so in a way they are more special than balanced metrics, which drew a lot of attention in the study of non-K\"ahler Calabi-Yau manifolds. In particular we derive various formulas on the diffrence between the Riemannian and Hermitian curvature tensors in terms of the torsion of the Hermitian connection. We beleive that these formulas could lead to further applications in the study of Hermitian geometry with curvature assumptions.

The development and deployment of parallel systems to perform large scale visual computing tasks have become widely available in recent years, making it possible to use them to process images with unprecedented resolution. However, these processing platforms still lack the necessary tools that enable users to conveniently access their resources to solve data driven problems. In this work we describe techniques for performing parallel and scalable image analysis using distributed iterative region growing methods running over a range of different computational models including shared memory threads, message passing interface (MPI), Mapred and Spark based clusters on both small laptops as well as huge supercomputers. We show two key points; firstly how to adapt clustering methods so they can be implemented efficiently across a wide variety of hardware ranging from single processor machines up to petascale clusters. Secondly, rather than just providing benchmarks about these systems we focus our efforts towards developing an end user toolkit around large image segmentations so people interested in performing such analyses are no longer required to know how or what type of system would best fit their requirements. Our current software allows us to test various segmentation tools such as Otsu, Mean Cut, Hue Saturation Value, Chocolate Box algorithm or watershed transformer to name some few which all run very easily through our library. We tested extensively different configuration strategies like SIMD, MPI+OpenMp, hybrid MPI/shared memory programs among others against a number of real life applications which include 100’s Millions of pixels per second. As future goals our toolbox will provide not only implementations but also the corresponding performance results on top cluster architectures along with the availability of several segmented databases generated over time which might serve other researchers to further examine new analysis approaches on high dimensional datasets coming from either astronomy or biomedicine fields of study.
